News.title: M5 closed in BOTH directions for ‘safety-critical emergency repairs’ as drivers face long delay & diversion
News.content:
A MAJOR motorway has closed in both directions for emergency repairs.

The M5 has shut between Junction 22 and Junction 23 near Bridgwater, in Somerset.



Drivers have been warned to avoid the stretch of the motorway and take a diversion via the A38 instead.

It spells rush hour chaos for thousands commuting home from work, who have been told to allow extra time for journeys.



National Highways posted on X: “We are supporting National Grid with an emergency closure of the M5 both directions between J22 and J23 near Bridgwater to allow for the inspection and repair of safety critical infrastructure above the carriageway.”

It added: “The M5 is now closed in both directions between J22 (Burnham-on-Sea) and J23 (Puriton) to facilitate emergency repairs by National Grid to safety-critical infrastructure above the carriageway.



“The closure is required to allow the works to be carried out safely.”

Those travelling southbound have been told to exit the M5 at J22 then take the A38.

Drivers on the northbound should exit the M5 at J23 (Dunball Interchange) and take the 1st exit on to the A39.

News.title: Argentina’s invasion threat is ‘bull****’ – RAF jets would ‘hammer’ their troops, says Falklands war commander
News.content:
A HEROIC Falklands war commander has blasted Argentina’s latest threats to take the islands as “bull****”.

Ex-Royal Marine Commando Major General Julian Thompson said RAF jets would “hammer” enemy troops if the Argentinian President Javier Milei dared to pick a fight with Britain.



Maj Gen Thompson, 91, who led 3 Commando Brigade in the deadly 1982 conflict, said: “They are just bull****ting as usual.”

He added: “They won’t be able to take the Falklands because the Air Force will hammer them.”



There are four RAF Typhoons fighter jets permanently based in the South Atlantic as well as an infantry company, a Royal Navy patrol ship and Sky Sabre air defence missile batteries.

Maj Gen Thompson added: “The Typhoons will take care of them. I just hope Donald Trump isn’t stupid enough to take Argentina’s side.

“Russia and China would love that.”

It comes after Donald Trump suggested he would not back the UK if Argentina invaded the archipelago, citing the lack of support in the war on Iran.

It follows a leak of an internal Pentagon email in April implying the US may review its position on the islands.

But he warned the dire state of Britain’s forces meant there was almost “nothing to send” if London had to dispatch a task force as it did in 1982.



The veteran continued: “It’s really pathetic. What would we send?”

The Royal Navy has shrunk to its smallest size since it was founded by Henry VIII.

It lost more warships under Keir Starmer’s government than the eight that were sunk in the Falklands War.



Today, the Navy boasts barely five working frigates, no amphibious assault ships and all its hunter killer nuclear submarines are stuck in ports in the UK.

Thompson said hunter killers were “what the Argentines are really afraid of”.

But only one of the six Astute class subs has been put to sea this year.



Three have been tied alongside each other for three years.

And The Sun revealed the Army has been ordered to halt training as the MoD is out of cash mid-way through the financial year.

Falkland Islanders put two fingers up to Milei and insist they want to stay British DEFIANT Falkland Islanders put two fingers up to Javier Milei today by insisting they want to stay British. They dismissed “threats and claims” as old hat and vowed to press on development – code for drilling for oil off the coast. In a statement the islands Legislative Assembly said their right to be British was enshrined in law and would not be threatened by leaders’ hot air. They said: “Our future is a matter for the people who live here to decide. That is a right grounded in international law, and it is not altered by the statements of any other government.” Donald Trump hinted America would not back Britain over the islands due a lack of UK support for his war of choice in Iran. He said US support for Britain’s claim to the Falkland Islands was currently under review. Milei vowed to fight “tooth and nail” for the islands and threatened to sanction companies drilling for oil in the Falklands territorial waters. The Falklands’ elected government added: “Statements like the ones made this week are not new to us. “Our long-established community has faced pressure of this kind many times over the decades, and despite this the Islands have continued to grow, develop, and thrive. “Threats and claims have never held back the Falkland Islands development in the past, and they will not now.” A 2013 referendum saw 99.8 per cent of islanders voted to remain a self-governing Overseas Territory of the United Kingdom. They said: “That democratic choice is clear, and it stands. “We remain confident, settled and focused on the future our people have chosen.”

A Falkland official dismissed Milei’s rant as “nothing new”.

They said: “We have been dealing with this for years. Nothing has changed.



“Of course we are monitoring it, but we are perfectly confident in our relationship with the UK government and we have had assurances from them today.”

It comes as Milei insisted the islands are a crucial part of Argentina’s “future”, while announcing sanctions on oil companies working off the islands “under the British occupation”.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

He warned the UK is facing “multiple crises” that are “unlikely to be resolved” while “Argentina‘s future is flourishing and will prevail”.

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband denounced Milei’s outlandish claim, as he doubled down on Britain’s “unwavering position”.

News.title: Young Brits three times more likely to be targeted by scammers than older generations, new poll finds
News.content:
YOUNG Brits are three times more likely to be targeted by scammers than older generations, despite many believing their grandparents are the ones most at risk online.

A study of 3,000 UK adults found 61 per cent of 25-to-34-year-olds and 59 per cent of those aged 18-24 have been personally targeted by a scam, compared to just 20 per cent of over-65s.



Among 25-to-34-year-olds who have fallen victim to a scam, 21 per cent were caught out by fake investment schemes, including fraudulent cryptocurrency, trading and NFT opportunities.

The figure is almost double the rate among the younger adults (11 per cent), with victims losing an average of £414 per incident, according to the research commissioned by insurer SquareTrade.



Social media and messaging apps account for 41 per cent of scam encounters among under-25s, compared to just seven per cent which arrive via email.

Instagram and TikTok are each responsible for 11 per cent of scam approaches.

While fake giveaways (17 per cent), fraudulent influencer promotions (14 per cent) and gaming scams (10 per cent) are among the biggest threats facing young people online.

Yet 28 per cent of Gen Z adults say a grandparent is the person they worry most about being scammed online, while only nine per cent worry most about themselves.

Alex Wood, reformed scammer turned counter-fraud advisor, said: “Fraud in this country is evolving fast.

“Social media has given criminals a direct line into the lives of millions of young people, and AI is making every scam more convincing, more personalised, and harder to identify.



“Fake investment schemes can now be generated in minutes. Phishing messages are flawless. Voice clones are good enough to fool your own family.

“This is not a niche problem – it is a crisis that is scaling by the month, and the people being hit hardest are the ones everyone assumed were safe.”

The study also found phone theft can leave victims vulnerable long after their handset has been stolen.

Among Britons whose accounts had been hacked, 32 per cent believe the breach began with a stolen smartphone, giving fraudsters access to banking apps, personal data and social media accounts.

However, 42 per cent of scam victims blamed themselves for what happened, almost identical to the 43 per cent who held the criminal responsible.



Among 25-to-34-year-olds who have experienced a scam, 34 per cent admitted the experience left them feeling stupid or naïve.

As a result, 18 per cent confessed they would be too embarrassed to tell anyone what had happened.

But among 18-to-24-year-olds who had been scammed, 10 per cent turned to an AI chatbot to discuss the experience, roughly the same proportion as those who told nobody at all (11 per cent).

The research, which was conducted by OnePoll, also revealed alarming levels of money muling among young people, where criminals pay people to let money pass through their bank accounts.

More than four in 10 (42 per cent) 18-to-24-year-olds have been approached to do so, while six per cent admitted they had gone through with it.



With AI becoming more prevalent, 49 per cent of all respondents believe it is making scams more convincing and harder to spot, while 38 per cent think the technology is advancing faster than the tools designed to stop it.

One in five (20 per cent) 18-to-24-year-olds have already encountered scam deepfake videos, while 12 per cent have received AI-generated voice calls impersonating somebody they knew.

Worryingly, 26 per cent would struggle to tell the difference between a real video call and a deepfake.

Aditya Hindocha, vice president of strategic partnerships at SquareTrade Europe, added: “The UK is one of Europe’s most tech-forward markets, but the risks facing consumers are evolving just as quickly.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“It’s concerning to see how wide the protection gap is becoming, particularly for younger people whose finances, identities and day-to-day lives are increasingly managed online.



“Consumers shouldn’t feel they have to tackle these risks alone, and greater awareness is vital if people are to stay protected in an increasingly complex digital world.”

News.title: Nigel Farage signs giant pact with his French counterpart vowing to ‘stop small boat crossings’ at Reform conference
News.content:
CHANNEL PACT Nigel Farage signs giant pact with his French counterpart vowing to ‘stop small boat crossings’ at Reform conference

NIGEL Farage has signed a migration pact to “stop the boats forever” with French prime ministerial front-runner Jordan Bardella.

Mr Bardella confirmed that he would give the green light to Britain to stop boats sent from French shores and send them back to France.



Both leaders signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) on the main stage of the conference centre to put an end to Channel crossings.

The National Rally President committed to accepting the return of illegal migrants which make their way to Britain.



Mr Farage hailed the new deal as a commitment to stopping illegal immigration between the two nations.

He said: “We are about to sign a memorandum of understanding between our two parties, and we hope and believe our next two governments, where we reaffirm our commitment to stopping illegal immigration, where France say they’ll do their utmost to stop all departures and maybe this time, with him as prime minister, they will actually mean it.”

Mr Bardella hailed the agreement as the “beginning of the co-operation”.

It comes after the conference is at risk of being overshadowed by a foreign donations row engulfing the party.



The Reform leader described comments made by two former senior aides as “loose pub talk” and insisted the party had broken no laws.

Mr Bardella waded into the row and claimed the investigation looked like a “smokescreen” and was wary of what had been “written in the press”.

Mr Farage described the timing as “no coincidence” as the documentary dropped on the first day of its party conference.

The Reform leader said he was disappointed to lose trusted aide Dan Jukes.

He said: “Of course, I don’t like it at all. I’ve worked with Dan [Jukes] closely for many many years. I described it as loose pub talk and that’s what it was because what he said simply wasn’t true.



“But he got put in a position… I believe the investigation will find that he should not have said any of those things that he said.”

News.title: Having fewer meaningful conversations & preferring to scroll phones are key signs a relationship is fading, poll finds
News.content:
HAVING fewer meaningful conversations is one of the top signs your relationship spark is fading, according to a poll.

This was followed by preferring to scroll through phones rather than talk to one another and retreating to separate rooms to watch TV.



A survey of 2,000 adults found other key warnings included no longer doing fun activities together, sleeping separately, and not making an effort with date nights.

Among those who admitted to staying in a romantic relationship longer than necessary, 63 per cent did so because they hoped things would improve, while 33 per cent were afraid of change.



But this tendency to stay loyal to things that simply aren’t delivering anymore extends beyond relationships and into possessions.

Nearly (47 per cent) have owned a microwave for longer than they were in a romantic relationship and, 36 per cent admitted to holding onto one even though it was no longer performing well.



The research was commissioned by SharkNinja, which are launching the Ninja Crispi Microwave with AirFryer technology and also partnered with Olivia Attwood to highlight this inertia when it comes to our relationships.

Attwood appears in a tongue-in-cheek film that begins like a heartfelt break-up conversation – before revealing that she’s in fact addressing her microwave.

Olivia Attwood said: “The fact that so many people have owned a microwave for longer than a relationship shows just how attached we become to things we’re familiar with.



“As much as I see the value in holding onto things that have served us for long periods of time, it’s so important to upgrade certain elements of our lives.”

The study found microwave owners expressed similar reasons for staying put as they do in relationships.

Among those hanging onto an old appliance, 59 per cent said it was because it still worked and 36 per cent had just not got around to replacing it.

But this leads to many people continuing to put up with common frustrations, such as unevenly cooked meals (16 per cent), slow cooking times (15 per cent), and crispy food losing its crunch (13 per cent).

It also emerged many struggle to let go of all sorts of things long past their useful life, such as old chargers and cables (52 per cent).



Along with clothes that no longer fit (52 per cent), dated receipts and paperwork (46 per cent), and birthday cards and handwritten notes (43 per cent).

Appliances can also become a surprising source of conflict during break-ups, as 13 per cent have argued with an ex-partner about who would keep household items.

Televisions (43 per cent), gaming consoles (29 per cent), and microwaves (27 per cent) were among the most disputed possessions.

Meanwhile, 19 per cent admitted they had kept an appliance following a split mainly because they did not want their ex-partner to have it.

Carolyn Anderson, from SharkNinja UK, which is marking the launch of its Ninja CRISPi Microwave, said: “There’s something very British about putting up with something because it technically still works, even when we know it could be delivering much better results.”

News.title: Is YOUR name dying out? Use our interactive tool to find out
News.content:
IS your name the height of fashion – or starting to show your age? If you’ve ever wondered just how popular your name is, try our new tool. It reveals how your name is faring, and charts its popularity through the years.

It’s bad news for the Jessicas, Matthews, Ellies and Ryans who grew up in the 90s, who are seeing their names tumble out of fashion as a new generation of parents looks elsewhere for inspiration.





Comment below to share how your name has changed in popularity

Jessica was the third most popular girls’ name in 1996, when 6,711 babies were given the name. Last year, it had fallen to 139th, with just 360 registrations.

Its decline appears to be gathering pace. Jessica dropped 44 places in the space of a year, while Ellie fell 31.

Matthew fared little better, plunging from sixth in 1996 to 153rd last year. Ryan dropped from seventh to 135th over the same period.

Today, The Sun has launched a search tool allowing readers to discover whether their own name is enjoying a revival or falling out of favour.

The tool allows readers to compare up to five names, and see how they have feared since 1996.

It comes as new figures reveal Muhammad was the most popular boys’ name in England and Wales in 2025, while Olivia held on to the girls’ crown for a tenth consecutive year.

The rankings cover the names given to 585,396 babies born during the year, including 284,681 girls and 300,715 boys.

Olivia was given to 2,386 baby girls, ahead of Lily, with 2,249, and Amelia, with 2,153.

Isla came fourth, followed by Florence, Freya, Poppy, Elsie and Ivy. Isabella was the only new entry in the top ten.

Olivia’s decade-long reign continued despite registrations falling by 375 from 2024.





Muhammad, by contrast, gained 236 registrations to reach 5,957, putting it well ahead of Noah on 4,075.

Leo moved into third place, pushing Oliver out of the top three, while Luca came fourth. Arthur, Oliver, George, Oscar, Theodore and Freddie completed the top ten.

Luca climbed from seventh to fourth after 3,266 babies were given the name, an increase of 452. Freddie also broke into the top ten, while Oliver fell to sixth after losing 338 registrations.

It was the third year running that Muhammad, counted as one exact spelling, had topped the chart after first overtaking Noah in 2023.

Alternative spellings remained high too. Mohammed was 20th and Mohammad came 55th.

Grouping together the five most common versions suggests the name has been the most popular choice for boys for more than a decade.

Clare Green, an expert at baby-naming website Nameberry, said she was not surprised to see Olivia and Muhammad remain at the top.

She said: “Change happens so slowly at the top and once a name becomes popular it normally stays there for quite a long time.

“Names can build momentum. The more people give their child a name, the more other parents hear it and like the sound of it, so it snowballs.”

Olivia came first in three of England’s nine regions and also topped the list in Wales.



Muhammad was number one in four English regions but ranked only 34th in Wales.

Further down the chart, Eliana soared 54 places, making it the fastest-climbing girls’ name. Anaya and Alba each rose by 24.

Vinnie made the biggest leap among boys, climbing 33 places, while Ruben rose 26 spots and Vincent was up 25.

Eliana, Gracie, Anaya, Alba, Marnie, Lilah and Frankie all entered the girls’ top 100, joined by Vincent, Carter, Stanley and Ruben among boys.

Bodhi fell 18 places, Grayson dropped 14 and Brody slipped seven, taking all three out of the top 100.

Andrew was given to just 127 babies and fell to 334th, its lowest position on record after once reaching third in 1964.

The Kardashian-Jenner effect can still be seen on birth certificates. There were 114 boys named Reign last year, alongside 98 Saints and 11 girls called Stormi.

Poppy climbed to second place among girls born in November, around the time of Remembrance Sunday.

Holly tends to rise in December, while Summer is more popular during the warmer months.

Just 9.1 per cent of babies were given one of the ten leading names last year, making the once-common sight of several children in a class sharing a name less likely.



Every spelling is counted separately, based on what is recorded when a birth is registered.

A mother’s age appeared to make a difference too.

Among those under 25, Delilah was the most popular girls’ name, followed by Arabella and Mabel. Willow, Harper and Lottie also featured highly.

Mums aged 35 and over stuck to more traditional choices. Olivia came first, ahead of Lily and Charlotte.

Younger mothers also put Arlo, Archie, Oakley, Elijah, Roman and Reggie in their boys’ top ten.

None appeared in the list for mums aged 35 and over, who instead favoured Oliver, George, Oscar, Arthur and Jack.

Muhammad topped the boys’ rankings among mothers of every age.

Name consultant Colleen Slagen said: “The top ten girls’ names are very nicknameable, which parents find very appealing.

“People will say, ‘I want them to have a CEO name, but be able to give them a more playful name while they’re younger’.”

News.title: Virtually extinct predator is RETURNING to England’s forests after vanishing 150 years ago
News.content:
AN ENDANGERED predator could soon return to England after becoming largely extinct for more than a century.

The cat-sized species were once commonplace across the UK, but were lost due to hunting and the decline of their preferred woodland habitat.

Pine martens, a small animal belonging to the mustelid family (which includes stoats, weasels, and badgers), may soon return to their natural habitat in south east England.



According to new research from Kent Wildlife Trust, the omnivores – who feed on voles, fungi and bunnies – thrive in landscapes with extensive woodland cover.



As a result, highly suitable habitats have been identified across southeast England, as well as wooded parts of the Southwest and Gloucestershire.

Other suitable areas include East Yorkshire, East Anglia and sections of Britain’s western coast.

Ella Lewis, lead author of the study and a nature-based evidence officer for the trust, said: “These new findings present the exciting potential for pine martens to return to their former range in the future.



“As well as being a native species, pine martens are an important woodland predator and create complex interactions with other animals, contributing to more balanced and resilient ecosystems.”

Reintroduction efforts have also proved successful in areas such as Devon, Somerset, Wales and the Lake District.

Pine martens were considered largely extinct from England and Wales by the early 20th century, as a result of being hunted for sport and the loss of 95 per cent of woodland cover in Britain.

Despite becoming one of the country’s rarest predators, the species population grew in Scotland where they remain largely confined to.



However, as woodland cover has doubled again in England, there is hope the species can now reclaim their home in the nation’s forests.

News.title: When does winter start? The first day of the UK 2026 season explained
News.content:
WITH temperatures starting to drop across the UK and the colder months on the horizon, many Brits will be wondering when winter officially rolls around.

There is still Autumn to look forward to in the meantime, but when does the festive winter season officially begin this year?



The official answer depends on who you ask, with meteorologists and astronomers ordering the seasons in different ways.

Meteorologists have a fixed date on the calendar, while astronomers follow the movement of the Earth and stars.



When does summer end?

The end of summer marks the return of autumn, which brings a drop in temperature and much darker skies.

Autumn acts as the transitional season between the hot, vibrant summer months and the frosty winter period, but can have two different start dates depending on which system you use.



Meteorological summer always finishes on August 31, meaning those who follow climate records to determine the season consider autumn to have started on September 1.

Meanwhile, astronomical summer ends on September 23 as that’s when the autumnal equinox will take place this year.

When do the clocks change?

The end of summer means a change in time zone, as British Summer Time (BST) comes to a close.



This transition takes place on the last Sunday of October – that’s October 25 this year, with clocks going back an hour to return the UK to Greenwich Mean Time (GMT).

Although Brits will lose an hour of evening daylight, it means brighter starts to the day and an extra hour of sleep on the Sunday morning.

When does winter start?

Like the change from summer into autumn, there is no official date for the return of winter as it depends on how you order the seasons.

Meteorologists, who divide the calendar year into four equal periods of three months each, view winter as spanning across the exact three-month period of December, January, and February.



That means that under this system, the last season of 2026 begins on December 1.

On the other hand, those who follow the solar system will view winter as arriving later in the month.

Astronomical seasons are determined by the position of the Earth’s orbit relative to the sun – using key events like equinoxes and solstices.

This year, the winter solstice – the shortest day of the year – marks the start of winter, with that set to take place on Monday, December 21.

News.title: England’s most depressed places revealed in map exposing scale of mental health crisis
News.content:
England’s most depressed places revealed in map exposing scale of mental health crisis

New figures have exposed the scale of depression across England, with around one in four adults diagnosed in the worst-hit constituency and rates even higher in some neighbourhoods

View 3 Images Birkenhead, Merseyside has the highest overall rate, with around one in four adult GP patients diagnosed with depression (Image: Getty Images)

The scale of England’s mental health crisis is exposed in new official statistics revealing the most depressed parts of the nation - with one in four people diagnosed with depression in one area of Merseyside.

‌



Figures published by the House of Commons Library show the North West has the highest rate of adults with a diagnosis of depression. The six parliamentary constituencies with the biggest proportion of residents diagnosed with depression are all in the North West, while 15 of the top 20 places suffering most from depression are in the region.

‌



Birkenhead in Merseyside has the highest overall rates, with around one in four adult GP patients diagnosed with depression (25%). High rates are also recorded across Blackpool South (24%), Wallasey (24%), Blackpool North and Fleetwood (22%), Knowsley (22%), and Carlisle (22%).

‌



View 3 Images Blackpool had the second-highest depression rate among England's parliamentary constituencies (Image: Getty Images)

Neighbourhood data shows that diagnosis rates are even higher in smaller communities. In Brinnington, Stockport, the area with the highest rates, one in three adult residents have a formal diagnosis of depression recorded by their GP practice (32%). Before the pandemic, in 2019, Brinnington was revealed as the most depressed neighbourhood in Britain, when one in four residents had a formal diagnosis of depression (24%). The situation has deteriorated since then. There are likely to be multiple reasons why so many residents in Brinnington are struggling.

The area suffers from deprivation, which is known to contribute to depression - with sufferers often struggling to manage their finances, causing a spiral. Brinnington has more affordable housing than many neighbourhoods, which may funnel more people into the area who are likely to already be suffering from depression. It is physically hemmed in by the M60 motorway and steep valley terrain, cut off from broader economic opportunities, while the decline of industry has stripped it of stable employment.

‌



Previous reports about the scale of depression in Brinnington have also highlighted a lack of mental health stigma, which could mean that residents are more likely to seek help and receive a formal diagnosis, laying bare a crisis that remains hidden in more reserved suburbs.

The stark figures arrive as Andy Burnham is now settled into 10 Downing Street after becoming Prime Minister following the resignation of Sir Keir Starmer. The former Manchester Mayor, dubbed the “King of the North”, has promised to tackle deep-seated regional inequality which may be triggering poor mental health in some parts of the country. Setting out his vision, Mr Burnham declared that “Westminster is broken” and has long failed the regions. He has promised to “drive good growth in every postcode”.

‌



Responding to the figures, Gemma Byrne, Policy and Influencing Manager at mental health charity Mind said: “Depression might feel like you get less enjoyment from the things you previously enjoyed, it might make you want to withdraw from loved ones, you might have trouble eating, sleeping, and exercising, and you can feel isolated or hopeless. You might also be thinking about ways to harm yourself or struggling with suicidal thoughts. These can all have a huge impact on your day-to-day life and make it difficult to manage tasks and self-care. It can affect your work, relationships, finances, and hobbies.

“No matter what kind of symptoms you have, everyone deserves to be able to access the help that they need. These figures show a significant number of people reporting poor mental health across the North West. While the exact reasons are unclear, we do know there are huge links between deprivation and mental wellbeing.

“For example, we know that struggling financially can take a huge toll on your mental health and equally, struggling with your mental health can make it harder to manage your finances. That’s why we need to see a shift in our mental health system towards better understanding of people's needs upfront and providing care that is holistic, appropriate, and person-centred.”

‌



The figures show the proportion of GP patients aged 18 and over diagnosed with depression.

Mind has several helplines available for advice and support for anyone experiencing a mental health problem: Support Line: 0300 102 1234 (lines open 9am - 6pm, Monday – Friday, except bank holidays)

Mind Infoline: 0300 123 3393 (lines open 9am - 6pm, Monday – Friday, except bank holidays)

Welfare benefits line: 0300 222 5782 (lines open 9am to 5pm, Monday to Friday, except bank holidays).

Legal line: 0300 466 6463 (lines open 9am to 6pm, Monday to Friday, except for bank holidays).

Mind’s Our online mental health community Side by Side is a safe space where anyone aged 18 and over with experience of a mental health problem can share their story, connect with others, access Mind’s wider information and resources, and give support in return. Find out more at www.sidebyside.mind.org.uk

News.title: Reform UK conference LIVE: Nigel Farage tries to downplay donations row as 'loose pub talk' ahead of major speech
News.content:
Nigel Farage has finally addressed allegations the party knowingly accepted foreign donations to pay for polls that weren't declared, hours before he speaks at Reform UK's conference

Nigel Farage has tried to downplay a donations scandal overshadowing Reform UK conference as "loose pub talk" ahead of major speech

The annual gathering has gone off the rails after explosive allegations over foreign donations saw two high-profile aides forced to step down. Comms chief Dan Jukes and head of policy James Orr were recorded allegedly plotting for a foreign donor to pay £32,500 for off-the-books polling on behalf of the party, in a potential breach of electoral law.

Ahead of his main speech at around 4:20pm, Mr Farage told reporters he is "not particularly worried" about anything he said during his meeting with fake donors. But he admitted he is "annoyed" about the situation, saying the meeting should not have been allowed to happen.

He added: “The loose pub talk, frankly, there was a bit of boasting, a bit of jack-the-lad-dery going on there... Am I annoyed? Am I annoyed that these people even got to meet me? Yes, I am. It should not have happened. It should not have happened."

Mr Farage has insisted Reform UK has “broken no laws” and had not “taken any dodgy money” amid allegations the party breached political donation rules. Foreign companies are not a permissible source of funding for parties, including for payments for studies and research, and accepting donations from them could constitute a criminal offence.

If the conference was already not going to plan, a brutal Labour ad van made matters worse for Reform. The van demanded answers on a £5million gift he received from crypto tycoon Christopher Harborne. It was spotted near the conference centre bearing the words: "You have 5 million questions to answer, Nigel - tell us about the money."

News.title: Gatwick Airport live: Flights grounded as emergency crews race to Norse plane
News.content:
Passengers at Gatwick Airport are facing hours of delays after a Norse Atlantic Airways jet reportedly aborted takeoff at around 138mph, forcing the runway to close.

Flights at London Gatwick Airport are facing hours of delays after a Norse Atlantic Airways plane was forced to abort takeoff at around 138mph, according to the Aviation Herald.

Flight Z0701, bound for New York’s John F Kennedy International Airport, was accelerating along runway 26L when a reported problem with the nose landing gear forced pilots to reject the takeoff.

Emergency vehicles surrounded the aircraft as the runway was closed for around 50 minutes, with incoming flights diverted to other airports. No injuries have been reported.

Gatwick said the closure was caused by a “technical issue” with a departing aircraft. The runway has since reopened, but passengers are still facing significant knock-on disruption, with some flights delayed by more than two hours.

News.title: Dad of woman who died after Turkey surgery pays tribute to 'passionate and caring' daughter
News.content:
Dad of woman who died after Turkey surgery pays tribute to 'passionate and caring' daughter

An inquest concluded Morgan Ribeiro, 20, died as a result of complications from gastric sleeve surgery in Turkey in January 2024

View 3 Images Morgan died as a result of complications from the gastric sleeve op

The heartbroken dad of a woman who died after a gastric sleeve op in Turkey has paid tribute to his daughter, telling an inquest: “She was a very passionate person. She cared.”

‌



Richard Ribeiro shared memories of his girl Morgan Ribeiro, 20, moments after an inquest found she perished as a result of complications from the cosmetic procedure.

‌



Tragic Morgan, who worked in a nursery for disabled children, travelled to Istanbul from her home in Croydon, South London, on January 5, 2024, for the weight loss surgery. Three days later, medics gave her clearance to fly back to the UK. But she took a turn for the worst during the return flight to London Gatwick, forcing the plane to make an emergency landing in Belgrade, Serbia, where she was admitted to ICU. She died five days later on January 13.

‌



View 3 Images Dad Richard Ribeiro left the court with his head in his hands (Image: Humphrey Nemar/daily mirror)

Turkey surgeon still dodging questions over British woman who died after gastric band operation READ MORE :

Assistant Coroner Laura Stephenson told South London Coroner's Court many attempts had been made to contact Morgan's surgeon, Dr Serkan Bayil, but that these were unsuccessful. She said: “It has not been possible to establish contact with the clinic or surgeon who performed it. I have [therefore] relied on the post mortem conducted in Serbia, information from the Serbian police..and information from Morgan’s partner about her travel.”

‌



The court heard how Morgan underwent emergency surgery in Serbia where medics discovered her intestinal wall had ruptured. Ms Stephenson concluded her medical cause of death was peritonitis caused by the rupture, which likely happened as a result of the gastric sleeve surgery.

Medical notes from the private hospital Ozel Medivitia in Istanbul, where Morgan was treated, state she was deemed stable and fit for discharge. But her partner Jamie Brewster told the court she was suffering from abdominal pain and a fever, which worsened when they boarded the London-bound flight.

View 3 Images Morgan travelled to Turkey with her partner Jamie Brewster

Article continues below

Devastated dad Richard sat alongside a friend at Friday’s inquest. Speaking through tears after being asked if he wanted to share anything about his daughter, he told the inquest: “Morgan was working in a nursery for disabled children, looking after children with special needs. She was a very passionate person. She cared.”

Morgan's mum, Erin Gibson, previously spoke to the Mirror emphasising her need for justice. She said: “It’s wrong, it shouldn’t be happening. My daughter had her whole life ahead of her. It’s hard to adjust. Grief-stricken is an understatement."

After years of suffering bullying due to her weight, Morgan decided to undertake weight loss surgery. A gastric band operation in the UK costs between £8,000 and £10,000 and Morgan paid £2,500 for the surgery in Turkey, it was previously said. In 2024, The Mirror confronted surgeon Dr Bayil in Istanbul. He denied botching it, saying Morgan suffered an embolism and insisted he did nothing wrong.

News.title: Andy Burnham to approve controversial Jackdaw North Sea gas field 'within weeks'
News.content:
Andy Burnham to approve controversial Jackdaw North Sea gas field 'within weeks'

The PM and new energy secretary are set to take on critics by approving gas field - but alongside green projects

View 3 Images Climate activists have taken their fight against the Jackdaw and Rosebank fields to the heart of Westminster (Image: Wiktor Szymanowicz/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock)

Andy Burnham is set to give approve the controversial Jackdaw North Sea gas field within weeks.

‌



Reports say the PM will give the go-ahead for drilling, but alongside a wave a green energy projects.

‌



The expected approval of the field - off the cost of Aberdeen - has been brought condemnation from environmental campaign groups, which argue it makes a mockery of the government’s net zero ambitions. However, it comes against a backdrop of concerns about supplies of gas amid the ongoing war in the Middle East, and soaring household energy bills.

‌



According to reports, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh is likely to make an announcement on September 15 and Mr Burnham will then confirm the news during a visit to Aberdeen.

View 3 Images Police officers arrest a demonstrator as climate activists from Just Stop Oil block the road outside the Houses of Parliament during Andy Burnham's first Prime Minister's Questions (Image: Wiktor Szymanowicz/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock)

Should Nigel Farage resign as Reform UK leader? Take our poll and have your say READ MORE :

The decision on a second controversial North Sea project, the Rosebank oil field, is expected to be made at a later date. Both projects were approved by the last Conservative government but were struck down by the courts after a challenge from environmental campaigners, with ministers told they had not fully considered their environmental impact.

‌



Asked if approval of Jackdaw was imminent, a No 10 spokeswoman told reporters: “I don’t have an update for you basically. It’s a quasi-judicial decision.”

The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) said: “We do not comment on speculation”.

Andrew Bowie, Tory shadow energy secretary, said approving the Jackdaw gas field was “common sense”.

‌



“Labour’s ban on new oil and gas licences has been disastrous for the North East and cost thousands of workers their jobs as they continue to dither over a decision,” he said.

View 3 Images A decision on the Rosebank oil field could be delayed, reports suggest (Image: Andrew Milligan/PA Wire)

Jackdaw and Rosebank are operated by Adura, a joint venture between Shell and Norwegian energy firm Equinor, with Aberdeen’s Ithaca also owning 20% of Rosebank. Adura says Jackdaw could produce 6% of the UK’s gas output at its peak, although environmental groups put the figure at 2%.

‌



Friends of the Earth Scotland said the UK Government must not “cave in to fossil fuel company pressure”. The group warned that the burning of more fossil fuels would worsen extreme climate change-related events such as heatwaves.

Caroline Rance, head of campaigns for the group, said: “New fossil fuels means deadly new climate disasters like the devastating floods in Nepal or the extreme heatwaves that have killed nearly 3,000 people in the UK this summer.

“It is terrifying that the UK Government is considering caving to pressure from oil and gas lobbyists, and listening to their lies rather than looking at the evidence and prioritising our collective safety.

‌



“New fossil fuels can never be compatible with our climate commitments. Both Jackdaw and Rosebank must be rejected once and for all.”

Tessa Khan, executive director of environmental group Uplift, said further drilling in the North Sea would “do nothing” to cut energy bills in the UK and make “no meaningful difference to UK energy supply”.

“After 50 years of drilling, the UK has now burned most of its gas and the majority of what’s left in the basin is oil, which is largely exported,” Khan said.

‌



“Jackdaw, a relatively small gas field, would - optimistically and assuming none of its gas is exported - provide just 2% of UK gas demand over its roughly 10-year lifetime.

“A new oil field on the scale of Rosebank, which is overwhelmingly oil for export, is fundamentally incompatible with safe climate limits and the UK’s international commitments.

“The science is clear that the world already has far more oil and gas than can ever be safely burned if we are to limit warming.”

‌



Industry body Offshore Energies UK (OEUK) has said Rosebank and Jackdaw would support a peak of more than 3,500 jobs during construction, and 880 jobs externally throughout during their lifespans.

A spokesperson for Adura: “With the conclusion of public consultation on the Jackdaw and Rosebank fields, we now await a government decision on consent to allow the two projects to move forward to production. Together, Jackdaw and Rosebank represent a significant opportunity for the UK. They can provide 10% of our gas production, 10% of UKCS oil output and contribute over £28billion in value to the economy, supporting over 3,500 jobs at peak construction.

“The projects represent total investment of £10.8 billion, unlocking £1.4 billion in tax revenues by the end of this Parliament, rising to £3.8 billion before the end of the next Parliament in 2034.

Article continues below

“Jackdaw and Rosebank will be among the lowest emissions oil and gas developments in the UK Continental Shelf, itself one of the most highly-regulated and lowest emissions basins anywhere in the world.”

News.title: Fraudster who pawned ex-Prem star’s £188k art misses sentencing after bag 'knocked her out’
News.content:
Fraudster who pawned ex-Prem star’s £188k art misses sentencing after bag 'knocked her out’

Nabila Habiby, 39, secured £31,500 in loans by taking Edgar Davids' art collection to pawnbrokers after he trusted her to move the pieces into storage during a house move

View 2 Images Edgar Davids (Image: PA)

A fraudster who pawned ex-Premier League star Edgar Davids' £188,000 art collection has failed to turn up to court to be sentenced, claiming she had been struck with a bag on her way to the airport.

‌



Wealth manager Nabila Habiby, 39, was trusted to put 37 of Davids' paintings and other artworks into storage during a house move.

‌



Instead, she used them to secure £31,500 in loans before the pieces were sold to collectors around the world.

‌



Mr Davids, a former Spurs and Ajax midfielder, only discovered the pieces were gone when a buyer contacted him asking about the history of one of the paintings.

Habiby pleaded guilty in September 2025 to two counts of fraud, and was set free on bail with a warning that she could face up to 34 months in prison. But more than a year later, she still has not been sentenced.

The first attempt to sentence her, in March, was derailed when she made a failed bid to withdraw her guilty pleas.

‌



View 2 Images Edgar Davids spent a short time with Spurs (Image: John Peters/Manchester United via Getty Images)

Today, Habiby was absent from the dock at Wood Green Crown Court, where she was due to be sentenced again.

Defence barrister Hannah Thomas said: "I received correspondence this morning from my solicitor, at around 9.30am, saying on her way to the airport to come here she had been hit on the head by a piece of luggage en route.

‌



"She had a concussion, since she passed out, and was taken to the hospital where she remains on a drip."

Judge Emma Deacon KC said she had been handed "inadequate" medical evidence from Belgium, where Habiby now lives, to support her story.

But the judge agreed to adjourn the sentencing hearing anyway, so that the original judge who oversaw the case when guilty pleas were entered could pass sentence.

‌



Habiby was first charged after a probe by the Metropolitan Police over fraud offences dating back to 2015 and 2016.

The court heard Davids had given Habiby the keys to his home in Hadley Wood, Hertfordshire, when he was moving to an apartment in central London in December 2014.

She took his collection of works by artists Paul Insect and Ron English, which he had bought from the Opera Gallery in New York between 2006 and 2012, to pawnbrokers.

Article continues below

Some of the paintings have since been recovered, but 25 works of art are gone.

Habiby has been ordered to come to court on September 23 to be sentenced. She has also been told to provide a full medical report to back up her absence from court on Friday.

News.title: Huge UK backlash after Buenos Aires makes new claim on Falkland Islands
News.content:
Huge UK backlash after Buenos Aires makes new claim on Falkland Islands

Alarming new claims by Argentina's leader on The Falkland Islands triggers huge backlash in the UK as Britain brands its commitment to the South Atlantic territory 'unshakeable'

View 4 Images British Type 42 Destroyer HMS Sheffield hit by Argentine missile 1982 (Image: PA)

Argentina's renewed claim on the Falkland Islands sparked UK political and military backlash today as Britain vowed its right to the territory is “unshakeable.”

‌



Bolstered by President Trump reconsidering the US position on the Falklands, Buenos Aires leader Javier Milei claimed Argentinian ownership of the South Atlantic archipelago. In a national address he said the “winds of change” back his demand for the Islands and threatened to sanction firms exploiting oil close to the British territory.

‌



He even cited signs that Trump may be ambivalent on the islands’ sovereignty after the US President hinted as much, because the UK has not fought in his war on Iran.

‌



But Downing Street was resolute, saying its position is “unwavering” and that the Falkands Islanders’ wishes are “paramount.” Asked if Prime Minister Andy Burnham was disappointed by Trump’s comments, a No 10 spokeswoman insisted: “I think those remarks are a matter for the US President.”

She added: “US foreign policy is a matter for them, but our position is clear: the Falkland Islands are a British overseas territory and they will remain so as long as the islanders wish.” UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting underlined the Argentine leader’s turbulent position in Buenos Aires, which is marred by rising dissent and controversy.

View 4 Images British commandos patrol towards Port Stanley: Falklands War 1982 (Image: PO(Phot ) Pete Holgate/MOD / SWNS)

‌



Kremlin sabotage bid sparks major diplomatic row with Germany READ MORE :

He said: “Milei’s statement overnight tells us more about domestic politics in Argentina than it does about the Falkland Islands. The Falklands are British because Falkland Islanders choose to be British. Our commitment to the Falklands is absolute and unshakeable.”

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has said the UK will "resolutely uphold" the self-determination of the Falkland Islands. He said: "The UK's position on the Falkland Islands is unwavering. The Islands are British and will remain so because that is the overwhelming position of the Islanders. Their right of self-determination is paramount, grounded in international law and we will resolutely uphold it."

British Falklands War veterans branded the Milei outburst “nonsense,” including ex-soldier Simon Weston, 65, who was badly burned on the ship RFA Sir Galahad. He said: “He's tanking in the polls, the country is in economic crisis - that's what caused them to invade 44 years ago.

‌



"Nothing has changed. And to sanction all the oil companies…is ridiculous, because they haven't got a footprint in Argentina, they're just empty words. They mean absolutely nothing. It's just rhetoric and he's just rattling the sabre again and unsettling the islanders and playing to the crowd as you can see in images there. That's all great for him, that's politics.

"But unfortunately for him his politics isn't working for a lot of people in Argentina. And this is why he's having to try and rally the troops, trying to create a cabal of nations in South America that will also support him.

View 4 Images RFA Sir Galahad after Argentinian attack kills 32 Welsh Guards (Image: Stefan Rousseau/PA Wire)

‌



"It's just nonsense again, but he's been emboldened by the fact of what Mr Trump has said. But it's got nothing to do with Mr Trump. We've never shirked our responsibility, certainly not after 9/11 and we followed them into Afghanistan, into Iraq, into Kuwait. So, you can't say we haven't been there. But what we didn't do was follow him into a war that really should never have taken place."

Earlier Milei said: “I want to be quite clear with everybody. The Falklands are Argentinian. Historically and legally. There can be no argument. They are part of the Argentine territory. The islanders on their usurped territory do not have a legitimate right to self-determination and any argument on any such self-determination is invalid.” British and Argentinian troops fought a bitter two month war over the islands in 1982, after then military dictator Leopoldo Galtieri ordered an invasion of the territory.

View 4 Images HMS Invincible returns to Portsmouth after war 1982 (Image: Getty Images)

‌



It lasted 74 days and ended with an Argentine surrender on June 14, formally passing back possession to Britain, whose Prime Minister was Margaret Thatcher. In total, 649 Argentine military personnel, 255 British military personnel, and three Falkland Islanders were killed during the hostilities.

Trump had been asked if America would support the UK in the event of a conflict and answered that the UK had not agreed to join his war on Iran. He said: "So, your country's not doing well. Don't forget, you get a big percentage of your oil from the Strait of Hormuz, and you weren't there to help me.

"Your country was not there to help me. We didn't need help, but I did ask Nato, and I asked your former leader, 'why didn't you send a couple of ships?' Trump said then prime minister, Sir Keir Starmer, told him no vessels were available, which "was pretty sad.” He also said: "Nato was not there, even though they get – most of those countries get – a big portion of their oil from there. So we're doing that by ourselves.”

Article continues below

Milei- whose government is facing corruption probes and unpopularity over massive health cuts- added that the UK was facing “multiple crises on multiple fronts.” He vowed he would sign decrees to introduce sanctions against any companies working on oil production in the area. Milei declared the Sea Lion oilfield, owned by an Israeli and a British firm where production is expected to begin in 2028, a “clear and present danger” to the country’s claims.

In a 2013 referendum, the Falkland Islanders voted overwhelmingly to remain a British overseas territory, with 99.8% voting in favour and just three votes against.

News.title: Princess Diana crowned greatest female style icon of all time - beating host of legends
News.content:
Princess Diana crowned greatest female style icon of all time - beating host of legends

Research has confirmed the enduring impact that the late Princess Diana still has - even among those who weren't alive when she died nearly 30 years ago

View 4 Images The late Princess Diana has topped the all-time style charts - nearly 30 years after her death (Image: Tim Graham Photo Library via Getty Images)

Princess Diana has been named the greatest female style icon of all time in a new survey. She came above such famous names as Marilyn Monroe, Beyoncé, and Kate Middleton.

‌



Such is Diana’s enduring impact that she also came top among Gen Z, despite them being born after her death in a car crash nearly 30 years ago.

‌



Overall, just under a third of the 2,000 people polled for clothing brand Cotton Trader said the late princess remains the ultimate benchmark for timeless fashion.

‌



Hollywood icon Marilyn Monroe came second in the rankings (22%), followed by Audrey Hepburn (16%) and Catherine, Princess of Wales (14%). Beyoncé was fifth (13%), ahead of Rihanna (12%), Madonna (12%), Grace Kelly (11%), Jennifer Aniston (10%) and Jennifer Lopez (10%).

View 4 Images Princess Diana's 'revenge dress' has been named among the most iconic in history (Image: PA)

When it comes to male style, football superstar David Beckham was crowned the greatest, with one in five people (20%) choosing the former England captain. He came above Elvis Presley (18%), and ahead of David Bowie (14%), Sean Connery (13%), Freddie Mercury (13%) and Brad Pitt (13%).

‌



Marilyn Monroe’s white halter neck dress from The Seven-Year Itch was voted the most iconic dress in history (15%), narrowly beating Diana’s famous “revenge dress” (12%).

Many of us aren’t content simply admiring their favourite stars, with almost a third (31%) admitting they have tried to copy the style of a fashion icon. However, almost nine in 10 of those surveyed reckon celebrities were more stylish in previous generations than they are today.

View 4 Images Marilyn Monroe’s white halter neck dress from The Seven-Year Itch was voted the most iconic dress in history

‌



Jools Dickson, Cotton Traders stylist, said: “Many women dream of being a princess for the day, and what Diana did so effortlessly was make that possible for every woman. She didn’t have a stylist or the luxury of the relaxed protocol that royals enjoy today, but she managed to steal the show wherever she went and her ongoing impact on fashion is as relevant now as it was then.

“From jaw-dropping ballgowns to slick suiting, and from sweats and joggers to country tweeds, she could make any look her own.

View 4 Images Football legend David Beckham named the number one make style icon (Image: Shaun Brooks - CameraSport, CameraSport via Getty Images)

‌



“Her simple styling trick was to add the unexpected. Her trademark frill collars were seen under dungarees or with jeans, while she would throw her favourite tailored blazer over a sweatshirt and cycling shorts. These sorts of styling tricks are commonplace now, but fashion in the 1980s was not as individual and free as it is today.

“She was a style pioneer long before Instagram and online shopping, and her distinct way of dressing was literally all her own work. The fact people still look to their favourite stars for inspiration shows just how powerful a genuine style icon can be.”

News.title: Farage unveils small boats deal with French National Rally party
News.content:
Nigel Farage has agreed a deal with France's hard-right National Rally (RN) party on returning small boat Channel migrants, should both parties win power.

It comes after Reform UK last month announced a plan to intercept boats and return migrants to French ports using the Royal Navy.

The proposed agreement with RN states that France would "ordinarily accept" those on board, and then repatriate them to their home country.

It was signed at Reform's annual conference in Birmingham by RN President Jordan Bardella, whose party is currently leading in opinion polls ahead of presidential elections in April next year.

In a speech in the main conference hall, ahead of the deal being unveiled, Bardella told delegates that an RN government would "do everything in its power to ensure that France is no longer the gateway for illegal migration into the United Kingdom".

Hailing Farage as the UK's next prime minister, Bardella pledged to work with a potential future Reform government to tackle illegal migration.

News.title: 'A rare moment of joy': Nepal tunnel rescues bring hope for more flood survivors
News.content:
Two people have been rescued from a tunnel in Nepal more than a week after flash flooding hit the Nepal-Tibet border, killing more than 1,300 people.

Nepal's army is continuing its search for survivors, but mud and rocks are making rescue efforts difficult.

The BBC's South Asia correspondent Azadeh Moshiri, reporting from Nepal, describes how the rescues have given renewed hope to some families still waiting to find out what happened to missing relatives.

News.title: Stock up on food to prepare for extreme weather, minister says
News.content:
Households should stock up on food to prepare for extreme weather as the strongest El NiÃ±o event in a generation develops over the Pacific Ocean, a government minister has said.

Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle told the Guardian the powerful natural climate phenomenon will lead to "more extreme storms in this country".

Her comments came as the National Audit Office (NAO) warned Britain's food supply chain is at risk given the growing threat of cyber-attacks and the climate crisis.

The NAO said the government was too reliant on the private sector to deal with food supply disruption. The government is due to unveil a strategy about preparing for national emergencies later this year.

Dame Angela said, external: "We're about to experience probably the largest El NiÃ±o that has ever been seen, and that will lead to drier summers, wetter winters, with more extreme storms in this country.

"It will do a lot more damage in Asia with flooding, and therefore I think that we need to take it seriously.

"If you've got a store of a bit of food that can keep you going for a while before the emergency services can get to you, you're going to be a lot better off than if you haven't.

"So some of it is that kind of preparation for just being a bit more resilient."

Her comments came as an NAO report warned Britain's food supply chain is vulnerable to plant or human disease outbreaks, cyber-attacks and extreme weather.

It also cited climate change as a longer-term chronic risk which could leave Britain's food supply at risk.

The disruptions could push up prices and leave vulnerable people struggling to buy food, it said.

The NAO said the Department for Food, the Environment and Rural Affairs (Defra) was too reliant on private companies to handle disruptions to food supply.

It added the department had not done enough in recent years to improve supply chain resilience.

UK households are less prepared for emergencies than those in several other countries such as Finland, Sweden and European Union nations, the NAO added.

It said ministers should encourage households to prepare for supply chain disruptions and learn from the approaches taken by other countries.

News.title: 'We expect our sons to be killed,' father of teen shot dead in West Bank tells BBC
News.content:
Funerals have taken place for two Palestinian teenagers who were shot dead this week when settlers and soldiers entered a Palestinian village in the occupied West Bank.

The killing of Omar al-Naasan and Khalil Abu Alia comes amid near-daily attacks by Jewish settlers in the village of al-Mughayyir, south of Nablus.

"We expect that when our sons walk in the street, they are likely to return to you injured or killed," Mohammed Al-Naasan, Omar's father, told the BBC.

Israel's military says it fired on "instigators of a violent riot" and that the incident is under review.

The United Nations says more than 80 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli forces or settlers in the territory since the beginning of the year.

News.title: Woman whose XL bully dog killed her cousin given suspended prison sentence
News.content:
A woman has been given a suspended prison sentence after her XL bully dog attacked and killed her cousin.

Kelcie Reed, 24, of Bristol, previously admitted being in charge of a dog dangerously out control, causing the death of Morgan Dorsett.

The 19-year-old, from Shrewsbury, died from neck injuries caused by the attack, which happened at Reed's flat in south Bristol in February 2025.

At Bristol Crown Court, Judge Anna Richardson sentenced Reed to 18 weeks in prison, suspended for 18 months. She will also be required to undergo mental health treatment.

Emergency services were called to the dog attack at a flat in Cobhorn Drive, Bishopsworth, but despite their best efforts, Morgan died from bites to her neck and face, a post-mortem examination ruled.

The dog, named Prince, which belonged to Reed and her boyfriend, was sedated at the scene and later "humanely destroyed", police said.

News.title: Xbox caps cloud gaming at 15 hours a month for Game Pass subscribers
News.content:
Xbox is introducing strict monthly time limits for Game Pass subscribers who stream games online through its cloud gaming service.

The changes, which come into effect in November, will see a subscriber to the Â£16.99 Ultimate monthly plan able to stream games for up to 15 hours a month - before having to purchase additional cloud play time.

Xbox said the limits were due to the rising cost of cloud gaming, and they would allow the firm to "continue to invest" in the service's "reliability and performance".

While some questioned, external whether the service was used by many to begin with, others called out, external the additional limits for subscribers.

Cloud gaming allows players to stream and play games online from a remote server using a phone, tablet or controller, rather than downloading and running it on a PC or console at home.

Different tiers of subscription to Game Pass will have different limits.

Premium users will get 10 hours, while those on the basic Essential tier will get five hours a month before they have to pay for extra time.

Xbox claimed just 4% of the people who use Games Pass - its Netflix-style subscription plan for games - use its cloud gaming service.

A recent Wall Street Journal article, external reported Game Pass has 30 million subscribers, which would leave the number of people affected by the cloud gaming changes at roughly 1.2 million.

"This is a pretty awful change, hopefully Xbox adds an extra zero on the end cause 15hrs is abysmal. 30 minutes a day, really?" posted one commenter on X, external.

Jez Corden of Windows Central told the BBC the announcement showed that "absolutely nothing is safe from the AI-driven component crisis," but he added it also highlighted "where Microsoft's priorities are".

Both cloud gaming and AI use data centres to process information.

"For them to continue to offer unlimited access to Microsoft Copilot [AI] for free but restrict paid cloud gaming in this way shows some contradiction," he added.

Xbox said in a blog post, external that from November, users would also be able to use the company's cloud gaming feature without subscribing to Game Pass, but by buying "cloud playtime hours" through the Xbox store.

It has not revealed how much extra hours of cloud gaming would cost.

News.title: Schools close early for A66 crash funeral
News.content:
Supt John Wrintmore from Cleveland Police said there was potential for traffic disruption and delays from 15:00 to 17:00 BST on Friday.

"This will affect areas of South Bank, Normanby Road through Teesville, Ormesby and Marton, and Acklam Road," he said.

"We are aware of some school closures in the area and have liaised with partners in the local authorities regarding the expected disruption today.

"Any decisions made by schools or other services to close has been a decision made by those organisations in isolation, and has not been a police recommendation.

"We are working closely with highways departments from the local authorities, who are leading on the traffic management for this event, in order to minimise disruption.

"There will be a proportionate visible police presence in the affected areas to ensure public safety, in line with our plans for any significant gathering."

A spokesperson for Redcar & Cleveland Borough Council said: "A number of schools in the South Bank area will close earlier than usual on Friday afternoon due to anticipated traffic congestion and transport disruption associated with a local funeral taking place in the area.

"The decision was made after careful consideration of the potential impact on home-to-school transport and the departure of pupils, staff and families at the end of the school day.

"Schools have worked with the Local Authority and transport providers to consider arrangements for pupils, including those who travel to and from specialist educational settings.

"We recognise that early closure may cause inconvenience for some parents and carers, and we thank them for their understanding and cooperation."

The decision comes after a vigil last week, for one of the young men who died, was followed by disorder in Haswell, County Durham, where a number of cars were set on fire.

The incident prompted criticism from MPs and police.

The Volkswagen Passat involved in the collision was being pursued by police until 10 seconds before the crash, according to the police watchdog.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct said the Passat was believed to be using cloned registration plates.

Police said a total of 24 people had been arrested as part of a wider police operation against organised crime, following the crash.

News.title: How could US-Iran conflict end? Three experts give their views
News.content:
Nicholas Hopton, Distinguished Fellow in international security at the Royal United Services Institute think tank in London and former UK ambassador to Iran

The latest spike in military action is not going to produce Iran's capitulation - it is just the latest twist. Economic pressure is also unlikely to work because China, Russia and many other countries which trade with Iran are not going to support unilateral US sanctions.

Iran can continue to disrupt the Strait of Hormuz - they have a thumb on the jugular of the global economy.

What is the White House's exit strategy?

Well, the US has already found it. If Trump was able to put a sustained effort into negotiating the deal outlined in June's MoU, that is the off-ramp.

Not only would a deal give the US a kind of victory because it would weaken the hardliners in the Islamic Republic, but also reassure everyone that Iran is not going to get a nuclear weapon.

There is a silver bullet in the MoU which is the lifting of all US sanctions on Iran.

What lifting those sanctions would do over time is weaken Iran's powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corp (IRGC). Economic engagement between the outside world and Iran in a new way would gradually force radical political and social change - so you end up with an Islamic regime, but of a very different nature.

Of course, that would not be straightforward to achieve, because of extensive IRGC penetration of the Iranian economy. But it should work, if given enough time and if the US and its partners exercised strategic patience which, sadly, is in short supply at this point.

For the time being, I think we're going to carry on with a messy, inconclusive situation that is bad for everyone.

News.title: Answers needed on transgender surgery pause, says health minister
News.content:
A meeting to discuss the decision to immediately pause referrals for gender-affirming surgeries in Wales has been called by the health minister.

The Welsh Gender Service paused surgery last week after concerns from an NHS committee about the number of referrals and whether they were all appropriate.

Wales' health minister, Mabon ap Gwynfor, is meeting with members of the NHS Wales Joint Commissioning Committee (NWJCC), which instructed Cardiff and Vale University Health Board to halt both new referrals and planned surgeries, on Friday.

The health board is responsible for the running of the NHS gender identity clinic which provides specialist care and support for adults in Wales.

The decision was prompted by data which indicated "significantly higher rates of referral for gender affirming surgery... compared with English gender services" in 2025-26, according to the health board.

The NWJCC has requested an independent clinical review be carried out, describing the move as "precautionary and clinically-led".

First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth previously said the review into surgery services at must be quick.

Plaid leader ap Iorwerth said while the committee at the heart of the row had taken the decision "for the right reason" on service quality grounds, he wanted a "resolution quickly".

News.title: Controversial Jackdaw gas field set to be approved in weeks, sources say
News.content:
The UK government is set to give the go-ahead for a controversial new gas field off the coast of Aberdeen, the BBC understands.

Approval for the Jackdaw project could come in mid-September, just before Parliament breaks for party conference season, according to government and industry sources.

The gas field was approved by the former Conservative government in 2022 but was delayed by a legal ruling from a Scottish court, after environmental groups argued consent was given without fully considering the climate impact.

Jackdaw's owner says it will account for 6% of UK gas output when at peak production but environmental groups say it will provide only 2% of UK use when imports are included.

Campaigners launched legal challenges after Jackdaw was approved in 2022 and when the Rosebank oil field off Shetland was given the green light in 2023.

The Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled last year that Rosebank and Jackdaw had been unlawfully approved because the government had failed to take into account the climate impact of burning extracted oil and gas from the sites.

A judge ruled that more detailed climate assessments had to be published, and further estimates were put out for consultation in July.

News.title: Man who died near Notting Hill Carnival is named
News.content:
A man who died after jumping into a canal while fleeing from police near Notting Hill Carnival has been named.

Karnell Kelly, 25, died in hospital after entering the Grand Union Canal off Kensal Road, west London, while being pursued by police officers.

He had fled on foot after the officers attempted to stop him near Harrow Road as he approached the carnival wearing a face covering at about 15:20 BST on Monday, the Metropolitan Police said.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC), which is investigating, said it was reviewing body-worn video from officers who had chased Kelly down Hormead Road.

Officers and members of the public entered the canal to pull him from the water and he was rushed to a central London hospital, where he was pronounced dead at about 16:40.

News.title: Planes grounded at Gatwick after aircraft stuck on runway
News.content:
Flights at Gatwick Airport were brought to a standstill for nearly an hour after a plane became stuck on the runway.

A Gatwick spokesperson said the runway was closed on Friday afternoon because of a "technical issue with a departing vehicle".

The airport said the runway was shut for 50 minutes while the plane was towed away before reopening shortly afterwards. Some flights were diverted to other airports including London Stansted and Birmingham.

A spokesperson said: "As always, safety and security is our number one priority."

Flights arriving at the West Sussex airport on Friday afternoon were showing some delays, ranging from 20 minutes to two hours.

Many departures, including those to major European tourist destinations, were also delayed.

Travellers can check Gatwick's official website for more information.

Tracking website Flightradar24 showed just after 16:00 BST on Friday that 40% of flights were delayed, with 1% cancelled.

It listed an average delay time of just over 60 minutes.

News.title: How Oasis fans cracked the Celtic Park gigs code in chip shop video
News.content:
Oasis fans have uncovered a set of cryptic clues in a promo video from the band, suggesting that they will stage gigs at Celtic Park in Glasgow next year.

The Manchester rockers released the 23-second teaser on their social media accounts, showing two boys in what appears to be a Scottish chip shop.

Internet sleuths spotted sets of numbers in posters around the chippy which they worked out to be the map co-ordinates for Celtic's Parkhead stadium.

It has fuelled speculation that the band will be playing at the venue next year- possibly as the first date of a new tour.

It follows the Gallagher brothers' hugely successful reunion tour which saw them perform at 41 sold-out stadium shows in 14 countries.

This included three dates at Murrayfield Stadium, Edinburgh, in August 2025, when they played to 200,000 fans.

News.title: Sheep stolen from Clarkson's Diddly Squat Farm
News.content:
Eleven sheep have been stolen from Diddly Squat Farm belonging to presenter Jeremy Clarkson.

Thames Valley Police said it received reports on Wednesday that the animals had been taken from the farm in Chadlington, Oxfordshire, within the last 10 days.

It said officers spoke with Clarkson at the scene on Thursday, adding that no arrests had been made and anyone with information should get in contact.

The 66-year-old told The Sun, external he discovered the animals were missing when he went to count his flock with Clarkson's Farm co-star Kaleb Cooper.

News.title: 'No reports' made to Stormont's Donaldson review
News.content:
A review by the Northern Ireland Assembly into Jeffrey Donaldson's conduct during his time at Stormont has found "no relevant information" requiring further investigation.

No reports were received as part of the exercise, which was commissioned in July following the former Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader's conviction for child sex offences.

Donaldson was convicted in June of 18 counts of sex abuse including one count of rape, which he committed against two women when they were children. Donaldson is to appeal.

The Northern Ireland Assembly said the review was "necessarily limited" and "does not determine that no incidents occurred", but added the process had "now concluded".

Donaldson was a member of the legislative assembly (MLA) from 2003 until 2010 and at one point a junior minister in Northern Ireland's power-sharing government.

In subsequent years he was often a visitor at Stormont in his role as an MP and DUP leader.

The assembly's speaker Edwin Poots asked its chief executive to conduct the review.

It aimed to enable any current or former MLAs or staff, or other users of Parliament Buildings, to report "any incidents of abuse or inappropriate behaviour they directly experienced".

In a statement an assembly spokesperson said the review "has now concluded".

"No reports were received through the dedicated review contact route and no relevant information was identified through the internal information search," they said.

"The report therefore concludes that no matter has arisen within the scope of the review requiring further investigation, referral to the PSNI (Police Service of Northern Ireland), or referral to another statutory agency."

The assembly spokesperson said the report, which has been published online, external, was "clear that this conclusion is necessarily limited".

"The absence of reports or relevant records does not determine that no incidents occurred," they added.

"It means that, within the scope and methodology of the review, none were reported to the review and no relevant information was identified."

The assembly said any subsequent approach received would be handled under Assembly Commission policies and procedures "with urgent referral to the PSNI or another statutory agency where appropriate".

The review was one of several launched in the wake of Donaldson's conviction.

The DUP commissioned Jim Gamble, a child safety expert and former senior police officer, to lead an independent review into Donaldson's behaviour while he was in the party.

Staff in the Northern Ireland Civil Service have been asked to come forward with any experiences of abuse or inappropriate behaviour during Donaldson's time as a junior minister.

The Ulster Unionist Party (UUP), of which Donaldson was previously a member, also said it would appoint an external organisation for people to confidentially share any information.

News.title: Five jailed after kidnap victim jumped from window
News.content:
Five people have been jailed after a man jumped from a first-floor window to escape kidnappers.

The victim was lured to a property in Market Rasen in July 2025 because of "personal matters linked to a past relationship breakdown", Lincolnshire Police said.

The force said he was "repeatedly assaulted, threatened, humiliated and tormented by his captors, while those involved filmed the abuse on their mobile phones and laughed as it unfolded".

After being held overnight he was driven to a house in Lincoln, where he was caught on CCTV leaping into a tree and climbing down before running into the street and flagging down a passing police car.

Armed police intercepted two of the kidnappers in a car, and the others were arrested at the house in Market Rasen.

The gang were jailed at Lincoln Crown Court on 28 August.

Brad'Lee Ranyard, 20, of Portland Street, Lincoln, was jailed for nine years after being convicted of kidnap and pleading guilty to false imprisonment.

Jackson Nicholson, 25, of Lindsey Drive, Gainsborough, was also jailed for nine years after being convicted of kidnap and pleading guilty to false imprisonment and possessing a bladed object in public.

Craig Ranyard, 42, of Barsey Walk, Horncastle, was sentenced to five years and three months in prison after pleading guilty to false imprisonment

Danielle Thompson, 38, of Lime Walk, Market Rasen, was given four years and nine months after pleading guilty to false imprisonment.

Nathan Gladwell, 36, of Union Street, Market Rasen, was sent to prison for three years and seven months after pleading guilty to false imprisonment.

Det Con Liam Henderson said: "This was a sustained and deeply distressing ordeal in which a man was subjected to violence, threats and humiliation at the hands of people who appeared to find amusement in his suffering.

"The victim showed remarkable courage in seizing the opportunity to escape. The CCTV footage captures a desperate moment in which he quite literally risked everything to get away from those holding him captive."

News.title: Judge ready to declare mistrial in Lindsay Clancy case but allows last-minute Hail Mary by defense
News.content:
