The judge in Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial says he’s ready to declare a mistrial but gave her attorney a last-minute “Hail Mary” before doing so.

The judge said in court that he saw no choice but to declare a mistrial, but then allowed Clancy’s defense attorney one hour to get a stay from the Supreme Judicial Court.

The mistrial ruling is now on hold.

Jurors have deliberated for seven days and repeatedly told the judge they were unable to reach a unanimous verdict.

Over a five-week trial, the jury heard testimony from doctors, first responders, relatives and even Clancy’s former husband. The jurors were tasked with determining whether she should be held criminally responsible for killing her three young children at her Massachusetts home in 2023.

Both sides agree Clancy did it. But her attorneys argued the former labor and delivery nurse was suffering from postpartum psychosis at the time, and that poor mental healthcare exacerbated her condition. Prosecutors argued she intentionally planned the killings.

open image in gallery Lindsay Clancy’s ex-husband, Patrick Clancy, testified at trial about the day he found his children dead and wife badly wounded ( Reuters )

Clancy faced life in prison for a murder conviction. If found not guilty at trial, she could have been released or remained confined in a mental health facility.

Clancy's former husband made anguished 911 call

Clancy's former husband, Patrick Clancy, was first to take the stand at trial. In emotional testimony, he described the day he found his wife after she tried to kill herself.

Lindsay Clancy had sent him out to get takeout food and medication for their daughter, which prosecutors argue was an excuse to get him out of the house.

He came home to find the house unusually silent, before finding blood throughout the main bedroom and a window open.

Jurors listened to the 911 call Patrick Clancy made after finding his wife outside in the snow. Clancy can be heard speaking with his wife, then tells the dispatcher he’s going to check on the children.

open image in gallery Lindsay Clancy poses with two of her children alongside her ex-husband, Patrick Clancy ( Facebook )

Moments later, he howls and cries after finding his children in the basement. The confused dispatcher repeatedly asks what happened.

“She killed the kids!” he yells.

Everyone knew Clancy was struggling

Clancy's mother, mother-in-law, sister, friends and co-workers testified that Clancy struggled with her mental health after giving birth to Callan, the youngest of her three children.

Clancy's mother-in-law, Susan Clancy, said she and her former daughter-in-law were close. Both worked as labor and delivery nurses. She described Lindsay as a wonderful mother.

But Susan Clancy testified that Lindsay had become anxious, paranoid and suicidal, and that the psychiatric care she was getting wasn't helping.

“She felt unwell. She had insomnia. She was losing her appetite. She was very anxious and sad,” Susan Clancy said. “She was begging for help.”

Lindsay Clancy’s mother, Paula Musgrove, testified that her daughter was scared of sleeping alone, became paranoid and believed the medications she was taking “were destroying her mind.”

open image in gallery Lindsay Clancy has to use a wheelchair after a suicide attempt left her paralyzed from the waist down ( via REUTERS )

“Mom, will you please come up and stay with me for a bit? I’m really sick. Something is wrong,” Clancy wrote in an October 2022 text message that Paula Musgrove read in court. “I had horrible insomnia all night, and I just don’t know how I am going to get through the day. … It’s just really scary, and I don’t want to be alone.”

The defense questioned the quality of Clancy's medical care

Clancy saw several doctors about her declining mental health, and eventually checked herself in to a psychiatric hospital. Her lawyer, Kevin Reddington, argued that she was misdiagnosed and overmedicated.

As he cross-examined one of her psychiatrists, Dr. Jennifer Tufts, Reddington questioned her expertise, prescribing decisions and use of 25-minute video appointments with limited time for talk therapy. At one point, Reddington implied that Tufts was a box-checking “robot.”

“What did you do? You had a woman who was telling you she felt hopeless,” he asked as they discussed an appointment about two months before the killings.

“I told her that this was something we could address, that there was hope, that there are treatments, that there are different types of programs,” Tufts said, “so she knew that she still had options and a reason to hope.”

Clancy said she heard a voice telling her to kill

Paul Zeizel, a clinical and forensic psychologist who visited Lindsay Clancy in the hospital after she killed the children, testified that he overheard her saying that a disembodied male voice had told her she had no choice but to kill her children and then herself. Zeizel said he believed Clancy wasn't responsible for her actions because of her deep mental illness.

open image in gallery Lindsay Clancy strangled her three young children with exercise bands ( GoFundMe )

Prosecutors called a rebuttal witness, forensic psychologist Kirk Heilbrun, who said he didn’t believe Clancy had hallucinated voices.

“One of the things that she said when I asked about what happened, is that in the course of strangling each child, she said, ‘Go to God, baby. Go to God,’” he said. “That was part of her expectation that she and the children would be together in heaven with God.”

Dr. Gregory Saathoff, a senior psychiatrist for the FBI’s Behavioral Analysis Unit, testified for prosecutors that Clancy “had the capacity to know right from wrong.”

The lawyers got the last word

After testimony was complete, each side got about an hour to make their closing argument to the jury.

Reddington showed the jury a photograph of the Clancy family, looking happy, and a second one of Lindsay Clancy in the hospital.

“How does this turn into this?" Reddington asked. “How? Because of the damn medicine and the lousy medical care that she got.”

Prosecutor Jennifer Sprague said criticizing the mental health system was “a distraction.” She said Clancy chose to kill her children because doing so would make it easier to kill herself.

“She was depressed. She was exhausted. She was done. She didn’t want to try anymore. She felt damaged,” Sprague said. “But those kids, those kids were her protective factor. Those kids were keeping her from ending her misery.”

If you are experiencing feelings of distress, or are struggling to cope, you can speak to the Samaritans, in confidence, on 116 123 (UK and ROI) or visit the Samaritans website to find details of your nearest branch.

If you are based in the USA, and you or someone you know needs mental health assistance right now, call or text 988, or visit 988lifeline.org to access online chat from the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. This is a free, confidential crisis hotline that is available to everyone 24 hours a day, seven days a week. If you are in another country, you can go to www.befrienders.org to find a helpline near you

President Donald Trump threatened to halt trade with every country that runs a surplus with the United States unless the Federal Reserve cuts interest rates, tying together two things that are not connected by any mechanism of American economic policy.

In a 183-word post Friday on Truth Social published hours after Bureau of Labor Statistics released a better-than-expected jobs report, Trump wrote in capital letters: "LOWER THE RATE OR I'LL STOP TRADING WITH COUNTRIES WITH WHICH WE HAVE A DEFICIT."

The president does not set interest rates, and the central bank’s Federal Open Market Committee does not set trade policy. The two are handled by different institutions under different statutes, and the Fed's rate decisions are made without reference to the bilateral trade balance.

Yet Trump inexplicably argued that the central bank should slash rates by comparing the Fed’s interest rate to the interest one might pay on a home mortgage, automobile loan or business loan based on one’s individual credit score.

"Lower the interest rates because the U.S.A. is a much stronger credit than it was just a short time ago!" he wrote. "A STRONG COUNTRY MEANS A LOWER INTEREST RATE - IT'S A BETTER CREDIT…Very simple!"

open image in gallery Trump’s Truth Social post appears to have no relationship to economic reality as he threatened to stop trade if interest rates aren’t lowered ( AFP via Getty Images )

That is a description of how consumer lending works. A borrower with a higher credit score is offered a lower rate by a bank, because the bank is pricing the risk that the borrower will not repay.

But that process has absolutely nothing to do with the Federal Reserve’s federal funds rate, which is an administered rate the central bank sets to pursue its congressional mandate of maximum employment and stable prices.

In short, it’s a tool for cooling or stimulating the economy, not a price quoted to the U.S. government by a lender assessing its creditworthiness.

The rate the government actually pays to borrow is the yield on Treasury securities, and that is set by investors in the bond market rather than by the Fed. Creditworthiness does affect it. But no rating agency has upgraded the United States. Moody's stripped the country of its last AAA rating in May 2025, cutting it to Aa1; S&P affirmed the U.S. at AA+ with a stable outlook in June, one notch below the top; Fitch has had the country at AA+ since 2023.

Additionally, his threat to cut off foreign trade — something that could be beyond his authority despite his claim that a recent Supreme Court ruling would permit him to do so — would actually raise the borrowing costs he claims should be lower because of his administration’s policies.

open image in gallery In a lengthy Friday post, Trump threatened to stop trade with numerous countries ( Getty Images )

Countries that run trade surpluses with the United States accumulate dollars, and a large share of those dollars are recycled into U.S. Treasury securities. That demand is one of the things that holds American borrowing costs down. Cutting off trade with surplus countries would reduce it.

Trump’s post came hours after Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Friday that employers added 162,000 jobs in August, with the unemployment rate holding steady at 4.1 percent. The August gain also ran well above the average of about 31,000 a month over the previous year, reversing a summer slowdown.

The federal funds target range has stood at 3.50 to 3.75 percent since December. At the July meeting — the first full one chaired by Kevin Warsh, who was nominated by Trump, confirmed 54-45 in May and sworn in on May 22 — the committee voted 9-3 to hold. All three dissenters, Cleveland's Beth Hammack, Minneapolis' Neel Kashkari and Dallas' Lorie Logan, wanted a quarter-point increase.

Continuing a years-long trend of publicly bullying Federal Reserve chairs over interest rates, Trump called Warsh a “great new leader” but warned that the Fed “must get smart” and urged the board to “BE PATRIOTS for a change.”

"High interest rates put the U.S.A. at a very unfair disadvantage, and I won't allow that to happen,” he said.

News.content:

A Georgia inmate is back in police custody after escaping from a sheriff’s office car wash Thursday morning in a sedan driven by a woman.

Isaac Kindle, a 21-year-old inmate trustee, escaped around 9:30 a.m. while working at the Douglas County Sheriff’s Office car wash, the department said in a Facebook post. Inmate trustees are prisoners who get extra jobs and trust because of good behavior.

Kindle was being held without bond on charges of failure to appear and theft by shoplifting, according to jail records reviewed by CBS Atlanta.

The woman driving the sedan was later stopped and arrested in Cobb County but Kindle was no longer in the vehicle. Authorities believed he had left Douglas County but said there was no known threat to the public.

The escape drew criticism from Reform Room Solutions Group, a community justice and reform organization. The group commented on the sheriff’s office’s initial Facebook post, accusing the department of delaying its report and suggesting it acted only after Reform Room reported the escape.

open image in gallery Inmate Isaac Kindle, 21, escaped Thursday while working at a Georgia sheriff’s office car wash, fleeing in a woman’s car ( Douglas County Sheriff's Office )

“We hope you catch him, we know your office and county has challenges with ineptitude,” the Reform Room’s comment read.

Kindle was apprehended later Thursday in Powder Springs, Georgia, police said, some six miles from where he went missing. He was escorted back to Douglas County around 5:45 p.m.

“While the ‘Reformers’ were talking, the DCSO was working. This is NOT what ‘inept’ looks like,” the sheriff’s office wrote in an updated Facebook post, announcing his capture.

open image in gallery 'What makes you think you can do what you do?' Douglas County Sheriff Tim Pounds asked Kindle upon his return to the jail ( Douglas County Sheriff's Office )

The department also shared video of Sheriff Tim Pounds meeting Kindle when he arrived back at the jail. “What makes you think you can do what you do?” Pounds asked.

As he escorted Kindle into the jail, Pounds added: “We don’t put up with no foolishness in Douglas County.”

The Independent has contacted the sheriff’s department for comment.

A Pennsylvania coroner has confirmed a second child measles death in the state.

The measles deaths are the first reported in the United States this year amid a 35-year high in infections.

“Just today, we received a report of another child who died with measles, and we’re in the process of doing an investigation,” Lancaster County Coroner, Dr. Stephen Diamantoni, told WHTM Wednesday.

It is unclear if the second death reported by the coroner is further clarification of two deaths already reported, or if this brings the death toll to three.

There has been unusual friction between the state and the federal government after Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. asked his newly appointed CDC director to remove a reference to two Pennsylvania fatalities from the agency’s online measles tracker after questioning whether the virus contributed to the deaths, according to a new report.

open image in gallery Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. speaks in Washington, D.C., Tuesday. Kennedy’s CDC and Pennsylvania officials are at odds over measles deaths in the state ( Reuters )

CDC staffers had accepted the state’s characterization of the deaths as linked to measles before recently-appointed Director Erica Schwartz ordered the edit, Reuters reported, citing three sources familiar with the matter.

A Health and Human Services spokesperson told the outlet the agency had requested details needed to determine the cause of the deaths - but did not comment on Kennedy's or Schwartz’s reported actions.

The Independent has reached out to HHS for comment on the report.

A spokesperson for the Pennsylvania Health Department told The Independent Tuesday that every reported measles case is “thoroughly reviewed to confirm it meets the CDC’s case definition for a measles case.”

Diamantoni contested the cause of one of the deaths reported by the department last month, telling WGAL that a ruptured the spleen of a newborn infected with measles was the actual cause of death.

That drew outrage from doctors including Philadelphia pediatrician Dr. Paul Offit, who told The Independent not saying the cause of death was measles was “absurd.”

The Independent has contacted Diamantoni for comment on the deaths, which are Pennsylvania’s first in 35 years.

However, a CDC tracker still shows zero deaths from measles nationwide this year.

open image in gallery This Pennsylvania Department of Health shows measles cases across the state's counties this year. The darkest blue counties have the most cases ( Pennsylvania Department of Health )

The CDC told The Independent earlier this week that the deaths have not been confirmed based on the information currently available to the agency.

The CDC has not said what information it will rely on to determine whether the Pennsylvania deaths were caused by measles.

The virus causes brain-swelling, fever and pneumonia, with the majority of infections in people who have not been vaccinated.

Two doses of the vaccine - which also protects against the mumps and rubella - are 97 percent effective against infection, offering lifelong protection, according to the CDC.

The nation’s ongoing resurgence in measles cases is fueled by rising vaccine hesitancy spurred by misinformation, experts tell The Independent.

Figures from the CDC and state agencies show that vaccination rates have been falling since before the Covid-19 pandemic.

Pennsylvania is one of the states with the highest number of cases, CDC data last updated August 30 shows. The state reported 540 cases on Tuesday, with 242 in Lancaster County alone.

There is a reason eight of the most expensive 10 transfers between English clubs this summer involved central midfielders.

Of all the factors that go into valuing a footballer – age, length of contract, performance metrics, injury record, Tottenham’s desperation – the starting point for any negotiation is to benchmark a player against the market. Once Spurs bought Mateus Fernandes for a club record £85m from West Ham in June, and then broke that record buying Sandro Tonali from Newcastle for £100m four days later, the reference points were set for Bruno Guimaraes, Morgan Rogers, Elliot Anderson, Carlos Baleba and Enzo Fernandez later in the window.

At the end of a two-month frenzy in which Premier League clubs spent roughly the GDP of Andorra, plenty of supporters and figures inside football are still trying to wrap their heads around the numbers. Each individual transfer is a unique case, but together they raise wider questions, about what players are worth, about what value they truly add. In short: can a footballer really be worth £100m to a football club?

open image in gallery Manchester City have splurged on a entirely new midfield ( Manchester City )

There are two connected parts to the answer: a player’s impact on performance, and a player’s impact on the club’s commercial success. On the latter point, only a handful of global stars have the ability to move the needle of a major Premier League club’s commercial revenues.

On the point of performance, there are some dramatic examples of individual influence. Virgil van Dijk missed most of Liverpool’s 2020/21 season with injury, and they fell 30 points short of the previous campaign. The true impact of Van Dijk’s absence is impossible to know, given he was part of a wider injury crisis in Jurgen Klopp’s squad, and given poor finishing was Liverpool’s main weakness. Man City had a similar collapse without Rodri in 2024/25, but again, his absence was only one factor in a wider malaise.

Omar Chaudhuri is chief intelligence officer at Twenty First Group, which advises football clubs on transfer strategy. The company has spent years researching and understanding the market, and has found that most transfers do not drastically change a club’s outcomes on their own.

So is there any justification for the £100m footballer?

“In intrinsic value, no,” says Chaudhuri. “Because if you analyse how much any one individual footballer can influence the outcome of a team over the course of the season, it’s never going to be more than three, four, five points – unless you’re Lionel Messi at Inter Miami, where the gulf between you and the other players is so big.

“Enzo Fernandez is a good player, but he’s not a transformative player, and it’s very hard to get transformative players in the Premier League because the quality is already so high. It’s a £125m transfer fee, but over the course of a deal you might be spending £200m on a player. You couldn’t really say that the difference between having Enzo Fernandez and not having Enzo Fernandez is worth £200m in revenue to Manchester City, it’d be difficult to make the sums add up. But ultimately you have to pay the prices that the market dictates. And if everyone is prepared to pay those prices, then you just have to accept that you’re operating in an inflated market.”

open image in gallery Enzo Fernandez has joined City in a £125m transfer ( Reuters )

The market has become increasingly distorted as clubs are drawn into spending huge sums, often under pressure after a run of poor results, or simply because they see transfers as a shortcut to improvement. And this idea of the market as a route to rapid success has repeatedly proved itself to be misguided.

“The transfer market is a vastly overrated opportunity to improve your team,” Chaudhuri says. “It’s obviously seen as the main opportunity because fundamentally you look at the quality of your players being the driver of your on-field success. But if you look historically, the amount a club net-spends in its transfer window has no bearing on the extent to which they improve or get worse over the following season – literally no bearing – which is kind of staggering. A club that spends £200m net is not expected to improve their position any more or less than a club that generates £200m net income.”

The reality is that a steady, focused execution of a long-term plan outperforms scattergun spending – although the big clubs’ prodigality offers opportunity for the rest. Brighton and Brentford have been able to punch above their weight by selling players at the most extreme end of the Premier League market, while finding replacements in more realistic waters.

“Whenever we advise clubs, they’re looking for that silver-bullet strategy or market you can recruit from,” says Chaudhuri. “The slightly more boring fact is you just need a plan and you need the discipline to execute against it. It almost doesn’t really matter what the plan is. The failing of most football clubs is that they don’t have a really clearly defined plan.

“We talk a lot about Brentford and Brighton. It’s very rare that you have clubs that are almost tunnel-vision in the way in which they operate. The amount of clubs that flip-flop from one season to the next in the way in which they set up their structure and management, their coach, playing style, recruitment, it’s all over the place. But having a plan and being consistent against it – it sounds so basic, but it’s lacking in so many clubs.”

open image in gallery Brentford signed Mamadou Sangare during the summer window for £38m ( Getty )

There is another element of the modern transfer market, which is that many of these large transfer fees are somewhat superficial. Most include add-on clauses that may not be triggered. Almost all fees are now amortised, so the outlay is spread over the length of the player’s contract. The £125m Manchester City spent on Fernandez will be parcelled up at £25m per year for the next five years, and even if he is sold for only half that price after three seasons, the money recouped will be enough to write off the remaining debt.

As The Independent’s alarming report explained this week, this almost casual reliance on debt is now the pile of sand on which the Premier League is built, and some figures within the game are warning it could give way to a serious collapse. Yet until that day comes, nothing is going to stop clubs spending wild sums in an overhyped market.

Chaudhuri suggests there is another way. “I think too few clubs actually focus on improving their own players. The amount of times we see performances ebb and flow, and over one part of the season a club could be demonstrating Champions League form when over an earlier part of the season it might have had mid-table form. That shows that clubs have the ability to generate much better performance out of the same group of players, rather than needing to recruit. There’s so little focus on what clubs can actually do to build cohesive teams and improve their own players, and I think many clubs have lost sight of that in the last few years.”

News.title: Former Liverpool winger Jordan Ibe avoids jail after assaulting girlfriend
News.content:

Read our Privacy notice

Former Liverpool winger Jordon Ibe pulled a braid out of his ex-girlfriend’s hair during an argument where she called him a “druggy”.

Ibe, 30, assaulted his former partner Amie Mayson outside her home in Lambeth, south London, on 14 December.

The attack happened after she confronted him and demanded he repaid her money she said he owed her, Croydon Magistrates’ Court heard on Friday.

Prosecutor Aya Alshekhili said that after Ms Mayson asked to be reimbursed, Ibe told her: “No, I’m going to be a prick.”

Ibe had a bag containing drinks, snacks and flowers, but when she called him a “druggy” he grabbed her arm “hard” and then grabbed her hair, the court was told.

The footballer, who made 58 appearances for the Anfield side before spells at Derby County, Birmingham City and AFC Bournemouth, pulled a braid from Ms Mayson’s hair, the court heard.

open image in gallery Ibe, 30, assaulted his former partner Amie Mayson outside her home in Lambeth, south London, on 14 December ( PA )

On Friday, magistrate Brij Kalia sentenced Ibe to a 12-month community order, 80 hours of unpaid work and 27 days of rehabilitation activity.

Ibe was also handed a £764 fine, including £114 of surcharge and £650 in court costs.

The footballer, who represented himself at the hearing wearing a black coat and black trousers, told the court: “I made a serious mistake.”

He added: “I understand it is wrong. I am genuinely remorseful. I’ve had to look at myself in the mirror. I cannot change what I did but will take responsibility for what I do next.”

Ms Alshekhili said the attack left Ms Mayson’s confidence, self-esteem and self-worth “on the floor”.

In a victim impact statement read to the court, Ms Mayson said: “I want the court to understand the impact that this incident has had.

“The assault has had a significant impact on me both physically and mentally.”

open image in gallery Jordan Ibe made 58 appearances for the Anfield side before spells at Derby County, Birmingham City and AFC Bournemouth

She said despite remaining “feelings of fear”, she felt “compassion” for Ibe, adding forgiveness had been part of her “healing journey”.

Ibe, of Chislehurst, south-east London, pleaded guilty to the charge of assault occasioning actual bodily harm in July, after denying it in March.

On Friday, Ms Alshekhili said that prior to the assault the pair had been on an “on and off” relationship since late 2024.

The former England under-21 international played for Lokomotiv Sofia in the Bulgarian First League until June.

In the last two years, he had been playing non-league football before securing the move to the Bulgarian capital in November 2025.

News.title: Could making fewer clothes create a fairer fashion industry?
News.content:

Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging. Fashion has become remarkably skilled at presenting small improvements as systemic change. A garment made with recycled fibres, a lower-impact collection or a resale scheme may suggest progress, yet the industry continues to manufacture clothes in quantities the planet cannot sustain.

For Safia Minney, the pioneering ethical fashion entrepreneur who founded People Tree and went on to establish Fashion Declares, and Indilisi incremental improvements are no longer enough. A genuine response to the climate crisis requires the industry to confront a far more difficult question: how can fashion produce dramatically fewer clothes without abandoning the millions of workers whose livelihoods depend upon making them?

open image in gallery Safia Minney, founder of People Tree, Fashion Declares and Indilisi, believes fashion must replace relentless volume with craft, regenerative agriculture and dignified livelihoods ( Odi Caspi )

“Science tells us that we should be cutting back production and consumption of new clothing by between 75 and 95 per cent,” Minney says. “That is a reduction of 75 to 95 per cent, not 5 or 25 per cent.”

Such a contraction would represent far more than a change in seasonal trends or consumer habits. It would fundamentally reshape a global industry built on speed, volume and cheap labour. Factories would receive fewer orders and jobs would disappear, many of them in countries where garment work provides a vital, if often precarious, source of income.

“Obviously, what that means is that a lot of people will lose their jobs in fashion supply chains,” Minney says.

It is a reality that can be obscured by the seemingly simple instruction to “buy less”. Reducing consumption is essential, but without a plan for the people making our clothes, environmental progress risks coming at the expense of those who have benefited least from fashion’s profits and suffered most from its inequities.

For Minney, the answer lies in replacing volume with value. Rather than continuing to rely on vast quantities of industrially produced clothing, fashion could redirect investment towards handweaving, traditional textile skills and regenerative agriculture, creating work that supports communities rather than extracting from them.

“There is now a global trend for craft, but at the moment it is considered to be high-end luxury,” she says. “It’s incorporating craft, handweaving and traditional hand-skilled techniques into mid-market fashion and above.”

open image in gallery A weaver at Swallows in Bangladesh creates fabric for Indilisi, preserving traditional hand skills while supporting lower-impact production and dignified livelihoods ( Safia Minney )

Craft is frequently celebrated on fashion’s most expensive runways, where evidence of the human hand helps justify the language and price of luxury. But Minney believes it should play a much broader role. If consumers bought fewer clothes, repaired what they owned and made greater use of resale and charity shops, they might also be able to spend more on an occasional handwoven garment.

“As consumers start to consume less and consume better and more consciously, there’s no reason at all why they wouldn’t be able to afford a handwoven shirt or dress or trousers,” she says. “We can buy second-hand very affordably through the various platforms or charity shops and, of course, we can repair clothes as well. We can keep things in circulation for longer.”

This is not simply about preserving beautiful techniques. Minney points to the millions of handweavers in India, Bangladesh and across Africa whose knowledge could form part of a lower-volume fashion economy. Investment in these skills could also create livelihoods outside the industrial centres to which many garment workers have migrated.

open image in gallery A craftswoman at Lesedi Cultural Village in South Africa uses traditional hand skills, an example of the knowledge and livelihoods Safia Minney believes fashion’s just transition must value and protect ( Getty )

“Retraining people, providing livelihoods and opportunities in craft production in rural areas could actually make life much more comfortable for a lot of people who are living quite far away from their families, maybe only seeing their children a couple of times a year,” she says.

“There are some real advantages in creating craft livelihoods in rural areas, where people can live more affordably with their extended families and with their children.”

This is the social dimension of climate action that the language of lower-impact materials can miss. A just transition is not only concerned with how much carbon a garment produces, it asks who is being supported, who carries the risk and whether the new system gives people the means to build secure lives.

Minney describes conventional sustainability as an attempt to improve an existing model, protecting basic human rights, preventing excessive overtime and moving towards lower-impact materials or mono-fibre garments that are easier to recycle.

Important though those measures are, she argues that many should already constitute the basic conditions of doing business.

open image in gallery Safia Minney with a handweaver at Swallows in Bangladesh, where traditional skills are used to create fabric for Indilisi and support dignified, lower-impact livelihoods. ( Safia Minney )

“Sustainability should be ticking all the boxes in terms of better practice, looking at what should be illegal, not covering people’s basic human rights in the supply chain, whether it’s paying workers badly or excessive overtime,” she says. “Sustainable fashion has been an embracing of human rights and nature, but I think we needed to go beyond that.”

Regenerative fashion demands a deeper relationship with the landscapes and communities which clothing depends. It means working directly with farmers through organic and Fairtrade agriculture, investing in soil health and GMO-free seeds, and paying producers fairly for fibres such as organic cotton.

Craft belongs within that model because its value can extend beyond lower-impact production. “Craft does use low-impact materials. It does use traditional hand skills. It can pay people a living wage,” Minney says. “If we were to use craft, that would be highly regenerative in its practices.”

For designers, buyers and merchandisers, this requires more than adding an artisanal piece to a collection. Brands need to change their production calendars and allow time for garments and textiles to be made by hand.

open image in gallery Indilisi brings traditional handwoven fabric into contemporary fashion, proving that heritage craft can feel every bit as modern as it is meaningful. ( Steve Nyman )

“They can start to look at their critical path so that they can make allowances for hand production,” she says. “It’s not difficult. It’s perfectly doable. We did it at People Tree. We’re currently doing it at Indilisi.”

The guiding question, she suggests, should be: “How are you going to make products with as low an environmental impact as possible, but with as high a social impact as possible?”

Craft-based production cannot be expanded responsibly simply by placing larger orders. Brands must form close partnerships with craft organisations, learn what makers can produce and offer design input so that finished fabrics become high-quality garments people will want to keep.

Crucially, they must also reconsider when people are paid.

“Whilst working capital sounds really unsexy, it’s critical,” Minney says. A handwoven fabric can take three-and-a-half months to complete and sometimes as long as five. During that period, artisans still need to support themselves and their families.

“You need to be paying the handweaver, the hand-embroidery artisan or the hand-block printer as they’re finishing their work,” she says. “Every week or every month, not nine months, or three months after the product has arrived with you in the UK.”

Minney’s work in Bangladesh includes training in design, production and quality management, as well as the use of safe, GOTS-certified dyes and links to certified organic cotton. The aim is to make the journey of a garment traceable back to the people growing its fibres, while ensuring that respect for the farmer and the natural world is embedded in the product.

It is a slower system, but that is precisely the point. Craft cannot become another means of feeding fashion’s appetite for endless growth. The industry must reduce overall production while building strong networks that allow makers to work at a human pace.

After more than 30 years of campaigning, Minney’s vision extends beyond emissions reduction. Fashion companies must also prepare their supply chains for the climate disruption that is already unavoidable.

“We are not thinking about extreme heat and floods and how that’s going to impact the people within our supply chains,” she warns, “especially women who already carry the burden of making ends meet.”

Environmental, social and governance frameworks need to become more than corporate reporting exercises. They must help communities build resilience and adapt to increasingly dangerous conditions while recognising fashion’s dependence upon both people and nature.

The transition Minney describes is radical, but it is not a rejection of fashion. It is an argument for restoring value to it. Fewer garments, made with greater skill, from fibres grown in healthier soil, by people able to earn a dignified living close to their communities.

Buying less is only one part of that transformation. The greater challenge is ensuring that as fashion relinquishes its dependence on volume, it does not relinquish its responsibility to the people who have sustained it. A just transition cannot simply close the door on the old system. It must invest in what comes next.

open image in gallery Mountains of discarded clothing expose the scale of fashion’s waste crisis, a challenge explored through repair, reuse and circularity at Craft, Clothing & Circularity: Out of Fashion on 11 September ( Tim Mitchell )

Minney will continue this conversation at Craft, Clothing & Circularity: Out of Fashion at Conway Hall in London on Friday 11 September. A Fashion Declares event in collaboration with Selvedge magazine.

“Fashion needs a wake-up call,” Minney says. “If you’re a fashion practitioner or fashion lover, join our interactive discussion and create powerful action with us.”, for evening-only tickets book here.

News.title: Indonesia wildfires triggers 50,000 respiratory infections
News.content:
More than 50,000 people have contracted respiratory infections in Indonesia, as raging wild fires blanket huge swathes of the country in a thick, toxic smoke.

The vast archipelago is only a month into its fire season, but intense blazes have proven hard to control across Sumatra and Indonesian Borneo. There are fears the situation will only get worse, because the “Godzilla” El Niño is set to suppress rains that would normally have helped extinguish the flames.

“Our problems are not over. September is the peak of El Niño,” said Raja Juli Antoni, the forestry minister. “September is the main fight for us.”

Already the toxic haze has spread across Southeast Asia. On Friday Kuching, a city in Malaysian Borneo, was the most polluted city in the world on the IQ Air Index, followed by Jakarta and Singapore.

The wildfires have brought memories of record-breaking blazes in 2015. Then, the smoke was linked to roughly 100,000 excess deaths in Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore, according to one study. The World Bank said Indonesia alone saw economic losses of $16.1bn, or 2 per cent of GDP.

News.title: Global hunger is a threat to Britain’s national security, report says
News.content:
Global hunger poses a direct threat to Britain’s national security, and tackling it should be a government priority, a new report from the London School of Economics has warned.

It says hunger is a major driver of mass migration, extreme violence and war – events that threaten significant repercussions for Britain and Europe’s national security.

“Hunger prevention is an important part of national security policy, not an optional act of charity,” Stuart Gordon, professor of International Development at LSE and author of the report, told The Telegraph.

Recent hunger crises in places like Sudan, Afghanistan and across North Africa have contributed significantly to rising numbers of people moving to the West.

Between January and November 2025 alone, 12,684 migrants from Sudan – which is facing what has been described as the worst hunger crisis in Africa’s history – arrived in Europe, roughly three times as many as the previous year.

Last year, an estimated 155,000 African refugees arrived in Europe.

“Food insecurity tests one of the most basic expectations people have of government: that it will protect access to the essentials of life,” said Prof Gordon.

“Food price shocks can rapidly escalate into political instability when governments are perceived to have failed to protect access to basic subsistence goods,” he added.

News.title: Congo’s Ebola outbreak slows at epicentre but widens elsewhere, modelling suggests
News.content:
Congo’s Ebola outbreak shows signs of slowing at the epicentre of the flare-up, but is widening as the infection spreads further afield, modelling suggests.

The daily tally of new cases in Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) was falling at the end of August, but more cases were being found outside Ituri province, where the infection burst out.

Latest official figures say the outbreak has now killed more than 3,000 people out of over 6,100 confirmed cases, with the infection spreading faster than any previous epidemic of the viral haemorrhagic fever.

Modelling by Airfinity, a health analytics firm, suggests the true toll of cases could be more than four times higher than reported.

The outbreak remains on track to eclipse the 2014 West Africa outbreak later this month, to become the largest ever recorded.

Airfinity said that data from late August showed the seven-day averages of reported cases and reported deaths had fallen by 16 per cent and 18 per cent respectively.

The firm said it was “too early to confirm the decline will hold, and it may mask subnational variation: The outbreak has fluctuated before and a week of falling case and death counts does not rule out another surge.

“Even if the decline continues at this current pace, low case levels remain weeks away.”

News.title: Bank of England must raise interest rates, says chief economist
News.content:
Thanks for joining me. Government borrowing costs edged lower on Thursday as Andy Burnham continues to face scrutiny over the public finances.

The yield on 10-year US treasury bonds – considered a benchmark for what governments pay to borrow money – declined slightly to 4.78pc on Thursday after a drop in oil prices.

Pre-market trading of bonds in Britain, France and Germany suggested the market was poised to rally after a brutal first half of the week.

However, Mr Burnham and Chancellor John Healey remain under intense pressure, with analysts estimating that as much as half of the country’s fiscal headroom has been wiped out by the jump in bond yields.

Borrowing costs surged after a jump in oil prices caused by fresh strikes between the US and Iran.

The yield on 10-year gilts, as UK bonds are known, hit levels not seen since the global financial crisis in 2007, while longer-term debt costs hit their highest point since 1998.

It means the Chancellor will have less room for manoeuvre in the Budget next month, with some economists predicting the rise in borrowing costs has wiped out up to £14bn of breathing room.

The rise in bond yields across major economies had deepened concerns about deteriorating financial conditions.

Central banks in the US and Europe are increasingly expected to raise interest rates this month to combat inflation caused by the Iran war, although the Bank of England is expected to hold rates steady for now.

Gavin Friend, an analyst at NAB, said: “If this war ‌were to be ‌put to bed, then that ⁠would certainly be something very positive to bring yields back down again across the board.” Here is what you need to know.

5 things to start your day

What happened overnight

Oil prices slipped, helping boost stocks and bonds.

Renewed fighting between the US and Iran pushed oil prices sharply higher earlier in the week.

However, Brent crude was trading near $94 a barrel after Donald Trump said he does not expect the US bombing campaign to last “much longer”.

Tokyo’s Nikkei 225 advanced 0.2pc to 64,455.83. Among major gainers, OpenAI investor SoftBank Group rose 2.9pc, memory chipmaker Kioxia rose 0.6pc, and chip equipment manufacturer Tokyo Electron gained 0.8pc.

South Korea’s Kospi rose 1.4pc to 6,656.81. Samsung was 1.3pc higher, while memory chipmaker SK Hynix was up 1.4pc.

In Hong Kong, the Hang Seng edged 0.1pc higher, to 25,344.80. The Shanghai Composite index climbed 0.4pc to 3,958.79.

Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 gained 0.5pc to 9,025.10.

The Taiex in Taiwan rose 0.6pc, while India’s Sensex climbed 0.3pc.

It comes after Wall Street bounced back after its sharp sell-off at the start of September, as investors snapped up shares that had fallen in recent days.

The S&P 500 rose, with almost 350 companies ending higher. Dell was among the biggest winners, jumping 14pc after giving an upbeat outlook, while investors were also looking ahead to results from chipmaker Broadcom.

The recovery came despite continued concerns over inflation, with oil prices remaining high as fighting between the US and Iran escalated. Brent crude briefly climbed close to $97 a barrel before easing back after Donald Trump said he did not expect the renewed bombing campaign to last “too long”.

US government bond yields were little changed after surging to their highest levels in several years earlier in the week.

Investors also got a mixed picture from the Federal Reserve’s latest assessment of the US economy. Economic activity increased modestly over the past two months, helped by strong demand from data centres, while companies added jobs at a slower pace in August.

The figures come ahead of Friday’s closely watched US jobs report, which could influence expectations for the next move in interest rates.

News.title: Weapons and mercenaries from foreign states fuelling Sudan’s war, UN report finds
News.content:
The war in Sudan is being fuelled by weapons and mercenaries from external states including the United Arab Emirates, Colombia and Turkey, a United Nations report has found.

An investigation by a UN fact-finding mission published on Thursday found that the supply of drones in particular to both sides in the civil war was extending the fighting’s reach and contributing to war crimes.

“Increasingly sophisticated drone capabilities [has] enabled both parties to strike far beyond immediate front lines”, says the report.

“The [UN] mission calls on States to enforce the Darfur arms embargo and suspend transfers of weapons, drones, components, or military assistance where there is a substantial risk of their use in serious violations”.

Sudan’s civil war erupted in April 2023 following a power struggle between the head of the military and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) as part of a planned transition to civilian rule. Hundreds of thousands have died and some 14 million people have been displaced in what has become the world’s deadliest conflict.

In a previous report in February, following the capture of El Fasher in which at least 60,000 people were killed, the UN said the RSF’s mass killings of Black African ethnic groups, including Zaghawa and Fur, bore the “hallmarks of genocide”.

The latest report said “individuals and entities” in the UAE were part of a transnational network supplying weapons, logistics, training and foreign personnel to the RSF – including NORINCO AH-4 howitzers, FK-20000 air defence systems and Chinese-made CH-95 strike drones.

The Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), meanwhile, separately obtained Turkish-manufactured drones, including Bayraktar Akıncı combat drones and Yiha III loitering munitions.

The Turkish embassy in London has been contacted for comment.

News.title: The Ukrainian children struggling to survive alone in Europe
News.content:
Every day begins and ends in the same way for Arsenii, 17: calling his mum back home in Kyiv. A year ago he moved from Ukraine to a school boarding house in Slovakia. One night he fell asleep before phoning. When he woke, his mobile was flooded with messages from the few adults his mum knew in the country: the dorm security guard and agent she paid to become his temporary legal guardian. “She woke up everybody,” he says, still with a sense of guilt. She had been trying, agonisingly, to account for her son from over 1,000km away.

Russia’s unprovoked full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 triggered Europe’s largest displacement of children since World War II. More than 1.8 million crossed into neighbouring countries in the first month – 90 per cent of them with their mothers or other female relatives. But as bombardments battered the country in the following four years, children continued to leave – only without their relatives.

A year-long investigation by the Telegraph has discovered thousands of Ukrainian children are living in Europe alone in the hope of a better life. Some have adapted to independent living, studying and learning the local language. Others have fallen into illegal work, experienced insecurity and discrimination. A few attempts end in tragedy.

The exact number of Ukrainian children who are now living alone in Europe is unclear. Data collected by EU statistical database Eurostat suggests the total cases since 2022 could be almost 23,500. It shows that 19,580 unaccompanied Ukrainian minors in European Union (EU) countries received EU Temporary Protection Status (TPS) between March 2022 and July 2026.

Non-EU countries offer parallel protection schemes. Eurostat data revealed that in the same time-frame, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland granted their protection status to an additional 3,905 unaccompanied Ukrainian minors.

However, the data is incomplete. Only 20 out of 27 EU members declared their numbers. Among those missing are key Ukrainian refugee destination countries, such as Germany and Poland. Poland alone issued 42,332 temporary guardian orders to Ukrainian minors between 2022 and 2025, according to Polish Ministry of Justice data requested by The Telegraph.

In theory, any child granted TPS protection should have a locally appointed legal guardian to sign their papers. However, our investigation revealed loopholes in the system, leaving this category of children vulnerable to abandonment or poor guardianship arrangements.

Arsenii is among at least 1,024 Ukrainian children aged 14 to 16 who have evacuated to Slovak school boarding houses, according to a snapshot 2025 survey by the Slovak Children’s Commissioner. The real figure is likely to be thousands higher, as this research covered just over half of secondary schools in five of the country’s eight regions. It concluded some 5,000 Ukrainian minors in Slovakia have no responsible adult “close to them”, of whom around 1,000 have no legal representative at all.

News.title: Zika virus mosquitoes breed in Britain for first time
News.content:
The UK has historically been too cold for the tropical mosquitoes to survive, but they have been slowly making their way up through Europe.

As temperatures warm, it is predicted that the mosquitoes could become widespread, potentially bringing with them diseases associated with Africa and the tropics.

“The timing of this detection is particularly interesting because the UK has just experienced its provisionally hottest summer on record,” Dr César López-Camacho, a researcher at the University of Oxford, said.



“Warmer conditions can accelerate mosquito development, extend the period in which mosquitoes remain active and, critically, increase the rate at which viruses such as dengue or chikungunya replicate within a competent mosquito,” Dr López-Camacho added.

Previous government modelling suggested that the mosquitoes would be unlikely to get a foothold in Britain until 2040, but the new discovery of the colony in London suggests it may happen sooner.

It means diseases such as dengue fever – which causes high fevers and severe joint pain, and can be fatal, particularly in the elderly and young children – could become common in southern England.

Sports.title: Tottenham ban LUXURY HANDWASH from opposition dressing room and decide to paint the walls ‘badly’ in bizarre move
Sports.content:
TOTTENHAM have ditched luxury TOLIETRIES from their opposition dressing room in Roberto De Zerbi’s bid to change the club’s mentality.

The Spurs boss and the club’s hierarchy are understood to believe opponents have been treating their world-class stadium like a pleasant day out rather than an intimidating football ground.



And that has led to a bizarre overhaul of the away dressing room at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium – with Molton Brown products now BANNED.

A video posted on X by a fan showed all the central tables have been removed from the room to leave one cavernous open space, while the walls have been painted badly and shower products have also been taken away.



A source told The Times: “No more Molton Brown handwash and body lotion.”

Tottenham have had a long-standing relationship with Molton Brown, which was previously the club’s official supplier of toiletries, including products used at the stadium and training centre.



But the changes are symbolic of the much bigger cultural reset being attempted by De Zerbi after he took charge in March.

The Italian has made it clear that he wants players who are completely committed to Tottenham and has been prepared to let even established stars leave if they want a fresh challenge.

When De Zerbi first arrived he held individual meetings with his players to discuss their futures The Sun was told.

Among those who told him they wanted to leave in the summer were captain Cristian Romero and goalkeeper Guglielmo Vicario.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

De Zerbi’s response was simple: help him keep Tottenham in the Premier League and then he would help them leave.

He later explained that he did not want to force anyone to stay, regardless of their status or importance to the team.

Romero eventually left for Atletico Madrid, while Vicario joined Juventus on loan, with De Zerbi insisting he respected their decisions.

Djed Spence and Luka Vuskovic were also allowed to depart, while Kevin Danso’s request to leave came as recently as last week after he was left out of the Carabao Cup squad.



Even then, Spurs granted his wish, with Danso joining Sunderland on loan.

That ruthless approach is at the heart of De Zerbi’s attempt to change Tottenham’s mentality after back-to-back 17th-place Premier League finishes.

The club have backed him with an extraordinary summer rebuild, spending around £400million on a squad overhaul, with the final figure potentially rising further through add-ons.

And the new arrivals have not simply been chosen for their footballing ability.



Tottenham have deliberately targeted players with experience, leadership qualities and reputations for having the right mentality to help transform the culture inside the dressing room.

Sandro Tonali arrived from Newcastle in a club-record deal, while Mateus Fernandes, Savio and Jan Paul van Hecke were among the other major additions.

Experienced campaigners including Andy Robertson and Marcos Senesi were also brought in, while Omar Marmoush arrived from Manchester City on loan.

And deadline day saw Spurs make two more moves designed to strengthen the squad, signing Chelsea defender Tosin Adarabioyo permanently and bringing in Mykhailo Mudryk on loan.



Tosin is particularly interesting because he fits the profile Tottenham appear to be targeting, a player regarded as a strong team man, with leadership experience and a willingness to embrace the standards demanded by his new manager.

The defender himself stressed the importance of mentality when he arrived, saying he wanted to bring the right attitude to training every day and help push Tottenham towards where they “deserve to be”.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

But despite the huge investment and sweeping changes, De Zerbi’s new-look Tottenham have endured a nightmare start to the Premier League season.



Spurs lost their opening two matches against Brentford and Newcastle, leaving the Italian with plenty of work to do to turn the club’s new mentality into results.

Sports.title: Ex-Aston Villa star Lucas Digne LEFT OUT of PSG squad ‘on sporting grounds’ despite completing shock transfer
Sports.content:
LUCAS DIGNE’s return to Paris Saint-Germain is off to a rocky start as he was left out of the side’s latest squad.

The Frenchman joined up with his former side this summer as part of an exodus of talent leaving Villa Park.



But now Digne, 33, may be regretting that decision after being completely omitted from Luis Enrique‘s side to face Monaco on Friday.

According to L’Equipe, “sporting reasons” are behind the decision after the full-back’s lacklustre start to life in the French capital.



Any hopes of finding regular football with his new side were quickly quashed when he was left as an unused substitute in their season opener against Rennes.

He saw some action against Lille the following week, coming on in the 71st minute with his side 2-0 down.

PSG rallied to score goals in the first and fifth minutes of extra time to steal a point, but apparently Digne’s hand in the turnaround was deemed unsatisfactory as he has since been dropped entirely from the squad.

His selection woes are made all the more concerning considering Nuno Mendes, the first choice option in the left-back position, is serving a suspension.

The Portugal international was handed a straight red card against Lens in their Trophee des Champions match before the season’s start, leaving him sidelined for the opening three Ligue 1 matches of the season.

Versatile centre-backs Lucas Beraldo and Lucas Hernandez were selected to start on the left side of Enrique’s back four in the Lille and Rennes games respectively, making Digne a third choice at best.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

But even he is faring better than Villa, who were thumped 4-0 by Brighton in their Premier League opener.

They put up a more robust defence against defending Champions Arsenal the following week, but still fell to a 1-0 loss.

The results have left them at the bottom of the Premier League table after two games on goal difference.

Sports.title: Brighton star Mats Wieffer ruled out for four matches with bizarre knee injury after getting smacked in FACE by ball
Sports.content:
BRIGHTON star Mats Wieffer has been ruled out for up to four matches after suffering a bizarre knee injury when he was SMACKED in the face by the ball.

The versatile midfielder-turned-right-back picked up the unusual injury during Brighton‘s 4-3 defeat at Chelsea on Sunday.



Wieffer, 26, was struck in the face by the ball before his legs ended up in an awkward position, leaving him with a knee problem.

And Brighton boss Fabian Hurzeler admitted it was one of the strangest injuries he has seen.



He said: “We expect Mats to be out until the international break.

“It’s a very unlucky one.

“I can explain it quite easily, because I like boxing and sometimes in boxing when somebody gets a hit, a knockout, you see how weak the legs go and the legs get in very strange positions.

“It might happen that your knee gets injured or your ankle gets twisted.

“It was a similar situation with Mats where he was hit in the face by the ball.

“He had control of his body, then his legs got in a strange position and therefore this injury happens.”



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

Hurzeler revealed Wieffer was initially more concerned about his head than his knee.

He added: “Luckily it isn’t a bad one, but how it happened is very unlucky.

“Not a normal injury, something to do with the knee.

“He held his head, stood up and felt his knee, that is how the players explained it to me.

“It was a strange and unlucky one.”



Wieffer was eventually substituted in the 80th minute at Stamford Bridge.

The Dutchman has already endured injury problems during his Brighton career, missing eight Premier League matches between December and February last season with a toe injury.

But his latest setback comes at a particularly awkward time, with Brighton facing a packed schedule before the next international break.

Hurzeler’s side host Leeds on Saturday before travelling to Coventry on September 13.



They then face Manchester United at Old Trafford in the third round of the Carabao Cup on September 16 before hosting Arsenal three days later.

The international break then begins, with Brighton not returning to action until their trip to Sunderland on October 10.

There was some better news for Hurzeler, with midfielder Yasin Ayari and striker Georginio Rutter potentially available against Leeds after missing the Chelsea defeat with minor injuries.

New signing Chema Andres is also in contention to make his Brighton debut after arriving from Stuttgart in the final hours of Tuesday’s transfer deadline.



However, fellow new arrival Femi Azeez is unavailable for the Leeds clash after arriving from Millwall carrying a slight injury.

Austrian defender Michael Svoboda has also returned to training following a minor knee problem.

Wieffer’s absence is not quite the blow it might have been before Brighton’s summer transfer business.

Hurzeler converted the defensive midfielder into a right-back towards the end of his first season in charge in 2024-25.



And Brighton have since strengthened their options in that position following Joel Veltman’s move to West Ham, with Costinha arriving from Olympiacos and Jaouen Hadjam joining from Young Boys.

Wieffer could also have been considered for the No.6 role following Carlos Baleba‘s move to Manchester United.

But Brighton moved quickly to fill that gap by signing Andres from Stuttgart on deadline day.

The bigger concern for Hurzeler is the growing injury list at the start of the new campaign.

Wieffer has joined Jack Hinshelwood and Liverpool target Yankuba Minteh on the sidelines for several weeks.

Brighton are also without Kaoru Mitoma, Stefanos Tzimas and Evan Ferguson, who have all suffered injuries at different stages stretching back to last season.

Sports.title: Mike Dean breaks silence after bombshell ‘mini-games’ confession as Premier League clubs open probes into former referee
Sports.content:
MIKE DEAN has broken his silence on his claims that he played “games” while officiating Premier League matches – after top-flight sides opened their own internal probes.

The former referee, 58, made the sensational revelations during an appearance on Jamie Vardy’s podcast earlier this week.



Dean said that during his professional days as a pre-VAR official, he would take part in challenges, such as seeing how long he could go without having to blow his whistle.

Now he has reaffirmed that he “always applied the Laws of the Game” accurately, regardless of any games he might have played.



In a statement released on his Instagram account, Dean wrote: “Throughout my 25 years as a professional referee, I have always applied the laws of the game to the best of my ability.

“My approach as a referee was always to allow the game to flow and whenever possible I preferred to apply a high threshold for contact which the players liked.

“However, if I saw a foul challenge that needed me to take the appropriate action I would give it from the correct position.

“At no stage was it my intention to question, criticise or undermine the integrity of refereeing in this country.

“I have always respected the profession and the responsibility that comes with being a referee.”

Dean’s original claims revealed multiple different mini games the official said he would play, and he even boasted that he once made it as long as 25 minutes without blowing his whistle.



CASINO SPECIAL – BEST CASINO BONUSES FROM £10 DEPOSITS

He told The Vardy Party Podcast: “There used to be games we’d have, as a laugh.

“We used to say, ‘we’ll kick-off now, right, see how long we can go without blowing a whistle’.

“I done that a few times in the Premier League, before VAR obviously. Went 20, 25 minutes without blowing a whistle.

“Few times… let it go, let it go, let it go.”



Dean also referenced another game in which he attempted to remain in the centre circle for as long as possible.

He added: “I used to do another thing in the Premier League. I used to stand in the centre circle, see how long I could stay in the centre circle, before I had to leave.

“That was just me, joking about. The lads that used to be on the line would say ‘you can’t’.

“I got to about 15 minutes once, in one game.”

The bombshell claims caused uproar among supporters and clubs, who began scouring pre-VAR clashes for any evidence of the antics in question.



A number of top club chiefs have asked their video match analyst teams if they can find any evidence of misconduct.

But SunSport understands the reaction from officiating chiefs at Pro Ref was immediately one of deep scepticism.

Dean’s apparent admissions brought shock, anger and disbelief at the refs’ organisation, where he is felt to have fallen into the trap of becoming little more than an attention-seeker.



Pro Ref does not believe there is anything to back up the comments, with some convinced Dean was simply playing to the audience.

Since hanging up the whistle, Dean has embarked on a career in the media, and is a regular fixture on Soccer Saturday.

And some former refs seemed to feel he had leant too far towards his new life in showbiz with the comments.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

SunSport’s whistleblower and Dean’s former colleague Mark Halsey dismissed the boasts – which referred back to the pre-VAR era – as “nonsense” and accused the former ref of being on an “ego trip”.

Another ex-top flight ref, Graham Scott, described Dean’s claims as “dispiriting clickbait”.

Sports.title: Michael Carrick gives verdict on Manchester United transfer window as he claims squad player is ‘like a new signing’
Sports.content:
MICHAEL CARRICK is adamant Manchester United have a stronger squad following the closure of the transfer window amid the club’s “financial situation”.

United spent £155million on midfielders Andrey Santos, Youri Tielemans and Carlos Baleba but missed out on a left back after Newcastle refused to sell Lewis Hall.



All three promoted sides posted a higher net spend than United, who failed to negotiate a single genuinely first-team sale in the summer.

Chelsea and Tottenham spent more than £300m on signings while Manchester City broke the £400m barrier.



United have been up against it in recent years to comply with the Premier League’s profitability and sustainability rules but had the headroom to invest more heavily in their squad.

Carrick said: “We went into the window wanting to come out stronger from the group that we had last season, and we’ve definitely added to that.

“I think we’ve done a lot of good work in that respect. The situation is what it is, in terms of finances and what we can work with and what we’re trying to get the most of.

“Certainly, the players that we’ve brought into the group, I’m delighted with, absolutely delighted with.

“I think we’ve done some really good business there for the quality and the level of player that we’ve got. I’m really, really happy with that.

“You can always look at it and there are other things you can do or possibly could have done. Some things become available, some don’t. That’s just part of evolving the group and trying to push all the time.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

“We obviously had certain things that we needed to fill and try and improve the group. Largely, I think we’re in a good place.

“We’ve got pretty good balance within the whole squad. Dynamics, strengths, what we might need in certain games.

“So, we’ve got players that are flexible as well throughout the whole team that can play in different positions as and when and if we need it.

“As you go through a season, you always need that. So, largely pretty happy.”

When pressed on the “financial situation” comment, Carrick replied: “I didn’t say restrictions. It’s the situation we have.



“Whatever the amount is, we want to make the most of it. For what we’ve spent we’ve made the most of it, without a shadow of a doubt.

“I only focus on ourselves and what we can do and maximising what we can do.

“What squad is ever perfect? You always have to find ways of adapting, when you’re building and going through a period when we’re trying to get to the top, you have to make steps.



“It’s not going to be one hit. It’s the whole thing, improving as a group, as a squad. It’s not an instant fix.

“There’s a whole road we have to go down with that and make sure we keep improving. There’s always things that we’re looking at and trying to improve.”

First-choice left back Luke Shaw, 31, has entered the final year of his contract and although he started every Premier League game last season, he has been historically injury-prone.

Dorgu, 21, joined United in February 2025 from Lecce, where he played at left back but his four starts under Carrick have come on the left wing.

The Denmark international missed more than three months last season under Carrick due to a hamstring injury and was dropped after the opening weekend defeat at Hull.



Carrick still believes Dorgu has brought a freshness to the United squad even though he has been at the club for nearly two years.

Carrick said of Dorgu’s left back credentials. “He can certainly play there, He has done, without doubt.

“I’m not sitting here saying he can’t do that. It’s just the way we’ve been since I’ve been here.



“He actually has been injured unfortunately for some time. He played three or four times for us last season.

“So, for me, he’s almost like a new player, you know, to have, and it’s almost like a new signing in some ways because he’s added so much to the group.

“He’s played off the right for Denmark, scored a great goal in the summer playing off the right in a forward position.

“He can play left back. He’s that type where he can do a number of things.

“I’m certainly not saying he can’t do that at all. It’s something he can, we just haven’t had to explore that.



“At some point we might have to, at some point he might do that. He can do that, absolutely no problem.

“There’s times in training when he does it. And then he’s only young.

“Being such a young age and having the attributes that he’s got, we’ve just got to keep trying to get the most out of him.”

Sports.title: Hearn: Talks 'reopened' for Fury vs AJ at Wembley
Sports.content:
Promoter Eddie Hearn has announced that talks have "reopened" to stage the Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua fight at Wembley Stadium.

Negotiations for the Fury vs Joshua fight had hit a major stumbling block after Madison Square Garden in New York emerged as the preferred venue to stage the blockbuster bout.

But Hearn has released a statement on social media, revealing that Wembley is again being considered as the venue for the fight.

He wrote: "I want to thank everyone for the unbelievable support!"

"You have been heard and talks have now re-opened for Wembley.

"Let's make history with one of the biggest sporting moments (British flag) has ever seen."

Sky Sports has contacted Fury's promoter Frank Warren for a response.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Tyson Fury took to his Instagram to call out Anthony Joshua for stalling his fight, claiming that he will fight anywhere and that AJ doesn't really want to fight. Credit: @tysonfury.

Fury had taken to social media earlier this week to label Joshua a "coward" while insisting he had been "conning" boxing fans amid the continued hold up.

Mayor of London Sadiq Khan has meanwhile urged Fury and Joshua's promoters to "get the fight to London".

"I understand the temptation of going to Madison Square Garden," Khan told Sky Sports News. "I understand the temptation of the money and offer, but the fans are here.

"We've been loyal to Tyson and to Anthony. We love them both, and we'd love to see them boxing here in London.

"I'm positive Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua know how much we love both of them. I'm not sure how much the promoters know how much we love both of them, but my message to the promoters is why don't you do what Tyson and Anthony want, which is get the fight in London.

"We'll get 100,000 people watching them live, plus millions watching across the globe fighting amongst the fans who've loved them from the beginning."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Mayor of London Sadiq Khan has called for Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury to fight in London.

Khan also revealed he had been in direct contact with Joshua's promoter Eddie Hearn, saying the Matchroom chairman had approached him for help with organising the fight:

"We've hosted some of the biggest boxing events in history in London during my mayoralty.

"Many British fans are fans of Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua. Many Londoners love both Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua. Both Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua recognise the importance of British boxing fans.

"The promoters know we're here to help. We've approached those in the know to say we're here to help.

"Eddie Hearn has approached us and we're keen to work with Eddie and the team."

Joshua is coming off a second-round knockout victory over Kristian Prenga in July, during which he was notably floored twice in the first round.

Fury also last fought in July when he took on Mariusz Wach, with the 46-year-old retiring in the seventh round.

Sports.title: Arrow gets emotional farewell on 100th Rabbitohs appearance after MND diagnosis
Sports.content:
Jai Arrow retired from rugby league in May following an MND diagnosis; NRL gave South Sydney Rabbitohs special dispensation to include Arrow in their squad and feature as an extra player for the last two matches of the regular season, allowing him to pass 100 appearances for the club

South Sydney Rabbitohs player Jai Arrow receives an emotional welcome as he leads out the side for the last time after his MND diagnosis

Jai Arrow made an emotional 100th NRL appearance for the South Sydney Rabbitohs to mark his farewell from the sport, following his Motor Neurone Disease diagnosis.

Special dispensation had been granted by the NRL and Rabbitohs to allow Arrow the opportunity to take to the field for the opening kick-off another two times, with the game against Sydney Roosters marking a century of appearances.

Arrow walked his team out onto the field for the Sydney derby, with 'Stand By Me' playing before 'You'll Never Walk Alone' then rang around the Allianz Stadium.

Image: Arrow (left) received a standing ovation as he entered the field

The 31-year-old forward had made 178 appearances overall in the NRL before his retirement announcement earlier his year, playing at Brisbane Broncos and then Gold Coast Titans ahead of joining the Rabbitohs in 2021.

Arrow, also having featured 12 times for Queensland in State of Origin, fought back tears as he was presented to the crowd, who all stood in applause, many holding up banners of support in his name.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Arrow was also welcomed onto the field ahead of last week's match against former club Gold Coast Titans

Ahead of kick-off, Arrow waved to the crowd before being embraced by his team-mates and then substituted off, with the Rabbitohs having been allowed an extra player in their squad list and an additional rotation.

Rabbitohs head coach Wayne Bennett offered out his arms to Arrow, who was overcome with emotion and could not hold back his tears before sharing an embrace with his wife Berina Colakovic.

Sports.title: Arsenal’s ever-improving defence meets one that got away in Rogers
Sports.content:
Welcome to The Radar, a Sky Sports column in which Nick Wright uses a blend of data and opinion to shed light on need-to-know Premier League stories. This week:

🔺 Arsenal's defence still getting stronger?

🔺 Rogers making instant Chelsea impact

🔺 Hull's unsung hero in defence

🔺A player to watch this weekend

Arsenal's ever-improving defence

Sunday's game at the Emirates Stadium pits the Premier League's best defence this season against its best attack. While Arsenal are yet to concede a goal, picking up where they left off in May, Chelsea have top-scored with seven in two games.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Take a look back at when Mikel Arteta and Xabi Alonso faced off as players

Arsenal are not the only side to have kept back-to-back clean sheets. Hull have defied expectations to do the same. But while Hull have needed their goalkeeper Konstantinos Tzolakis to be at his best, Arsenal's David Raya has mostly been a bystander.

A Jack Rudoni header remains his only shot on target faced. Raya played a huge part in last season's success, of course. But Arsenal retain an extraordinary capacity to supress chances.

Since the start of last term in the Premier League, they have allowed under 0.50 expected goals in 20 out of 40 games, a figure which includes their first two games of the new campaign.
