No other side even gets close to their total, with Liverpool next on the list on eight. Last season's runners-up Manchester City have only managed it twice. Chelsea are only just ahead of them on four.

Arsenal fans are justifiably lamenting the club's failure to strengthen their attack in the transfer window. But the numbers highlight the gulf between them and the rest out of possession.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player David Ornstein discusses Arsenal missing out on Morgan Rogers, Julian Alvarez and Vinicius Junior

It speaks to the standards they have set as a collective, too, that the absence of their best defender, William Saliba, not to mention another starter in Jurrien Timber, has barely even registered during the opening weeks of the new season.

The club have of course invested heavily to provide cover. But Ezri Konsa's playing time so far amounts to only 11 minutes, with Cristhian Mosquera deputising ably alongside Gabriel at centre-back, and Ben White stepping in at right-back.

There is added depth and steel in midfield, too, thanks to the signing of Bruno Guimaraes. But, like Konsa, he has been eased in.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch the best moments from Bruno Guimaraes' debut

The key to Arsenal's defensive excellence lies instead in the strength of the tactical foundations put in place by Mikel Arteta. Consider the fact that, before the opening two games of this season, the back four of White, Mosquera, Gabriel and Riccardo Calafiori had never previously started a Premier League fixture together.

Arsenal's solidity provides cause for optimism for the fight that lies ahead to retain their Premier League crown, even as they face their toughest test yet against free-scoring Chelsea.

Instant impact from Rogers

The visit of Xabi Alonso's side will give Arsenal a glimpse of what have been at the other end of the pitch. Before their fruitless attempts to land Vinicius Junior and Julian Alvarez, there was the unsuccessful pursuit of Morgan Rogers, who opted for Chelsea.

Watching him in their 4-3 win over Brighton on Sunday from the press box at Stamford Bridge, a few rows behind the dugouts, almost at ground level, was a first-hand reminder of the devastating power and incisiveness that made him so coveted.

Image: Morgan Rogers has played off the left in his first two Chelsea games

Operating from the left, in precisely the position in which Arsenal have seemingly left themselves light, he drove past two Brighton defenders to set up Chelsea's second goal, then produced the turn and through-ball to launch the break for their third.

Those moments highlighted his technical and physical prowess and there were plenty of others to catch the eye, as there were in Chelsea's opening game against Fulham. Many felt Chelsea had overpaid at £117m. He looks determined to prove otherwise.

Image: Rogers ranks second for shots and chances created combined

Rogers already has a goal and an assist, while only Manchester United's Bruno Fernandes has a higher combined total of shots and chances created across the opening two games.

It is no surprise to see Cole Palmer and Joao Pedro, the other two members of Chelsea's front three, next on the list. Their challenge now is to produce the same level of threat against a stronger foe. Rogers, Arsenal's one that got away, may feel added motivation.

Egan showing his worth

Back to Hull's defensive record and while Tzolakis has undoubtedly been key, keeping out shots with an xG of 1.92, giving him the best underlying data of any goalkeeper in the Premier League's opening two games, it would be remiss not to mention John Egan.

The 33-year-old centre-back, formerly of Sheffield United, might have felt his Premier League days were over before Hull's unlikely promotion but he was one of six Hull players to sign a new and improved contract this week and he is certainly doing his bit.

Image: Hull's John Egan has made more clearances than any other player

Egan made a remarkable 17 clearances in their win over Manchester United on the opening weekend and followed it up with another 10 against Coventry, putting him on an average of 13 per game and giving him by far the highest total in the division.

It might not be pretty but it is certainly effective. Hull will hope for more of the same when they face Aston Villa on Sunday.

Player Radar: Who else to keep an eye on

Best of luck to Everton's one-man strike force Thierno Barry against Manchester United. The club's sale of Beto and failed moves for Richardson and Folarin Balogun in a nightmarish transfer window have left him as their only option up front. No pressure, son.

Four Premier League games will be shown live on Sky Sports this weekend, starting with Ipswich vs Liverpool on Friday night.

Saturday's action sees Hull host Aston Villa in the evening kick-off, before a Sunday double-header. Everton take on Manchester United at 2pm, followed by Arsenal face Chelsea at 4.30pm.

Manchester United's issues defending corners and the growing (or should that be lengthening?) threat of Ethan Ampadu's long throw went under the microscope in the last column.

Sports.title: Former referees’ boss says Dean ‘in fantasy land’; Richarlison axed; away fans banned from Old Firm games – live
Sports.content:
4m ago 10.56 EDT Arteta also said that Bruno Guimarães and Cristhian Mosquera, who both picked up injuries in Monday’s 1-0 victory at Aston Villa, will be given Saturday’s training session to prove their fitness. Jurrien Timber is close to making his comeback from a groin problem and Arteta revealed he could be involved for the first time since the Champions League final. Share

6m ago 10.53 EDT London Colney calling. Mikel Arteta has been giving his thoughts to the press before Arsenal’s play Chelsea on Sunday. His thoughts are mostly how delighted he is with Arsenal’s squad. The Gunners were linked with Morgan Rogers, Vinícius Júnior and Julián Alvarez over the summer, but none of them arrived. Greek winger Christos Tzolis came in from Club Brugge, but Leandro Trossard, Gabriel Jesus and Gabriel Martinelli all left. Arteta told reporters: double quotation mark I love the players that we have, that is for sure. It is what it is, this is what we have and we already have some very, very good players. Let’s trust them and let’s make sure we are right behind them, and I will do everything we can to help the incredible talent that we have. I don’t know [if failing to secure any of Arsenal’s targets was a missed opportunity]. These are just opinions. The window is closed and I prefer to look at all the incredible things that we have in the squad and not spend any more time on things that are not a part of us right now. That’s it and that’s my main responsibility. Share

23m ago 10.36 EDT Andrew Beasley WSL transfer talking points: three things we learned from the data The Women’s Super League’s summer transfer window has closed before the start of the 2026-27 season. The finances involved are microscopic compared with the £3.4bn that Premier League clubs spent on new players but the data provides three key points of interest: which club has made the biggest improvement to their squad, who is banking on stability, and how the women’s game has outsmarted its male equivalent. Read Andrew Beasley’s full analysis: WSL transfer talking points: three things we learned from the data Read more Share

33m ago 10.26 EDT Hello, me again. Another point of intrigue from Maresca’s press conference, he confirmed that Erling Haaland is among four players named as City captains this season, the striker is joined by Rúben Dias, Marc Guéhi and Gianluigi Donnarumma in the armband squad. That decision sees Maresca go back on his previous statement about having the striker as a captain, back on 11 August: “At Leicester and Chelsea, I had a rule that when we scored, the captain had to come to the bench not to celebrate for instructions but if he scores, then he can celebrate. So if Erling is the captain, we have a problem.” Share

1h ago 10.00 EDT Time to hand you back to Tom Bassam for the next flurry of managerial chat … Share

1h ago 09.55 EDT Back to De Zerbi, who is still refusing to pepper his pre-game quotes with 80s musical references. Instead, he tells the assembled journos that everyone is available to play against Nottingham Forest, aside from James Maddison, who is back in training. Even Mykhailo Mudryk could get a run out, having not played competitively since November 2024. “He’s ready to play 15, 20, 30 minutes,” De Zerbi adds. “I think he’s ready to play part of the game.” Share

1h ago 09.45 EDT I can guarantee none of these Premier League lot gave as good a presser as Southend manager Kieron Dyer delivered yesterday. Allow Instagram content? This article includes content provided by Instagram . We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'. Allow and continue Share Updated at 09.58 EDT

1h ago 09.33 EDT Unai Emery has admitted leaving striker Brian Madjo and new signing Taylor Harwood-Bellis out of Aston Villa’s Champions League squad was a “hard decision”. Teenage striker Madjo suffered an injury setback after impressing in the Uefa Super Cup final, while defender Harwood-Bellis was a deadline-day signing from Southampton – but both will miss out on Villa’s league phase campaign. Another summer signing, Johan Mazambi, is still injured and won’t travel to Hull for their next game; Emery was tight-lipped on whether Leon Goretzka, Ibrahim Mbaye or Harwood-Bellis might feature on Saturday. Share

2h ago 09.28 EDT Tottenham manager Roberto De Zerbi has revealed that Richarlison told him he wanted to leave the club earlier this summer. The striker has been left out of Spurs’ Premier League squad. “He spoke with me at the start of pre-season and his idea was to leave … I only want the players that want to stay here with pride, passion to stay. Then every other problem is not my business, it’s the responsibility of the club. I can’t say anything because I didn’t decide anything. “The message from Richarlison from the beginning of the season was clear and I accepted that,” De Zerbi added. “I don’t know if there is an offer from Turkey. I don’t know if the club has accepted it. I know there was an offer before the end of the transfer market, but [Richarlison] didn’t accept it.” Share

2h ago 09.26 EDT Moyes accepts that Everton have a “real small squad” but is backing fringe and youth players to make the step up. “Ultimately, we didn’t want to lose a lot of the players, but for different reasons that had to happen. They’re all going to have to be able to muck in as we’ve got a real small squad now. “It gives opportunities to some people who have not had them … sometimes you need to be given that chance [to] show what you can do. Let’s see if some of them can do that. I have no concerns. I am sure they will be fully at it.” Share

2h ago 09.24 EDT Moyes is magnanimous about the failure of Folarin Balogun’s deadline-day move, saying: “It wasn’t anyone’s fault. The player had a problem in his medical, and that was simply it.” The Everton manager also accepts that business may have been limited by the decision not to sell Harrison Armstrong to Forest. “I don’t do the financials, but I think that’s right. We were looking to get some money in. We didn’t want to lose Iliman Ndiaye, but it’s difficult when City come looking for your players.” Share

2h ago 09.21 EDT Here’s David Moyes on Everton’s frustrating end to the transfer window. “Disappointed we didn’t do more business and things didn’t go our way in the end. Sometimes in football you have to live with disappointment and we will move on.” Share

2h ago 09.04 EDT No away fans at Old Firm games this season Celtic and Rangers fans will not be present in each other’s grounds for the rest of the season. The absence of away allocations has been announced by the SPFL after Celtic challenged Rangers’ decision to give them just 300 tickets for the Premier Sports Cup tie at Ibrox on 13 September. Rangers cut the allocation from the recently-agreed total of about 2,500 seats in response to the trouble that marred the Scottish Cup quarter-final clash between the Glasgow rivals in March, when Celtic were given the traditional allocation of about 8,000 under competition rules. An SPFL statement read: “After further discussions involving both clubs, agreement has been reached that there will be no away supporters for matches involving Rangers and Celtic in SPFL competitions for the remainder of the 2026-27 season. “All parties have committed to working constructively during this period, with safety and security remaining the priority. The position will remain subject to review should circumstances materially change during the season.” Press Association Share

2h ago 08.59 EDT More from Xabi Alonso, who says he’ll make a decision “tomorrow” on whether Moisés Caicedo can be involved against Arsenal on Sunday. Chelsea stole a march on the Gunners to sign Morgan Rogers, a signing that delighted their new manager. “For sure, Morgan was a big, big one to get a player of his stature in the present and future. He will be a key player for the next six, seven years. He’s had a great impact.” Share

2h ago 08.51 EDT Next to Chelsea, where Xabi Alonso gives his view on Enzo Fernández’s departure. “We take all the decisions together. We work together with big ones, small ones. We knew ultimately the goal is to have the best for the team. We want to build a good spirit, a good team.” “In football many things happen. With Enzo, we have had conversations and always with respect. What he has done for the club has been great, but now it’s time to move forward. We have players with quality in every position and now we are ready to go.” Share

2h ago 08.47 EDT Now we cross Manchester to hear from Michael Carrick on Manchester United’s transfer business. “We went into the window wanting to come out stronger [than] last season and we have definitely added to that. Certainly the players we have brought in [I’m] absolutely delighted with, think we have done some really good business. “You can always look at it and think there are other things we could have done or might have don … Largely, I think we are in a good place with the squad, we have players that are flexible throughout the team.” Share

2h ago 08.39 EDT Enzo Maresca says his namesake, new City recruit Enzo Fernández, should be part of the squad for their home game against Coventry. Fernández will also be part of the “captaincy group” at the Etihad, along with Erling Haaland and Ruben Días, who has worn the armband in City’s opening two Premier League games. Share Updated at 08.42 EDT

3h ago 08.06 EDT We’ll hear from Alvaro Arbeloa shortly, before eight news conferences at the same time (1.30pm BST), so many big hitters. Arteta, Alonso, Maresca, Emery, Carrick, Moyes, De Zerbi … Andrews. Share

3h ago 07.59 EDT Some more from Frank Lampard. “Do I have affection for Manchester City? Yes. I had a fantastic year there and it is a fantastic football club. I am very happy to go back to a place where I have a good feeling. It will be a big challenge for us, but also a good challenge to see what we can do.” Share Updated at 08.41 EDT

4h ago 07.09 EDT My time is up on the blog for now, up next is Niall McVeigh. Share

4h ago 07.01 EDT Frank Lampard says his Coventry side will have to get used to that losing feeling this season. The Sky Blues have endured a tough return to the Premier League with back-to-back losses against Arsenal and Hull and things do not get any easier this weekend as they travel to Manchester City. Speaking ahead of Coventry’s trip to his former club, Lampard has warned his players they need to pick themselves up after defeats: double quotation mark I think we all know that it will not look like last season, and the quicker we realise that the better, because last season was an incredible season for us because we won a lot and everything becomes easier in that moment. So it’s important that we understand the rigours of the Premier League, how it may feel different and that mindset has to be clear on that to be able to get up after a difficult result like Hull in whatever way or shape it may come. We train well through the week, prepare for the next one. Share

4h ago 06.49 EDT Crystal Palace are still searching for their first point under Pierre Sage, but the new man in charge does at least still have Adam Wharton to call on after another deadlne day passed without the midfielder leaving. Sage described Wharton as “really smart” for prolonging his career at Selhurst Park after Palace rejected offers from clubs in England and around Europe for the 22-year-old. Ahead of Saturday’s derby against Fulham at Craven Cottage, Sage said: double quotation mark The club was strong with his situation and the player is completely in line with that. He never spoke with me about a possible departure, that’s why I think he is in a project to manage his career and he is really smart to do it like this. He did the job every day without a bad mindset and that’s why I understood quickly he wanted to stay and prepare his future with us. He is really smart to stay one more year and maybe more, because he has 10 years (playing) after that. Share

4h ago 06.43 EDT Women's Champions League draw There are three English clubs in the competition this year. Here’s who the WSL sides got in this morning’s draw in Switzerland: Arsenal: Lyon (h), Barcelona (a), Benfica (h), Paris FC (a) HB Koge (h), Inter Milan (a). Chelsea: Paris Saint-Germain (h), Lyon (a), Roma (h), Hacken (a), Austria Wien (h), OH Leuven (a). Manchester City: Paris Saint-Germain (h), Bayern Munich (a), Real Madrid (h), Hacken (a), Austria Wien (h), Inter Milan (A). Share Updated at 06.51 EDT

5h ago 06.17 EDT There are a few interesting tidbits from the English club squads submitted to Uefa for the Champions League. Federico Chiesa and Wataru Endo have been left off Liverpool’s list, while Unai Emery’s 23-man Aston Villa squad does not feature new signings Taylor Harwood-Bellis and Modou Kéba Cissé. Teenage striker Brian Madjo, who scored against Paris Saint-Germain in the Super Cup but is currently injured, also misses out. William Saliba has been included in Arsenal’s squad, despite being sidelined. While Enzo Maresca has put Nico O’Reilly on Manchester City’s ‘B list’ to retain senior slots. The England international is joined in special list for homegrown players by Ryan McAidoo. View image in fullscreen Federico Chiesa has been left off Liverpool’s Champions League squad list. Photograph: Kamil Krzaczyński/AFP/Getty Images Share Updated at 06.45 EDT

5h ago 05.52 EDT The vibesman cometh… Former Wolves captain Conor Coady is part of a refreshed support team for England Under-21 boss Lee Carsley. Coady has not officially retired after he leaving Wrexham earlier this month, but is still without a club. He will join Carsley’s coaching set-up for the European Championship qualifiers with Kazakhstan, Slovakia and the Republic of Ireland over the next month. Paul Williams will also be part of the England Under-21 backroom staff after holding a number of roles within the FA. The duo will help fill the void of Ashley Cole, who left Carsley’s team earlier in 2026 after a successful five-year spell. Share Updated at 05.53 EDT

5h ago 05.40 EDT It’s been a tough week for Folarin Balogun. Someow a solid but not exceptional striker has become a main character in 2026. The USA striker has been left out of Monaco’s squad for the Conference League amid uncertainty over his future after the collapse of his proposed transfer to Everton this week. Balogun will also miss Monaco’s match at Paris Saint-Germain in the French league on Friday after being omitted from the group traveling to the capital. Monaco say Balogun is back in group training. He hasn’t featured in any of the team’s four games so far this season. The American striker was close to joining Everton on Tuesday but opted to pull out of a deal because he felt uncomfortable that the English club raised doubts about his health in a medical examination, according to Monaco’s sporting director. Additional reporting courtesy of the Associated Press. Share

5h ago 05.33 EDT Hackett: 'Dean in fantasy land over podcast claims' Mike Dean’s former boss insists the referee would not have been able to play the “games” he claims to have done while officiating. Dean, who refereed in the Premier League until 2022, generated controversy after claiming on the ‘Jamie Vardy’s Having a Party’ podcast he would “joke about” during matches, seeing how long he could go without blowing his whistle or leaving the centre circle. Keith Hackett, Dean’s former boss at Professional Game Match Officials Limited (PGMOL) between 2004 and 2010, insisted he could not have got away with doing so. Hackett wrote on X: “Mike Dean is in fantasy land!! The examination of performances assessors is forensic. When I was boss referee’s performances were forensically examined. Dean on my watch could not have done what he said with the monitoring systems in operation.” Hackett added he was “satisfied [Dean] is talking nonsense” and said: “He clearly has damaged his reputation. The fallout does not help current refs.” Dean has been approached for comment. Press Association Share Updated at 06.45 EDT

The Tigers host Villa on Saturday, Unai Emery’s side having brought in a raft of new faces. 6h ago 05.03 EDT Matt Hughes Broadcasters and governing bodies make tax plea for TV coverage of women’s sport The chief executives of the Football Association, Rugby Football Union and England and Wales Cricket Board have joined forces with leading broadcasters and YouTube in writing to the chancellor requesting tax credits for production companies to help deliver more television coverage of women’s sport. In a letter signed by 25 representatives of the country’s biggest sports and broadcasters, including Sky Sports and ITV, the government is urged to extend to women’s sport production the audio-visual expenditure credit scheme that provides tax relief to independent films and children’s television. The WSL is the second-richest league in women’s sport after National Women’s Soccer League in the US, but faces challenges attracting broadcasters in a congested market. 7h ago 04.16 EDT Barry Glendenning More on Dean’s loose lips from Barry Glendenning in yesterday’s Football Daily: Dean appears to blow the whistle on himself over in-match game claims While Football Daily likes to think we have our finger on the cultural pulse, before this week we were oblivious to the fact that Jamie Vardy has his own podcast. Called Jamie Vardy’s Having a Party, it is a far more sedate affair than the name suggests, given the only episode we have seen features our t1tular hero and his sidekick the comedian Josh James listening to Mike Dean reminisce about his time as a referee. While Football Daily can’t think of any social gathering that wouldn’t be enhanced by the presence of a 61-year-old former match official from the Wirral on its guest list, this isn’t so much a party as an occasionally awkward conversation. Its claim to be “a hilarious look back at Mike’s career at the heart of English football” is as bold as it is false, but what the episode lacks in laughs it has more than made up for in controversy. During the course of the chat, Dean revealed to his hosts that in the pre-VAR era he and his assistants used to keep themselves amused by playing little games within games of top-flight football. “We used to say: ‘Right, we’ll kick off now, right? See how long we can go without blowing a whistle’. Done that a few times in the Premier, before VAR obviously. Went 20-25 minutes without blowing a whistle a few times. Let it go, let it go, let it go.” Dean went on to tell his inquisitors that he also used to see how long he could go without leaving the centre-circle while games were being played around him, claiming that he once set up camp in one for almost 15 minutes. “That was just me joking about,” he honked, promptly eliciting not entirely convincing laughs from a clearly surprised Josh and Jamie. 7h ago 04.11 EDT I thought nonsense and transfers were over for a while, alas. Dean claims he played secret games for a laugh while refereeing matches View image in fullscreen Mike Dean stood down as a referee in 2022. Right, see how long we can go without blowing a whistle,’” he said. “I’ve done that a few times in the Premier League, before VAR obviously – [I] went 20, 25 minutes without blowing a whistle. “I used to do another thing. I used to stand in the centre circle – see how long I could stay in the centre circle before I had to leave. That was just me joking about. I got about 15 minutes once.” Officials within the refereeing organisation, Pro Ref, are understood to be puzzled by the claims, with the suggestion that a referee could stay in the centre circle for 15 minutes without someone noticing, for example, seen as highly improbable. Sports.title: Women’s Super League Q&A: football writer Suzanne Wrack answers your questions now
Sports.content:
2m ago 10.57 EDT That's all, folks! Suzanne Wrack That’s a wrap! Thanks for joining me for this Q&A and hope you enjoy the opening weekend of the new WSL season. If all goes well, it promises to be the most competitive and unpredictable season yet. Hear more from Suzanne on our Women’s Football Weekly podcast and 

13m ago 10.46 EDT How to challenge accusations that women’s football is inferior to men’s? Trentwarrior asks: I spend time trying to rebut misogyny and characterisations of women’s football as inferior to the men’s game. I have quite a few ready and polite responses, most of which boil down to the idea that the games are different, not inferior or superior. Do you have any responses yourself, particularly to the accusation that women’s football is parasitic on the men’s game? double quotation mark Suzanne: Absolutely! History: The women’s game was banned for 50 years when it was drawing big crowds of over 50,000. It was condemned to being played in parks and rugby grounds and that scale fizzled away. In many respects the FA and men’s game owe the women’s game for stamping it down for so long. Agreement: Of course men’s players will be better, be faster, be technically better, because they’ve been trained and conditioned in elite academies and clubs from as young as five years old, sometimes younger. We are only now reaching a stage where a girl can play football for a living without having to work while they do it, but in many cases they still have to study because there aren’t the wages to set you up for life. Meanwhile, only those that make it into the top academies get top environments, coaching and other staff support, and even then it is nowhere near what the boys get. Stick a generation of five-year-old girls in the same academies the boys are in with all the same opportunities and then let’s talk about the technical/quality differences. They are different: The women’s game, if anything, has the potential to be better technically than the men’s. Bold? Yes. Why? Because women players have to compensate for their relative lack of physicality with technical skill. Allow them to develop that side of the game with the same resources, coaching and facilities afford players in the men’s game and you’ll see the full potential of the women’s game, and it could look very different but as exciting in different ways. There’s a few! I have more but running out of time! View image in fullscreen Women’s football has come a long way since Dick Kerrs Ladies from Preston were the top team in the land. ‘The women’s game, if anything, has the potential to be better technically than the men’s’. Photograph: Firebird/Alamy Share Updated at 10.49 EDT

23m ago 10.37 EDT Can women's football culture keep its connection with fans as it grows? double quotation mark IanMH71 asks: I was introduced to women’s football through my daughter some 12 years ago and I/we’ve been avid football (and AWFC) supporters since. Seeing the game grow and develop over the years in terms of attendances, skill levels and improved player welfare, the pessimist in me worries we will lose what is so great about the women’s game and its surrounding culture - that we feel an important part of it. The optimist feels it will merely change. How do you see the culture changing? And how do we avoid the contempt men’s football appears to have for its supporters?



Suzanne: I share your fears, but am hopeful that enough within the women’s game, in the WSL, in the playing group, are as keen to hold onto that relationship with fans. How players interact with fans is obviously having to evolve with more and more fans attending, but I think there is a will across the board to maintain that connection. Of course that could change in the future, particularly as players become more insulated as they earn bigger and bigger wages and become less socially conscious, which they kind of inevitably will do when they don’t have to work or study alongside their football to the same extent they’ve had to until now. Hopefully though, there’s enough people that care deeply about retain the best aspects of the women’s game from the preceding years to push back against a separation developing. Share

36m ago 10.23 EDT Why does Arsenal get the biggest crowds? Rhinog asks: Do you have any insight into why Arsenal - and only Arsenal - are able to draw big crowds? It’d be interesting to see a breakdown of their fanbase: those who are also fans of the men’s team (hardcore/casual); those who are fans of other men’s teams; those with no interest in the men’s game. I’d imagine this is shared with other clubs, but none come close to matching Arsenal. double quotation mark Suzanne: Good question, and something I’ve spent a lot of time thinking about and discussing. I think Arsenal have really benefited from their longevity in women’s football. When I was a kid, at the parades for the men’s double wins in 1998 and 2002, the women’s teams were there on a bus behind them with all their trophies. They were visible and present and Arsenal were proud of them. In that sense, Arsenal have had a head start, because they’ve not had to explain that the women’s team exists or convince fans of the men’s team that the women’s team has value, because the club has always valued it (and I don’t mean financially, I mean more broadly). The women’s historic quadruple-winning team of 2007 is celebrated on the outside of the stadium equally alongside the men’s Invincibles team. Then, I think they’ve done an exceptional job at strategising on building attendances and a vibrant fan base, which has included things like their five-year plan to take them from three WSL games a season at the Emirates to all WSL games at the stadium and their Block by Block campaign, which they have worked on very with closely with the supporters’ club. Every club is on this journey and can reach the same levels but it will take time. Arsenal started a few steps ahead and have done a very good job in recent years at building on that innate love fans of Arsenal as a club have had for the women’s team for quite some time. View image in fullscreen Arsenal women’s team pictured when they were still the ‘Ladies’ – ‘Arsenal have really benefited from their longevity in women’s football’ Photograph: Linda Nylind/The Guardian Share Updated at 10.32 EDT

47m ago 10.13 EDT Which new WSL players will make the biggest impact? ProudHyphenate asks: Which new WSL players do you expect to make the biggest impact this season? I’ve been really impressed by Lisa Baum in pre-season but haven’t closely followed the new arrivals outside of Arsenal. Who are you looking forward to watching? double quotation mark Suzanne: So many teams have done great business. Writing the big WSL preview and going through them team by team really brought home just what a strong summer it’s been for the majority of teams. I agree Lisa Baum is an interesting one. I can’t wait to see how Georgia Stanway does at Arsenal. I’m very excited to see how Kirsty Hanson and Shekiera Martinez do under Martin Ho at Tottenham. Melvine Malard at Chelsea has already looked like a brilliant match in Champions League qualifying and then who isn’t interested in seeing how Alexia Putellas performs on a cold evening in Bromley? View image in fullscreen Kirsty Hanson has joined Spurs from Aston Villa is an exciting prospect this season. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian The WSL returns bigger than ever and with a mouthwatering title race Read more Share

55m ago 10.05 EDT Can London City Lionesses expensive names get results? Bobzzz asks: Can London City Lionesses really succeed in challenging the top four and how long do they have to do it? Money goes a long, long way, but eventually this collection of expensive names will have to produce results. double quotation mark Suzanne: I put in the Guardian’s team preview of London City Lionesses that they are an enigma this season. It’s so hard to predict what they’ll look like when they play this evening or how they’ll cope over the course of the season. Obviously some huge huge names have come in and big money has been spent, but whether Eder Maestre can gel them into a team after such a big turnover is a huge question. They’ve had a full preseason (as has everyone) with no major international women’s tournament this summer, which will help in that regard, but in the past teams that have embarked on big squad overhauls after promising seasons have gone on to struggle (in particular Everton and Aston Villa a few seasons ago spring to mind). The players they have brought in are also from lots of different teams and leagues with different styles of football and bringing them together stylistically will be a challenge. That said, there is so much individual quality in many of their players that that could help offset those issues while they iron them out. Either way, it’s going to be hugely exciting to watch their style and season unfold and how patient Michelle Kang and the rest of the club’s hierarchy are with Maestre given the big task ahead of him. View image in fullscreen With huge signings such as Mary Earps and Alexia Putellas (pictured) London City Lionesses ‘are an enigma this season’ Photograph: Catherine Ivill/AMA/Getty Images Women’s Super League 2026-27 preview No 10: London City Lionesses Read more Share

1h ago 09.54 EDT Is there a WSL highlights show? sanbikinoraion asks: Is *anyone* producing a highlights show that I can show my kids every week that ties everything together? YouTube highlights of matches are one thing but having it all together in context and wrapped up with the league table at the end was actually a really good way of getting my children interested. I know there’s the Guardian’s WFW podcast (and me and the football playing girls of the house listen to that on the way to training on Wednesdays!) but that’s not at all visual. double quotation mark Suzanne: Afraid there’s not a like for like replacement. Highlights of matches will continue to be put on YouTube by the WSL. It’s also understood that the BBC has given assurances that they are enhancing their women’s football coverage across their live matches and different BBC platforms. So, I think it’s a bit of a wait and see on what that looks like and how successful it is. The good news is that all matches from the WSL and WSL2 will be broadcast somewhere. Personally, I’m not against experimentation, but like you would like some sort of highlights package with analysis so I’m curious to see what delivery of that type of content looks like and how easy it is to find. If the new things work, great, if they don’t, hopefully things are tweaked for next season. Share Updated at 10.07 EDT

1h ago 09.52 EDT Should clubs’ academy teams play in the third tier? tyroneshoelaces asks: What is your view on the decision to allow clubs’ academy teams to play in the third tier? I see it as very retrograde and against the spirit of competition. double quotation mark Suzanne: Great question. Personally, I’m in two minds about it and still easily swayable on it until I delve a little deeper. On the one hand, I think it’s awful for Women’s National League teams to have their leagues potentially dominated by academy teams of top clubs, particularly when so many players are working part-time or fulltime alongside playing at that level. It also drains the loan pool of the best young talents that teams in the WSL2 in particular benefit from. That said, there are also fewer and fewer opportunities for young players that have come through the academies at top clubs to get competitive minutes. It wasn’t that long ago that a decent young player could end up starting for the first team at 15 or 16, but with the development of the game, the small maximum squad size and the increase in international players coming into the league, those opportunities are rarer. In part, that’s because the games are more competitive and there’s not the wiggle room, results wise, to give young players a chance at the top. That’s not totally a bad thing either, it’s a good thing that the game has developed to a point where it’s professional, you can play into your 30s and young players have more time to be developed before they are thrust in and overplayed. Basically, something needs to be done to get young players more minutes and improve academy games, but I’m unconvinced this is the solution. Share

1h ago 09.37 EDT Who are the main WSL2 challengers? Forzasmudge asks: Who do you see as being the main challengers from WSL2 this season? double quotation mark Suzanne: It’s hard to look past the side relegated from the WSL, Leicester City, and Bristol City and Newcastle, particularly with Bristol City now owned by Mercury 13 and Newcastle’s investment in the women’s team following the club’s takeover by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund. Other teams will likely struggle to keep pace with Leicester, who know what it takes to compete in the WSL and Bristol and Newcastle financially, as they invest season on season. Southampton, who finished fifth before Bristol City last season, with the top three teams all being promoted as the WSL expanded to 14 teams, will also fancy they can mount an outside challenge. I’m very curious to see how newcomers Watford and Wolves do and whether Durham, as an independent women’s team, which almost folded towards the end of last year before a new investor was found, can hang in there in the fully professional era of the WSL2. Women’s Super League 2 predictions: can Newcastle reach promotion and will Watford stay up? Read more Share Updated at 10.15 EDT

1h ago 09.30 EDT Will anything short of a trophy be failure for Arsenal? Bobzzz asks: What is the minimum Arsenal expect from this season? With the heavily refreshed squad, investment, and the largest fan base in the women’s game, surely anything short of a trophy would feel a failure? double quotation mark Suzanne: I agree, anything less than a trophy will feel like a failure. There is always the possibility for mitigating factors, a colossal injury crisis such as the one they faced a few years ago, would change expectations. However, as you say, the top-level new recruits, the investment in the team and wider set up around them, the lack of League Cup games stretching them thin, having secured automatic qualification the Champions League league phase, a proper summer off for international players and a full pre-season, are all the ingredients needed for the club to challenge on all fronts. They desperately want to win the league, having not lifted the WSL trophy since 2019, and they cannot afford the slow starts they had in the last two seasons that ruled them out before the campaign really got going. View image in fullscreen Arsenal Women’s bus after winning FIFA Women's Champions Cup 2026. ‘They desperately want to win the league having not lifted the WSL trophy since 2019’. Photograph: Avpics/Alamy Share Updated at 10.43 EDT

2h ago 09.28 EDT Any update on female players and ACL injuries? dfic1999 asks: What’s the latest evidence re female players and ACL injuries? double quotation mark Suzanne: I’m not totally up to date on the latest research, though it’s on my to-do list to revisit some time soon in detail, but Fifpro (the global players’ union) have just published the first findings of their Project ACL study, which was conducted with 12 WSL sides and looked at the modifiable factors that may contribute to ACL injuries for professional women football players, such as facilities, pitch conditions etc.

Share

2h ago 09.18 EDT Is it a worry that certain clubs seem to have unlimited funds? Noahfence asks: Is it a worry that certain clubs have what looks like unlimited funds? I wouldn’t want the league to resemble other two team leagues. double quotation mark Suzanne: Anything that would lead to an uncompetitive league is a worry. I personally think we’ve not learned enough from the men’s game and the WSL aren’t regulating strongly enough on club finances, but I know there’s a balance to be struck between wanting to allow investment of those committed to women’s football and setting up the long-term success, sustainability and competitiveness of clubs and the leagues that doesn’t negatively impact on the pyramid. I’d like to see a completely different financial structuring of women’s football with those things at the very centre of the discussion and decisions but I think we’re a world away from the type of radical plans that I would like to see. The good thing is that while Arsenal and Chelsea, and maybe now London City Lionesses, are spending most heavily, other teams are upping their expenditure too and there is a level of competitiveness that will be maintained if they continue to do so, but that’s not guaranteed or a long-term strategy that can be relied on. Share Updated at 09.22 EDT

2h ago 09.11 EDT Favourite player: Carpenter or Fowler? Weekender73 asks: Daughter’s favourite player: Ellie Carpenter. Mine: Mary Fowler. Who is right? double quotation mark Suzanne: Both. Who am I to say who an individual’s favourite player should be? It’s personal, and mine would probably be different - no I’m not saying who, probably because I’m not totally sure! They’re both top players, Ellie Carpenter has looked rampant in Chelsea’s two games against Real Sociedad in the last two weeks and both looked excellent last season when they featured. Hopefully Mary Fowler has an injury-free season back at her best following her recovery from her ACL injury. View image in fullscreen Ellie Carpenter looked ‘rampant’ in Chelsea’s two games against Real Sociedad in the last two weeks. Photograph: Gari Garaialde/Getty Images Share

2h ago 09.07 EDT Do the top three City, Chelsea and Arsenal face a challenge this season? Challengingviews asks: Would the real test of competitiveness this season be if the clubs from fourth to ninth can get results against the top three? For too many years City and Chelsea and Arsenal have only really had to worry about each other. double quotation mark Suzanne: This is what I think is really exciting this season. Each year, while you haven’t necessarily been able to predict exactly which of Arsenal, City or Chelsea will win the title, you could predict that the only points they would drop would be against each other, at least 99% of the time. This season, I think the likelihood of those teams dropping points to some of those in the chasing pack on a more frequent basis is much higher. We saw Brighton, Tottenham, London City Lionesses, Aston Villa, Liverpool and Manchester United all take points off the top three across the course of last season and I think that trend will continue. How the top three handle that and how those challenging for the ‘best of the rest’ mantle capitalise is going to be super interesting. Share Updated at 09.08 EDT

2h ago 08.54 EDT Can Man City retain their WSL title and win the Champions League? Paula2026 asks: After finally winning the WSL again last season, do you think City have built a squad capable of not only retaining the title but seriously challenging the Champions League – and where do you think they’re still vulnerable? Amoody51 asks: Why are Man City in Pot 3 for the Champions League? Feel bad for Bayern... double quotation mark Suzanne: I’ve predicted City to retain their title, though don’t get too excited as my predictions are notoriously bad. A lot think having Champions League football will stretch the squad but I think City have the depth to cope. The change to the League Cup, meaning UWCL teams will not take part, also alleviates the issue a little, while obviously the UWCL matches are few levels up from the League Cup intensity wise. Where are City vulnerable? I think an injury to any more key players beyond Miedema could cause problems, particularly to Bunny Shaw, Alex Greenwood or Lauren Hemp. For me, the centre-back options are a little lacking, particularly with Jade Rose out. City are in Pot 3 of the Champions League draw because their Uefa coefficient isn’t high enough. They weren’t in European competition last season and while they reached the quarter-final stage the preceding year, they failed to qualify for the 2023-24 edition and failed to escape the qualifying rounds in the two years prior to that. The good news is that despite being in Pot 3, the draw has been pretty kind to them. Arsenal arguably have a tougher draw from Pot 1. View image in fullscreen ‘An injury to any more key players beyond Miedema could cause problems, particularly to Bunny Shaw (pictured), Alex Greenwood or Lauren Hemp.’ Photograph: Paul Childs/Action Images/Reuters Share

2h ago 08.46 EDT Is Brighton's new manager a quick fix? Yorlow asks: Do you think the Brighton hierarchy see their new manager as the right coach for long term success or more of a quick fix to Dario’s departure? double quotation mark Suzanne: I think both. Dario Vidosic’s exit was a shock to everyone but the speed of the announcement of Arturo Ruiz’s appointment showed the club clearly had a little bit of advance notice. A big problem will have been the availability of top-rated managers with the WSL season on the eve of kicking off and many other European leagues having already gotten underway. Ruiz’s decision to switch to the WSL in between Real Sociedad’s two-legged UWCL qualifier against Chelsea and just before their domestic season got underway, shows what WSL sides can offer and the draw of the English league. Would he have been first choice if Vidosic had gone sooner? Hard to say. However, on the basis of his first press conference Ruiz has impressed and Real Sociedad looked very well organised against Chelsea despite their 6-2 aggregate defeat, so they may be landing on their feet with his appointment. Time will tell. View image in fullscreen Arturo Ruiz’s decision to switch from Real Sociedad to Brighton just before their domestic season got underway shows the draw of the WSL. Photograph: Europa Press Sports/Europa Press/Getty Images Share

2h ago 08.38 EDT Is coverage going backwards? FrankfurtView asks: The BBC have removed their Women’s football show from linear television. Already it was being shown in a broom cupboard, later than Match of the Day … Have BBC gone backwards in women’s football coverage? double quotation mark Suzanne: Their approach to coverage is changing across sport more widely. There seems to be a drive towards social platforms, as shown by the launch of their women’s football Youtube channel and expansion of their content on their TikTok account. Whether that strategy will drive audiences will show over time. The loss of the Women’s Football Show is a big one, in my view. It needed a better slot and greater investment but it provided fans with the most accessible week-by-week analysis with clips and highlights and it will be interesting to see whether the new 15-minute Women’s Football Fallout will be able to deliver enough depth for fans wanting game-by-game analysis. Share

2h ago 08.31 EDT Can Manchester United surprise ? Laughable asks: Do you think Manchester United can surprise people? How far can good tactics, high motivation and an attacking strategy take them? I think there will be new signings that fit Eva Olid’s style of play in the January window and that they will they do quite well this season and perhaps break into the top three within three years. Am I wrong? double quotation mark Suzanne: Interestingly, I did a profile of new manager Eva Olid when Hearts, the team she left in the summer after leading the Scottish side to the SWPL title, had five games of the season remaining. Having known nothing about her I got an incredible impression from the various interviews I read with her about her coaching philosophy and her time coaching boys in Spain and managing in the women’s game. My fear is that United won’t give her the resources required to punch as high above their financial weight as they will need to be doing to be competitive in the WSL. Yes, she worked wonders at Hearts, having arrived with the team having finished at the bottom of the league (only avoiding relegation thanks to the expansion of the SWPL), but Hearts did increase their support for the women’s team alongside her shrewd coaching and player development during her five years. Arguably, their transfer window was one of the most disappointing of all the WSL teams this season. Their four signings are promising, but they see some high-level WSL experience leave in their seven outgoing players. They will benefit from no Champions League football, but I don’t think they have the squad to be able to ‘do a Man City’ and take advantage of that significantly in the league, not when so many mid-table teams have looked to have strengthened really well. I hope I’m wrong, I would love to see United do well and Olid be really successful there, but without a greater commitment from the club from the top down, not just financially, I struggle to see much to be excited about. The League Cup is a great opportunity for silverware though, with no City, Arsenal or Chelsea involved, but others will be sensing that opportunity too. View image in fullscreen During Eva Olid’s five years at Hearts, the team saw increased support alongside her shrewd coaching and player development but Manchester United management needs to make a greater commitment. Photograph: Zuma Press/Alamy Leaving present? Eva Olid takes Hearts Women within sight of historic title Read more Share Updated at 08.48 EDT

3h ago 08.21 EDT Will failing to cover Miedama come back to bite Man City? trinder19 asks: How much will City’s failure to sign an attacking midfielder to cover for Miedama cost them? Benítez would have been quite the coup and they should try again for her next time. My view is that just about any side would miss Miedema’s intelligence and ability but if there’s one thing City have an abundance of, it’s attackers. Her absence will give Beney and Fowler a chance to shine in that central role, and of course Mead can play there too. double quotation mark Suzanne: Losing Vivianne Miedema is of course a huge blow for any length of time and I think her absence towards the end of last season coinciding with City’s slight faltering and lack of rhythm wasn’t a coincidence. As you say, you could view City’s lack of action in that area in the transfer window, bar the late attempt to Fiamma Benítez as costly, or you can view it as an opportunity for the likes of Mary Fowler or Iman Beney to step up and really make that position their own. Is that a risk or not getting Benítez a blow? Maybe, but I think I personally prefer players being given a chance rather than cautious clubs recruiting and blocking the route to starting games for those younger talents. However, if City didn’t think Fowler or Beney or anything else is ready for that role and they really wanted Benítez then they should have gone harder for her much much sooner, because Miedema’s injuries issues haven’t been a secret in recent years. View image in fullscreen Losing Vivianne Miedema is of course a huge blow for any length of time. Photograph: Nick Potts/PA Manchester City failed to land Spain pair in scramble for Miedema cover Read more Share

3h ago 08.13 EDT Is Arsenal weaker after letting Mead and McCabe go? FuzzyDunlop1982 asks: Arsenal: weaker or stronger after their big free-transfer spree but having released Beth Mead and Katie McCabe? Suzanne: Beth Mead and Katie McCabe are huge players and personalities to lose, particularly after the excellent seasons they both had last year. Arsenal’s handling of the McCabe situation showed they must feel they may be making a mistake in letting her go. That said, Arsenal’s recruitment has been very strong, Georgia Stanway in particular brings the battling spirit they lose with McCabe’s exit. Are Arsenal stronger? In my view, yes, given the players coming in and a refresh of the group. The biggest regret will be less about letting those two players go, but about where they let them go to (not that they had a huge amount of control over that with the players being free agents and able to join whoever they wanted) because, while Arsenal are stronger, Mead and McCabe strengthen their two main rivals. View image in fullscreen Katie McCabe’s move from Arsenal to rivals Chelsea stunned fans but Arsenal’s recruitment has been ‘very strong’. Sports.title: Nottingham Forest’s Liam Delap: ‘I play at my best on the edge of being horrible’
Sports.content:
“You can imagine it: he’s a centre-back, I’m a striker,” says Liam Delap, Nottingham Forest’s £45m club-record signing, smiling as he sets the scene. He is reliving taking on his younger brother, Finn, in the garden. These days, they are each other’s biggest supporters – Liam attended Finn’s victory for third-tier Burton on Wednesday – but as kids there was a friendly rivalry. The elder brother says: “There were probably a lot of tears, a lot of fights … whether it was playing Monopoly or football, it always ended in either the table being flipped or kicking the shit out of each other.”

It is a competitive streak that has stuck and Delap is determined to make his presence felt at Forest, for whom he could make his full debut against Tottenham on Saturday. It has been a testing 16 months; he left Chelsea a season into a six-year contract and after one goal in 28 top-flight appearances, a dozen of those starts. “It is never a linear path straight to the top,” Delap says, his right hand taking flight in the City Ground boardroom, the 1979 and 1980 European Cups shimmering behind him. “I just want to get my head down, focus and keep improving because I’m still so young and I have so much to learn. I even at times probably think I’ve been in football a lot longer than I have. I’ve still, hopefully, got a long career ahead.

“I think you just have to accept that sometimes things go bad, things happen … it might [prove to] be a good thing, I think. My first loans to Stoke and Preston [from Manchester City, across 2022-23] didn’t really go well at all and it was probably one of the best things that happened because I learnt so much from that season and went to Hull [for 2023-24] and kicked on from there. I’m still young, I’ve still got a lot of learning to do. Sometimes injuries happen, sometimes you don’t play. I don’t think anything is lost … Everyone has rocky moments. I’ve just got to use them to learn and kick on.”

Last summer, Delap was hot property. Oliver Glasner tells a story of Delap having proposals from 18 Premier League clubs and jests that the 23-year-old knows every top-flight manager owing to the various Zoom calls he held while deciding his next move. After all, one of those was with Glasner, then at Crystal Palace. Forest wanted him then, too. “It was a tough decision,” recalls Delap. “I remember the conversation we had, I was really impressed and I thought: ‘This guy [Glasner] is really good.’ He spoke incredibly well and you can see he has done really well with the strikers he has had in the past. That definitely stuck in my mind.”

Glasner wants Delap to play to his strengths: physicality, power and finishing. He doesn’t mean the forward’s hidden talent: cube roots. At the start of the year a clip of Delap showing off his maths skills went viral. “I didn’t enjoy maths one bit but I was always quite good at it. One of my friends taught me in school how to do it and I didn’t forget it. I hated school, [the] work, but I was always quite intelligent.”

The Austrian head coach said it was apparent in conversations with Delap this summer that the player had learnt lessons from a trying year: “I think it shows his attitude and his character that he said: ‘Yeah, I want a team and a club that values my strengths and wants to play to my strengths.’ Because I never want to change a player: it doesn’t make sense to say: ‘OK, now you should play like Messi: false nine, drop into midfield and combine play with one or two touches.”

View image in fullscreen Liam Delap scored once in 28 league appearances for Chelsea. Photograph: Adam Davy/PA

A tally of 12 goals in the Ipswich side relegated in 2024-25 triggered widespread interest. At that point Delap was talked up as a potential heir to Harry Kane as England’s No 9. He has been capped by his country at every age group and was in the same under-16s team as Jude Bellingham. “As a little kid, all you want to do is play for your country,” Delap says. “So, of course, in my mind that’s where I want to get to. But it’s not as easy as that. I have to work hard and improve and that’s all I can do.”

An imposing 6ft 2in striker, Delap has long been viewed as the next big thing. He spearheaded Manchester City to FA Youth Cup victory over Chelsea in 2020, a couple of months after Pep Guardiola handed him his senior City debut aged 17. Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers, now teammates at Chelsea, were part of that same under-18s side, together with the new Aston Villa defender Taylor Harwood-Bellis and James McAtee, one of his best friends and now a clubmate again.

“He was a No 10 and quite often he would give me the ball and we just had that really good relationship off the pitch and it translated on to the pitch,” Delap says of McAtee. “If we didn’t win, we’d all be fuming. It probably instilled that winning mentality into us early. I think it’s worked because you can see from that team that almost everyone is playing somewhere in the Premier League, abroad, the Championship and that is probably because we pushed each other so much.”
