Gunnun said the restrictions were particularly difficult for traders dealing in perishable goods such as bananas, apples and watermelons, which can spoil quickly if not sold.

“If I don’t sell today, I will get a lot of losses,” she said, adding that many vendors rely on daily sales to support their families and pay school expenses for their children.

According to Gunnun, traders believe the measures may be linked to activities surrounding a recent presidential visit, during which crowds gathered along the roadway. She said ordinary vendors should not be penalized for events in which they played no part.

“We are all here doing our business,” Gunnun said. “We were not part of the people that were here yesterday.”

She described herself as a single mother who depends on fruit sales to support her daughter and other family members.

The vendors said the sudden loss of their stalls has left them without a source of income and are calling for an opportunity to return to the junction or be provided with an alternative location where they can legally conduct business.

An entrepreneur J.U. Dempster Hennings, said business has been slow and customers had stopped coming to buy this morning since police officers were deployed, creating fear among potential buyers and disrupting normal business activities.

“I have been doing business here for many years and I know the inflow of customers,” Dempster said. “Right now, with the presence of the police, it sends some kind of signal to our customers.”

Dempster said many traders and money exchangers operating in the community depend on daily sales and participate in local savings and credit schemes, commonly known as “susu,” under which members make daily, weekly, or monthly payments.

He said some business owners, including himself, had also taken bank loans to finance their operations.

“Most of the petty traders out there took money from banks,” he said. “Even my very self. I have to pay suppliers today.”

According to Dempster, the demolition of business structures and the removal of traders from their usual locations could immediately affect their ability to generate income and meet repayment obligations.

“With the police presence and the businesses being removed, it will affect their ability to pay their susu and other commitments,” he said, warning that prolonged disruptions could place financial strain on vendors, money exchangers and small business owners who depend on daily transactions.

Dempster said business owners had not been informed of the reasons behind the security operation and appealed for a return to what he described as a conducive business environment.

“We don’t know why the police are here,” he said. “We pray that tomorrow we’ll have a conducive atmosphere for our business.”

Questions Over Timing

Critics of the administration say the sequence of events raises concerns about whether the government’s response was disproportionate.

They argue that if the demolition was part of an existing plan to clear the junction, the government should explain why it occurred immediately after the President was booed at the location.

The controversy also comes against the backdrop of heightened political tensions between the ruling Unity Party and the CDC, particularly following Weah’s return and renewed political activity ahead of the 2029 elections.

For the vendors, however, the political contest is secondary to survival.

They say they should not become casualties of Liberia’s growing political rivalry and are urging President Boakai to intervene before they lose their livelihoods permanently.

World.title: Liberia: South Africa Pledges High-Powered Technical Mission for Liberia’s Peace and Reconciliation Memorial Museum
World.content:
Pretoria— A delegation appointed by H. E. President Joseph Nyuma Boakai, Sr. has successfully concluded the South African phase of its two-country study tour with a major commitment from the South African Government to send a fully funded, high-powered technical, tourism, and cultural delegation to Monrovia at the soonest time. The mission will support Liberia’s efforts to establish the proposed National Peace, Reconciliation and Memorial Museum.

The commitment followed high-level discussions led by Liberia’s Minister of State without Portfolio, Hon. Hadja Mamaka Bility, and South African Minister of Sport, Arts and Culture Gayton McKenzie. Minister McKenzie directed that the mission become the largest delegation ever sent abroad by his department, describing it as a practical demonstration of the historic bond between Liberia and South Africa.

The delegation will include specialists from South Africa’s leading museums, memorial sites, archives, cultural institutions, artifact-repatriation initiatives and the country’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission process. The experts will conduct workshops, share technical knowledge and help Liberia develop credible systems for collecting, preserving and presenting its history without altering the truth of the country’s past.

Minister Bility warmly welcomed the commitment and assured the South African Government of Liberia’s full cooperation. She said the planned visit would coincide with efforts to convene the museum’s inaugural steering committee, allowing both sides to hold several days of intensive technical discussions and begin moving the initiative from concept to implementation under President Joseph Nyuma Boakai’s leadership.

Minister McKenzie described Liberia and South Africa as brother and sister nations whose relationship was strengthened during the anti-apartheid struggle, when Liberia provided refuge and support to South African freedom fighters. He stressed that the upcoming mission would be based on mutual learning. “We are not going there only to teach. We are also going there to learn from the Liberians,” he said.

During its four-day engagement in South Africa, the Liberian delegation met with senior officials responsible for planning, monitoring and evaluation, as well as representatives of the Department of International Relations and Cooperation. The team also met with the leadership of the University of South Africa, (UNISA) where both sides agreed to explore knowledge-sharing, specialized training, and postgraduate opportunities for Liberians in fields connected to museum development, archives, peacebuilding, and reconciliation. The delegation also visited the Nelson Mandela Foundation, Hector Pieterson Museum, UNDP South Africa, Mandela House, Freedom Park, Apartheid Museum, and other key cultural and historical institutions.

UNDP Resident Representative in Liberia, Ambassador Aliou Mamadou Dia, described the outcome as a major boost for Liberia’s museum initiative and reaffirmed UNDP’s commitment to supporting the government. With the Rwanda and South Africa phases of the study tour now successfully completed, Minister Bility and her delegation will return to Liberia to report to President Boakai, consolidate the lessons gathered and begin preparations for the arrival of the South African delegation.

World.title: ⁠’Growth Has to Put Bread On the Table’: Dan Saryee Gives ‘Honest’ View On Liberia’s Economy
World.content:
MONROVIA – A prominent Liberian democracy advocate , policy advisor and former government official, Dan Torkamawon Saryee, has given what he described as his honest view on Liberia’s economy.

Saryee said the Liberian economy is growing, saying that is headline and that is true.

But Saryee pointed out that he has sat with enough farmers, traders and young graduates to know that a growth number doesn’t mean much if it never reaches their pockets.

Saryee, who has been a notable voice in Liberia’s civil society, governance and public administration sectors for over two decades, told the FrontPage Africa(FPA) in an interview in Monrovia Thursday, September 3 that growth only matters if it shows up as jobs, better incomes, less hunger and a better quality of life.

By Augustus D.R Bortue-augustusd.rbortuefrontpageafricaonline.com

The former Deputy Managing Director of the Liberia Water & Sewer Corporation during the regime of former President George Manneh Weah recalled that in 2025 was a strong year on paper, driven largely by mining, with agriculture and services pulling their weight too.

Encouraging, no doubt.

‘‘But ask the average person on the street what matters and the question gets a lot more basic, a lot faster: Where are the jobs? Can I afford food, transportation, rent, school fees, and healthcare,?” he asserted.

That’s really where the conversation should start.

Saryee, who also served as Acting Director General of the Liberia Agricultural Commodity Regulatory Authority (LACRA) in President Joseph Nyuma Boakai’s Administration, noted that, ‘‘we have a real employment problem. Too many Liberians are stuck in informal work — petty trading, subsistence farming, small hustles just to get by. It keeps families afloat. It rarely gets anyone ahead. ’’

According to him, he does not say that to dismiss the market women or the roadside sellers — they’re working harder than most of us.

‘‘The point is that we need an economy where people aren’t just looking for jobs, but where businesses are actually creating jobs,’’ the prominent Liberian democracy advocate and policy advisor stated.

Agriculture should be creating jobs, not just food

Speaking further, Saryee averred that Liberia can’t fix unemployment while still treating agriculture as mostly subsistence farming, stressing ‘‘we should be producing more rice, cassava, and vegetables — more of nearly everything we grow, really — not just to feed ourselves, but to build real businesses around it.’’

‘‘Take cassava. A farmer grows it. Someone else buys it, processes it, package it, moves it, sells it — or finances and equips the people doing all of that. One crop, handled right, can quietly create a dozen jobs along the way.

That’s why we need serious investment in agro-processing, storage, transportation, irrigation, farm-to market roads and agricultural financing. Government has initiated these processes but the need to accelerate is like yesterday. The World Bank has pointed to agro-processing and expanded production as real opportunities for more inclusive growth,’’ Saryee intimated.

Let’s track business growth, not just business registration

The former LACRA boss intoned that Liberia doesn’t just need more businesses — it needs businesses that can actually grow and hire.

‘‘Recent World Bank data found that 86% of firms in the National Establishment Census were micro-sized, and nearly 89% were one-person operations. So, the real question isn’t “how many businesses do we have, it’s: How many grew from one worker to five? From five to twenty? From twenty to a hundred? That’s where the real job creation happens. Government should make it easier for legitimate small businesses to get financing, electricity, land, technology, and markets — and tie that support to results: production, compliance and jobs,’’ Saryee uttered as he expressed the hope that policymakers will consider his view on Liberian economy with constructive lenses if they must change the paradigm shift.

Government can’t be the employer of last resort

‘‘Government has a role. But let’s be honest — the public payroll was never going to be Liberia’s employment strategy, no matter how much we wish it could be. The real job of government is to create the conditions that let private businesses invest, produce and hire: reliable power, better roads, working ports, affordable financing, rules people can actually plan around,’’ he continued.

He said Liberia should also work to cushion food-price shocks by producing more locally and improving storage, transport, and processing — WFP has flagged how much risk our heavy reliance on food imports creates.

Young people need a real path to work

‘‘Our young population is one of our biggest assets — but it turns into a serious problem when people leave school with no realistic way to earn a living. We should be more aggressively expanding practical training — construction, electrical work, plumbing, welding, agribusiness, IT, healthcare support, and a dozen other trades that this country will need for decades,’’ Saryee accentuated.

‘‘But training on its own solves nothing. We can’t train people for jobs that don’t exist. It has to connect directly to employers, apprenticeships, and real projects on the ground — otherwise we’re just handing out certificates,’’ Saryee uttered.

Touching on how to deal with corruption and waste, Saryee said no economic plan works if public resources leak out through corruption, waste, poor procurement and weak accountability.

‘‘Every public dollar should be treated as money that could have built a school, fixed a road, backed a farmer, or helped launch a business. Development runs on trust. Investors need confidence, entrepreneurs need predictability and citizens need to know public resources are actually being used for the public good,’’ Saryee said.

Meanwhile, the prominent Liberian democracy advocate, policy advisor named five things to focus on right now.

1.

2.Feed Liberia — grow local food production and agro-processing.

3.Power businesses — expand reliable, affordable electricity to productive areas.

4.Finance entrepreneurs — make real financing available to businesses that can grow and hire.

5.Build market infrastructure — roads, bridges, storage, ports, electricity, and digital connectivity that link producers to markets.

6.Measure job creation — make jobs, business growth, local production, and household income the actual targets.

What success really looks like

Saryee concluded by saying Liberia shouldn’t judge its economy only by GDP growth, investment headlines or government revenue. He acknowledged that those matter, but they’re not the finish line.

He further noted that the real test is whether an ordinary Liberian can honestly say:

“I can find work.”

“My business can grow.”

“My children can eat.”

“My income is improving.”

“I have hope for tomorrow.”

‘‘We have the land, the young people, the coastline, the agricultural potential — most of what we need is already here. I don’t pretend to have every answer for how we turn that into businesses, jobs, and income. But I know what the wrong answer looks like: waiting.

The goal isn’t just a bigger economy. It’s stronger households. Because at the end of the day, this was never really about statistics. It’s about putting bread on the table,’’ he said.

World.title: Chifwanakeni urges accountants to drive wealth creation
World.content:
The University of Lusaka Vice Chancellor, Professor Pinalo Chifwanakeni, has challenged the new 884 ZICA Graduates accountants to go beyond traditional accounting roles and use their skills to drive wealth creation and national development.

Professor Chifwanakeni said accountants should not limit themselves to bookkeeping, but should become strategic thinkers, entrepreneurs and advisers capable of identifying and exploiting business opportunities.

He was speaking at the 20th Graduation Ceremony of the Zambia Institute of Chartered Accountants at Mulungushi International Conference Centre today.

Professor Chifwanakeni said Zambia is operating in an increasingly complex economic environment characterized by rapid technological change and digital transformation, making it important for professionals to continuously upgrade their skills.

He further challenged ZICA to take advantage of its expertise by developing short courses for newly elected councilors, Members of Parliament and mayors to strengthen accountability and financial management of public resources, including Constituency Development Fund, CDF resources.

The Vice Chancellor has further urged the graduates to uphold ethical standards, saying accountants have a critical responsibility in safeguarding corporate and national resources.

Professor Chifwanakeni also urged the graduates to embrace entrepreneurship and create businesses and employment instead of relying solely on formal employment.

He said the country’s economic growth will depend on professionals who can turn knowledge and qualifications into practical solutions, businesses and lasting wealth.

And Zambia Institute of Chartered Accountants (ZICA) President, Joseph Matimba urged newly qualified accountants to look beyond traditional accounting practices and embrace emerging technologies, particularly artificial intelligence.

Mr Matimba said the accounting profession is changing rapidly due to digital transformation, climate change, evolving governance expectations, and growing demands for transparency and accountability.

World.title: Civil Service Commission extends health workers verification deadline
World.content:
The Civil Service Commission has extended the verification deadline for applicants under the recruitment of 2,600 health workers, from September 11 to October 9, 2026.

Speaking to the Media today, Commission Chairperson Choolwe Beyani said the extension follows concerns raised by applicants over the limited time available for verification, as well as the logistical and financial challenges involved in travelling to Provincial and District Health Offices.

Dr Beyani said verification will continue until October 9 at Provincial Health Offices for medical doctors and pharmacists, while applicants in other health professional categories will verify their details at District Health Offices.

He said the decision is intended to give applicants adequate time to confirm the accuracy and completeness of information submitted during the recruitment process.

Dr Beyani explained that verification covers applicants’ personal details, academic and professional qualifications, positions applied for, professional registration details where applicable, and other supporting documentation.

He said the exercise is also aimed at ensuring that the recruitment database accurately reflects applications received by health authorities.

“The Commission initially scheduled the verification exercise to run from September 1 to 11, 2026, but it commenced on September 2 following the declaration of September 1 as a public holiday for the Presidential Inauguration Ceremony,” added Dr Beyani.

Dr Beyani has further clarified that verification is not mandatory.

He stressed that choosing not to verify will not, in itself, disadvantage an applicant in the recruitment process.

Dr Beyani has urged applicants wishing to verify their details to use the extended period and follow official guidance issued by the Civil Service Commission.

He has since directed Provincial and District Human Resource Officers under the Ministry of Health, to provide applicants with the necessary assistance and guidance during the verification exercise.

World.title: FRA assures against maize spoilage
World.content:
The Food Reserve Agency (FRA) has assured that it has put measures in place to secure maize at its storage facilities and prevent spoilage, in areas where rainfall is expected over the next few days, in the Country.

FRA Head of Corporate Communication, John Chipandwe has told ZANIS in a telephone interview that the Agency distributed materials such as tents and chemicals to its depots around the Country.

Mr Chipandwe has explained that the materials were sent to the depots prior to this year’s crop marketing season, adding that more tents are currently being dispatched to areas where they may be needed.

He has indicated that satellite depots serve as temporary purchasing points, noting that maize bought is then transported to the main depots for safe and long-term storage.

According to the Zambia Meteorological Department, isolated rainfall is expected in some parts of the Country between Friday, September 4th to Monday, September 7th, 2026.

Mr Chipandwe further emphasised that fumigation and other scientific measures are conducted regularly, beginning at satellite depots and continuing through to main holding depots.

“So the stock is safe and all necessary measures are being taken to prevent any spoilage,” he assured.

World.title: Mundubile, Zulu Remain in Mukobeko as Treason Case Proceeds
World.content:
Mundubile, Zulu Remain in Mukobeko as Treason Case Proceeds

National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity presidential candidate Brian Mundubile and his running mate Makebi Zulu remain detained at Mukobeko Maximum Security Prison in Kabwe, facing treason charges that stem from an August 14 security operation at Mundubile’s residence in Lusaka’s Kabulonga suburb.

The operation, during which former cabinet minister Mutotwe Kafwaya was shot dead, has become one of the most closely watched legal proceedings to emerge from Zambia’s disputed August general election. Government has acknowledged responsibility for Kafwaya’s death.

Human Rights Commission Chairperson Dr Pamela Towela Sambo said 18 people, including Mundubile and Zulu, are facing treason charges connected to the Kabulonga raid, alongside Bishop Trevor Mwamba, senior lawyer George Chisanga and businessman Patrick Mwansa.

Security forces reported discovering military-grade equipment, including firearms, at the premises during the operation, along with what officials described as other sophisticated weaponry. The discovery has featured prominently in Government’s public defence of the arrests.

Mundubile and Zulu initially escaped to a United Nations facility in Lusaka, where they remained for several days before being handed over to Government authorities. According to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the handover was facilitated personally by the UN Secretary-General’s Special Envoy, Parfait Onanga-Anyanga, on the basis of assurances that the two leaders’ constitutional rights would be respected throughout the ensuing legal process.

Upon being handed over, the two men were immediately detained and charged with treason. Other individuals connected to the case were taken into lawful custody and held at the same Mukobeko facility.

Prior to surrendering, Mundubile said he and his colleagues were being targeted for opposing poverty, injustice and what he described as shrinking space for free expression in the country.

The case has drawn international attention. United Nations Special Rapporteur Gina Romero described the eleven opposition leaders facing treason charges as “political detainees” and called for their immediate release, prompting a sharp rebuttal from Government, which said the term prejudged matters still before the courts.

Government has separately disputed Romero’s characterisation of treason as a capital offence, noting that Zambia abolished the death penalty under the Penal Code in December 2022 and subsequently removed it from military law as well.

Human rights groups, including the Human Rights Commission, have continued to seek clarification on the welfare of Mwamba, Mwansa, Chisanga and other co-accused persons connected to the case, while continuing to press for their access to legal representation and family visits in accordance with constitutional protections.

Six international observer missions, including the European Union, the Southern African Development Community, the African Union and the Commonwealth, have expressed concern over aspects of the broader post-election environment. EU observers cited intimidation during the electoral process, while SADC noted delays in vote counting and the deployment of security forces as factors that had eroded public confidence.

Zambia has been recognised since 1991 for peaceful transfers of power, a record reaffirmed as recently as 2021. That continuity was tested on August 13, when vote counting was suspended for six hours and the army was deployed in Lusaka, with reports of direct interference in the counting process.

The Mundubile Ecl Movement, chaired by Davies Mwila, has said Mundubile remains the substantive Tonse Alliance leader despite his detention, and has called for the immediate release of Mundubile, Zulu and 18 others unless credible evidence is produced to sustain the charges against them.

The case continues to work its way through the legal process, with the accused entitled under Zambian law to the presumption of innocence, access to legal representation and a fair hearing before an independent court.

World.title: HRC Presses Police, Prosecutors to Charge or Release 84 Election Detainees
World.content:
The Human Rights Commission has urged the Zambia Police Service and the National Prosecution Authority to immediately charge, grant bond to, or release at least 84 people who remain in custody in connection with the August 13 general elections.

HRC Chairperson Dr Pamela Towela Sambo said prolonged detention without a court appearance violates Articles 13 and 18 of the Constitution, as well as international human rights law to which Zambia is a party.

“The commission is monitoring several cases,” Sambo said in a statement issued this week. She cited the case of Alphonso Daka and 42 others arrested on August 14 in Roma Township, Lusaka, who remained in custody at Chelston as of September 1 despite investigations having been concluded.

Sambo also flagged the case of six men arrested in Ng’ombe on August 13, Newton Miti, Joseph Phiri, Collins Kavwali, Kennedy Chimfwembe, Emmanuel Banda and Fredrick Machali, who she said had spent 19 days in custody without formal charge. A seventh man, Enock Roosevelt Tonga, arrested at the National Results Centre on August 17, remained in detention as well.

In Kalabo, 16 people, including musicians known as Chester and Felix Phiri and comedian IDC Light Comedy, were granted bail only after spending an extended period in custody on riotous behaviour charges, according to the Commission.

Sambo said 18 others, including National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity presidential candidate Brian Mundubile and his running mate Makebi Zulu, are facing treason charges following the August 14 arrests in Kabulonga.

The HRC chairperson also raised the case of opposition figure Kennedy Kamba, who she said had been detained for around two weeks after being granted bail, and whose whereabouts were only recently established at Kabwata Police Station.

Sambo rejected suggestions that overcrowded police cells justified continued delays in processing detainees, and called on police to review all outstanding cases, disclose the whereabouts of those held, and ensure access to family members and legal representation.

“…Release all those whose continued detention exposes the risk of ill-treatment, restricts access to legal representation and undermines public confidence,” Sambo said, according to the Commission’s statement.

She said the Commission would continue engaging the National Prosecution Authority to ensure dockets were processed promptly, and would maintain its monitoring of detention facilities across the country.

The 84 cases form part of a wider pattern of arrests and detentions the Commission says it has tracked since the disputed election period, spanning multiple provinces and a range of charges, from riotous behaviour to treason.

Government has separately disputed the characterisation of the post-election period as a “crackdown,” and has rejected the description of those detained as “political detainees,” arguing that the term implies a conclusion about the nature of the charges that has not been established through due process.

The Commission has said its monitoring role is independent of that political dispute, and that its concern centres on constitutional compliance regarding the length and conditions of pre-charge detention, irrespective of the underlying nature of individual cases.

Human rights groups, including the Commission, have separately sought clarification on the welfare of Bishop Trevor Mwamba, businessman Patrick Mwansa, lawyer George Chisanga and other co-accused persons connected to the broader treason proceedings.

The Commission said it would issue further updates as cases progressed through the legal system, and reiterated its call for authorities to ensure that constitutional protections around detention were consistently observed regardless of the political sensitivity of individual cases.

World.title: Court Grants Mukandila Habeas Corpus, Orders State to Justify Detention
World.content:
The Lusaka High Court has granted Tonse/Pamodzi Alliance Secretary General Celestin Mukandila leave to issue a Writ of Habeas Corpus, compelling the State to bring him before the court and explain the basis for his continued detention.

Mukandila was arrested on August 20 and charged with concealing his true national identity and unlawful possession of a National Registration Card. He has denied the allegations and is seeking his immediate release, arguing he has been detained since his arrest without being taken before a court or granted police bond.

According to court documents, the Department of Immigration opposed Mukandila’s application for habeas corpus, citing that he had not produced credible sureties to facilitate his release on police bond.

Principal Immigration Officer Ian Mutamina told the court that Mukandila was arrested on August 20, 2026 and charged with concealing his true national identity and unlawful possession of a National Registration Card. He said all required procedures had been followed and that a docket had been submitted to the National Prosecution Authority on September 2 to facilitate Mukandila’s court appearance.

The State’s application to further delay Mukandila’s court appearance was declined, with the judge ordering that the applicant be brought before the court to allow the matter of his continued detention to be tested judicially.

Mukandila’s legal team argued that his continued detention without a court appearance was unconstitutional, and that the delay in processing his docket had exceeded what was reasonably justifiable under Zambian law.

The case forms part of a broader pattern of legal challenges emerging from Zambia’s post-election period, in which several individuals connected to opposition parties have sought habeas corpus relief after prolonged periods in custody without formal court appearances.

Mukandila’s case has drawn attention in part because of his position within the Tonse/Pamodzi Alliance, a grouping that has featured prominently in the broader political tensions following the August 13 general elections.

The State maintains that its officers followed proper procedure throughout the arrest and subsequent investigation, and that the delay in bringing Mukandila before the court reflected ordinary processing timelines rather than any deliberate attempt to circumvent his constitutional rights.

Immigration officials said the docket had been forwarded to the National Prosecution Authority in early September, and that the matter would now proceed through the normal court process following the judge’s order.

The Human Rights Commission has separately raised broader concerns about the treatment of detainees connected to the post-election period, calling for prompt disposal of cases involving prolonged detention, particularly for persons arrested in connection with the August general elections.

Legal observers say the outcome of Mukandila’s habeas corpus application could have implications for how similar cases are handled going forward, particularly where questions arise over the timeliness of docket processing and the availability of bail.

The matter remains before the Lusaka High Court, with Mukandila expected to appear as directed following the judge’s ruling.

World.title: Government Contrasts UN Envoy’s Ground Engagement With Rapporteur’s Distant Criticism
World.content:
Government has drawn a sharp contrast between the conduct of two United Nations representatives during Zambia’s post-election period, arguing that the Secretary-General’s Special Envoy engaged constructively on the ground while the Special Rapporteur issued condemnation from a distance without similar engagement.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation said Special Envoy Parfait Onanga-Anyanga was present in Zambia during the events surrounding the August 14 arrests in Kabulonga and personally facilitated the handover of two opposition leaders to the Church before their transfer to security agencies.

The handover took place on the basis of assurances from Government that the fundamental rights of the suspects would be respected at every stage of the legal process, the ministry said.

“The UN Special Envoy engaged directly on the ground and chose constructive facilitation. The Special Rapporteur, from a distance and without such engagement, has chosen condemnation by news release,” Government said in its statement.

Special Rapporteur Gina Romero had issued a statement from Geneva earlier in the week urging Zambian authorities to release all political detainees and restore democratic accountability. Her release did not reference the Special Envoy’s earlier involvement in the case.

Government said the contrast between the two approaches illustrated what it described as a deeper problem with the Rapporteur’s statement: that it was built on distant assessment rather than direct verification.

Officials said the Special Envoy’s role in personally overseeing the handover, and securing assurances regarding the treatment of the two leaders, reflected the kind of engagement Government said it welcomed from international partners.

By contrast, the ministry argued, the Rapporteur’s release adopted language describing the arrests as a “crackdown” and the detainees as “political detainees” without direct verification of the circumstances on the ground.

“Zambia values the contribution of the United Nations Special Procedures to the promotion and protection of human rights. But engagement must rest on accuracy, objectivity and respect for the specific mandate entrusted to each office-holder,” the statement read.

Government said sweeping assertions about electoral flaws, intimidation, abductions or deaths, without substantiated evidence, did not strengthen democracy but instead risked sowing doubt and confusion.

United Party for National Development legal and constitutional affairs chairperson Jack Mwiimbu said the party had reviewed the Rapporteur’s statement and concluded that she had exceeded her mandate by making broad pronouncements on Zambia’s electoral conduct.

Mwiimbu said the Southern African Development Community’s Electoral Observer Mission had reported that the political environment in most areas was peaceful and represented an improvement on the 2021 elections, a finding he said the Rapporteur’s assessment failed to reflect.

The UPND International Relations Committee separately urged the UN to allow competent Zambian authorities and courts to independently determine the facts surrounding the cases, describing the Rapporteur’s call for the release of suspects as premature and potentially prejudicial to ongoing judicial processes.

UPND media director Mark Simuuwe said the UN should respect Zambia’s sovereignty and the credibility of its legal institutions in presiding over matters relating to treason. He said the world body should not provide what he termed sanctuary to those who may have violated Zambian law.

Government said it remained committed to constitutional democracy, political pluralism, freedom of peaceful assembly and association, and constructive cooperation with the UN human rights system, provided that engagement was conducted on the basis of the same standards it was demanding of others.

The ministry has formally requested that the Rapporteur and the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights correct the record with the same prominence given to the original statement, though no response had been received by the time of publication.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - September 4, 2026
World.content:
Zimbabwean Street Vendors Vow to Defy Eviction Order

Street vendors in Harare have vowed to defy a government order to leave illegal trading sites. They said informal trading was their only means of survival in the current economic climate and amid high unemployment. As the September 9 deadline approaches, the government is preparing to launch a zero-tolerance operation against illegal vending in the capital before extending it nationwide. Vendors and civil society groups have warned that removing traders without providing adequate alternative spaces could deepen poverty and leave thousands of people without an income.

South African Anti-Immigrant Group Raids Durban Refugee Camp



Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

A vigilante group known as March and March raided a camp housing hundreds of refugees outside Durban's Home Affairs offices. Several people were injured, and at least four refugees were hospitalised. The refugees, mainly from the DR Congo, Burundi and Rwanda, have been living at the site for more than three months after being displaced by xenophobic threats. They have been verified by the department as being in the country legally. They have asked for protection from xenophobic attacks. Activists have condemned the violence and accused authorities of failing to provide the refugees with adequate protection, shelter and support.

Cholera Outbreak Kills 10 in Sudan's West Kordofan

At least 10 people have died and more than 40 others have been infected in a cholera outbreak in Sudan's West Kordofan. Conflict has severely restricted access to healthcare, medicines and humanitarian aid. The World Health Organization has recorded more than 2,600 cholera cases across several Sudanese states. Kordofan has been identified as the latest outbreak hotspot. UN spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric has said that the UN and its partners are intensifying efforts to combat cholera. Health workers are continuing to treat the sick, conduct vaccination campaigns and distribute vital medical supplies. Officials and aid groups have warned the outbreak could worsen as fighting, poor access to medical supplies and deteriorating environmental conditions continue to hinder efforts to contain the disease.

Ruto Orders Tata Chemicals to Vacate Kenya

Kenya's President William Ruto has ordered Tata Chemicals to leave the country. He accused the company of failing to generate sufficient benefits for Kenyans during its long-running operations at Lake Magadi. Ruto criticised the company for exporting soda ash rather than expanding local processing. He said that the government had identified new investors to take over its operations and create more jobs. Ruto's comments come five weeks after Kenya's mining minister directed Tata Chemicals Magadi to suspend operations, reportedly citing its failure to make royalty payments and meet other regulatory requirements. Tata Chemicals, which has operated the plant since 2005, said it respected the government's decision and remained committed to resolving outstanding matters through legal and regulatory channels.

Close 

Driver in Fatal Anthony Joshua Crash Appears in Nigerian Court

The driver of a vehicle carrying former heavyweight boxing champion Anthony Joshua has appeared in court in Nigeria over a crash that killed two of Joshua's close friends and team members last December. Prosecutors have alleged that the driver lost control of the vehicle while attempting to overtake a moving truck before colliding with a stationary lorry, killing Joshua's personal trainer Latif Ayodele and strength coach Sina Ghami. The driver has denied charges including causing death by dangerous driving. The court also heard that police have yet to take a statement from Joshua, who was a passenger in the vehicle. The trial has been adjourned until September 10.

Concern Grows Over Missing Niger Journalist

Reporters Without Borders has called for an urgent investigation into the disappearance of prominent Nigerien journalist Moussa Kaka, who vanished after leaving his office in Niamey days after a failed coup attempt. Kaka, a former Radio France International correspondent and director of a private television station, has not been heard from, raising concerns among his family, colleagues and press freedom groups. His disappearance comes amid rising political tensions and pressure on journalists under Niger's military government, with RSF calling on the authorities to reveal his whereabouts and the circumstances of his disappearance.

World.title: South Africa: Illegal Mining Wrecks Johannesburg - South African News Briefs - September 4, 2026
World.content:
An aerial view of the abandoned mine in Stilfontein in the in North West Province where hundreds of zama zama miners were underground.

Illegal Mining Wrecks Johannesburg

Illegal mining is causing widespread infrastructure damage and insecurity across Johannesburg and other parts of South Africa, reports AFP. Underground blasting and excavations have created cracks, sinkholes and collapsing roads. The so-called zama zamas, or irregular miners, work in abandoned shafts and in newly dug tunnels, damaging electricity and water infrastructure. They also contribute to violent crime and instability in surrounding communities. Despite increased police and military patrols, residents continue to face dangerous conditions. Mining experts warn that the damage could worsen.

MK Party Slams Ramaphosa's Phala Phala Court Bid

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The uMkhonto we Sizwe Party's legal representative, Advocate Dali Mpofu, has criticised President Cyril Ramaphosa's attempt to have the Section 89 Independent Panel report reviewed and set aside, describing the court action as a delaying tactic, reports SABC News. The report found prima facie evidence that Ramaphosa may have seriously violated his oath of office in connection with the theft of $580,000 from his Phala Phala farm. Mpofu argued that the review application was aimed at avoiding accountability and delaying answers that South Africans are seeking from the president.

Durban Migrants Plead for Temporary Shelter

Foreign nationals who have been camping outside the Home Affairs refugee offices in Durban for more than three months are calling on the government to provide temporary shelter after being displaced from their homes and businesses, reports EWN. Tensions around the camp escalated after clashes broke out during a protest by March and March demonstrators. At least five people were hospitalised and three others arrested. The group, which includes refugees and asylum seekers, said that it was promised temporary accommodation while its members underwent identity verification. However, the government has instead urged them to return to their communities or go to the Lindela Repatriation Centre in Limpopo.
