“[I told him that] our perspective is very different because here there is a large majority of Mexican people who support the transformation and the results we’ve achieved, and the people are happy with the work the government is doing,” Sheinbaum said.

“… They were some of the issues we spoke about,” she said, adding that she had invited Petro to return to Mexico to speak at the National Institute of Historic Studies of the Revolutions in Mexico.

World.title: Colombia’s New President Dismantles ‘Total Peace’, Signs Extraditions
World.content:
COLOMBIA · POLITICS & SECURITY

Key Facts — What happened Colombia’s new President Abelardo de la Espriella signed extradition orders for five drug traffickers linked to the previous government’s peace talks.

— How big The president also closed three negotiation tables and claims 41 extradition orders signed in his first 19 days in office.

— What it means The moves dismantle “Total Peace,” the signature negotiation policy of former President Gustavo Petro, in favor of a tougher security line.

— The catch Only the extradition orders are signed; none of the five men has been confirmed physically transferred to U.S. custody yet.

— Who it affects Three of the five men are in Colombian prisons; two remain fugitives at large and would be sent once captured.

— What comes next Former President Petro publicly defended his record, setting up a political clash with his successor.

Colombia’s new right-wing president is rapidly dismantling his predecessor’s “Total Peace” policy, signing extradition orders for five traffickers who once sat at government negotiation tables.

Casa de Narino, Colombia’s presidential palace in Bogota. President Abelardo de la Espriella took office there on August 7, 2026. (Photo: “Casa-narino-1-fachada” by Juanjo70000, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.)

Colombia’s new president, Abelardo de la Espriella, has signed extradition orders for five drug traffickers who once negotiated with the state under his predecessor’s “Total Peace” policy. The move, announced Aug 26-27, marks the most concrete step yet in the new administration’s rapid dismantling of that flagship program.

De la Espriella, a conservative who took office Aug 7, 2026, succeeding Gustavo Petro, is reversing course on a policy that defined the previous government. The five men are described by multiple outlets as former negotiators or representatives in Petro’s peace process with armed groups.

A New Administration Reverses Its Predecessor

De la Espriella won the June 21, 2026 presidential runoff with 49.66% of the vote, narrowly beating Iván Cepeda’s 48.70%. Cepeda was the candidate preferred by Petro, whose term ended with the Aug 7 inauguration in Cali.

The new president’s actions echo a campaign pledge from the right-wing bloc. Reuters reported in May that candidate Paloma Valencia vowed to end “Total Peace” and replace it with what she called “Total Security.”

De la Espriella has embraced that same stance since taking office.

What Was “Total Peace”?

Petro’s flagship security policy sought negotiated demobilization with armed groups, including FARC dissident factions, the ELN guerrilla group, and Clan del Golfo, Colombia’s largest drug-trafficking network. It favored talks over pure military confrontation.

The policy was already weakening before the transition. The Rio Times reported in April that Petro’s own team had described the two remaining active tracks as closed or collapsed.

Some officials were calling “Total Peace” over even before Petro left office.

A Rolling Dismantlement, Not a Single Stroke

The end of Total Peace unfolded over about a week rather than in one dramatic announcement. On Aug 26, De la Espriella said he had signed the five extradition orders.

The next day, UPI framed it as a “definitive end” to the plan.

But El País reported Aug 28 that the founding decrees creating the negotiation tables had not yet been formally repealed at that point. On paper, the tables still legally existed even as extraditions were announced.

Concrete closures followed on Aug 28. El País reported Aug 31 that De la Espriella had formally closed three dialogue tables via resolutions signed that day.

Estrella Digital counted nine resolutions in total, closing two peace tables and one “socio-legal” conversation space.

The Five Men Named in the Orders

Geovanny Andrés Rojas, alias “Araña,” led the Comandos de la Frontera group and was a key negotiator in the Total Peace talks. His extradition was approved by Colombia’s Supreme Court in Oct 2025 but suspended while he negotiated.

Semana reports he remains at La Picota prison “awaiting transfer” as of Sept 2.

Willington Henao Gutiérrez, alias “El Mocho Olmedo,” commanded Front 33 of the FARC dissidence and was arrested in 2025. His extradition had been delayed due to his negotiator role.

Carmen Evelio Castillo Carrillo, alias “Muñeca,” is tied to the Autodefensas Conquistadoras de la Sierra Nevada structure and is in custody. His brother, Fredy Castillo Carrillo, alias “Pinocho,” belongs to the same armed group but was still a fugitive when the order was signed.

Gabriel Yepes Mejía, alias “H.H.,” is linked to Comuneros del Sur, an ELN dissident faction. His extradition was previously approved by Colombia’s Supreme Court, and he was a fugitive when the order was signed.

Orders Signed, Transfers Pending

Of the five, three were in Colombian custody when the order was announced: Rojas, Henao Gutiérrez, and Carmen Evelio Castillo Carrillo. The other two, Fredy Castillo Carrillo and Yepes Mejía, remain at large and would be extradited upon capture.

No source through Sept 2 confirms any of the five has been physically flown to the United States. The orders were signed Aug 26-27, but the actual transfers remain unconfirmed and pending.

Rojas, for instance, is still reported at La Picota prison awaiting transfer.

Petro Fights Back Publicly

The former president has not gone quietly. Infobae reported Aug 30 that Petro publicly defended his Total Peace record after the tables closed.

Petro said the policy “saved thousands of lives.”

The exchange sets up a live political conflict between the two men. It is now a clash between a former president and his successor, not a struggle within one government.

De la Espriella, for his part, claims 41 extradition orders signed in his first 19 days in office.

More: Colombia news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Abelardo de la Espriella?

He is Colombia’s sitting president, inaugurated Aug 7, 2026, for the 2026-2030 term. He won the June runoff with 49.66% of the vote, succeeding Gustavo Petro.

What was the “Total Peace” policy?

It was former President Petro’s flagship security strategy of negotiating demobilization with armed groups rather than relying on military force. De la Espriella has been dismantling it since taking office.

Have the five men been extradited to the United States?

No. Only the extradition orders have been signed; physical transfer to U.S. custody is not yet confirmed as of the latest reporting on Sept 2.

Who are the five men facing extradition?

They are Geovanny Andrés Rojas, Willington Henao Gutiérrez, Carmen Evelio Castillo Carrillo, Fredy Castillo Carrillo, and Gabriel Yepes Mejía, all linked to armed groups that negotiated under Total Peace.

How did the policy end?

It was a rolling process across late August, with three dialogue tables formally closed by resolutions signed Aug 28. Some outlets called it a “definitive end” a day before others noted the tables were still technically open on paper.

Sources: Reuters, Associated Press, CNN, NPR, Le Monde English, UPI, Infobae, El País, DW, Anadolu Agency, Semana, Estrella Digital, Ground News, Rio Times, Edelman analysis, Wikipedia.

World.title: Geles Cabrera, Mexico’s pioneering sculptor, dies at 100
World.content:
MEXICO · CULTURE

Key Facts — What happened Geles Cabrera, long hailed as Mexico’s first professional female sculptor, died Sept. 1, 2026, at age 100.

— How big Her career spanned more than seven decades, with works centered on the human figure.

— What it means She helped found the Salón de la Plástica Mexicana in 1949 and opened her own museum in 1966.

— The catch No cause of death has been disclosed by her family or by Mexican cultural authorities.

— Who it affects She was based in Mexico City, where her self-funded museum in Coyoacán ran for decades.

— What comes next Tributes have poured in from Mexico’s National Institute of Fine Arts and Literature (INBAL).

Geles Cabrera, the Mexican sculptor who spent seven decades shaping the human form, has died at 100. She opened her own museum in Coyoacán.

Geles Cabrera pictured at a public event. She died on September 1, 2026, at the age of 100. (Photo: “TesorosRegistroCivilPresentation13” by AlejandroLinaresGarcia, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.)

Geles Cabrera, long celebrated as the first woman to practice sculpture professionally in Mexico, died Sept. 1, 2026, in Mexico City. She was 100 years old, having marked her centenary on Aug. 2, 2026.

Her death was confirmed by Mexico’s National Institute of Fine Arts and Literature (INBAL), which oversees the country’s cultural institutions. No cause of death has been disclosed.

A Pioneer of Mexican Sculpture

Born Ángeles María Cabrera Alvarado in Mexico City on Aug. 2, 1926, she trained at the Academia de San Carlos. She also studied at La Esmeralda in Mexico City and at the Academia de San Alejandro in Cuba.

Mexican cultural institutions have long described her as the first woman to practice sculpture professionally in the country.

At just 22 years old, she became the first Mexican woman to exhibit her work abroad, according to INBAL. She was also among the first female sculpture students at the Academia de San Carlos.

Founding Institutions

In 1949, Cabrera was invited to help found the Salón de la Plástica Mexicana (SPM), a major Mexican artists’ association. Her first solo show there made her the first Mexican woman sculptor with her own exhibition, per Mexico’s Ministry of Culture.

In 1966, she founded the Museo Escultórico Geles Cabrera in the Coyoacán district of Mexico City. The self-funded museum remained open with free admission for roughly four decades, according to multiple sources including La Jornada and Artishock.

A Body of Work on the Human Figure

Over more than seven decades, Cabrera developed a body of work centered on the human figure. Her sculpture “opened the way for new generations of women artists,” INBAL said in a statement quoted by ArteInformado.

Her 1965 piece “Perfil del viento” is among her most frequently cited works.

In late 2025, Mexico City’s Museo del Palacio de Bellas Artes hosted “Partituras Corporales,” a retrospective of her work. La Jornada reported at the time that it was her first individual exhibition at that venue.

Awards and Recognition

Cabrera received numerous honors, including the First Prize at the XXXI Salón de Bellas Artes in Havana, Cuba, in 1949. She also earned an honorable mention at INBAL’s III Bienal Nacional de Escultura in 1967.

In 1985, she won the Gran Premio de Escultura “Kiter Peter” in Gabrovo, Bulgaria. She also received the Premio Coatlicue in 2011.

In September 2024, she received the Medalla Bellas Artes de Oro en Artes Visuales, one of Mexico’s highest cultural honors.

More: Mexico news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who was Geles Cabrera?

Geles Cabrera was a Mexican sculptor born Ángeles María Cabrera Alvarado in Mexico City in 1926. She was widely described as the first woman to practice sculpture professionally in Mexico.

When did Geles Cabrera die?

She died on Sept. 1, 2026, in Mexico City, at the age of 100, one month after her birthday. Her death was confirmed by INBAL, Mexico’s National Institute of Fine Arts and Literature.

What was Geles Cabrera known for?

She was known for a seven-decade body of work centered on the human figure. She helped found the Salón de la Plástica Mexicana in 1949 and founded her own museum in Coyoacán in 1966.

What awards did Geles Cabrera receive?

Her honors include the 1949 First Prize at the Salón de Bellas Artes in Havana, Cuba. She also received the Medalla Bellas Artes de Oro en Artes Visuales in September 2024.

What was the cause of Geles Cabrera’s death?

No cause of death has been reported by her family or by Mexican cultural authorities.

World.title: Chile Reports Homicide Drop and 188 Fugitives Arrested
World.content:
CHILE · SECURITY

Key Facts — What happened Chile’s government reported a 17.2% drop in homicides this year and the arrest of 188 fugitives in 48 hours.

— How big The homicide decline equals 117 fewer cases, and violent robberies fell 13.2% compared with last year.

— What it means The figures back President José Antonio Kast’s campaign promise to restore order and security after taking office in March.

— The catch Opposition party Frente Amplio disputes the government’s shifting crime-reporting methods, and prosecutors logged a 36.8% rise in organized-crime homicides after the inauguration.

— Who it affects Police made 36 arrests in Santiago and 152 across other regions, with 184 fugitives caught on active warrants.

— What comes next Carabineros has captured 1,295 fugitives so far in 2026, an 82% jump, as the government keeps issuing periodic security balances.

Chile’s security ministry touts falling homicides and a mass fugitive sweep. Opposition figures and prosecutors offer a more mixed picture of crime under President Kast.

A Carabineros de Chile patrol vehicle in Valparaiso. The force reported a 17.2 percent year-to-date drop in homicides in its August 31 balance. (Photo: “Carabineros de Chile Nissan patrol vehicle in Valparaiso” by Jay Galvin, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.)

Chile’s government reported a 17.2% year-to-date drop in homicides, or 117 fewer cases, alongside a 13.2% fall in violent robberies. The figures come from the Ministry of Public Security’s security balance released on August 31, 2026.

The same report highlighted the capture of 188 fugitives during a 48-hour national police operation. The announcement bolsters President José Antonio Kast’s central campaign pledge to restore order after he took office on March 11, 2026.

The Fugitive Sweep

Carabineros de Chile, the national police force, ran the “Macro Operativo” from August 25 to 27, 2026. Officers detained 188 people nationwide, with 36 arrests in the Metropolitan Region of Santiago and 152 in other regions.

Of those detained, 184 were captured on active arrest warrants, while four were caught in the act of committing a crime. Twenty-six of the 188 were listed in the National Fugitives Registry.

The operation was carried out by the Carabineros’ fugitive-search unit, known as SEBV, and its regional sections. Chilean outlets covering the sweep did not report individual cases or specific crime types.

A Year of Declining Numbers

The August 31 balance is the latest in a series of government reports showing falling crime throughout 2026. In his June 1 state-of-the-nation address, Kast cited 378 homicide victims through May 31, versus 444 in the same 2025 period.

That specific claim was independently verified by the Chilean fact-checking outlet factchecking.cl. A first-semester balance on July 6 showed 442 homicides from January to June 28, down 13% from 508 a year earlier.

Cumulatively, Carabineros reports capturing 1,295 fugitives so far in 2026, an 82% increase over the same period of the prior year. Security Minister Martín Arrau has been the public face of these balances since taking office in May 2026.

The Opposition’s Objection

The opposition party Frente Amplio disputes the government’s methodology. The ministry ran weekly homicide reports from April to June 2026, then switched back to monthly.

Frente Amplio says the changing cadence and moving comparison windows make it harder to verify long-term trends. The fluctuating year-to-date percentages, from 13% to 17.2%, reflect each report’s shifting cutoff date.

A Counter-Narrative on Organized Crime

A separate statistic complicates the government’s framing. According to the Fiscalía’s organized-crime unit, ECOH, homicides linked specifically to organized crime rose 36.8% in the weeks right after Kast’s inauguration.

That measure covers March 11 to April 6, 2026, when prosecutors logged 26 such cases versus 19 in 2025. This is a different metric from the government’s broader year-to-date figures, which include all homicide victims over a much longer window.

In early April, prosecutors and the Subsecretaría de Prevención del Delito (crime-prevention agency) publicly disagreed over how to interpret the March uptick. The dispute highlights a genuine institutional divide over the state of public security.

Political Context

Kast, of the right-wing Partido Republicano, won the December 14, 2025 runoff with 58.2% of the vote against Communist-backed Jeannette Jara. His inauguration marked Chile’s biggest right-wing shift in decades, according to Reuters.

Crime, migration, and the Venezuelan gang Tren de Aragua were central to the election. Prosecutors attributed a large share of rising homicides and kidnappings to organized crime.

The Ministry of Public Security was created by law in 2025 under former President Gabriel Boric. It split security functions off from the Interior Ministry.

Arrau, the current minister, is a civil industrial engineer from the Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile and a Partido Republicano militant. He took up the role in May 2026 after serving in various government and party positions.

More: Chile news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Chile’s government report on August 31, 2026?

The Ministry of Public Security reported a 17.2% year-to-date drop in homicides, or 117 fewer cases, and a 13.2% decrease in violent robberies. It also highlighted the capture of 188 fugitives during a 48-hour police operation.

How many fugitives were arrested in the operation?

Carabineros detained 188 people nationwide from August 25 to 27, 2026. Of these, 184 were captured on active warrants, four were caught in the act, and 26 were listed in the National Fugitives Registry.

Why does the opposition dispute the government’s crime figures?

Frente Amplio criticizes the government for repeatedly changing its crime-reporting methods. The ministry ran weekly homicide reports from April to June 2026, then switched back to monthly.

What does the Fiscalía’s data show about organized crime?

The Fiscalía’s ECOH unit recorded a 36.8% rise in organized-crime-linked homicides from March 11 to April 6, 2026, compared with the same days in 2025. This narrower metric contrasts with the government’s broader year-to-date figures.

Who is Martín Arrau?

Martín Arrau is Chile’s Minister of Public Security, appointed in May 2026. He is a civil industrial engineer and a militant of President Kast’s Partido Republicano.

Sources: Revista Seguridad & Defensa, BioBioChile, T13, Emol, El Dínamo, Cooperativa, ADN Radio, El País (Chile), Reuters, factchecking.cl.

World.title: TV Azteca bankruptcy: Mexico court declares broadcaster insolvent
World.content:
MEXICO · BUSINESS

Key Facts — What happened A Mexican court formally declared broadcaster TV Azteca bankrupt on July 7, 2026.

— How big The company owes roughly 24 billion pesos (about US$1.4 billion) plus a defaulted bond claim of US$500-600 million.

— What it means This is a reorganization process, not a liquidation, so the network keeps broadcasting under court oversight.

— The catch No outlet confirms company-wide layoff numbers; only a newsroom shake-up with named on-air departures is documented.

— Who it affects Viewers of Hechos and adn Noticias newscasts, plus creditors and employees of the Salinas-owned network.

— What comes next A conciliation phase runs up to 185 days, extendable, before any possible conversion to liquidation.

Mexican broadcaster TV Azteca is navigating a court-supervised bankruptcy reorganization while its news division undergoes a visible on-air talent shake-up.

The Mexico City skyline. TV Azteca, one of the country’s largest broadcasters, is based in the capital. (Photo: “Mexico City Reforma skyline (cropped2)” by Jonathan Salvador, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.)

A Mexican federal judge formally declared TV Azteca bankrupt on July 7, 2026, granting court protection under the country’s concurso mercantil process. That ruling caps a months-long slide that began with a voluntary filing announcement on February 26, 2026.

A Mexico City court had already admitted the case on March 23, 2026, a procedural step ahead of the final ruling. That admission cut off legal protection for many TV Azteca subsidiaries, court filings showed.

The concurso mercantil is Mexico’s equivalent of Chapter 11 reorganization, not a liquidation. TV Azteca has said the goal is to preserve value and keep operations running while it restructures its debts.

A Debt Problem Years in the Making

The bankruptcy stems from accumulated insolvency, which courts described as “generalized nonpayment” of obligations. A central piece is a 2017 bond issue, originally US$400 million in unsecured notes, on which TV Azteca defaulted.

Reporting on the claim’s current size varies. El País cited “more than US$580 million” in late February, while El Imparcial reported “nearly US$600 million” around the same time.

Total liabilities in the filing reached roughly 24 billion pesos (about US$1.4 billion). Liquid assets totaled only about 1.1 billion pesos (about US$65 million).

Infobae put the total debt figure at 23,961,373,218 pesos (about US$1.41 billion). Zeta Tijuana cited 23,345 million pesos (about US$1.37 billion) across 1,970 separate debts.

Separately, Expansión reported a tax debt of more than 5,000 million pesos (about US$295 million). The company was settling that debt in installments with Mexican authorities.

A Banco Azteca-related liability of about 1,708 million pesos (about US$100 million) also appears within the broader debt picture.

A Long Legal History

This is not TV Azteca’s first brush with bankruptcy courts. In March 2023, holders of about US$63 million in the same notes filed involuntary Chapter 11 petitions in New York.

They named the company and 34 subsidiaries as debtors.

A US judge dismissed those petitions in November 2023, ruling the bondholders’ claims faced a “bona fide dispute.” That litigation has continued in parallel in US courts.

Creditors alleged in July 2026 that TV Azteca hid valuable assets in a newly created company before filing for bankruptcy. The company contests that allegation.

Owner Ricardo Salinas Pliego has dismissed bankruptcy concerns publicly. “See you in 2030, and we will see if it is true that I am bankrupt,” he posted on February 27, 2026.

Mexico News Daily and Vallarta Today both reported the remark. It followed an online exchange with a Mexican state broadcasting official who had criticized the filing.

Newsroom Shake-Up, Not Confirmed Mass Layoffs

The most concrete recent event is a restructuring of TV Azteca’s news division. Grupo Salinas spokesperson Luciano Pascoe announced it starting August 27, 2026.

The changes, effective around August 31 to September 1, merged programming under the Hechos and adn Noticias brands.

Several on-air figures departed, per Infobae. Carolina Rocha left Hechos Sábado after eight years, and Ricardo Raphael exited A Ras de Tierra after four.

Vaitiare Mateos, Otoniel Martínez, and Leonardo Arriaga all left Hechos AM.

Uriel Estrada departed Al Extremo, while Roberto Ruiz was reassigned to adn Noticias’ night slot rather than laid off. Manuel López San Martín joined as solo host of the morning show Hechos AM.

He did not replace Javier Alatorre, despite earlier speculation to that effect. Alatorre remains anchor of the flagship evening newscast, Hechos Noche.

No outlet reviewed has confirmed a company-wide headcount or percentage of employees laid off in 2026. Ámbito, an Argentine outlet, used the phrase “mass layoffs” for the news division alone, without citing a number.

SDPNoticias reported only that the restructuring “could involve” layoffs in different areas. Neither outlet cited company-wide figures.

What Happens Next

Under Mexican law, the conciliation phase runs up to 185 days after the July 7 declaration, extendable by two additional 90-day periods. If no restructuring agreement is reached, the case can convert to liquidation, or quiebra.

For now, the company continues operating under court oversight, with asset seizures and most creditor enforcement actions halted. TV Azteca is pushing bondholders to pursue claims through the Mexican process rather than US courts, per Bloomberg on August 19, 2026.

The network’s last public workforce disclosure, cited by Expansión, showed headcount falling from 4,102 employees in 2020 to 3,500 in 2022. That reduction predates the bankruptcy filing.

No more current public figure exists.

More: Mexico news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a concurso mercantil?

It is Mexico’s bankruptcy reorganization process, similar to Chapter 11 in the United States. The goal is to restructure debts while keeping the company operating, not to shut it down immediately.

How much debt does TV Azteca have?

Total liabilities are roughly 24 billion pesos (about US$1.4 billion). A defaulted 2017 bond claim is cited at US$500-600 million, and a separate tax debt exceeds 5,000 million pesos (about US$295 million).

Did TV Azteca lay off mass numbers of employees?

No outlet has confirmed a company-wide headcount or percentage of layoffs in 2026. What is documented is a news-division reorganization with several named on-air departures and some reassignments.

Will TV Azteca stop broadcasting?

No — the company continues operating during the conciliation phase under court oversight. Broadcast signals have not been disrupted, and the newsroom changes are framed as a programming refresh.

What happens if TV Azteca cannot reach a creditor deal?

If no restructuring agreement is reached within the maximum conciliation period, the case can convert to liquidation, or quiebra. That is the fallback scenario, not the current path.

Sources: Reuters, Bloomberg, El País, Expansión, Infobae, El Imparcial, Mexico News Daily, Vallarta Today, Zeta Tijuana, Ámbito, SDPNoticias, Snell & Wilmer, Santa Marina & Steta, Mexico Business News, adn40.mx, La Sociedad del Contenido, Cleary Gottlieb.

World.title: Mexican musician Jonathan Meléndez, family killed in Mexico City attack
World.content:
MEXICO · SECURITY

Key Facts — What happened Musician Jonathan Meléndez, his pregnant wife, their three-year-old daughter and their nanny were shot dead in their apartment near Mexico City on September 1.

— How big Four people died in the attack, and the family dog was found dead and tied up alongside them.

— What it means Meléndez was a keyboardist in Camilo Séptimo, a nationally known indie and synthpop band, making the case a shock to Mexico’s alternative music scene.

— The catch Prosecutors say the killers likely entered through a relationship of trust, not a random break-in, and no cartel link has been confirmed.

— Who it affects Two suspects, including a reported business associate of Meléndez, are detained in the State of Mexico pending formal homicide charges.

— What comes next Authorities are preparing arrest warrants for aggravated homicide while the motive remains under investigation.

State of Mexico prosecutors are treating the killings of Camilo Séptimo keyboardist Jonathan Meléndez and three others as a targeted attack tied to a business relationship, not a random home invasion.

A street in Atizapan de Zaragoza, the Greater Mexico City municipality where the killings took place. (Photo: “Calzada San Mateo, Atizapan de Zaragoza, Estado de Mexico” by ProtoplasmaKid, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.)

Musician Jonathan Meléndez, his pregnant wife, their three-year-old daughter and their nanny were found shot dead on September 1. They were killed inside their apartment in Greater Mexico City, authorities said.

State of Mexico prosecutors — the Fiscalía General de Justicia del Estado de México, or FGJEM — confirmed the deaths. They said two suspects have been detained.

Meléndez, 38, was a keyboardist, composer and co-founder of Camilo Séptimo, a nationally recognized indie and synthpop band from Mexico City.

The case has shaken Mexico’s alternative music scene. Proceso called the band one of the country’s most recognizable alternative acts of the last decade.

The Attack

The killings took place inside the family’s apartment in the Grand Viure development, in the Zona Esmeralda area of Atizapán de Zaragoza. The municipality sits on the State of Mexico’s edge, bordering the capital.

Municipal police discovered the bodies around 11:50 p.m. on September 1, according to CNN en Español, citing the FGJEM.

Investigators place the attack window at roughly 5:30 p.m. to 7:40 p.m. that day, Excélsior reported, citing the FGJEM investigation. Two of the victims were found tied up, and all four had apparent gunshot wounds.

PorEsto! reported that Meléndez’s body was found in the main bedroom, while his wife and child were found in the bathroom. The family dog was found dead and tied up nearby, according to the Fiscalía’s communiqué relayed by CNN en Español and Telediario.

A young child in the household was found unharmed, according to multiple Mexican news outlets.

A Trust-Based Intrusion

The residential complex has 24-hour private security with controlled access for vehicles and pedestrians, Telediario reported, citing the state prosecutor’s office. Security camera footage and entry logs were decisive in identifying the suspects.

Prosecutors’ initial hypothesis is that the attackers had direct authorization to enter from Meléndez himself or were part of his circle of trust. Excélsior reported that one suspect, described as Meléndez’s business associate, used a pre-existing relationship of trust to gain entry to the residence.

N+/Foro TV reported that the two detained men were allegedly Meléndez’s business partners in a vacation-rental company. The venture operated in Valle de Bravo, Acapulco and Tepoztlán.

The outlet also noted prior fraud complaints against one of the suspects. Social-media groups of alleged victims are now reportedly part of the FGJEM investigation file.

Suspects Detained

Two suspects are in custody: Diego Sebastián “N,” described by Excélsior as Meléndez’s commercial partner and an Argentine national, and Gerardo “N.” Mexican legal convention uses “N” in place of full surnames until formal charges are filed.

Both men were initially held at the Fiscalía de Asuntos Especiales, or FAE, in Toluca. They were held on grounds of bribery and being caught in the act, Excélsior reported.

The FGJEM is preparing to execute formal arrest warrants for aggravated homicide, known in Spanish as homicidio calificado.

Once the warrants are executed, the suspects would move to a state penitentiary in the Valle de México region.

An FGJEM statement, relayed by ADN Noticias, confirmed the two detentions. It said the investigation is coordinated with federal and Mexico City authorities.

Investigation Ongoing

No outlet reviewed has quoted prosecutors formally attributing the killings to organized crime or a cartel.

The framing across Mexican and international coverage is a targeted attack tied to a personal or business relationship. It is not described as a narco-style hit or a random home invasion.

The motive is not officially confirmed, and the investigation is reportedly examining the business relationship and the alleged fraud angle. As of September 4, no trial date or formal charges beyond the arrest-warrant process had been reported.

The case has drawn wide attention because of Meléndez’s standing in Mexico’s indie scene. Camilo Séptimo formed in 2013 and built a national following with the 2014 EP “Maya” and the 2017 album “Óleos.”

The band has played major festivals including Vive Latino.

More: Mexico news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who was Jonathan Meléndez?

Jonathan Meléndez, 38, was a keyboardist, composer and co-founder of Camilo Séptimo, a nationally recognized Mexican indie and synthpop band from Mexico City. The group has been active since around 2013 and has played major festivals including Vive Latino.

Where did the killings take place?

The four victims were found dead in their Grand Viure apartment in Atizapán de Zaragoza, State of Mexico, near Mexico City. Municipal police discovered the bodies around 11:50 p.m. on September 1.

Who are the suspects in the case?

Two suspects are detained: Diego Sebastián “N,” described as Meléndez’s commercial partner and an Argentine national, and Gerardo “N.” Prosecutors are preparing arrest warrants for aggravated homicide, and the motive remains under investigation.

Was this linked to organized crime?

No outlet reviewed has quoted prosecutors formally attributing the killings to organized crime or a cartel. The investigation is focused on a targeted attack tied to a personal or business relationship, with the motive not yet officially confirmed.

Why is this case getting so much attention?

Meléndez was a working, nationally recognized musician, and the deaths of four people including a young child have shocked Mexico. The case has been covered independently by Reuters, CNN, El País and major Mexican outlets.

Sources: Reuters, CNN en Español, CNN International, El País, Infobae, Excélsior, Telediario, PorEsto!, N+/Foro TV, Proceso, ADN Noticias.

World.title: Colombia Earthquake Recovery Enters Fourth Week
World.content:
COLOMBIA · DISASTER RECOVERY

Key Facts — What happened A magnitude-7.4 earthquake struck western Colombia on August 10, 2026, near San José del Palmar in Chocó department.

— How big Official figures now count 331 dead and 4,519 injured, with more than 466,000 people affected across five departments.

— What it means A joint UN and government study now puts direct physical damage at about US$13.4 billion, far above earlier estimates.

— The catch Starlink’s free internet in affected zones is funded by SpaceX itself, not by the Colombian government, and only runs through September 12.

— Who it affects Survivors in Chocó, Valle del Cauca, Risaralda, Caldas, and Quindío, including the cities of Cali, Pereira, and Quibdó.

— What comes next Authorities are still counting losses, and no official plan has been announced for internet service after September 12.

Four weeks after Colombia’s strongest earthquake in a century, the confirmed death toll has held steady at 331. Damage estimates have climbed sharply, and a free Starlink internet lifeline is nearing its deadline.

Quibdo, capital of Colombia’s Choco department, seen from the air. The region is still recovering from the August 10 earthquake that struck nearby. (Photo: “Ciudad de Quibdo” by Danielcuesta, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.)

Colombia is entering its fourth week of recovery from the magnitude-7.4 earthquake that struck Chocó department on August 10, 2026. The quake, which hit at about 7:34 a.m. local time, has been widely described as the country’s strongest in a century.

The disaster has affected more than 466,000 people across at least five departments, including Chocó, Valle del Cauca, Risaralda, Caldas, and Quindío. Major cities such as Cali, Pereira, Quibdó, Manizales, and Armenia have all reported damage.

Death Toll Climbed, Then Held Steady

The official death toll climbed steadily in the first days after the quake. On the first day, reports counted at least 20 dead, but that number rose to more than 130 within 24 hours.

By August 13, figures ranged from 265 to 281 dead depending on the source, with hundreds more listed as missing. Colombia’s national disaster agency, UNGRD, has since updated its count several times after cross-checking records.

The most current official figure, reported by UNGRD on August 25–26, stands at 331 dead and 4,439 injured. That number supersedes the earlier 265 figure, which was only accurate as of August 13 and is now outdated.

The toll has not risen since. UNGRD’s latest update, on September 3, still counted 331 dead, though the injured count had climbed to 4,519.

Damage Cost Climbs Sharply

Early damage estimates have also been revised sharply upward. On August 18, President Abelardo de la Espriella announced preliminary losses of about US$9.6 billion.

That estimate was based on modeling by Ingeniar Risk Intelligence, a private catastrophe-risk firm. The figure, roughly 30 trillion Colombian pesos, was widely reported as preliminary and represented roughly 1.5%-2% of the country’s GDP.

President De la Espriella’s government cited the same figure days later when it declared an economic emergency. However, a joint evaluation by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and UNGRD, published August 31, found far higher losses.

Direct physical damages reached 42.1 trillion pesos, roughly US$13.4 billion, about 40% above the earlier US$9.6 billion estimate.

Starlink Provides Free Internet

SpaceX’s Starlink satellite internet service has been providing free connectivity in the affected regions since mid-August. The company confirmed the program in its own posts and support materials, covering Chocó, Caldas, Valle del Cauca, Risaralda, and Quindío.

The free service is funded directly by SpaceX through account credits, not by any Colombian government subsidy. Existing customers receive account credit, while cancelled customers get a reactivation credit, and new customers must buy a kit first.

The Colombian government’s role has been limited to distributing Starlink hardware kits in the epicenter area. The free service itself is scheduled to run through September 12.

What Happens After September 12

No official announcement has been made about what happens to internet service after the September 12 cutoff date. Starlink’s own materials do not specify whether free service will continue, be extended, or convert to paid plans.

This remains an open question for the hundreds of thousands of people still recovering from the quake. Relief workers and residents in remote areas of Chocó have relied heavily on the satellite connection for emergency coordination.

Meanwhile, recovery efforts continue across the affected departments, with authorities still counting the full scale of the damage. The revised US$13.4 billion estimate suggests reconstruction will be a long and costly process.

More: Colombia news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many people died in the Colombia earthquake?

The official death toll stands at 331 as of August 25–26, according to Colombia’s national disaster agency UNGRD. Earlier figures of 265 were only accurate as of August 13.

How much damage did the earthquake cause?

A joint UN and government study published August 31 puts direct physical damages at about US$13.4 billion. That figure supersedes an earlier preliminary estimate of US$9.6 billion from a private modeling firm.

Who is paying for the free Starlink service?

SpaceX itself is funding the free Starlink service through account credits, not the Colombian government. The government only distributed the physical hardware kits in affected areas.

When does the free Starlink service end?

The free service is scheduled to run through September 12, 2026. No official plan has been announced for what happens after that date.

Which areas were most affected by the earthquake?

The hardest-hit departments are Chocó, Valle del Cauca, Risaralda, Caldas, and Quindío. Major cities including Cali, Pereira, Quibdó, Manizales, and Armenia all reported damage.

World.title: Haiti Kenscoff Funeral Held as UN Urges Faster Gang Force Deployment
World.content:
HAITI · SECURITY

Key Facts — What happened Mourners buried four victims of a gang massacre in Kenscoff, Haiti, on August 30.

— How big The UN says at least 47 people died, though Haitian officials confirmed 25 dead.

— What it means The UN Security Council urged faster deployment of the Gang Suppression Force to Haiti.

— The catch Only about 1,000 of the authorized 5,550 troops are on the ground so far.

— Who it affects Residents of Kenscoff, a hillside town near Port-au-Prince, and all of Haiti.

— What comes next The UN wants the force at full strength, but no newer troop count has been released.

As Haiti buries victims of the Kenscoff gang attack, the UN Security Council is pressing for the rapid, full deployment of the international Gang Suppression Force to a country where only a fraction of the authorized troops have arrived.

A hillside neighborhood near Kenscoff, Haiti. A funeral was held nearby on August 30 for victims of a gang massacre in the area. (Photo: “Gfp-final26” by Yinan Chen, via Wikimedia Commons, Public Domain.)

Haitians gathered in Kenscoff on Sunday, August 30, to bury four of the people killed in a gang attack that has shaken the hillside town near Port-au-Prince. Hundreds of mourners packed a Baptist church in Kenscoff, per the Haitian outlet Vant Bèf Info, before the burial at a nearby cemetery.

The service came less than a week after the Viv Ansanm gang coalition struck Kenscoff overnight on August 23-24, an assault that included a church where residents had sought refuge. Kenscoff Mayor Jean Massillon attended the funeral, according to Vant Bèf Info, and Pastor Jean Robert Dorlus spoke at the service, according to the AP.

A Death Toll Still in Dispute

The United Nations says at least 47 people were killed and 50 kidnapped in the attack, a figure the Security Council itself uses and the most widely repeated. But Haitian judicial officials have confirmed a lower toll, with Kenscoff Mayor Jean Massillon telling the Miami Herald that 25 deaths were verified and 15 people remained missing as of August 25.

The human-rights group RNDDH initially estimated 30 to 40 killed, cautioning that the count could change, Reuters reported. One unverified report from HaitiLibre put the number at “at least 60 victims,” but that figure has not been corroborated by other outlets.

UN Council Urges Faster Force Deployment

Two days before the funeral, the UN Security Council held an urgent briefing on Haiti and called for the Gang Suppression Force (GSF) to reach its full strength quickly. The UN’s top envoy for Haiti called for the force’s “swift and full deployment,” and members urged it to reach its planned size of 5,500 personnel as soon as possible, according to a UN readout dated August 28.

That statement is Council meeting language, not a new binding resolution. The briefing followed directly from the Kenscoff killings, with the UK calling the violence “horrific and unacceptable” and the US Mission to the UN also delivering remarks.

The Force’s Mandate and Its Gaps

The Gang Suppression Force grew out of an earlier international mission. UN Security Council Resolution 2699, adopted October 2, 2023, authorized the Multinational Security Support (MSS) Mission under Kenya’s leadership for an initial 12-month period.

Resolution 2751, passed September 30, 2024, renewed that authorization for another year. Resolution 2793, adopted September 30, 2025, then transformed the MSS into the Gang Suppression Force.

That same resolution created a UN Support Office in Haiti (UNSOH), which provides logistics and operational support to the GSF, Haiti’s national police, and its armed forces.

The authorized ceiling for the force is 5,550 personnel, according to a UN press release from July 20, 2026, though a later UN statement cited the “planned strength” as 5,500. As of that July 20 count, only about 1,000 troops were actually deployed, a gap the Dominican Republic’s foreign minister flagged explicitly in Council remarks.

Who Is on the Ground

Kenya leads the force, which is “largely populated by Kenyan troops,” according to UN materials. Jamaica, Belize, Guatemala, El Salvador, and the Bahamas have also contributed personnel, and were thanked by name in the UN press release marking the MSS-to-GSF transition.

No source with a deployment figure newer than July 20, 2026, was found, and no country-by-country pledge breakdown specific to the GSF was located. The predecessor MSS force numbered “just over 1,000” personnel as of March 2025, per the US Congressional Research Service.

The AP reported it was not clear when funerals for the other victims of the Kenscoff attack would be held. The town hall in Kenscoff separately declared three days of mourning, according to the Haitian newspaper Le Nouvelliste.

More: Haiti news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happened in Kenscoff, Haiti?

The Viv Ansanm gang coalition attacked the hillside town of Kenscoff near Port-au-Prince overnight on August 23-24, 2026, including a church where residents had taken refuge. The UN says at least 47 people were killed, though Haitian officials confirmed 25 deaths with 15 people still missing.

What is the Gang Suppression Force?

The Gang Suppression Force (GSF) is an international security mission in Haiti, led by Kenya, that replaced the earlier Multinational Security Support Mission. It was authorized by UN Security Council Resolution 2793 in September 2025 to help Haitian police and armed forces fight gangs.

How many troops are deployed in Haiti?

About 1,000 of the authorized 5,550 personnel were deployed as of July 20, 2026, the most recent confirmed count. No newer deployment figure has been released since that date.

Did the UN Security Council pass a new resolution on Haiti?

No. The August 28, 2026 statement urging faster Gang Suppression Force deployment came from a Council briefing and press release, not a new binding resolution. The force’s mandate rests on earlier resolutions from 2023, 2024, and 2025.

When was the funeral for the Kenscoff victims?

The funeral was held on Sunday, August 30, 2026, at a Baptist church in Kenscoff, with hundreds of mourners attending. The service honored four of the people killed, and it was not clear when funerals for the other victims would take place.

Sources: Associated Press, PBS NewsHour, UN News, UN Press, Reuters, Al Jazeera, NPR, Miami Herald, Vant Bèf Info, Le Nouvelliste, HaitiLibre, UK Government (gov.uk), US Mission to the UN, US Congressional Research Service, Security Council Report.

World.title: Guyana Output Nears One Million Barrels Per Day as Uaru Ship Lands
World.content:
Guyana · ENERGY

Key Facts — What happened The Errea Wittu production vessel arrived offshore Guyana for the Uaru oil project.

— How big The vessel is built to produce about 250,000 barrels of oil per day.

— The catch Actual output was 869,000 barrels per day in June 2026, below peak capacity near 918,000.

— Who it hits The project raises government revenue and confirms ExxonMobil as operator, with Chevron now a partner.

— What comes next ExxonMobil guides to the fourth quarter of 2026 for first oil, while officials have floated September.

Guyana’s oil vessels can produce more than 900,000 barrels a day, though actual output has recently dipped. A new vessel for the Uaru project could push the country past one million barrels per day.

A floating production, storage and offloading vessel. The Errea Wittu is Guyana’s fifth, built for the Uaru project. (Photo: The Rio Times archive.)

Guyana’s oil vessels have capacity for more than 900,000 barrels per day, though June 2026 output was lower. A fifth vessel for the Uaru project should push the country past one million barrels per day.

Current Production and the Uaru Project

Guyana’s oil output depends on whether you mean actual production or capacity. The two figures are different, and reports often mix them up.

The country’s four current oil vessels have combined capacity of roughly 900,000 to 920,000 barrels per day. Actual production has recently run below that peak.

A fifth vessel, the Errea Wittu, arrived offshore in August 2026 for the Uaru project. It should push both capacity and output above one million barrels per day.

The Errea Wittu Vessel

The Errea Wittu is a floating production, storage and offloading vessel, known as an FPSO. It arrived offshore Guyana around August 20-21, 2026, according to Guyana’s government and local media.

This is Guyana’s fifth FPSO, confirmed by Guyana Chronicle and other outlets. It is built to produce about 250,000 barrels of oil per day, dedicated to the Uaru project.

The vessel can also handle 540 million cubic feet of gas a day. It can inject 350,000 barrels of water and store about two million barrels of crude.

What Is an FPSO?

An FPSO is a large ship that processes oil and stores it until tankers carry it away. Guyana uses these vessels because its oil fields sit far from shore.

Each vessel anchors above the oil field and connects to wells on the seabed. This lets companies produce oil in deep water without building a fixed platform.

FPSOs can later be moved to a new field once a project winds down. That flexibility makes them popular in deep offshore basins like Guyana’s.

Guyana’s Five FPSOs

Guyana already has four FPSOs producing oil before Errea Wittu. Liza Destiny works the Liza Phase 1 project, with a design capacity near 120,000 barrels per day.

Liza Unity serves Liza Phase 2, with a design capacity near 220,000 barrels per day. Prosperity works the Payara project, also near 220,000 barrels per day.

ONE GUYANA serves the Yellowtail project and can produce about 250,000 barrels per day. It began producing in August 2025, the newest vessel before Errea Wittu.

Uaru Project Details

The Uaru project covers three fields: Uaru, Mako and Snoek. ExxonMobil sanctioned it in April 2023 with an investment of about US$12.7 billion.

The project should recover more than 800 million barrels of oil over its lifetime. That estimate comes from ExxonMobil and independent industry analysts.

The development includes up to ten drill centers and 44 production and injection wells. Guyana’s government approved the plan after ExxonMobil submitted it in 2023.

First Oil: What the Operator Says

Sources differ on exactly when Uaru will start producing oil. Guyana’s government has pointed to September 2026 as a possible start date.

ExxonMobil, the project’s operator, has consistently guided to a fourth-quarter 2026 startup. That is the timeline most investors and analysts rely on.

Early output from Uaru is expected to start below the vessel’s full capacity. Production usually ramps up gradually over the following year.

Stabroek Block Ownership

The Stabroek Block is operated by ExxonMobil, which holds a 45% stake. Chevron holds 30%, and China’s CNOOC holds the remaining 25%.

Some older reports still list Hess as the 30% partner. That information is now outdated.

The block holds more than 11 billion barrels of discovered recoverable oil and gas resources. It sits roughly 120 miles off Guyana’s coast in deep water.

Offshore oil activity off Guyana. The country averaged about 750,000 barrels per day in 2025. (Photo: The Rio Times archive.)

The Ownership Change Explained

Chevron bought Hess in a deal completed on July 18, 2025, gaining Hess’s Guyana stake. ExxonMobil and CNOOC had tried to block the sale using contract rights.

An arbitration panel in Paris ruled against ExxonMobil and CNOOC in 2025. ExxonMobil said it disagreed with the ruling but accepted Chevron as a partner.

Chevron’s chief financial officer has said the Hess assets, including Guyana, add about 250,000 barrels per day to Chevron’s overall production growth.

Production History

Guyana’s oil production averaged about 750,000 barrels per day across all of 2025. Output first passed 900,000 barrels per day on average in November 2025.

Production has since fluctuated. It eased to 869,000 barrels per day in June 2026, the latest confirmed month, according to government data reported by OilNOW.

Guyana has produced oil since December 2019, when the Liza field first came online. Output has grown quickly with each new project since then.

How Guyana Earns Money From Oil

Guyana’s contract with ExxonMobil sets a 2% royalty on all oil produced and sold. After companies recover their costs, remaining profits are split 50-50 with the government.

Guyana earned about US$1.2 billion in royalty and profit-oil payments in the second quarter of 2026. That brought first-half 2026 earnings to almost US$2 billion, according to OilNOW.

Guyana’s finance minister has projected total 2026 oil earnings near US$2.8 billion. That includes profit oil, royalties and one signing bonus for new exploration.

The Natural Resource Fund

Guyana saves its oil money in the Natural Resource Fund, held at the Bank of Guyana. The fund passed US$4 billion for the first time in mid-2026.

Money can only leave the fund for national development or disaster response. Parliament must approve every withdrawal before it can be spent.

Since 2020, the fund has taken in roughly US$10.5 billion in oil money. About US$6.7 billion of that has already moved into the national budget.

Future Production Targets

ExxonMobil has said it aims to reach about 1.3 million barrels per day in Guyana by 2027. That would require projects beyond Uaru to come online.

The company has approved a seventh offshore development in the Stabroek Block. Each new project also brings jobs and contracts for Guyanese companies.

ExxonMobil is also studying a Hammerhead project that could add further capacity. These projects aim to keep Guyana’s output rising through the rest of the decade.

What Comes Next

Guyana’s oil output should keep climbing once Uaru begins producing. The exact timing depends on whether the government’s September estimate or ExxonMobil’s later guidance proves right.

Either way, the Errea Wittu FPSO marks another step in Guyana’s rapid rise as an oil producer. The country now ranks among the fastest-growing oil economies in the world.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Guyana’s current oil production?

Actual production was 869,000 barrels a day in June 2026, the latest confirmed month. Capacity across existing vessels is higher, near 900,000 to 920,000 barrels a day.

What is the Errea Wittu FPSO?

It is Guyana’s fifth floating production vessel, built to produce about 250,000 barrels a day. It serves the Uaru project and arrived offshore in August 2026.

When will Uaru start producing oil?

Guyana’s government has suggested September 2026. ExxonMobil, the operator, guides to the fourth quarter of 2026.

Who owns the Stabroek Block?

ExxonMobil operates the block with a 45% stake. Chevron holds 30%, after buying Hess’s stake in July 2025, and CNOOC holds 25%.

Sources: OilNOW; Rio Times Online; Guyana Chronicle; ExxonMobil; U.S. Energy Information Administration; Rigzone; Kaieteur News.

World.title: Why is Daniel Ortega Shutting Nicaragua’s Opposition Out of Elections?
World.content:
Nicaragua approved a constitutional reform that bars the opposition from participating in elections and extends Daniel Ortega’s term in office, a measure aimed at securing a presidential succession within the family of the octogenarian former guerrilla leader.

Ortega and his wife and co-president, Rosario Murillo, tightened their grip further by pushing through the amendment, which closes the door to a political transition after two decades of rule marked by the concentration of power and harsh repression.

What was approved?

The National Assembly, controlled by the Sandinista National Liberation Front (FSLN), voted Tuesday to prohibit “traitors to the homeland,” people linked to attempted coups, or those who call for “military intervention” or “economic blockades” from participating in elections. The couple routinely levels those accusations against all their opponents.

Lawmakers also extended the terms of current elected officials and the heads of the Armed Forces from six to seven years. The reform also granted new powers to electoral authorities to dissolve political parties and sanction candidates. If reelected in late 2028, Ortega and Murillo could remain in power until 2036.

The reform must be ratified during a second legislative session in January 2027. In practice, it would pave the way for a one-party system controlled by the FSLN.

What is the objective?

Ortega, 80, and Murillo, 75, tightened their control over society following the 2018 protests, whose repression left more than 300 people dead, according to the United Nations. The co-presidents describe the demonstrations as an attempted coup sponsored by the United States.

Thousands of people went into exile following the protests, including opposition leaders, intellectuals, journalists and members of the clergy who were stripped of their nationality after being accused of “treason.” During the 2021 election campaign, Ortega’s main rivals were imprisoned before the vote, leaving virtually no domestic opposition today.

Ortega suffers from lupus and kidney problems and has difficulty walking. Most of his children hold key government positions, while opposition figures warn that an internal purge is underway to secure a family succession. Rebecca Bill, president of the Inter-American Dialogue, said Ortega and Murillo do not need tougher measures to win elections because the opposition “has already been crushed and democratic institutions destroyed.”

“The objective is to ensure there is as little uncertainty as possible about what happens after Ortega. Elections create uncertainty, as do independent institutions and a genuine opposition, which is why they have eliminated all three,” Bill said. Extending their terms would also allow the co-presidents to outlast the current period of pressure from U.S. President Donald Trump and postpone any possible negotiations over electoral conditions, according to former Nicaraguan lawmaker Eliseo Núñez.

What could the consequences be?

The United States on Wednesday urged its partners to sever ties with Nicaragua, arguing that “dictatorships” should not enjoy the political and economic benefits afforded to democracies. Washington, Nicaragua’s largest trading partner, has already imposed sanctions on government figures and is pushing for a meeting of foreign ministers from the Organization of American States (OAS) to consider measures against Managua.

The European Union also condemned the amendment before it was approved. “The international community needs to coordinate more effectively and raise the cost of repression in a targeted manner, while avoiding measures that primarily punish ordinary Nicaraguans,” Bill said.

World.title: How El Nino is choking the Panama Canal
World.content:
The Panama Canal will restrict the number of vessels transiting the crucial waterway from Friday for the second time ever due to drought caused by the El Nino climate phenomenon. Five percent of global trade passes through the canal that connects the Pacific Ocean with the Atlantic.

The waterway is set to reduce daily traffic from 36 to 32 ships a day in an effort to conserve water amid a severe drought likely to last until mid-2027. Canal authorities are also reducing the permitted draft of vessels — how deep they sit in the water — from 15.24 to 14.63 meters.

Panama has declared an emergency over El Nino, which raises surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean and causes global changes in winds and rainfall as well as erratic weather conditions. The canal’s incoming administrator Ilya Espino de Marotta has acknowledged the current “challenging” conditions.

Nothing without water

The 80-kilometer (50-mile) canal draws on freshwater that comes mainly from rainfall and is stored in artificial lakes. Without water, its locks that lift and lower ships at the beginning and end of the journey would not function. Each transiting ship requiers about 200 million liters of water, which is then discharged into the sea.

Water “is the most important resource for operations,” but “between April and August the accumulated rainfall deficit was 35.8 percent below the historical average,” the canal’s water manager Erick Cordoba said. And there are “no signs of recovery in the short term,” Cordoba added.

No signs of recovery

Forecasts indicate that the 2027 dry season, normally between January and April, will start a little earlier than usual and extend into May. In 2023 and 2024, El Nino forced a reduction in daily transits to 22 and the maximum draft to 13.41 meters.

That led to 20 percent fewer vessels and a 17 percent drop in tonnage, not to mention longer lines of ships queuing up. Further restrictions could follow those imposed on Friday. “If we don’t manage to fill the lakes in November, we’re going to have to tighten our belts,” former canal administrator Jorge Quijano said.

Worldwide repercussions

Long-lasting restrictions will lead to “higher shipping costs and longer waiting times” and therefore higher prices for consumers, Rebecca Bill Chavez, president of the Inter-American Dialogue said. A ship loses around 200 containers for every 30-centimeter draft decrease, according to Quijano.

That amounts to hundreds of units for large vessels that can carry up to 16,000. “We’re going to see a significant impact on the container sector,” which is the canal’s biggest source of revenue, he said. But Danish shipping company Maersk believes it is still “too early” to “speculate” about the impact.

The route mainly connects China, South Korea and Japan with the United States — the origin or destination of seven in ten containers that pass through the canal. Rising costs could “potentially affect US trade,” said analyst Natasha Lindstaedt of Britain’s University of Essex. If he wanted to, US President Donald Trump could argue “that trust and reliability in the channel have been lost,” Lindstaedt said.

The US-Israel war on Iran has pushed up traffic in the Panama Canal given the standstill the conflict caused in the Strait of Hormuz, through which around a fifth of the world’s oil and gas normally travels. The difficulties on both routes “put real pressure on global supply chains,” noted Bill.

Future-proofing

The canal authority plans to build a new 4,600-hectare reservoir on the Indio River to the west as a way to limit the effects of future droughts on operations. But this project would not be ready before 2031.

The canal’s watershed also supplies drinking water to half of Panama’s 4.6 million inhabitants via infrastructure that was designed almost a century ago.

World.title: Belize City mechanic charged in fatal Phillip Goldson Highway accident that killed 77-year-old Erleen Gillett
World.content:
Belize City mechanic charged in fatal Phillip Goldson Highway accident that killed 77-year-old Erleen Gillett

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 58-year-old Belize City mechanic and supervisor has been arraigned on three traffic-related charges stemming from last week’s fatal road traffic accident that claimed the life of 77-year-old Erleen Elizabeth Gillett of Burrell Boom Village.

Gregory Nicholas appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Thursday, where he was charged with manslaughter by negligence, causing death by careless conduct, and driving a motor vehicle without due care and attention.

No plea was taken because the charges are indictable.

There was no objection to bail, and Nicholas was granted bail in the sum of $6,000 with one surety of the same amount. As conditions of his bail, he must surrender his passport, cannot leave the jurisdiction without permission from the court, and must report to the Belama Police Station every two weeks on a Friday.

He is due back in court on October 9, 2026, for disclosure.

The charges arise from a fatal collision at about 11:00 a.m. on Thursday, August 27, along the Phillip Goldson Highway near Enriquez Martinez & Sons Ltd.

Police allege Nicholas was driving a gold Dodge Caravan toward Belize City when Gillett, who was crossing the highway, stepped from the median divider into the path of the vehicle. She was struck and reportedly hit the windshield before falling onto the pavement.

Gillett was transported to the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital, where she was pronounced dead on arrival.

Nicholas was subsequently detained, his vehicle was impounded, and a blood sample was obtained. Police also served him with a Notice of Intended Prosecution.

A post-mortem examination conducted on September 1 determined Gillett’s cause of death to be multiple blunt force trauma injuries due to a road traffic accident.

World.title: ‘What if something happens?’ Parents blast school policy leaving children outside locked gate before 7:30 a.m. at Raymond Sheppard Primary
World.content:
‘What if something happens?’ Parents blast school policy leaving children outside locked gate before 7:30 a.m. at Raymond Sheppard Primary

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A group of concerned parents is calling on the administration of Raymond Sheppard Nazarene Primary School in Roaring Creek Village to reconsider its morning drop-off policy, arguing that children who arrive before 7:30 a.m. are being left outside the school compound without supervision.

The concern was raised in a letter sent to Breaking Belize News on Friday morning. According to the parents, the school recently circulated a notice advising that the gate will remain closed until 7:30 a.m., with the school bell reportedly ringing at 8:00 a.m. The notice lists the official drop-off time as 7:30 a.m. and pickup between 2:30 and 3:00 p.m.

The parents say the arrangement creates difficulties for those who must report to work early and have little choice but to drop their children off between 7:00 and 7:30 a.m.

One parent alleged that on Thursday morning several children were waiting outside when a teacher arrived, opened the gate to allow herself and her own children onto the compound, and then locked the gate again, leaving the other students outside.

“This raises a serious question: Who is responsible for the children who arrive before 7:30 AM? What happens if something happens to a child while they are waiting outside the locked school gate?” the parents wrote.

They are asking the school to consider opening the gate at 7:00 a.m. or establishing a safe, supervised area where students who arrive early can wait.

“Children should not be left outside a locked school gate without supervision. Their safety should always be the priority,” the letter stated.

Raymond Sheppard Nazarene Primary is a government-aided primary school located in Roaring Creek Village, Cayo District, according to the Ministry of Education’s school directory.

BBN has not independently verified the allegation involving the teacher, and no response from the school administration was immediately available.

World.title: “The timing is not right”: Mahler pushes back on hotel tax increase
World.content:
“The timing is not right”: Mahler pushes back on hotel tax increase

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Minister of Tourism Anthony Mahler says the announcement of a proposed increase in the hotel accommodation tax came out too early, and that discussions on it have been running for nearly two years.

Speaking to 7 News, Mahler said he met with the Belize Tourism Board’s Board of Directors before taking a Cabinet paper, and that both major industry organisations were present.

“There has been negotiations and discussions about this for almost 2 years,” he said. “In fact, private sector individuals have met with the Ministry of Finance, the Prime Minister and other people without the BTB there, and they knew it was coming.”

Mahler said he personally does not believe the timing is right and has told both the BTIA and the Belize Hotel Association as much.

He tied the proposal directly to sargassum.

“We have a significant problem in sargassum. It is killing us on the coastal communities that are important for our tourism product. How can we fund this?”

Mahler said around $20 million in equipment is needed to fight it, and that BTB has funded the effort alone so far.

“I had always opposed new taxes on the tourism industry, always, and that is a fact.”

World.title: Two charged after 625 pounds of seafood seized on Hattieville-Boom Road
World.content:
Two charged after 625 pounds of seafood seized on Hattieville-Boom Road

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The Belize Fisheries Department has seized a substantial quantity of seafood suspected to have been illegally imported into the country.

Fisheries officers, with assistance from the Belize Police Department, intercepted a pickup truck along the Hattieville-Boom Road following a brief pursuit during an early morning enforcement operation on Thursday.

An inspection of the vehicle turned up 290 pounds of tilapia fillets, 335 pounds of jumbo shrimp and 14 octopus.

The vehicle and the seafood were seized and secured.

Two adult males were detained and charged with offences relating to the alleged illegal importation of fisheries products. They are expected to appear before the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Friday.

The Fisheries Department reminded the public that importing fish and fisheries products into Belize requires the appropriate permits and full compliance with applicable laws.

The Department said unauthorised importation poses food safety and phytosanitary risks, and undermines legitimate local businesses that follow the regulatory requirements.

The Department thanked the Belize Police Department for its assistance.

World.title: $100,000 unaccounted for at a government school
World.content:
$100,000 unaccounted for at a government school

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): An audit has been completed at Louisiana Government School after reports that roughly $100,000 went missing over several years.

Minister of Education Francis Fonseca confirmed the audit is done, and that the next step is meetings with the principal, the bursar and others working in finance at the school.

Whether those meetings have happened, he could not say.

“I haven’t gotten any feedback if they’ve had the meeting yet,” Fonseca said.

He was clear on what should follow if the audit found what it was looking for.

“If there are any misappropriation that took place, they would make sure that those who were involved would be held responsible.”

Government schools operate on tight budgets, funded by taxpayers and supplemented by fees and fundraising that parents contribute to. A sum of that size, missing across multiple years, is money that did not reach classrooms, supplies or students.

Nothing has been made public from the audit itself and nobody has been named.

We will keep following the story.

Should the audit findings be made public?

World.title: “It was just time”: Espat explains Gamboa’s transfer after 11 years at SPU
World.content:
“It was just time”: Espat explains Gamboa’s transfer after 11 years at SPU

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Minister of Home Affairs Julius Espat says the transfer of Superintendent Aaron Gamboa from the Special Patrol Unit came down to management, not misconduct.

Gamboa led the SPU for 11 years, possibly a record for any police unit in Belize. He was moved with immediate effect on Monday.

Speaking to 7 News via Zoom, Espat said Gamboa is already officially retired and had been serving on an extension.

“He has been officially retired for, I think, six months now, if I’m not mistaken, and he was given an extension,” Espat said. “But if you have to plan for the future, you have to be able to look at things and bring in new people.”

He said the Commissioner recommended the transfer to a more administrative position.

“SPU for 11 years, that’s a good run. And we need other people now to have an opportunity.”

Espat was clear on his reasoning.

“There’s no bad intention in this move. But change is necessary, especially in the Police Department, it’s necessary to not have a commander in one position for too long.”

World.title: Rain targets the south while most of Belize stays warm and mostly dry
World.content:
Rain targets the south while most of Belize stays warm and mostly dry

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Conditions are slightly moist and marginally unstable over Belize today, according to the National Meteorological Service.

Skies will be cloudy with sunny breaks this morning, becoming partly cloudy this afternoon and tonight.

A few early morning showers and isolated thunderstorms are likely to affect mainly the southern districts this morning, and again late tonight into early tomorrow morning. Elsewhere, showers or thunderstorms will be isolated.

Inland temperatures will reach 96 degrees Fahrenheit before dropping to 74 overnight. The coast reaches 90 with a low of 84, while the hills stay at 84 and fall to 68.

At sea, winds will blow from the east to southeast at 5 to 15 knots with a light chop and waves of 2 to 4 feet.

Saturday brings mostly dry and warm weather across most of the country with only isolated showers, except for the southern districts where there is a high chance a few showers and isolated thunderstorms will persist Saturday morning.

Tropical cyclone formation is not expected over the region during the next 48 hours.

Sunset comes at 6:03pm.

World.title: Belize Fisheries Department Intercepts and Seizes Suspected Illegally Imported Jumbo Shrimp and Other Seafood
World.content:
Belize Fisheries Department Intercepts and Seizes Suspected Illegally Imported Jumbo Shrimp and Other Seafood

GOVERNMENT OF BELIZE PRESS RELEASE: During an early morning fisheries enforcement operation on Thursday, September 3, 2026, Fisheries Officers, with assistance from the Belize Police Department, intercepted a pickup truck along the Hattieville-Boom Road following a brief pursuit. A subsequent inspection of the vehicle resulted in the seizure of a substantial quantity of seafood suspected to have been illegally imported into Belize, including:

• 290 lbs. of tilapia fillets;

• 335 lbs. of jumbo shrimp; and

• 14 octopus.

The vehicle and seafood products were seized and secured by the Belize Fisheries Department. Two adult males were detained and subsequently charged with offences relating to the alleged illegal importation of fisheries products. They are expected to appear before the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Friday, September 4, 2026.

The public is reminded that the importation of fish and fisheries products into Belize requires the appropriate permits and must comply fully with applicable laws and regulations. Unauthorized or unregulated importation of fisheries products is prohibited. Such activities can pose food safety and phytosanitary risks. Illegal importation also undermines legitimate local businesses and persons who comply with the established regulatory requirements. The Fisheries Department therefore urges all importers, traders, and members of the public to ensure that all fisheries products entering Belize are properly authorized and meet the applicable regulatory and health requirements.

The Department further reminds members of the public that suspected illegal fishing activities and other violations of fisheries laws should be reported to the Fisheries Department. Information provided by members of the public plays an important role in supporting enforcement efforts and protecting Belize’s fisheries resources. Compliance with fisheries laws is a shared responsibility, and safeguarding Belize’s fisheries resources requires the collective efforts of the Department and the public. Illegal activities can undermine the sustainability of our fisheries and negatively affect the livelihoods of communities and fishers who depend on these resources.

The Belize Fisheries Department continues to work closely with national enforcement agencies to combat illegal fishing and the unauthorized importation and trade of fisheries products. The Department thanks the Belize Police Department for its assistance during this operation.

World.title: Gift from the heart
World.content:
Minister of Health and Wellness Dr Christopher Tufton (second right) checks out specialised equipment donated to the University Hospital of the West Indies (UHWI) by Abigaye Smythe (second left), founder and managing director of I Have a Heart Foundation, on Thursday, as consultant cardiothoracic surgeon Dr Sunil Stephenson explains its function. Sharing in the moment is chief executive officer at UHWI Dr Sydney Powell. The equipment will give surgeons at the hospital the ability to perform minimally invasive open-heart surgeries. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

A cardiac patient facing her sixth surgery this December has donated US$4,000 in specialised equipment to the University Hospital of the West Indies (UHWI), directly upgrading its training resources and capabilities for minimally invasive open-heart surgery.

Speaking at the handover ceremony of the medical equipment at UHWI on Thursday, Abigaye Smythe, founder and managing director of I Have a Heart Foundation, revealed that leading this initiative is her life’s purpose.

Describing her connection to the project as lifelong, Smythe shared that she has battled heart disease since the age of seven, when she first began experiencing symptoms.

At 19, Smythe was delivered life-altering news when she was diagnosed with arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy — the same disease that took her mother’s life. The rare genetic condition causes fat and scar tissue to replace healthy heart muscle, disrupting electrical signals and triggering abnormal heart rhythms.

Since her diagnosis, the philanthropist has undergone five surgeries at UHWI, making this donation a profoundly personal milestone.

“Because of my own journey, and understanding the fact that cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death in Jamaica, I don’t advocate for heart disease patients from a distance. I understand what it means to be one [a cardiac patient], and I understand what it means to lose one. So this is my purpose. And that is why today is so meaningful,” she said.

“I’m not simply donating equipment to a hospital, I’m giving back to an institution that has cared for me, from testing and diagnosis in 2011, through five surgeries between 2012 and 2019, several emergency room visits and hospitalisations in-between, and an institution that will care for me again in December when I undergo my sixth heart surgery. I am investing in my fellow heart disease patients. I’m also investing in my country, in Jamaica,” added Smythe.

The donation builds on a partnership between the I Have a Heart Foundation, the Organisation for International Development, and a medical team from New York’s Montefiore Einstein Hospital. Since 2019, this partnership has provided more than $120 million in free open-heart surgeries at UHWI for 60 financially vulnerable patients.

Smythe noted that while this collaboration has been highly beneficial for both the patients and UHWI, she realised the hospital still lacked the capacity to perform minimally invasive open-heart surgeries without foreign assistance. She highlighted this gap as the driving force behind her efforts to lobby for and secure the new equipment.

“During the 2025 cardiac mission, the international medical team brought their specialised tools to perform minimally invasive open-heart surgery, and this resulted in the first such procedure being performed at UHWI, and possibly the first in Jamaica.
