They returned [home] and so did their equipment. And they came back in March 2026, for the mission. And when they performed the surgeries, and when they left, so did their equipment again,” she explained.

“So I said, ‘Okay, I want us to be independent, I want us to have our own, I want us to be able to perform minimally invasive open-heart surgeries outside of the mission’. And that is where the begging began. Thanks to our sponsors, we were able to raise the money, and we turned that vision into a reality, and purchased the equipment,” Smythe explained.

Looking ahead, she hopes this contribution will elevate care at UHWI, arguing that the island has no shortage of medical skill or talent but requires some help securing the tools to match that expertise.

“I’m excited to see how this capacity, this capability, will continue to grow. Today is not simply a handover, it is an investment in Jamaican lives, in our health care system, our medical professionals, and the future of cardiac care. My hope is that one day a Jamaican will never have to ask, ‘Can this procedure be done in Jamaica?’ They will simply know that it can be done here, and it can be done here at the University Hospital of the West Indies,” she said.

Expressing gratitude for the donation, Dr Sunil Stephenson, consultant cardiothoracic surgeon at UHWI, told the Jamaica Observer that the equipment was a necessity as the hospital continues to observe an increase in cardiac patients yearly.

“For a year, we perform about 80 to 90 heart surgeries. As a matter of fact, most deaths… in Jamaica are caused by cardiovascular diseases. So we do see quite a bit of patients who require our services and it’s mainly related to lifestyle illnesses. Some are genetic but most of what we do see is related to chronic non-communicable diseases. So there’s definitely an increase,” said Dr Stephenson.

He added that the equipment gave patients greater access to minimally invasive surgery which, he noted, offered significant advantages.

“The benefit in the sense that there’s less pain, they recover much faster. There’s still a shorter time in the ICU, and they need less time on the ventilator. So they recover much quicker and they’re more comfortable. And for females, they prefer the fact that they don’t have an incision in the middle of the chest because they’re very concerned about how the scar would look. So these instruments will actually help us to be able to do these procedures, and extend these procedures to the entire Jamaica, because that’s the population that we serve,” said the doctor.

For his part, Health and Wellness Minister Dr Christopher Tufton thanked Smythe and her team for the donation, and expressed confidence in the quality of staff at UHWI, adding that he had no doubt that the equipment would be put to good use.

“I just want to embrace the concept of ongoing effort to improve, and to make the services more efficient, embrace the concept of volunteerism and charity and gifting, and just say that for health, we have to see ourselves as a community and work together as a community. So thank you again, we appreciate it, and we certainly wish you the very best in terms of your own struggles and work, both as a foundation but also individually,” Tufton said.

World.title: Fit for purpose
World.content:
Mico CARE Centre interventionist Collette Demetrius (right) shows one of the centre’s retrofitted classrooms to (from left) permanent secretary at the Ministry of Education, Skills, Youth, and Information Dr Kasan Troupe; The Mico University College President Dr Asburn Pinnock; and portfolio manager, education and special needs, Digicel Foundation Jamilia Crooks Brown at Thursday’s official opening of the facility that caters to children with special needs. (Photo: Karl Mclarty)

AFTER more than four decades of supporting children with special needs, The Mico University College’s Child Assessment and Research in Education (CARE) Centre has upgraded its learning environment, unveiling renovations to five classrooms aimed at creating better spaces for students to learn, develop, and thrive.

The project, valued at approximately $24 million, was done in collaboration with Digicel Foundation and partners and provides classrooms with specialised sensory and occupational therapy equipment designed to aid concentration, emotional regulation, and physical engagement.

“The classrooms before were just regular classrooms. The rooms were very old, wooden floors, old aluminum windows, and so on, which are from the 1980s. Renovating these rooms makes the learning space more modern, more accommodating. So what we’ve done, we have looked at the needs of the clients that we serve,” Micro CARE Centre Director Dr Sharon Anderson-Morgan explained after the official handing over and ribbon-cutting ceremony on Thursday.

“So the rooms are now fit for purpose, they’re not just a regular classroom. We have children who are fidgety, for example, because they have attention-deficit disorder or any kind of disorder that causes them to want to move all the time. So we have the kick bands on the chair, they can put their feet on the chair. We have the wobbly things at the end of it, so they can rock and can move,” she added.

Anderson-Morgan pointed to several challenges faced by the institution prior to its renovation.

“The rooms were very, very hot. When you have spaces that are hot and you have bodies moving around, people are going to get a little agitated sometimes. So we’ve had children who react terribly to the heat. For example, we had some of our kids with autism and it gets hot and they would just start screaming,” she said.

“Also, we could not move the furniture as we would like to, because the old furniture did not allow for us to. If you’re going to move the chairs, it’s going to scrape the floor, some children are sensitive to that. They didn’t fit together the way these fit together,” Anderson-Morgan said, adding that the lighting at the facility was also an issue.

“We had these old fluorescent lights that also affected some children. There were children who would look up because they’re hypersensitive to visual stimuli. They would get scared because they think they’re seeing patterns in the ceiling. I remember one day we had to cover a portion of the ceiling with paper because the child kept looking up there because he thought he was seeing something else,” said Anderson-Morgan.

She underscored that the renovations will not only benefit students who enter the facility through its intervention programme, but also those who come in for assessment.

“Sometimes children come here for assessment and they are dysregulated. The clinicians now have the centre space to take them, calm them down before they can assess them, because before, sometimes they can’t get to assess them unless they come back because a child is screaming, running all over the place,” Anderson-Morgan said, adding that the centre assesses close to 1,000 children yearly.

She hastened to add that despite the centre being known to conduct assessments, its services extend beyond that.

“We do assessment, we do intervention, not just academic, because we have speech therapy. And we have occupational therapy, behaviour therapy, we have behaviour therapy for one group, and that’s only because we don’t have an on-site behaviour therapist, so we have to bring in the service. And we also have counselling services, we have a counselling centre up there, where even some of our kids in the intervention programme, they also receive counselling as needed, and sometimes their families need it as well,” she explained.

Permanent secretary in the Ministry of Education, Skills, Youth, and Information Kasan Troupe welcomed the upgraded facility and lauded Digicel Foundation and partners for their investment in the special needs sector.

“We’re going to have a room that teachers will be exposed to improve opportunities to train and integrate technology because it is technology-enabled. We’re going to have a room that will build confidence in learners because here they have a safer space, a modern space that they can make mistakes, learn and grow and be strong because they are fully supported with specialists that can train them and support them in the way they should grow,” she said.

“You’re going to have learners who cannot communicate confidently. You’re going to have learners who will learn new skills so they can transform their whole realities in the future. That’s the promise of this investment,” Troupe added.

The Mico University College CARE Centre states on its website that it was established in 1980 as a centre of excellence, dedicated to child assessment and research in education. It was formed through a partnership between The Netherlands and Jamaican governments.

World.title: Malie Donn releases debut album Golden Child
World.content:
Malie Donn.

Dancehall artiste Malie Donn today released his debut studio album, The Golden Child, marking a major milestone for the entertainer who has steadily carved out a place among dancehall’s new generation.

The 21-track project, released through VP Records, follows several years of building his name with songs including Van Cleef, Body Tea, V6, Dirty Mirror, Suspect, Crook and many others.

“The Golden Child represents everything that brought me to this point: the pressure, the growth, the wins and the lessons,” Malie Donn said. “This project gives people a chance to hear more of who I am as an artist, where I want to take the music next and the versatility I bring.”

On Thursday, Malie Donn released the album’s title track, Golden Child, featuring fellow dancehall artiste Squash. The collaboration pairs Malie Donn’s melodic delivery with Squash’s distinctive style, while exploring themes of confidence, ambition and resilience that also run through the wider project.

The official music video for Golden Child also premiered on Thursday, providing the final lead-in to the album. Born Kimalie Hylton, Malie Donn is originally from Jones Avenue, Spanish Town, St Catherine, but grew up in Waterford, Portmore.

His passion for music dates back to his days as a student at Waterford Primary School and developed further while he attended Bridgeport High School. Malie Donn has emerged as one of the acts in dancehall’s newer wave, building a catalogue that has helped expand his audience locally and internationally.

The Golden Child also continues his relationship with VP Records. In 2024, he released The Grand Rising EP through the label, followed by the Leak the Hard Drive EP in 2025.

The album was preceded by Holiday, which arrived on August 7 alongside its official music video and offered listeners an early glimpse of a different side of Malie Donn’s artistry.

For Malie Donn, the release of his first full-length album represents an opportunity to present a more complete picture of himself beyond the individual songs that first brought him attention.

World.title: GOJ TAPS MARKET FOR US$1B
World.content:
The Government of Jamaica (GOJ) has gone to the international capital markets to raise a US$1 billion ($157.62 billion) unsecured bond to support its liability management strategy and budgetary objectives.

The prospectus was published on Wednesday through the United States Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), three weeks after GOJ filed its registration statement to issue debt securities. According to a roadshow document seen by the Jamaica Observer, US$600 million is to be used to fund a tender/exchange offer, with the balance earmarked for general budgetary purposes. A source close to the matter also indicated that the new bond is expected to mature in 2037.

At the same time, GOJ launched the tender/exchange offer for holders of the three existing global bonds, tying the new borrowing directly to its wider effort to manage the country’s external debt.

“The Invitation is part of a broader program of Jamaica to proactively manage its external public debt,” stated the tender invitation to holders of the old bonds/notes.

The Government currently has US$837.53 million outstanding on its April 2028 notes, which carry a 6.75 per cent interest rate. The 2036 and 2039 notes have US$250 million and US$1.24 billion outstanding, respectively.

International Financing Review (ifre.com) reported that GOJ began holding fixed-income investor meetings on September 3, likely in connection with the new bond issuance, which will be listed on the Euro MTF Market of the Luxembourg Stock Exchange. Citigroup Global Markets Inc. and Scotia Capital (USA) Inc. are serving as deal managers and joint lead underwriters for the transaction.

If the value of bonds tendered exceeds GOJ’s maximum purchase amount, the government can determine how much of each series it will accept, applying different proration factors where necessary. This means it could accept less than the full amount tendered by holders of any of the eligible notes.

The new tender offer opened on September 2 and will expire on September 9, unless extended or terminated at GOJ’s discretion. Settlement is expected to be completed by September 17.

“The invitation is not conditioned upon any minimum participation of any series of Old Notes but is conditioned on, among other things, the pricing and closing of an international capital markets transaction in an amount and on terms and conditions acceptable to Jamaica,” stated the GOJ release.

The Government last executed a transaction of this nature in October 2023, when it spent US$237.4 million to redeem three notes with a nominal value of US$233.2 million. At the time, GOJ repurchased approximately US$99.7 million in two separate 2025 notes and US$165.15 million of the April 2028 notes. The tender on the 2028 notes represented 11.6 per cent of the amount outstanding before the GOJ offer.

That tender offer coincided with Jamaica’s first Jamaican dollar (JMD)-linked bond issuance on the international capital markets, worth $46.6 billion, or US$300 million. The instrument carried a 9.625 per cent interest rate and matures in November 2030.

Through the new tender offer, GOJ can extend the maturity profile of its foreign debt and reduce the amount that will need to be refinanced in the near term, in keeping with its broader debt management strategy.

The transaction, however, comes against the backdrop of a difficult start to the government’s 2026/27 fiscal year. According to the central government accounts for April to July 2026, revenue and grants came in eight per cent below budget at $353.84 billion for the four-month period. That was despite $18.04 billion in new taxes being implemented for the current fiscal year, with one company reporting that it paid $454 million in special consumption tax on sweetened drinks for May and June.

The revenue shortfall was largely driven by tax collections coming in $21.32 billion below budget, including a $13.27-billion shortfall in taxes on companies. Expenditure was also six per cent below budget at $387.27 billion. The Government recorded a fiscal deficit of $33.43 billion, wider than the budgeted $30.89 billion.

An overall surplus of $10.28 billion was recorded, compared with a budgeted deficit of $57.86 billion, largely because loan receipts of $130.62 billion were twice the budgeted amount. Based on the roadshow document, a successful bond raise would leave US$400 million, or approximately $63.05 billion, available for general budgetary purposes in the 2026/27 fiscal year.

“The effects of this natural disaster may continue to adversely affect the development and performance of key sectors of the country’s economy,” GOJ’s prospectus stated, regarding the impact of Hurricane Melissa.

The warning was included among the risk factors outlining Jamaica’s exposure to external shocks, including risks to the tourism sector.

The prospectus added that volatility in global energy prices may also contribute to higher domestic energy costs for Jamaica and could place upward pressure on inflation.

“While the full extent of the impact of these conflicts remains to be seen as of the date of this prospectus supplement, the effects of such conflicts could negatively affect Jamaica’s economic growth, inflation and fiscal revenues,” it said.

Final pricing details, including the interest rate on the new GOJ bond, are expected to be revealed in the coming days. Until then, recent sovereign issues elsewhere in teh Caribbean ofer some indication of where borrowing costs have been landing. Trinidad & Tobago refinanced a US$1-billion bond in January at 6.50 per cent for 10 years before issuing a US$800-million bond at 6.20 per cent for 12 years. Trinidad currently carries a higher international credit rating than Jamaica, although S&P Global Ratings has assigned it a negative outlook, compared with Jamaica’s stable outlook.

World.title: ELITE COMPANY!
World.content:
Oblique Seville (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

WORLD champion Oblique Seville will be gunning for his first Wanda Diamond League title when he lines up in the men’s 100m on the opening day of the two-day Diamond League athletics final at King Baudouin Stadium in Brussels, Belgium.

Seville is one of nine Jamaicans down to compete today with another eight set for Saturday.

He is coming off a confidence boosting win in Poland on August 23, and is hoping to join 100m sprinters Usain Bolt, Asafa Powell and Ackeem Blake as Jamaican men who have won the Diamond trophy.

Following his win in Poland, in which he clocked 9.83 seconds to break the meet record, Seville had said he was focused on ending the season on a high.

“I am just having fun. There are great things ahead of me. Many sprinters ran under 10.00s, that is really special. For the rest of the season I would like to keep winning and the next win should be in Brussels.”

He will have his hands full and will need to be at his best as he lines up against a tough field that includes Nigeria’s Kayinsola Ajayi, who has beaten the Jamaican twice this year, Commonwealth Games champion Emmanuel Eseme of Cameroon, Akani Simbine of South Africa and Trayvon Bromell of the United States.

Jamaicans have won at least one Diamond League title in the 16 years that the global series has been contested.

Today, Rushell Clayton, in the women’s 400m hurdles; Orlando Bennett, in the 110m hurdles; Tajay Gayle and Wayne Pinnock, in the men’s long jump; Romaine Beckford, in the men’s high jump; Roje Stona, in the men’s discus throw; Danniel Thomas-Dodd, in the women’s shot put; and Ackelia Smith, in the women’s triple jump, will be hoping to add their names to the list.

Clayton, who is coming off a win at the prestigious ISTAF Berlin on Sunday, has been consistent through the Diamond League series.

The event in Brussels could be decided between points leader Emma Zapletalova of Slovakia, who lost in the series for the first time after she hit a hurdle in Zurich as world leader Anna Cockrell sped to victory.

Veteran American Dalilah Muhammad, who has announced she will retire at the end of this season, and Belgium’s Paulien Couckuyt are expected to challenge for podium places.

Bennett, the World Athletics Championships medallist, is to take on a handful of Americans, led by world record holder Ja’Kobe Tharp in the 110m hurdles.

Tharp’s compatriots Jamal Britt and Trey Cunningham will be expected to give him competition,

Former world champion Tajay Gayle will be hoping to continue his late season improvement after he jumped a season’s best 8.43m in Zurich. There, he challenged world leader Miltiadis Tentoglou of Greece before falling just short.

Gayle and Pinnock will hope to provide robust competition for Tentoglou, who has lost just once in 15 outdoor meets this year.

Beckford is enjoying his best season as a professional and cleared 2.29m in Poland, just off his season’s best 2.30m. He is down to take on world leader JuVaughn Harrison of the United States, Gianmarco Tamberi of Italy, and Oleh Doroshchuk of Ukraine, all of whom have cleared 2.32m this year.

Stona is set to meet world leader Matthew Denny of Australia on Australia in the men’s discus throw, Mykolas Alekna of Lithuania, and Kristjan Ceh of Slovenia, all of whom have thrown over 72.00m this season.

Thomas-Dodd faces two of the best women’s shot-putters in the last decade or so, Jessica Schilder of Netherlands and Chase Jackson of the USA, both of whom have thrown beyond 21 metres this season. Back-to-back Commonwealth Games champion Sahara Mitton of Canada is also expected to feature.

Ackelia Smith is to line up in what is expected to be an explosive women’s triple jump that will see four jumpers who have gone over 15 metres.

World leader Thea Lafond of Dominica will hope to end the series on a high, but will be challenged by Cubans Davisleydi Velazco and Leyanis Perez Hernandez and Senegal’s Saly Sarr.

World.title: ATL Automotive drives  into Ocho Rios
World.content:
ATL Automotive’s new location at the Ocho Rios Bypass Plaza, St Ann, was officially opened on Friday, August 28.

The ATL Automotive Group opened its ninth location on Friday, August 28, at the Ocho Rios Bypass Plaza, St Ann.

“My late incredible father grew up about 1,000 feet east of where we are in this incredible town, and as a youngster his mother, my grandmother, ran a retail store here. And the genius of what became ATL 58 years later was consummated right here in the town of Ocho Rios. So, being here 58 years later, opening a brand new facility, I want to recognise my dad, and all the people that have worked for ATL all those years and that have gotten us to where we are,” Adam Stewart, executive chairman, ATL Automotive Group, told guests at the grand opening event.

Minister of Water, Environment and Climate Change Matthew Samuda, who is the Member of Parliament for St Ann North Eastern, welcomed the investment in the constituency.

“This evening is a night to congratulate and to mark a particular milestone. It is good to see commerce return to Ocho Rios in this way,” said Samuda.

Sloane Jackson, general manager, ATL Ocho Rios, was also on hand to reiterate the further economic contribution the new showroom will make.

“Almost 20 of the people that work for me come from St Mary or from St Ann. We’re hiring locally. We’re training local talent, and we’re using that local talent to bring the goods and services of ATL to the customer,” explained Jackson.

Pointing out that the showroom had been functional since April, Jackson said, “We’ve been selling cars in May, June, July, August, so we’ve been operational for four months. We’ve also been servicing for that time.”

The brand new facility will host sales, service and parts for nine of the ATL Automotive Group’s brands — Honda, Kia, Porsche, Audi, MG, Omoda Jaecoo, Foton, and BYD. The 3,150-square-foot showroom can accommodate six display cars, plus one space for customer delivery, while up to 12 models can be kept externally. The parts and service bays are of similar size to the main showroom.

“Our staff complement is 24. We’re looking to grow that to 30 before the end of the year, and with our continuous growth, it might get to 40 by the end of next year,” said Jackson.

The four service bays are set up to handle the Kia and Honda brands at a collective 16 units a day. Service support for BYD, MG, and Foton is expected to arrive at the end of the year.

Jackson explained that the showroom eases the burden on customers in the north-western side of the island, as they will no longer have to make the long trek to either Montego Bay or Kingston to view a unit, purchase one of the nine brands, or have general service done on their ATL Automotive vehicle.

“In the month of September we’re starting with a discount of 15 per cent on parts and labour,” said Jackson.

The site will also house an Appliance Traders Limited store, replacing the Newlin Street, Ocho Rios, location.

World.title: How Dis Mek? From bean to brew – Jamaican Blue Mountain coffee
World.content:
Jamaica’s Blue Mountain coffee, recognised among the finest coffees in the world, is a staple for many locals. But, how do we get the yummy aromatic drink from sweet red fruit?

This week, the Jamaica Observer travels high up into the Blue Mountains to hear from the Managing Director of the Mavis Bank Coffee Factory, Dr Norman Grant, who details ‘How Dis Mek!’

World.title: UPDATE: Robert Morgan orders investigation into MoBay perimeter road death
World.content:
A police vehicle at the scene where a engineer died while died while working on a section of the Montego Bay bypass.

KINGSTON, Jamaica — Minister with Responsibility for Works Robert Morgan says he is deeply saddened and has ordered an investigation following the death of a supervising engineer at the Montego Bay Perimeter Road Project on Thursday.

“On behalf of the Government, the ministry and our implementing agencies, I extend sincere condolences to the family, loved ones and colleagues of the deceased. We share their grief at this profoundly difficult time,” said Morgan.

The statement comes hours after the engineer died from injuries he sustained after being run over by a truck while carrying out his duties along a section of the roadway, also referred to as the Montego Bay bypass in St James.

READ: Engineer dies after being crushed by truck while working on MoBay bypass

In acknowledging the incident, Morgan said an investigation has been opened.

“I have directed that a thorough investigation be conducted into the circumstances surrounding the incident. The contractor, China Harbour Engineering Company (CHEC), is required to cooperate fully with all relevant authorities and ensure that the facts are established promptly and transparently.

He expressed deep regret at the death of the engineer.

“A tragedy of this nature should never occur on any of our worksites. No deadline, project target or operational consideration is more important than the safety and life of a worker,” he stressed

“The protection of every person working on our infrastructure projects is non-negotiable. We remain resolute in our commitment of ensuring the safety of every worker,” Morgan concluded.

World.title: French government promises €1B for drought-stricken farmers
World.content:
Three schemes account for the bulk of the government’s spending under the new plan.

France will speed up payments under its “national solidarity” scheme designed to compensate for crop losses. It will be topped up to a total of €520 million, provided the country's 2027 budget is duly adopted.

An “agricultural recovery fund” of €235 million aims to provide targeted support for the hardest-hit and most vulnerable farms across the produce, cereal and livestock sectors.

Finally, a targeted tax relief scheme on unbuilt land will cut €330 million in tax revenue for the state. The government is also considering extending a program helping farmers to purchase fertilizer and non-road agricultural diesel.

Genevard also suggested that the retail sector could "play its part" by keeping price rises in check.

Part of her plan is already funded for this year, but more cash will need to be allocated in next year's budget, which is set to be presented by Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu at the end of September.

World.title: Nigel Farage: Departing aides guilty of only ‘loose pub talk’
World.content:
The Reform UK boss said his party has done nothing wrong, but also that the comments captured in an undercover video were ‘human error.’

BIRMINGHAM, England — Two top Reform UK aides forced to step down amid an undercover donations sting were guilty of untrue boasts and “loose pub talk,” party leader Nigel Farage claimed Friday.

“There was certainly human error here,” Farage acknowledged during a press conference alongside National Rally vice president Jordan Bardella, invited to celebrate a joint policy rollout on migration. “It should not have happened.”

Dan Jukes, Farage’s long-term media chief, and James Orr, his senior policy adviser, stepped down Friday morning after Channel 4 broadcast footage apparently showing them agreeing to take donations from a foreign benefactor via a middle-man in the U.K. Experts allege taking the cash and then seeking to hide its provenance could be a breach of U.K. electoral law.

World.title: Le Pen rivals seize on National Rally’s Ukraine divide
World.content:
"We turn off the tap," Aliot said of aid to Ukraine in a television interview, pointing to France's fiscal overstretch and problems in financing areas like health and education. He stressed his party's strong support for Ukraine and condemned Russia for its invasion, but underlined: "Who pays for the war?"

Philippe and Attal — fighting to become the main center-right presidential candidate — both fired back.

"Cutting off aid to Ukraine means playing into Russia’s hands," Philippe posted on X. "The National Rally has changed its position on just about everything, except for its support of Putin’s regime — a stance that runs counter to French and European interests."

"You’ve just heard the 'foreign-backed' party speak ... The National Rally is once again demonstrating its subservience to Russia," echoed Attal.

Le Pen, who's currently leading in opinion polls, responded: "Since Russia's aggression against Ukraine, I have been demanding that France urgently convene a major conference for peace in order to contribute, not to the prolongation of a bloodbath, but to a diplomatic resolution of this abominable war."

However, she didn't repeat Aliot's comments on France's inability to continuing to provide military aid to Ukraine.

World.title: How a ‘dodgy money’ scandal hijacked Nigel Farage’s reset conference
World.content:
Jukes was uncharacteristically not seen at Farage’s side during Thursday night’s dinner. He had been there at his boss’s drinks with political editors shortly before the investigation aired. But his presence on the mind of Reform’s top brass was evident.

“The impression over dinner was Nigel was going to back them to the hilt,” said one senior figure in the party who was present at the business event. They were granted anonymity like others in this article to speak frankly about an internal party matter. The argument was that there had been “no law breaking” and that Farage could stand by the embattled duo.

“Different combinations of [deputy leader Richard] Tice, Orr etc. were regularly stepping away from tables, having hushed chats in the corners, then coming back,” said a second attendee. “They didn’t acknowledge or mention it to anyone, they certainly weren’t laughing it off.”

Meanwhile, there was what one invitee described as a “watch party” of the Channel 4 footage in a hotel room, where senior officials discussed how to handle the situation.

At the fifth-floor Sky Bar where many of the conference revelers gathered, senior figures in the party were asking each other “how bad is bad?” over 11.30 p.m. gin and tonics.

Most were insistent the row would blow over. If the support for Orr felt more rudimentary, the expectation that Jukes would be fine seemed certain.

World.title: US court ruling aggravates Brussels’ Google problem
World.content:
In a ruling from Washington’s own attempt to break up Google, Judge Leonie Brinkema, of the Federal District of Eastern Virginia, rejected the DoJ’s request for a forced divestiture of parts of its business.

That decision leaves the EU alone, at a time of transatlantic discord, in advocating that the online advertising giant break itself up.

“It’s obvious that the European Commission has been holding out for a decision in the parallel U.S. case, even if it has the authority to act independently and should have done so long ago,” Max von Thun, Europe director at the Open Markets Institute non-profit, told POLITICO.

One year after the Commission issued its fine, both the complainants who brought the case, and the civil society groups who see this as a test of the EU’s nerve in confronting Big Tech, fear the EU executive may find itself with limited options to loosen Google’s stranglehold on the online advertising ecosystem.

“As long as Google maintains the incentive and the means, they have an endless number of paths to achieve comparable anti-competitive goals,” said Arielle Garcia, CEO of Check My Ads, a U.S.-based watchdog, adding that while a Europe-only remedy might be technically possible, its effect would be minimal.

In her order, Brinkema said she didn’t see a structural divestment of part of Google’s business as necessary to remedy the finding of liability against the company.

World.title: Belgian PM’s chocolate gift to Modi doesn’t survive journey to India
World.content:
“But unlike the real India Gate, which has stood almost for a century, the chocolate version didn’t even survive the journey to India,” De Wever said. “Chocolate is excellent for diplomacy, but not excellent for diplomatic travel.”

The gift carried a more serious message. India Gate is a war memorial in New Delhi, and De Wever said the replica was meant to honor the more than 9,000 Indian soldiers who fought and died in Belgium’s Flanders Fields during World War I.

A backup version is still waiting in Belgium, De Wever said. He promised the replacement would fare better: “One way or another, I will get it to Prime Minister Modi in one piece.”

Diplomatic gifts have produced stranger outcomes.

A camel given to former French President François Hollande by Mali was left with a family in Timbuktu, which later slaughtered and ate it. In 2014, then-U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry presented Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov with two Idaho potatoes.

Beyond the protocol hiccup, De Wever and Modi agreed to deepen cooperation on defense, organized crime and renewable energy, while aiming to boost trade. De Wever also invited Modi to visit Belgium.

World.title: Sécheresse : le gouvernement promet un milliard pour les agriculteurs
World.content:
A la main des préfets dans les départements, qui recevront prochainement les organisations agricoles, un “fonds de réarmement agricole” de 235 millions d’euros doit permettre, dès les prochaines semaines, de cibler les exploitations les plus touchées et prioritaires parmi notamment les maraîchers, les céréaliers ou encore les éleveurs. La répartition entre les départements est encore en cours d’arbitrage, a indiqué le ministère de l’Agriculture. Si certaines productions baissent, “nous perdrons des paysages, des parts de marché, de la souveraineté”, a mis en garde Annie Genevard.

Autre volet important : des dégrèvements de taxe sur le foncier non bâti, pour soulager les exploitants les plus touchés — 330 millions d’euros de recettes fiscales minorées pour l’État. La prolongation cet automne des guichets d’aide à l’achat d’engrais ou de gazole non routier agricole est aussi sur la table.

Le financement de l’ensemble de ces mesures ? Un mix de dégel à court terme de crédits du ministère de l’Agriculture, des économies dans d’autres ministères... et un besoin de nouveaux crédits octroyés par la prochaine loi de finances.

“C’est de l’argent nouveau, ce n’est pas du recyclage”, a insisté Annie Genevard, passant sous silence les tensions existantes entre Matignon, le ministère de l’Agriculture, Bercy et le reste des ministères pour arbitrer ces derniers jours les contours du plan. Un message a également été passé à la grande distribution pour “contenir l’augmentation des prix” dans les rayons.

Dans les prochaines semaines, un "plan de rebond" pour l'agriculture doit également être détaillé par l'exécutif, qui en inclura les principales mesures dans le budget 2027.

Sébastien Lecornu en a déjà donné un avant-goût à la mi-août en promettant un futur “suramortissement fiscal pour les projets d’avenir agricole”, la création de ces futurs contrats ayant été votée dans la loi d’urgence avant l’été, ainsi que d’autres mesures pour “continuer d’adapter l’agriculture au changement climatique” ou encore “soutenir les investissements hydrauliques”.

World.title: Ukraine renews push for Russia’s frozen assets
World.content:
Using Russia's immobilized state assets to help fund Ukraine returned to the EU agenda after the Netherlands, Poland, Spain and Sweden last month called on the European Commission to explore “new options” for unlocking them.

More than €200 billion in Russian central-bank assets are immobilized across the EU, with most held by Belgian-based financial depository Euroclear. The Belgian government has resisted proposals to use the funds, citing the potential legal and financial risks it could face in the event of Russian retaliation or litigation.

Kyiv’s renewed appeal reflects the growing pressure to find additional money for Ukraine, with the country facing a substantial budget shortfall and Russia's full-scale invasion in its fifth year.

The EU and Ukraine "need to consider other options, to consider, say, different figures as a first step" to get at least some of the Russian assets released, Chentsov said in response to a question from POLITICO about how Belgium might change its mind.

Europe also needs new ideas about "how to guarantee this instrument," he added. "Maybe not only EU, but other players can step in and help to answer the concerns of Belgium. So it's important to start working again on the issue and look for the solution.

"I'm sure that if we want to find a solution, we will find a solution," he added.

World.title: TAP privatisation: Portuguese government opens talks with Air France-KLM and Lufthansa
World.content:
The Minister of the Presidency, António Leitão Amaro, announced on Friday that the Portuguese government is to open talks with the two groups bidding to buy TAP Air Portugal, Air France-KLM and Lufthansa, which submitted binding offers at the end of July.

 

Quoted by the Lusa news agency, Leitão Amaro said that the bids, although different, have an "overall valuation that is very close", which he believes justifies an "effort to negotiate" in order to obtain improved proposals from both contenders and allow the government to move towards "a single bidder for the very final negotiation".

Parpública, the holding company that manages the Portuguese state's stakes, delivered its report on the two binding offers for the privatisation of TAP to the government for analysis on 1 September.

Two binding offers

Air France-KLM and Lufthansa submitted their bids on 29 July, the last day of the deadline, binding offers to acquire 44.5% of TAP Air Portugal. Parpública then had 30 days to assess the documentation and submit a report to the Portuguese government. Once the bids had been evaluated, the government could invite one or both of the bidders that had submitted binding offers to negotiate and table a new final proposal.

The partial sale process for the national airline, relaunched in 2025 by Luís Montenegro's government, was reduced to two bidders after the withdrawal of International Airlines Group (IAG) - owner of Iberia - leaving Air France-KLM and Lufthansa still in the running.

The decree-law approved by the government a year ago provides for the sale of up to 49.9% of TAP to private investors, of which 5% is reserved for employees, while the state remains the majority shareholder.

The Minister for Infrastructure, Miguel Pinto Luz, has already said that the chosen investor could take on joint management of the airline as early as 2026, alongside the current board, but that the actual capital injection is only expected to take place in the summer of 2027.

World.title: Passport for a newborn: Birth tourism as part of Russia's new emigration
World.content:
Following the start of Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine and the subsequent wave of emigration, one notable trend has been the rise of so-called "birth tourism".

 

Thousands of Russian women, unwilling to tie their children's future to a country that started a war and concerned about Russia's growing isolation, began looking for opportunities to give birth abroad.

The main goal is not only to access quality healthcare, but also to obtain a second citizenship for the newborn, which can potentially open the way for the entire family to emigrate, study, work and travel freely around the world.

Countries that apply the principle of jus soli ("right of the soil"), under which citizenship is granted to every child born on the country's territory regardless of their parents' citizenship, have become particularly popular.

However, the growing number of such trips has already prompted several countries to reconsider their policies due to an "influx of applicants".

Argentina: From dreams of a new passport to tighter rules

Argentina became the most popular destination for Russian women after 2022. The country offered a unique combination of advantages: visa-free entry for Russians, relatively affordable healthcare, automatic citizenship for the child, and the possibility for parents to eventually obtain Argentine documents.

For many families, the main attraction was not only the newborn's passport, but also a broader range of related benefits. A child born in Argentina automatically became an Argentine citizen and received all the rights provided by law, including access to state social programmes and child benefits. Parents could apply for permanent residency and later for citizenship.

Obtaining residency status made it possible to legally live and work in the country, run a business and enjoy most of the rights available to permanent residents. Another advantage was the possibility of subsequently legalising the status of other family members through family reunification and naturalisation procedures.

The Argentine passport itself was also a significant advantage, providing broad visa-free access around the world. Russians were not required to give up their Russian citizenship. The absence of compulsory military service in Argentina was another factor.

Birth tourism agencies actively promoted this combination of benefits in their advertising. Potential clients were offered not simply assistance with arranging childbirth abroad, but effectively a ready-made emigration pathway for the entire family, with agencies promising help with paperwork, obtaining residency and eventually securing citizenship.

Maxim Levoshin and his wife Yekaterina Gordienko pose for a photo with their newborn son Leo in Buenos Aires, Argentina, on Saturday 18 February 2023. Natacha Pisarenko/Copyright 2023 The AP. All rights reserved

According to Argentine authorities, around 10,500 pregnant Russian women arrived in the country in 2022 alone. Many arrived shortly before giving birth and left the country soon after obtaining documents for their child. Authorities estimated that around 7,000 of these women left Argentina almost immediately.

According to The Wall Street Journal, by mid-2024, the total number of Russians who had moved to the country since the start of the war had reached around 75,000, with several neighbourhoods in Buenos Aires already forming a "Little Russia".

Argentine authorities eventually began openly raising concerns about abuses of the immigration system. Agencies selling Russians comprehensive service packages — including arrangements for childbirth, assistance with paperwork and support in obtaining citizenship — came under investigation. Advertising materials often emphasised that having a child in Argentina could be the fastest way to obtain a second passport and lay the groundwork for the entire family to relocate.

After President Javier Milei came to power, the rules were significantly tightened. Parents of a child born in Argentina can no longer use their child's birth as a fast-track route to obtaining citizenship themselves. Naturalisation now requires at least two years of legal residence in the country. At the same time, access to free healthcare was restricted for foreigners without legal status, and additional requirements were introduced for people entering the country.

The impact was significant: while Russians submitted more than 7,000 applications for residence permits in Argentina in 2023, by mid-2025 the number of such applications had fallen to fewer than 2,000.

Russian nationals Alla Priglovkina and Andrei Ushakov spend time with their son Lev Andres, who was born in Argentina, in the bedroom of their home in Mendoza, Argentina, 14.02.2023. Natacha Pisarenko/Copyright 2023 The AP. All rights reserved

Brazil becomes the new magnet

As the Argentine route closed, Russian families, particularly in 2026, shifted their attention to Brazil. According to Deutsche Welle, the number of Russians travelling to Brazil increased significantly after Argentina tightened its migration rules.

The Brazilian passport is considered one of the "strongest" in the world: it allows visa-free travel to 161 countries, including countries in the Schengen area and the United Kingdom, and also allows holders to apply for a US visa valid for up to 10 years.

A child born in Brazil automatically receives Brazilian citizenship and a birth certificate. At the same time, the child can also obtain their parents' citizenship through the relevant consulate, becoming a holder of two passports.

Older children in the family can obtain Brazilian citizenship through a simplified procedure within their first year of residence in the country. This opportunity is unique to Brazil.

The newborn's parents, as well as their grandparents, are entitled to a residence permit with the possibility of later naturalisation. For parents, one year of residence in the country and proof of Portuguese language proficiency are sufficient to obtain citizenship, while grandparents must live in Brazil for four years.

For many Russian families, Brazil is becoming more than just a place to give birth; it is part of a long-term emigration strategy. Statistics also reflect this trend: 477 Russians obtained Brazilian citizenship in 2024, rising to 613 in 2025. More than half of the new citizens were women.

Chile, the US, Canada and other destinations: What attracts Russian women

In addition to Argentina and Brazil, Russian families are considering a range of other countries where having a child can offer additional immigration advantages. The choice depends not only on the possibility of obtaining citizenship, but also on the quality of healthcare, the cost of services, how quickly documents can be processed and the prospects for the family to subsequently obtain legal status.

Chile holds a particularly prominent place among these countries. It has long been considered one of the most attractive destinations for birth tourism in Latin America. A child born in Chile receives citizenship, while the parents can benefit from simplified procedures to legalise their stay. The Chilean passport is also considered one of the strongest in the region and provides visa-free access to a significant number of countries around the world.

Another advantage of Chile is its well-developed healthcare system. Private clinics in Santiago and other major cities are often compared with medical centres in the United States and Western Europe in terms of their facilities and quality of care. At the same time, the cost of pregnancy care and childbirth is generally significantly lower than in the US.

It is this combination of high-quality healthcare, political stability and relatively moderate costs that makes Chile an attractive alternative for families who are not prepared to pay US prices but want a comparable standard of care.

A doctor examines a five-month-old girl during a routine appointment at UCSF Benioff Children's Hospital on 16 March 2011 in San Francisco, USA. Lea Suzuki/San Francisco Chronicle

The United States has also remained a popular destination and is perhaps the best-known destination for birth tourism in the world. Under the 14th Amendment to the US Constitution, a child born on US territory automatically receives American citizenship regardless of their parents' status.

However, the cost of this option is significantly higher than in Latin American countries. The total cost of childbirth, accommodation, insurance and legal assistance can run into tens of thousands of dollars.

In recent years, US authorities have also stepped up efforts to combat organised birth tourism, paying increased attention to cases in which foreign nationals use tourist visas solely for the purpose of giving birth in the country.

A similar principle applies in Canada, where a child also automatically receives citizenship by virtue of being born in the country. Canada is chosen for its high level of safety, well-developed healthcare system and reputation as a country with a strong social welfare system. However, the financial costs are also relatively high, while waiting times for some medical services can be longer than at private clinics in Latin American countries.

Among the less obvious but increasingly popular destinations is Mexico. The country grants citizenship to children born on its territory, while its geographical proximity to the United States makes it attractive to those seeking a second passport for their child at a more moderate cost. In addition, the cost of medical services at private clinics in Mexico is often significantly lower than in North America.

For wealthier families, Switzerland remains another option. Unlike countries in the Americas, it does not grant citizenship by birth, but is considered one of the world's leaders in the quality of maternity care. Giving birth there is therefore seen more as a premium medical service than as a means of obtaining a second passport.

How countries are tackling "birth tourism"

Many countries have previously faced an influx of foreigners travelling specifically to obtain citizenship for their children.

Ending automatic citizenship

The most radical approach has been to end unconditional birthright citizenship.

Ireland, Australia and New Zealand have taken this approach. In Ireland, following a 2004 referendum, a child no longer automatically receives citizenship solely on the basis of being born in the country. Today, in most such cases, at least one parent must be a citizen of the country or have the right to permanent residence.

The United Kingdom, Australia and New Zealand previously adopted a similar approach.

Restricting benefits for parents

Against this backdrop, Argentina has taken a less restrictive approach. Children still receive citizenship, but authorities have removed parents' ability to quickly obtain their own documents on the basis of their child's birth. This measure has significantly reduced the popularity of Argentina as a birth tourism destination.

A mother hugs her newborn baby in hospital shortly after giving birth. Natalia Deriabina, Shutterstock)

Visa restrictions

The US has retained birthright citizenship, which is guaranteed by the Constitution, but has begun tackling birth tourism through other means.

Since 2020, US consular officers have been able to refuse tourist visas if they believe the primary purpose of a trip is to give birth in the country in order to obtain US citizenship for the child.

In recent years, authorities have also stepped up action against intermediaries and begun revoking visas on a large scale for people involved in such schemes.

Checks at borders and maternity hospitals

Hong Kong offers a notable example, after authorities faced a large influx of pregnant women from mainland China. Mandatory advance registration at maternity hospitals, quotas for foreign women and tighter border controls were introduced. As a result, the number of such cases fell sharply.

Debate in Canada

Canada still maintains unconditional birthright citizenship, but the political debate over restricting birth tourism is becoming increasingly heated.

Canadian studies show that more than 5,400 births to non-residents were registered in the country during the 2024-2025 financial year. Against this backdrop, politicians are increasingly calling for the rules to be reviewed.

War as a driver of new migration

Russia's war against Ukraine has reshaped the migration strategies of thousands of families, with giving birth abroad becoming a way to secure citizenship and new opportunities for their children.

But as birth tourism grows, countries often tighten their rules. Argentina has already done so following an influx of pregnant Russian women, and Brazil could face similar pressure if the trend continues.

World.title: Inside the quiet luxury revival of the Venice Lido – home to the glittering film festival
World.content:
The crème de la crème of the world of cinema has been jetting into Venice for the 83rd edition of its International Film Festival.

 

The glittering event is centred on the Lido island, a narrow strip of land a short water bus ride from the historic centre.

The island has a character all of its own; a summer resort of beach establishments and historic hotels beloved by Venetians but often overlooked by international tourists.

That is, apart from when it transforms into a global hub of the silver screen for 11 days each September.

But there have been some signs that the quiet isle of Belle Époque architecture that gives way to campsites, pine forests and nature oases may be undergoing a revival with luxury in mind.

Its most famous hotel, where the film festival was originally hosted, has undergone a full revamp, while another storied establishment is set for renovation and a new four-star superior resort opened last year.

Film festival’s starriest hotel gets an upgrade

The Hotel Excelsior Venice Lido is the film festival’s most prestigious address, having hosted the inaugural edition in 1932 on its sea-facing terrace.

Since the property’s opening in 1908, it has become a favourite of royalty, politicians and, of course, film stars.

Greta Garbo, Audrey Hepburn and Elizabeth Taylor graced its Moorish-inspired interiors in the past, while current icons like George Clooney and Nicole Kidman continue to base themselves there during the festival.

The hotel’s reopening in May this year unveiled a series of stunning renovations to the storied property of domes, arches and minarets.

One of the most significant upgrades is to its Palm Court, an interior lobby of lush greenery restored to its former glory as the social heart of the hotel.

The space now features archival photography of royalty, famous directors, and Hollywood legends who stayed at the property over the last century.

As for accommodation, more than half of the 198 rooms and suites have been refreshed with soft Mediterranean colour palettes and custom Murano glass.

There is also a new signature terrace restaurant, pool bar and beach club with 299 cabanas, called Amù Venice. It combines Riviera flair from where the brand was born on the Côte d'Azur at the rooftop of the Fairmont Monte Carlo with the gastronomic traditions of the Veneto.

New four-star resort opens on Venice Lido

Last year saw another example of the Lido’s iconic 1920s architecture revived as a four-star superior resort.

Meliá Venezia Lido is far less extravagant than the Excelsior, but it adds an elegant and more affordable accommodation option to the island.

The communal spaces are flooded with the clear light off the Adriatic sea, while several of the 60 rooms have sweeping views over the lagoon to the historic centre.

There is also a restaurant, AcquaRiva, with an Art Deco-inspired design and fusion Mediterranean-Venetian dishes.

Storied Lido hotel to undergo €200 million restoration

The sprawling Grand Hôtel des Bains once also welcomed cultural icons and film greats. Author Thomas Mann stayed at the property in 1911, inspiring his novella Death in Venice.

The grand, Liberty-style hotel closed in 2010, but last year plans were announced for its reopening.

A €200 million investment will see the property and its beachfront restored and modernised as a high-end resort.

The sprawling Grand Hôtel des Bains once also welcomed cultural icons and film greats. Serge Le Strat

“This is more than a restoration – it is a revival of European legacy through modern excellence,” said Mohamed Alabbar, Chairman and founder of Eagle Hills, a real estate development company based in Abu Dhabi, which is financing the project along with the urban regeneration COIMA ESG City Impact Fund.

“Venice has always been a bridge between worlds, and we are proud to be part of its future, bringing our experience in luxury hospitality to one of the most symbolic hotels on the continent.”

World.title: Five EU countries aim to send migrants to return hubs by 2027
World.content:
Five EU countries say they expect to be ready to send irregular migrants to deportation centres built outside the European Union by 2027. The announcement came after a meeting in Copenhagen on Friday attended by the interior ministers of Denmark, Austria, Germany, the Netherlands and Greece.

 

The ministers agreed on a common model for "return hubs" — facilities set to host asylum seekers whose applications have been rejected by the five countries and who cannot be returned to their countries of origin.

The five-state group is currently negotiating the creation of the hubs on the territory of one or more partner countries, which have not yet been disclosed. Uganda and Rwanda are seen as the most likely possibilities, according to several press reports.

"Today's guiding principle forms the basis for the way forward [...] to be ready to transfer the first irregular migrants to a partner country outside of the EU in 2027," said Danish Migration Minister Morten Bødskov.

He claimed that the hubs are not "a prison" or "a detention camp", but facilities where "partner countries give irregular migrants a new chance".

The five countries are expected to fully finance the hubs and may also provide additional funding, commercial partnerships or other incentives to partner countries. "A return centre scheme will be established through equal and mutually beneficial partnerships with countries outside the EU," reads the guiding principles document.

The new model should also lead to a noticeable reduction in the number of people migrating illegally to the EU. "Our common goal is pushing illegal migration towards zero," said Austrian Minister Gerhard Karner.

In the meantime, meetings with potential partners are continuing and the discussions are "becoming deeper and more fruitful," said Greek Minister Thanos Plevris, who hopes to announce an agreement in the near future.

The five ministers are set to meet again in Munich at the end of September.

The agreements with the non-EU countries will define the procedures applicable to migrants in the return hubs, the conditions of their stay and the responsibilities of the EU states involved.

The ministers said the project will be carried out in partnership with international organisations, such as the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees and the International Organization for Migration, and in full accordance with EU law and international obligations.

In June, the European Parliament approved the 'strictest-ever' migration law, granting member states the right to set up return hubs by reaching agreements with non-EU countries. The adoption of the "return regulation" is likely to take place in the autumn, with final approval by EU countries, an EU official told Euronews.

The majority of EU countries seem interested in setting up return hubs, while Italy already has a similar project in place with Albania.

Nineteen EU governments are convinced that this is an "innovative solution" to pursue for migration management, as made clear in a joint letter sent to EU leaders last June, suggesting that the centres could become a reality sooner rather than later.

Return hubs have raised concerns in Europe over their compatibility with EU law and the protection of human rights. The idea has been harshly criticised by European civil society and non-governmental organisations.

"Sending people to deportation centres outside the EU means uprooting children, adults and families from the lives they’ve built in Europe and subjecting them to prolonged detention in places they don’t even know," said Michele LeVoy, Director of Picum, a Brussels-based NGO promoting the human rights of undocumented migrants.

So far, attempts to transfer migrants to non-EU countries have not been particularly successful.

The United Kingdom abandoned a scheme to deport asylum seekers to Rwanda, where their applications would have been examined. Denmark ditched a similar plan in 2023, changing its strategy from a national approach to a European one.

Italy initially projected housing around 3,000 migrants a month in its Albanian centres; the actual figure has reportedly been just 500 in total since the facilities were converted into deportation centres in March 2025.

The entire bill amounts to over €670 million, and, according to a recent study by an Italian university, detaining migrants in these centres has proven to be much more expensive for Italy than hosting them on its own territory.

World.title: Russian drone strikes Ukraine Security Service headquarters in central Kyiv
World.content:
A Russian drone struck the headquarters of Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU) in central Kyiv on Friday afternoon, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, adding that it had targeted the head of the agency's office.

 

The drone hit the SBU’s central building on Volodymyrska Street, opposite St Sophia Cathedral and close to Kyiv’s Golden Gate area, as Russia continued its campaign of daytime drone attacks on the Ukrainian capital.

“I spoke with the Head of the Security Service of Ukraine, Oleksandr Poklad. Unfortunately, a Russian drone struck the central building of the Security Service of Ukraine on Volodymyrska Street in Kyiv, across from St. Sophia Cathedral,” Zelenskyy said.

“The drone was aimed directly at the office of the Head of the Security Service in that building," he added.

Zelenskyy said emergency services were attending the scene. There was no immediate information on casualties.

The Ukrainian president said he had also instructed Poklad to prepare a response to the attack.

“I instructed Poklad to deliver an appropriate, tangible response and, where possible, one that mirrors this strike, to the Russians once everything is ready. Our military will support this response,” Zelenskyy wrote in a post on X.

Witnesses reported hearing an explosion at around 3.30 pm local time, with thick smoke rising from the area around the Golden Gate in the historic centre.

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko initially reported a fire in the city’s Shevchenkivskyi district after a drone fell on the roof of a non-residential building, adding that emergency services were heading to the scene.

The attack came during another air-raid alert in Kyiv, with Ukraine’s air force warning that several drones were heading towards the city.

Russia has significantly ramped up its drone attacks on Kyiv in recent days, disrupting daily life in the Ukrainian capital.

World.title: Ladies Only: Afghan pop star Aryana Sayeed takes on Taliban with European tour
World.content:
She was one of Afghanistan’s biggest stars. Then the Taliban returned to power and she fled the country. Now, Aryana Sayeed is taking her music and message across Europe - with one key difference: the audiences will be women only.

 

Sayeed remains one of the most recognisable faces in Afghanistan, building a huge following as a singer, an outspoken advocate for women's rights, and from her time as a judge on The Voice Afghanistan and other major talent shows in the country.

But when the Taliban retook control of Afghanistan in 2021, her life and career changed dramatically. Unable to return home or perform there, Sayeed has continued her work from abroad, using her platform and her organisation DEFAW (Defenders of Equality, Freedom, and Advancement for Women) to speak out for Afghan women and girls living under what she calls "dark days."

Five years on, she is taking her message of hope across Europe with her "Ladies Only_"_ tour, a series of concerts exclusively for women. The tour begins this Friday in Rotterdam, where Sayeed will perform at the Laurenskerk. She will then head to Stockholm on 5 September, followed by Hamburg on 26 September and Wiesbaden, near Frankfurt, on 3 October.

Ahead of the shows, Euronews Culture spoke to her about what sparked the idea behind her Ladies Only concerts, the current situation facing women and girls in Afghanistan, and the message she hopes to share through her music and activism.

When did you come up with the idea for a ladies-only tour?

Aryana Sayeed: Well, I have been planning to do this Ladies-Only tour for the past three or four years. Since the Taliban took over the power in Afghanistan, you know, they literally banned women from most things. Like, they have banned schools for girls past grade six, and women are not allowed to work anymore.They are not even allowed to go to the park. You know, like some simple things in life. They're not allowed to do it anymore.

So when all of this happened, obviously, besides my singing career, I am also an activist for women's rights in Afghanistan. And I thought, you know what? We need to stand against this injustice, against the Taliban and what they're doing. And so I thought initially it would be a great idea to do this Ladies-Only concert where we show the power of women, where we stand together as women, and raise our voice and raise awareness against the injustices that are going on in Afghanistan and stand up for the millions of voiceless women in Afghanistan.

Many people around the world will know you from The Voice of Afghanistan. How influential has your voice been in Afghanistan, and how big are you there?

Well, it's really hard to talk about yourself and say how big you are, but I know that the things that I have been doing in Afghanistan for the past, I would say, 15 years have been quite effective. It has had major effects on the society. It has been able to give so much hope to the hopeless women of Afghanistan.

Empowering them in a way to think differently, to know their rights and to stand up for their rights and things like that. As much as I've been focused on my singing career, as much I've been focused on my activist side as well, trying to give voice to the voiceless women of Afghanistan.

I used to be a judge on these talent shows, and I used to be present there during all of these problems and issues as well. Even before the Taliban came, Afghan women did not have their full rights at all. Before the Taliban came, things were getting along really well, and the things that we were doing in Afghanistan, the effect it had on society, was going really well.

Since the Taliban returned to power five years ago, do you feel more free and more heard outside Afghanistan, as a performer and as someone delivering a message of hope?

Even when I was in Afghanistan, I still had my concerts outside of Afghanistan. I still was touring all this time. For me, there's no major difference in that field. But I do feel that we are very isolated now. I do feel like there's so much that I could do in my country. There's so much more that I could. But right now, I am unable to do that because of the fact that I'm not allowed to go back to Afghanistan. I'm not allowed to physically be there, be on the screen of the TV, give out my messages, be that support and that hope for the Afghan women.

But the one thing that I'm grateful for is the fact that we were able to establish the organisation outside Afghanistan. I have this organisation called DEFAW, which stands for Defenders of Equality, Freedom and Advancement for Women. And through the organisation, I've been trying to be active and do my activism through that and raise awareness and try to be the support for the voiceless women of Afghanistan, do interviews all around the world and try to be, you know, as helpful as I can.

And the great thing is that in Afghanistan, we still have YouTube, we still have all these platforms where women can be connected with me, so they can still hear me, they can still see my videos.

Aryana Sayeed moderating a talk with Pakistani education activist Malala Yousafzai & Sahar Halaimzai, director of Malala Fund's Afghanistan Initiative, 15 August 2025, London Credit: DEFAW/Hasib Sayed

You can’t completely silence voices like yours, particularly when young girls can still access your work online. What message would you give to those girls who look up to you?

The one advice that I constantly keep giving them is not to give up hope because honestly, they are living in the dark, dark, dark ages right now. I speak to around 100 Afghan women or girls inside Afghanistan on a monthly basis through my organisation, through Zoom. And I actually get to speak to them, ask them questions, hear their stories. And what they tell me is heartbreaking, quite sad.

They literally talk without crying because of the fact that they've been abandoned from school and from work, and they feel so hopeless and they feel so useless as humans. Most of them have to just go ahead and get married, you know, at a young age because they don't see a future and they don't have another choice.

Let's say a woman who doesn't have a husband and doesn't have somebody to support the family with the income, with the food, with the money and everything. What is she going to do? And she's not allowed to go to work. So the only choice left for her is just go to bed. That's it. And so it's really sad to hear all these stories.

Because I honestly, I do feel from the bottom of my heart that these dark days will pass. They will not exist forever. This is, at least as a human, what I think, because what they have brought upon women in Afghanistan is ridiculous and inhumane, and this kind of a life, I don't think it's going to last forever.

People will eventually raise their voices. People will eventually stand up against them, and justice will prevail. Maybe it will. I don't know when. Maybe it will last another two, three, four or five years. But it cannot be forever. I don't believe that.

Men will obviously have a crucial role in making that change happen. What is your message to Afghan men, both inside Afghanistan and those living in exile?

I have literally made videos on social media and asked the Afghan men all around the world, and particularly in Afghanistan, to stand up for the rights of their women, for their mothers, for sisters, and for the women in general. And that's my message to them. I have a strong feeling that unless Afghan men come together and stand up for the women, women alone cannot do much for themselves.

And in order for this change to come, or for the women to have their full rights, men need to start supporting them. And I have seen a glimpse of, you know, their support here and there. Of course, not inside Afghanistan yet, but I have seen Afghan men getting together for protests outside the country, like, for example, in Germany and the U.S. and other countries like this, which is a good sign, which is a good thing to happen.

And hopefully, there will be more of that in the future.

How would you describe your music?

Well, I mostly sing pop. My songs are pop. That's how I started. I started with R&B and then pop music, but then I also have a lot of traditional songs. Funny enough, when I went to Afghanistan for the first time in 2011, I mixed a few songs of, like, old 40, 50-year-old songs and I made them with new music, and I presented them on the stage to people and people just loved those songs.

For me, that gave me kind of this indication that people still love the traditional music. So I do traditional music, but also a big portion of my songs are dedicated to the rights of Afghan women. And those are the ones that are the most effective in the society, I would say. And I actually performed some of them at the European Parliament, at UNICEF and all these big government gatherings that take place.

And it's been amazing. And this is the part of my career I love and enjoy the most. The songs actually, you know, give me something that is very fulfilling as a human being and that performing well.

You mentioned what music means to you as a human being, so I can’t let you go without asking about artificial intelligence. A significant proportion of music streamed these days is either created or influenced by AI. Are you open to using AI in your music?

I find it scary. I honestly am not for AI at all. I don't like it. It scares me and it makes me worried of where are heading. I know in a way it's - it can be really good. It can be fantastic. But in a way we are losing that human touch. For example, nowadays they can even create the sound of the singers, they can create my sound, they can create my videos when I'm not even there.

And that scares me. That's not nice. I feel like the human touch should exist, and it should be there. And you cannot even compare it with AI at all. And I don't like AI, and I don't use it, and I'm not for it. I don't support it at all.
