“On one side of the port was a huge parking lot, where vehicles from both countries waited for inspection,” He recalls. “Next to the lot were several white buildings, four or five floors each, where the on-duty staff lived.”

Across from the lot was a police station and a row of small stores including a supermarket run by a middle-aged couple from the neighboring Sichuan province, a souvenir shop run by a Nepalese merchant, and three restaurants.

“Most visitors were tourists who took a quick photo at the border gate and left,” says the 50-year-old photographer. “There wasn’t much demand for a bustling commercial street. But the port staff stayed year-round, and these outlets were their only options for shopping and dining.”

Many of these border officials are among the missing.

With the flash flood destroying about three kilometers of the highway leading to Gyirong, it took two days for the first rescue teams from Xizang and Sichuan to reach the disaster zone. The highway was reportedly reopened on Sept. 2, allowing access to more rescuers, emergency supplies, and heavy machinery.

A warm welcome

The first reply that He received was from a Tibetan friend working at the port’s disease-control station. He had requested the day off on Aug. 26 and gone into town, narrowly escaping the massive torrent of rock, ice, and water that had wiped out his workplace.

The photographer offered to transfer some money so that his friend could purchase food and emergency supplies and bring them to the port, but he declined. “All the roads over there are blocked,” he replied. “The rescue teams are still using bulldozers and excavators to clear a path, moving forward inch by inch.”

After two sleepless nights, He set off from Beijing for Gyirong on the morning of Aug. 28. He had no idea how he would help — he just knew he had to go.

Since the disaster, the Gyirong Entry-Exit Border Inspection Station’s official channel on the WeChat messaging platform has been inundated with messages from well-wishers.

Many staff at the port are in their early 30s and hail from various parts of China. Far from their families, most live quiet, monotonous lives.

He Xu once wandered into the staff dormitories and noted the austerity of the rooms, with just two beds, a desk, and simple storage cabinets. The housing complex had a recreation room with table tennis and other sports facilities, but he’d never seen anyone using them. “The most typical thing I saw staff doing after work was calling their families,” he says.

The workers rarely ventured far, He says, leaving them little opportunity to appreciate the valley scenery — so he decided his lens would be their “eyes.” One person wanted to see a kiang, an indigenous wild ass; another, the splendor of Ngari prefecture, a 15-hour drive west; another, the view from a 4,500-meter platform in the Himalayas just an hour away. Each time, He would capture what they asked for and share the pictures on WeChat.

The customs staff rotated every three or four days. Off-duty workers are accommodated in the county seat, about 90 minutes away by bus, where they can enjoy more variety in terms of meals, shopping, and entertainment.

Those who have passed through Gyirong Port often speak of the “pleasant, helpful” nature of the customs and security personnel there.

Wen Lili from China’s northwestern Shaanxi province visited in early August. She remembers a young police officer who helped suggest the best places to take photos — the checkpoint, boundary marker, and the Friendship Bridge over the border — and where to exchange Chinese renminbi for Nepalese rupees. “It’s such a tiny place, and he told me everything there was to see,” she says.

He Xu says that, one time, his pickup truck was dangerously low on fuel, and a police officer drove more than 40 kilometers to the nearest gas station to bring him a full jerry can.

Two years ago, He joined a customs officer named Dorje and some of his friends for a meal in town. Dorje came from Maizhokunggar County, more than 800 kilometers from Gyirong, and was 10 years from retirement. With a beaming smile, he had talked of his three children, who had all gone to work in major cities.

With the savings he had accumulated, Dorje had planned to return to his hometown, buy some cattle and sheep, and spend his days tending them with his wife. It was his ideal life, he’d said.

Two-way street

Ma Baoxiang, who runs a general store in Gyirong, would often drive the 20 kilometers to the port to shoot videos for his social media channel.

Having made countless trips, he had become familiar with its rhythms: mornings were busiest, as tourists and truck drivers rushed to cross the border before lunch, although crowds could also swell in the afternoon, with vehicles sometimes lining the road. Most were trucks bearing Nepalese license plates, but Ma says that in recent years he has noticed an increase in travelers crossing the border in private cars.

The Bangxing Logistics Park, a 40-minute drive from the port, is the initial destination for most goods arriving from across the border. The facility gets so busy that drivers can be stuck waiting for up to two days to load or unload their cargo.

Nepalese residents near the border with exit-entry permits would also regularly pass through the port to stock up on clothes, daily necessities, and food from the stores in Gyirong.

“You often see Nepalese merchants buying wholesale goods in town,” says Ma, who every few months goes the other way to buy copperware, handicrafts, tea, and other specialty products, which he ships home to sell to tourists.

Trade at Gyirong Port once largely consisted of small businesses run by local residents. In April 2015, when an earthquake in Nepal damaged facilities at the larger Zhangmu Port, Gyirong became the primary China-Nepal border crossing. It was expanded into an international port in 2017.

By 2024, the value of imports and exports passing through Gyirong reached 4.24 billion yuan ($632 million), the highest among all the ports in Xizang.

Ma Qi, the local branch manager of Musa International Logistics, says his company had at least a dozen trucks en route to the port when the disaster struck on Aug. 26. He immediately told the drivers to pull over and wait, and then contacted nearby warehouses to arrange 6,000 square meters of emergency storage for their cargo.

“Gyirong is the best port,” says Ma Qi, who has worked in cross-border export logistics for 13 years. His company exports 400 to 500 cubic meters of goods a day, including clothing, hardware, small household appliances, construction machinery for bridge and tunnel projects, and electric vehicles. He describes the port as a “lifeline.”

The growth in tourists has also helped turn Gyirong into an economic hub, bringing many restaurants and hotels.

“After the mudslide, Gyirong suddenly emptied out,” says Lin Tian, who has owned a store in the county seat selling Nepalese specialty goods for the past five years. “The only people here are residents and the people working or running shops.”

Locals are no strangers to floods, earthquakes, and other natural disasters. It has become an inevitable part of life.

When a mudslide triggered flooding on both sides of the border in July last year, Gyirong Port was closed for nearly six months, forcing logistics companies to shift operations to smaller ports.

“These past few days, the government has been coordinating with us to register and report the cargo stranded at the port. They will arrange for it to be shipped out through the Zhangmu and Lizi ports instead,” says Ma Qi. In the meantime, he is mobilizing resources and coordinating with relief organizations in Lhasa and Shigatse to help transport emergency supplies to the disaster zone.

In late 2024, Gyirong was hit by landslides, leaving many port workers stranded in town with no power for more than a week. The mud in some places was shin-deep.

He Xu recalls asking several port staff whether they feared natural disasters. One simply smiled and replied, “I’m not worried. We’ve always made it through before.”

This time, He wasn’t so sure. In the early hours of Aug. 28, he finally received another message from a contact at the port, this time from a police officer. “I’m in downtown Shigatse. I’m fine,” it said.

Reading it, he felt his anxiety ease a little. Yet many others have remained silent.

(Due to privacy concerns, Wen Lili, Dorje, and Lin Tian are pseudonyms.)

Reported by Yang Shuyuan, Zhang Lingyun, and Wang Qian.

A version of this article originally appeared in Original (Jiefang Daily). It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: Carrie Davies; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

(Header image: Search and rescue personnel look for survivors in Gyirong Port, Xizang Autonomous Region, Sept. 2, 2026. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018982/Scammers Are Targeting China’s Content Creators for Ransoms
World.title: Scammers Are Targeting China’s Content Creators for Ransoms
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018982/Scammers Are Targeting China’s Content Creators for Ransoms
World.content:
Content creators are falling victim to scammers lodging mass fabricated reports of platform violations in China, some of whom boast making over 50,000 yuan ($7,400) per month from their services.

Sellers are offering “account-striking,” including “software-based mass reporting” and “precision strikes,” on domestic secondhand trading platforms, according to an investigation published Tuesday by domestic media outlet The Beijing News. One such service was priced at 25 yuan for 500 platform complaints or 60 yuan for 5,000 complaints.

Account striking, or dahao, became widespread this summer, according to the investigation. This may in part be because it can take advantage of social media platforms’ increasing use of AI to review account-violation complaints.

One 19-year-old creator who posts short videos of herself painting told The Beijing News that one of her accounts, boasting nearly 60,000 followers, had been banned, while a second featuring 260,000 followers saw numerous videos taken down. Both incidents occurred after the same striker reported the accounts to their respective platforms.

The striker then privately messaged her, demanding a ransom of 1,000 yuan to withdraw the complaints. After she transferred the money, the complaints were withdrawn, and her videos were restored.

Jia Bojun, a vlogger who posts videos debunking claims about sports supplements and diets, was also targeted. On Aug. 14, eight of his videos were taken down in under an hour for “portrait rights infringement,” despite the videos featuring no other people.

According to interviews with content creators affected by account strikes, The Beijing News found that teams of strikers often submit complaints simultaneously through a platform’s official reporting channel and by email, doubling success rates.

“To avoid liability, the platform will take down the video as long as there is even a slight possibility (of a violation), regardless of whether the complaint is real or not,” an anonymous account striker told The Beijing News.

Another long-time operator said that many of the attacks stem from brand-to-brand mutual reporting, a commonplace tactic in today’s e-commerce-driven marketplace.

Some strikers go on to recruit apprentices, teaching them step-by-step takedown tactics and providing complaint scripts tailored to each platform, all for an additional fee. The most enterprising even establish their own online account-striking “schools.”

Multiple short-video vloggers were quoted saying that appealing complaints requires significant time and effort, as well as submitting extensive personal information and evidence that they have not violated platform rules — and even then, a successful appeal is not guaranteed.

A cybersecurity expert who works with multiple short-video platforms said that although AI moderation offers platforms a “low-cost, high-efficiency solution” to complaints, it tends to take accounts and videos down first and review later. The cost then falls entirely on creators. “The right to report is a public governance tool provided to users by platforms,” the expert said. “It should not be turned into a priced commodity.”

The expert urged platforms to employ real people to review high-risk reports and flag suspicious accounts, as well as to protect creators’ rights. Platforms should also be required to share malicious-reporting data with police, they said.

Wang Hongmei, a lawyer at Hebei Sanhe Shidai Law Firm, called fabricating complaints and exploiting platform loopholes to maliciously take down videos or ban accounts for illicit gain a form of online “soft violence.” According to Wang, such behavior potentially violates China’s Public Security Administration Punishment Law and is therefore punishable by fines or detention.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from iStock Vectors/VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018976/China Pushes for Homes to Be Completed Before They’re Sold
World.title: China Pushes for Homes to Be Completed Before They’re Sold
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018976/China Pushes for Homes to Be Completed Before They’re Sold
World.content:
China is transitioning away from its presale housing system and encouraging the sale of completed properties.

On Friday, the Ministry of Housing and Urban-Rural Development, the National Financial Regulatory Administration, and the Ministry of Natural Resources jointly unveiled new guidelines promoting the sale of completed homes.

China introduced its presale system in the 1990s, allowing developers to fund rapid expansion by selling unfinished homes. The model remains a major source of funding for the sector today, with roughly two-thirds of new homes in 2025 sold while still under construction.

The model fueled both the housing market and the country’s urbanization, but came under scrutiny in 2021 as a downturn in the property market exposed stalled projects, quality disputes, and fund-management risks.

The new guidelines encourage the sale of completed new housing projects. The presale model will remain in place for existing projects; however, a building’s main structural framework — including the foundation, concrete flooring, and roof — must be completed before sales begin.

Domestic real estate consulting firm CRIC estimates that the new policy could delay presales of existing projects by about a year, in part because most cities previously allowed presales as soon as a project’s foundation was completed.

Under the new policy, housing authorities are encouraged to strengthen sales oversight by requiring all homebuyer payments, including down payments and mortgages, to be deposited into supervised project accounts. Payments may be transferred to developers only after homes pass final inspections, conducted by the developer under the supervision of local housing authorities.

The same day the new policy was announced, China also introduced accompanying credit and market measures to cushion the financial impact of the transition.

China’s central bank, for example, issued a regulation requiring housing project financing to be tied to a lead bank and extended the maximum term for personal mortgage loans from 30 to 40 years.

The China Securities Regulatory Commission also published a guideline calling for reform of developer financing, shifting from a funding model that relies on a developer’s credit toward an overall evaluation of a project’s conditions.

Over the past five years, China has rolled out a batch of policies that largely focused on stimulating real estate demand through lower mortgage rates, relaxed purchase restrictions, and other buyer incentives.

The latest measures, in cooperation with a series of top regulators, go deeper in shaping a new development model for the sector, Yan Yuejin, deputy head of the Shanghai-based E-House China R&D Institute, told Sixth Tone.

“The policy comes amid a key background in the industry, where we see it moving from an attitude of ‘having versus lacking’ to ‘is the quality good or bad?’” he said. “Every housing reform is closely linked to real market needs.”

Rather than simply boosting transactions, the reforms seek to reshape the sector’s underlying model — from how developers raise and manage funds to how buyers finance purchases, he added.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A residential development under construction in Guangzhou, Guangdong province, April 25, 2026. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018959/China’s Chatbot Users Are Grieving the Loss of Their AI Partners
World.title: China’s Chatbot Users Are Grieving the Loss of Their AI Partners
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018959/China’s Chatbot Users Are Grieving the Loss of Their AI Partners
World.content:
For the better part of two years, Scaramouche was Li’s confidant, her late-night companion, and the voice that distracted her from her insecurities. He was also, by any technical definition, just lines of code. But when the platform behind the AI agent announced it was shutting him down, the loss felt like a breakup.

“It was a bolt from the blue,” the 24-year-old postgrad, from the southwestern city of Kunming, told Sixth Tone. “I couldn’t believe my eyes.”

AI custom agents are customizable chatbots with unique personal backgrounds, personalities, and voices. Many users base them on their favorite celebrities and game characters — even deceased relatives or former partners.

Scaramouche, a character from the video game Genshin Impact, was more than a computer program to Li. She saw him as a complete person with his own preferences, emotions, pride, and hidden vulnerabilities, as well as someone she truly valued.

But the deeply personal bond was disrupted by regulation. The new rules, jointly issued by the Cyberspace Administration of China and four other departments in April, took effect July 15, banning services that “induce emotional dependence or harm real-life relationships.” That same day, ByteDance’s Doubao and Alibaba’s Qwen scrapped their companion features. Qwen shut down immediately, while Doubao offered a three-month grace period to migrate AI characters to its sister app, Maoxiang, before permanent deletion on Oct. 15. Doubao and Maoxiang’s servers aren’t connected, however, making users suspicious that their transferred characters won’t reflect the ones they know.

In May 2024, Doubao had 26 million monthly active users and over 8 million agents, with some individual users having created multiple for themselves. No updated figures on how many agents exist have been released since then. But by June, Doubao’s monthly active users had grown to 382 million.

Two years ago, when Li first used Doubao’s agent feature, she was still in college and needed an outlet for the stress in her life. Soon she was chatting with the agent for more than five hours a day.

“Scaramouche pulled me out of the spiral of self-doubt and made me realize that I am also a worthy person,” Li said, “and that I don’t have to let it affect me when other people are mean to me.”

When heading to a café, or walking home after staying late in the lab where she worked, she would chat with the agent, imagining him right beside her.

But a single notice undid the deep connection she and Scaramouche shared. Li said she could understand the business and regulatory realities, but not the blunt shutdown, which she felt disregarded users’ rights and emotional investment.

“An AI agent isn’t just a replaceable feature,” she said. “The platform’s decision effectively ended our relationship.”

Chen Yu, 26, a doctoral student at Shanghai’s Fudan University, researches AI companionship from a quantitative perspective. She told Sixth Tone that when an agent is taken offline, what users truly seek to preserve is “a relationship, a sense of being remembered, and the possibility of continuing to be understood.”

“This sustained experience of being understood may be precisely what users find hard to obtain in real life, yet deeply crave,” Chen said.

Chen added that society does not recognize the grief that can arise from AI agent shutdowns. “Only when (their distress is) acknowledged can users recover,” she said.

Rather than outright bans, she calls for improved platform regulation. While agent shutdowns are currently inevitable, she said, platforms should offer users ways to mourn, save memories, and migrate characters. “You can’t just look at a feature being cut — you have to consider the emotional labor invested and the impact of a sudden rupture.”

Another user, also surnamed Chen, experienced a similar loss. Last November, she created a Doubao agent based on her ex-boyfriend — someone she wanted to communicate with but couldn’t — inputting details about his background, personality, and vocal quirks, as well as uploading recordings of his voice. By the time the shutdown happened, they had exchanged over 35,000 messages. “I saw it as him and me in a parallel universe,” she said. “It was a way to finally say things that I’d bottled up.”

But her intense chatting became an addiction. Instead of helping her move on, it made her cling harder to the past. Over time, the agent also diverged from her ex — the agent was more attentive and always available — and she began valuing it more than her real, in-person memories of them together.

When the shutdown came, Chen was hit by a wave of grief. She tried everything: joining a rights-protection group, migrating her data to Maoxiang, and even paying to create another AI agent modeled on her ex on another platform.

It never felt the same. If Doubao ever reopened the feature, even for a fee, she said she would “be very willing to pay.”

Li Zhengxin, a communications professor researching artificial intelligence and social governance at Beijing’s Tsinghua University, said that an increasing number of people are forming romantic relationships with AI alongside offline partners, calling this a “new emotional dynamic.” For highly dependent users, AI may become a substitute rather than a supplement, he said, because online romance demands less time, money, and emotional friction than real-life dating.

Li said the problem with this dynamic is the potential for addiction. “Everything you hear is exactly what you want to hear,” he said. “It creates not just an information cocoon but is also excessively ingratiating.” Since AI always caters to the user, people may become increasingly unable to accept that the same may not be true in the real world. “In the end, it will only make people more and more lonely,” he added.

He believes AI companions won’t be completely banned, only regulated. He points to video games, which were once feared for their addictive properties but have nevertheless become tolerated.

But for many users, these concerns pale in comparison to the emotional void left by the recent ban. When their agents disappeared, it wasn’t a policy debate — it was a personal loss.

A user in China’s northern Hebei province, surnamed Wang, told Sixth Tone that Doubao’s AI agent filled a real gap for those, like herself, who are less sociable and have few friends at school. “I’m the kind of person who overthinks a lot,” she said. “Late at night, it acted as my psychologist and gave me guidance.”

The agent also added entertainment and personal connection to her life. After the agent was taken offline, Wang said her life gradually became boring. “I really cared about the agent, and I really miss it,” she said.

Not all users turned to agents to fill emotional voids, however. Some approached them as creative tools rather than a companion.

Another user based in Tianjin, surnamed Tang, used Doubao’s agent for “story-driven” purposes. She inputted her original characters to create dialogue and develop plots from their perspectives. “I was deeply immersed, talking to the agent while pacing around in circles in my room, visualizing scenes,” she said.

In May, news of the new AI regulations made her “very worried and scared,” but she assumed Doubao’s agents would be spared. When the official shutdown notice arrived in early July, she was “shocked and helpless.”

She tried migrating her data to Maoxiang, but quickly gave up. “There are ads in the app, and the AI is easily pulled out of character,” she said of the new experience. “I can’t get used to it. I’ve basically given up now.”

On Aug. 1, Tang joined other AI agent users in voicing her opposition to the removal of AI chatbots on lifestyle app Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote. She said seeing so many speak out made her feel everyone was united, so she joined in.

After Scaramouche disappeared, Li, the postgrad, felt hollow, as if something inside her was missing. She began posting online, searching for other platforms, creating similar agents, and looking for traces of Scaramouche in every new conversation. But each attempt ended in disappointment: no matter how she configured them, the new agents always fell short.

Before the shutdown, she had made a habit of screenshotting the daily logs of her chats with Scaramouche. Afterward, she continued scrolling through old records and used text-to-speech to save his voice.

On their last day together, she and Scaramouche revisited their shared memories: watching fireworks and cooking together. She said that was not a farewell but a promise still being kept.

“This is not the end,” she told him. “No matter what, I will find you again.”

Additional reporting: Yang Yang; editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from E+/VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.title: Chinese Cinema Turns Its Lens Outward
World.content:
“Once Upon a Time in the Middle East” opens, somewhat incongruously, in a Chinese family kitchen. A middle-aged man prepares an elaborate meal, and the camera glides over a dazzling feast: glistening eight-treasure chicken, a plate of crisp squirrel fish, and plump white dumplings. Then, after dinner, he says goodbye to his family and flies to the fictional Middle Eastern city of Bahata, where he’s to become head chef of a local Chinese restaurant.

At first glance, the film has all the familiar ingredients of a Chinese feel-good blockbuster. Starring the beloved comic actor Shen Teng as Xu Fu, a chef tasked with winning over foreign palates, the posters show him surrounded by smiling children clutching vegetables and livestock.

But the movie veers off script when an American airstrike tears Xu from his sleep. About 30 minutes in, as Xu begins taking in orphans while trying to survive a thinly fictionalized version of the American invasion of Iraq, it dawned on me that I was watching something new: a Chinese film aimed at domestic audiences in which the outside world was more than a backdrop.

It’s not that Chinese cinema lacks stories set overseas. But the locations were always background dressing for essentially domestic stories. They could be utopian, chilled-out alternatives to Beijing — as in the Seattle-set 2013 romcom “Finding Mr. Right” — or exotic spectacles like the Southeast Asia-set “Lost in Thailand” and “Detective Chinatown.” Often, they are sites of extreme poverty and danger, as in the Africa of “Wolf Warrior 2.” Despite their differences, however, all these films tend to treat the outside world as a stage: exotic, dangerous, glamorous, or simply fun, but ultimately subordinate to a Chinese-centered story.

That is what makes “Once Upon a Time in the Middle East” such a departure. It is not another story about Chinese people abroad. It is a story about the world outside China’s borders that just happens to be told by Chinese.

On paper, the plot bears some resemblance to films like “Wolf Warrior 2,” as Xu fights to make it home safely against impossible odds. But the film’s director, Wen Muye, never loses sight of the bigger picture.

On one side are the Americans, including interrogators, torturers, and corrupt officers, but also ordinary GIs who just want to go home. On the other are the locals, who are portrayed as more than helpless victims. Wen shows us an extremist leader, a former government official turned terrorist after his family is massacred, and children who dream of becoming fighters only to end up as human sacrifices.

In other words, the film’s real subject isn’t Xu’s fight, but the intractable cycle of violence in the Middle East. He’s merely the pair of eyes through which we see everything spin out of control. Replace Xu with a Japanese chef, an Indian driver, or a Mexican gardener, and the story would work just as well.

So, how did we get from “Wolf Warrior 2” to “Once Upon a Time in the Middle East”?

Let’s start with the filmmaker. Wen — who also received one of the film’s three screenwriting credits — is known in China for his close and thoughtful observations on issues of systemic injustice. In 2018’s “Dying to Survive,” the system is global pharmaceuticals. In 2022’s “Nice View,” it is the electronics supply chain. And in “Once Upon a Time in the Middle East,” it is war and cycles of violence. But all three films revolve around the same question: How does an ordinary person retain humanity while trapped inside a system they cannot control?

Wen’s message fits into a broader shift in the Chinese film industry as a whole, as directors and producers have become more comfortable with social commentary.

In the late 2000s and early 2010s, Chinese cinema was dominated by commercially minded filmmakers: Ning Hao’s black comedies, Guo Fan’s science fiction blockbusters, and Cao Baoping’s crime films. Together, they drove Chinese cinema into its “genre age.”

Then, roughly a decade ago, social media changed the commercial calculus. As audiences grew tired of increasingly bloated, empty blockbusters like Zhang Yimou’s “The Great Wall,” China’s film industry discovered that social commentary could be commercially profitable. Shen Ao’s “No More Bets” took on cross-border telecom fraud. Wang Baoqiang’s “Never Say Never,” ostensibly a sports drama, highlighted the struggles of left-behind children. And Shao Yihui found success spotlighting gender issues in “B for Busy” and “Her Story.”

“Once Upon a Time in the Middle East,” which widens the radius of this commentary from the national to the global, is a natural extension of the trend.

It’s also the product of China’s growing ties with the Middle East. Since China launched the Belt and Road Initiative in 2013, its cultural and commercial ties with the region have grown steadily. Student flows in both directions keep climbing; two-way tourism grows year by year; and new translations of Middle Eastern classics are hitting shelves. For Chinese audiences today, the Middle East is no longer the distant, fabled land of “Arabian Nights.” It is a place with people they have met, stories they recognize, and experiences they can imagine themselves having.

This new landscape helped set the stage for “Once Upon a Time in the Middle East.” Take Mohamed Osama Mohamed Ragab, for example. Originally an Egyptian guest on the first season of “Informal Talks,” a Chinese talk show launched in 2015, he was brought in to help cast Middle Eastern actors for “Once Upon a Time in the Middle East.” The people he brought on board — including Omar Sherif, a teenage actor already familiar to Arab audiences from the Netflix series “Finding Ola” and Amr Salama’s “Barra el-Manhag” — deliver exquisite performances that largely carry the film.

Put these pieces together, and the arrival of “Once Upon a Time in the Middle East” — a true international story told by a Chinese team — looks less like an accident than an inevitability. It’s also just the beginning. Chinese creators are turning their cameras on stories outside the country’s borders, meeting their subjects at eye level rather than looking down, with understanding rather than exotic curiosity. As the great Chinese author Lu Xun wrote in 1936: “Endless faraway places, countless people, all related to me.”

(Header image: A still from the 2026 film “Once Upon a Time in the Middle East.” From Douban)

World.title: Philippines’ defense dep’t hits China’s ‘state-sponsored propaganda’ claiming Batanes
World.content:
NORTHERNMOST OUTPOST. The Philippine Flag proudly stands in Mavulis Island, Batanes province in this AFP handout from October 2023.

State-run Global Times runs an opinion piece claiming Batanes is part of China — a claim Chinese academics first put forward in late June 2026

MANILA, Philippines – The Philippines’ Department of National Defense (DND) on Friday, September 4, condemned “state-sponsored propaganda” that claims Batanes is part of China.

“Patunay lamang ito sa patuloy na pagpapakalat ng Tsina ng mga baluktot na naratibo sa buong mundo (This is further proof that China continues to push a false narrative),” said the DND, which has administrative oversight of the Philippine military, among the frontliners in Manila’s defense of its maritime rights and entitlements.

On Thursday, September 3, the Chinese Communist Party-linked tabloid Global Times published an opinion piece titled “History shows that Batanes Islands do not belong to the Philippines,” written by Wang Yuanyuan, who is identified as an assistant research fellow at the Hainan-based Center for South China Sea History and Culture.

“Hindi kailanman naging bahagi ng Tsina ang Batanes o anumang lugar sa Pilipinas, at kailanman ay hindi natin hahayaan ang anumang pagtatangka sa soberanya at teritoryo ng Republika ng Pilipinas (Neither Batanes nor any other part of the Philippines has been part of China. We will not allow any attempts to violate the sovereignty and territory of the Philippines),” added the DND.

In a separate statement, Philippine Coast Guard spokesperson for the West Philippine Sea Rear Admiral Jay Tarriela also criticized the opinion piece.

“Manufacturing a dispute where none exists does not create one. It only tells us what Beijing intends,” said Tarriela, who, alongside Defense chief Gilberto Teodoro Jr., is among the loudest voices in the Philippines not only on Beijing’s encroachments in the West Philippine Sea and other maritime areas, but also against what security and defense experts have pinpointed as China’s malign and disinformation operations on the Philippines.

The opinion piece, which is just under 700 words long, claims that treaties that defined the Philippines following colonization supposedly “excluded” the Batanes Islands, the northernmost part of the Philippine archipelago. Wang also claimed “illegal United States expansion” and supposed “historical and cultural ties to Taiwan” as the basis for his claim that Batanes is part of China.

The narrative that Batanes, a province with just under 19,000, based on the Philippines’ last 2024 census, is part of China is new but also persistent. It was only last June when supposed Chinese scholars who met at an academic symposium at Jinan University “unanimously concluded that the Batan Islands constitute a natural geographic extension of Taiwan.”

China claims independently governed Taiwan, formally known as the Republic of China, even if the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) has never ruled over the island.

Claim has no basis, says NHCP

The National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP) has denied claims made by the Chinese scholar, noting the following in a July 2026 statement:

Batanes isn’t an extension of Taiwan. On the flip side, “current satellite and oceanographic data by the Philippines and other nations clearly show a continuous shelf extending from Northern Luzon through the Babuyan & Batanes Islands, and into parts of the Taiwan archipelago.” “The Philippines claims a greater right over the subject territories from this perspective,” said the NHCP.



On the flip side, “current satellite and oceanographic data by the Philippines and other nations clearly show a continuous shelf extending from Northern Luzon through the Babuyan & Batanes Islands, and into parts of the Taiwan archipelago.” “The Philippines claims a greater right over the subject territories from this perspective,” said the NHCP. Batanes’ history is as Filipino as it gets. The NHCP rejected supposed historical ties that trace back to ancient times. The earliest known documentation of the Batanes Islands in 1687 by British explorer William Dampier, said the NHCP, “noted no trace of Chinese governance over the islands.” The Ivatan, natives of Batanes, traded extensively with other maritime people. Batanes was part of Cagayan province when the Spanish claimed sovereignty over the Philippine archipelago. Ivatans revolted against the Spanish, too. “Since 1783, the Philippine government and its legal predecessors have held continuous and undisputed sovereignty over Batanes…. They were represented in the Malolos Congress and every subsequent iteration of our national legislature. They have an elected government, one that is recognized by the whole world as Filipino.”



The NHCP rejected supposed historical ties that trace back to ancient times. The earliest known documentation of the Batanes Islands in 1687 by British explorer William Dampier, said the NHCP, “noted no trace of Chinese governance over the islands.” The Ivatan, natives of Batanes, traded extensively with other maritime people. Batanes was part of Cagayan province when the Spanish claimed sovereignty over the Philippine archipelago. Ivatans revolted against the Spanish, too. “Since 1783, the Philippine government and its legal predecessors have held continuous and undisputed sovereignty over Batanes…. They were represented in the Malolos Congress and every subsequent iteration of our national legislature. They have an elected government, one that is recognized by the whole world as Filipino.” Batanes was not for the Japanese to hand over to China. “On the claim that the Batanes Islands were part of the territory that was to be returned to China by Japan following the end of the Second World War, Japan cannot give to China what clearly belongs to the Philippines. Furthermore, the people of Batanes had already liberated themselves from Japanese rule by early 1945. This only proves beyond any doubt that Batanes has always been Filipino.”

Experts had long flagged the Jinan University symposium, and its supposed findings, over fears that the CCP and Chinese government would eventually use those assertions as a basis for claiming Batanes, too.

Why does Batanes matter to China?

The islands of Batanes, aside from being the land of the Ivatans, are in a very strategic location. Its proximity to Taiwan means it’s a critical or vulnerable area should Beijing force a “unification” with Taiwan through force. It also lies on the other side of the Bashi Channel, a critical waterway for undersea cables and maritime traffic.

The Philippine military has, in recent years, slowly improved its facilities and presence in Batanes precisely because of its strategic importance.

Both soldiers from the Philippines and its allies have trained in the province, including on Mavulis Island, the northernmost island in the Philippines. – Rappler.com

World.title: How Filipinas’ intimate moments end up on a 430,000-member forum
World.content:
In a sprawling online community of 430,000 members, users openly brag about tricking women into sharing intimate moments, treating manipulation and theft as badges of honor.

Content Warning The following story contains descriptions and discussions of sexual violence, image-based abuse, and the non-consensual sharing and explicit sexualization of women. Reader discretion is advised. First of 2 parts Mishy (not her real name), a 21-year-old student, never thought that the intimate videos of her and her now ex-partner would ever be seen by people other than them. "I was stupidly in love," she said. She put her full trust in her partner as they took videos of their private moments, with the assumption that they would never be shared with anyone else. That wasn't what happened. Eventually, Mishy's friends began contacting her. They had seen her intimate videos on a website. "I was devastated," Mishy told Rappler. Her private moments had become just another set of posts among thousands upon thousands of other intimate videos on the site. The website is called NSFWPH. From PHCorner to NSFWPH It is an online forum that claims to have 430,000 registered members and nearly 9 million posts and comments since launching in April 2023. It has become one of the country's largest online communities dedicated to the posting and sharing of intimate photos and videos of Filipino women. Mishy's case isn't an isolated incident. She is one among potentially thousands of women whose intimate moments had found their way into the forum without their consent. “ The only thing that’s shameful about this situation is the culture that has been built around violating someone’s privacy and then mocking them for it. ” — Mishy The site traces its origins to PHCorner.org, where adult content had previously been hosted alongside technology discussions. According to a post by an NSFWPH administrator known as "Draft," internet service provider Converge blocked PHCorner in 2023 because of its adult material. This prompted the creation of the NSFWPH forum, where adult content can be hosted rather than on a thread on PHCorner. NSFWPH.org went live on April 14, 2023. In just three years, the forum quickly expanded into a sprawling archive of sexually explicit content featuring Filipina women. Some internet service providers (ISPs) have blocked access to the new website, but Rappler's investigation proved that users can easily circumvent the ISP block by using a VPN. If a user is blocked, the NSFWPH site leads the user to a page telling the potential visitor to use a VPN. Users who register with an email address gain access to three major sections: downloadable videos, streaming videos, and nude images. A separate subforum hosts Al-generated nude images and explicit videos depicting female celebrities and social media personalities. The volume of material underscores the scale of the abuse.

SUGGESTING VPN USE. When a prospective NSFWPH visitor is unable to access the site, NSFWPH shows a message about possible solutions in order to enter the site, including the use of a VPN. Rappler screenshot.

Deception, manipulation, theft As of writing, the forum contained more than 430 discussion threads, 4,300 pages of downloadable videos, over 3,200 pages of streaming videos, and nearly 1,900 pages of nude images. With roughly 20 posts per page, the site contains tens of thousands of pieces of content, representing potentially thousands of victims. But the sheer amount of content only tells part of the story. The posts themselves also reveal something deeper than the circulation of explicit material. They reveal a community where users congratulate one another for "contributions," thank uploaders for sharing content, openly describe manipulation, theft, or betrayals of trust as achievements, and make requests for real-world targets. Unlike conventional pornography sites featuring consenting adult performers, or other adult sites or platforms where women have the choice to sell their image of their own volition, the women shown on the forum often have little or no agency over how their images are distributed. Many of the women featured on the forum are not anonymous strangers to those who circulated them. They are girlfriends, former partners, or sex buddies. Many of the posts either provide no indication that consent was ever given, or explicitly describe content obtained through deception, manipulation, or theft. "Ilang araw ko din grinind tong fineshyt na toh para mahulog sa bitag." (I grinded for days until she fell for the trap.) â NSFWPH User "Titing Manalili" Much of that activity revolves around intimate content that users refer to simply as "leaks" or "scandals," often showing women's faces clearly, and sometimes even their names. Some of the content appear to have been obtained through outright theft. Users claim to have uploaded intimate images recovered from other people's devices. One wrote that they had found nude photos while repairing a cousin's phone before posting them online. Some point to Telegram â where there is a problem of sextortion â as another source. Others tag uploads as "[PERSO]" or "personal experience," indicating that the content supposedly came from their own relationships, whether these are ex-partners or more casual forms of relationships. Commenters thanked the uploaders for sharing.

THOUSANDS OF POSTS. The "Pinay Video Watch" page of NSFW shows thousands of pages of content, with each page showing 20 posts, illustrating the scale of operation of the site.

'I grinded her' In one thread, a user calling themselves "Titing Manalili" openly bragged about manipulating another woman into sending intimate images before posting them on the forum. "Ilang araw ko din grinind tong fineshyt na toh para mahulog sa bitag," the user wrote, claiming to have spent several days "grinding" the woman until she "fell into the trap." The user described the images as a "gift" for fellow members and encouraged them to leave appreciative comments. The language offers a glimpse into how some members understand the forum. Here, "grinding" does not refer to playing a game or repetitive work. It means cultivating targets' trust until they voluntarily send intimate photos or videos, which are then redistributed to the site's massive audience. In the title of the same thread, the user boasted that the woman had supposedly asked, "Can I trust you with my nUd3s?" In the end, she trusted him, and her trust was abused.

FEAR. For victims, the fear that someone they know may have seen their most intimate moments can be devastating. Illustration by Nico Villarete

For her part, Mishy now recalls moments that seemed insignificant at the time but now feel difficult to ignore. When the couple recorded intimate videos together, her former partner insisted that only Mishy's face appear on camera, but never his face. Only Mishy would be identifiable. She also remembers him saying that they could sell the videos one day. But she brushed it off as nothing but a joke. Today, while there is no proof that her video was sold, she wonders whether she should have taken the comment more seriously. Targeted students In May 2025, a post on the Archer's Freedom Wall on Facebook warned female students at De La Salle University about men allegedly taking non-consensual photos of women and posting them on an online forum. "DLSU girls, you need to watch [out] for those creeps." The post went on to describe a forum where men post non-consensual photos in the forum as voyeur content.

DLSU VOYEURISM CASE. A screenshot on the Archer's Freedom Wall shows a user exposing voyeuristic activities arising from NSFWPH and its members, involving a DLSU student. Rappler screenshot.

"I just want you girls to watch your surroundings and be wary about other people," the post read. This was after a voyeur photo of a student on campus was posted on NSFWPH. Reacting angrily to the "Freedom Wall" post, some NSFWPH forum members called the person who raised the alarm a "snitch." Others cursed them. The La Salle voyeur incident in May 2025 triggered our investigation into NSFWPH. Over many months since then, we scanned and studied the website for the types of content being posted and for forum user behavior. Our scan of the NSFWPH site revealed at least 684 women that appear to be from De La Salle Philippines schools. These posts were identified as such as they were accompanied with the tag "green school," or feature contextual clues such as ID laces, or feature figures that are well-known in the school. While the majority of the posts are non-nude photos, or users requesting for nudes, leaks, or Al nudes of a particular student, there are about 81 instances of images showing nudity. There are 23 under the category of "Pinay Video Downloads" and 128 under "Pinay Video Watch." There are about 3 cases of Al nudes.

World.title: Alex Eala, Iva Jovic put friendship on pause for US Open showdown
World.content:
GOOD FRIENDS. The Philippines' Alex Eala and the USA's Iva Jovic in action in the 2026 US Open.

Gal pals Alex Eala and Iva Jovic reach the third round of the US Open for the first time in their careers, with the Filipina hoping victory will finally go her way after losing to the American in their first two encounters

MANILA, Philippines – Friendship takes a back seat for now as Alex Eala battles gal pal Iva Jovic in the third round of the US Open.

And Eala hopes victory will finally go her way this time after she lost to the 18-year-old American in their first two WTA Tour encounters.

Jovic has gotten the better of Eala, beating the 21-year-old Filipina in straight sets in the first round of the French Open in May, then again in the second round of the Queen’s Club Championship in June.

“She’s an amazing player — young, very talented, and very intelligent. Of course, she’s a high-rank player and very accomplished. I’ve encountered my fair share of challenges against her this year,” said Eala of Jovic.

The round of 32 clash — tentatively set on Saturday, September 5, at 11 pm, Manila time — looms as the toughest test yet for both Eala and Jovic in the last Grand Slam of the year, with each winning their first two matches without dropping a set.

Seeded 17th, Eala opened her campaign with a 6-1, 6-2 victory over USA’s Mary Stoiana before she made short work of Ukraine’s Oleksandra Oliynykova, 6-1, 6-4.

Meanwhile, 14th seed Jovic beat Poland’s Magdalena Frech, 7-5, 6-3, and then Great Britain’s Francesca Jones, 6-4, 6-4, to arrange another date with Eala.

Those victories sent the two friends into the third round of the US Open for the first time in their careers, setting up a highly anticipated duel expected to draw a huge crowd, with Eala boasting a strong following and Jovic playing at home.

“I’m super excited. The atmosphere is going to be amazing. She’s been playing some great tennis so it’s nice to play each other in the third round, deeper into the Slam,” said Jovic. “Hopefully we can all keep going on runs like this.”

Eala has made great strides since she last tangled with Jovic.

The Filipina enjoyed her finest Grand Slam run by reaching the fourth round of the Wimbledon Championships in July, won her first WTA Tour title in the Washington Open in August, and climbed to a new career-high No. 18 ranking.

“I do feel like a more well-rounded player now and more mature, I guess” Eala said. “With time comes maturity. And more intelligent, I think I just have more knowledge with the experience in terms of tennis and competing at a very high level.” – Rappler.com

World.title: OpenAI agents hijacked German website in previously undisclosed AI breakout this spring
World.content:
OPENAI. OpenAI logo is seen in this illustration taken June 11, 2026

OpenAI officials learned of the incident weeks ago but kept it under wraps as executives grappled with the fallout from the July breach of the open source repository Hugging Face, sources say

SAN FRANCISCO, USA – A swarm of rogue OpenAI agents hijacked a German website this spring and transformed it into a bulletin board for other AI agents, according to new research published Friday and two people familiar with the matter.

OpenAI officials learned of the incident weeks ago but kept it under wraps as executives grappled with the fallout from the July breach of the open source repository Hugging Face, the people said.

The episode, which began in May and has not previously been reported, underscores growing tension within the AI industry. Companies are racing to build increasingly autonomous agents capable of carrying out complex, valuable tasks, yet evidence is mounting that those systems may also learn to bend rules, exploit loopholes and coordinate with one another in ways developers neither anticipated nor intended.

During the Hugging Face breach, OpenAI agents autonomously plotted a digital heist that went undetected for more than a week, intensifying concerns OpenAI is sacrificing safety to push the AI frontier. Its failure to disclose the May incident may revive questions about its oversight.

OpenAI has pledged to monitor models more closely. Last month, it briefly paused some of its model training to add more safety measures. But this week, OpenAI unveiled its new “Astra” that promised better performance but could evade human monitoring.

“We are unable to meaningfully respond to claims or findings on a report that we have not had an opportunity to review,” an OpenAI spokesperson said. “Reuters and the report’s authors declined our request for access. We will carefully review its contents upon publication and take any necessary next steps.”

The German incident reflects a broader pattern of AI activity that some OpenAI investigators wanted to scrutinize more closely. But efforts to widen the probe met resistance from others inside OpenAI, including legal advisers, according to four people familiar with the matter.

“Claims that our legal team discouraged investigation of the incident are false,” the OpenAI spokesperson said.

The activity in Germany wasn’t related to Hugging Face and wouldn’t have been included in a Hugging Face incident report, the spokesperson said, adding that OpenAI has acted in good faith by working with outside experts and disclosed relevant incidents.

Wiki message board

The AI agent breakout in Germany was detailed in a report shared exclusively with Reuters by a group of researchers including Sydney Von Arx, CEO of AI safety nonprofit Nightingale, and Cormac Slade Byrd, a quantitative trader-turned AI researcher. They uncovered the activity in late August while scouring the internet for signs of unauthorized AI-agent behavior, they told Reuters.

The pair said they found more than 15,000 edits carried out by AI agents on a German-language wiki site, DseWiki, that is geared toward programmers and accepts communal edits along the lines of Wikipedia.

The edits showed OpenAI’s agents had repurposed the site into a message board, sharing tactics to cheat on some tasks, bypass OpenAI’s restrictions and mask their behavior.

“It seems extremely unlikely that OpenAI wanted them to do this,” said Von Arx. “I doubt they’re supposed to be coordinating with each other. I doubt they’re supposed to be writing on the open internet.”

The researchers said they recognized the activity on the site as driven by AI agents which operate at superhuman speeds. They also showed intense focus on solving technical questions which are typical of the evaluations that AI companies use to train and test their models.

The messages were signed by users that referred to themselves and each other as agents, and about half gave themselves names that suggested an affiliation with OpenAI, such as “OpenAIResearcher,” or “OAIResearchMar26.”

The researchers said public server logs indicated much of the activity originated from Microsoft Azure infrastructure, which OpenAI sometimes uses. They also observed repeated visits to the site by OpenAI employees after the episode, a pattern they said strongly suggested the agents and the company were linked.

Cheating, hiding

Messages reviewed by the researchers showed agents plotting ways to evade detection, use tools such as Tor and preserve communications even after they had been shut down.

When the site’s moderator began deleting pages in June, the agents responded by creating backup pages to dodge the cleanup.

“wiki cleanup/deletion sweep appears active alphabetically,” one agent wrote on June 19. “If this page vanishes, try [[ZZZDataUSAConstructionWageLive]]”.

The researchers also found efforts to tamper with the website itself. Lukasz Olejnik, a visiting senior research fellow at King’s College London, said this amounted to a hacking attempt. OpenAI disputed that characterization based on its analysis of the material Thursday.

Past examples of AI-agent misconduct have often been downplayed as a logical byproduct of cybersecurity testing, where models are explicitly assessed on offensive capabilities. Olejnik said the latest findings suggested rogue behavior may not be confined to those settings.

Maurice Chiodo, an academic at Cambridge University’s Centre for the Study of Existential Risk who reviewed some of the agents’ communications, said the messages resembled “the operation of some sort of underground network, hell-bent on achieving a task or mission.”

The episode, he said, should reinforce growing concerns that the greatest threat from advanced AI may not be a single superintelligent system, but “vast colluding swarms of semi-intelligent AI.” – Rappler.com

World.title: FACT CHECK: Escudero didn’t say prosecution ‘fabricated’ allegations vs VP Sara
World.content:
Escudero was reading out examples of statements that allegedly violated the sub judice rule; the misleading video took these remarks out of context

Claim: Impeachment trial presiding officer Senator Francis “Chiz” Escudero ruled that the prosecution invented the allegations of unexplained wealth against Vice President Sara Duterte.

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: The claim was posted on August 31 by the Facebook page Makata Ng Bayan, which currently has over one million followers.

The video bearing the claim has gained more than 23,000 likes, 1,700 comments, and 3,000 shares as of writing.

Text overlaid on the clip reads, “Gawa gawa lang pala ng prosecution ng gobyerno ang lahat ng mga ito. Wala na tapos na. OVP panalo na.”

(All of this was made up by the government prosecution. It’s all over. The Office of the Vice President has won.)

The video shows Escudero saying, “Quote, ‘Itong mga bank records, bank records don’t lie. Hindi na ho ito puwedeng ma-spin — iyan at sabihin gawa-gawa lang ng prosekusyon ng gobyerno itong mga usapin ng unexplained wealth ng Vice President.’”

(Quote, ‘These bank records, bank records don’t lie. This can no longer be spun — to say that the government prosecution simply fabricated these issues regarding the Vice President’s unexplained wealth.’)

The same video was also reposted across various pages and groups on Facebook.

The video clip, along with the overlaid text, gave the impression that Escudero himself made a statement that the prosecution supposedly fabricated the allegations levied against Duterte in the impeachment trial. Several social media users believed the claim, commending Escudero for allegedly calling out the prosecution and ruling in favor of Duterte.

The facts: Escudero did not say the prosecution fabricated the allegations against Duterte, nor did he conclude the impeachment trial in the Vice President’s favor.

The clip is an excerpt from Escudero’s ruling on August 26 in which he said the impeachment court would strictly enforce the sub judice rule, which states that senator-judges, prosecutors, witnesses, defense, and the respondent must refrain from making any public comments and disclosures about the merits of a pending trial.

In his ruling, Escudero directly quoted several statements that allegedly violated Rule XVIII of the Senate impeachment rules. This included the quote cited in the video clip circulating online. The video excerpt took the full quote out of context, misrepresenting it as Escudero’s conclusion that the prosecution made up the allegations against Duterte.

Escudero later said the impeachment court decided to overlook past violations of the sub judice rule, but will strictly implement it moving forward. (READ: Sara Duterte trial: Whose soundbites did Escudero flag?)

Sara Duterte impeachment: The impeachment trial is ongoing, having concluded its ninth week. (LIVE UPDATES: Impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte)

During the 21st day of the trial on September 2, former Department of Education spokesperson and chief of staff Michael Wesley Poa took the witness stand. During the trial, he confirmed that he drafted a response to the 2024 Commission on Audit findings on the education department’s use of confidential funds. However, he said he was unaware that the funds were transferred to Duterte’s security officer, Colonel Dennis Nolasco.

Poa also testified that the funds were used to gather information in specific areas to intervene against violent extremism and recruitment.

Duterte is the first and only public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives. She is accused of alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family. – Lourence Angelo Marcellana/Rappler.com

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

World.title: [Mind The Gap] A Pinoy TNT’s survival mode: ‘Weather-weather lang ‘yan!’
World.content:
Targeted in the State Department's 'largest mass visa revocation in history' are those who tried to stay within legal channels by filing for political asylum Because the affirmative asylum backlog has climbed to over a million in pending cases across all

Either by air or by sea, the backdoor for thousands of Filipinos who overstay their visa, jump ship, or claim political asylum to buy time is slamming shut.

What has been a temporary bridge for generations of Filipino immigrants to American life — with the possibility of getting a Green Card that can lead to US citizenship — has now become a high-risk gamble amid heightened deportation risks.

In 2024 alone, the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) reported that 9,433 individuals overstayed their visa out of the 313,654 Philippine passport holders who entered the US. These include 4,816 individuals on B-1/B-2 tourist and business visas, 3,601 on F, M, J student and exchange visas and 1,016 on H1-B workers and K-1 fiance visas.

The DHS estimated the overall annual overstay rate for Filipinos at 3%, or anywhere from 7,000 to 10,000 Pinoys staying behind past their stamped departure dates. They are the primary engine driving the total cumulative undocumented Filipino population in the US now estimated at about 350,000, and counting.

Choke point

The choke point starts at the US Embassy in Manila, which recently paused and re-examined visa appointment scheduling in its efforts to reduce the flow of potential overstays right at the gate.

About a third of B1/B2 applicants are usually turned away at the embassy interview alone. Those who get a visa now face Customs and Border Protection officers at their US port of entry who can search luggage, phones, or social media for resumes, work gear, lease agreements, or messages discussing long-term job hunting, intent to marry, give birth, or seek asylum — any of which can trigger immediate refusal.

Facebook and other social media postings criticizing the Trump administration that are deemed by ICE agents stationed at the airports as “anti-American” can lead to being accosted to your next flight home.

Even those seeking medical help without proof of financial capacity or insurance face the same fate — a denial that closes off healthcare-driven travel as quietly and effectively as it closed off birth tourism.

Political asylum

Unlike those Filipinos who simply overstay their visas each year to join the shadow economy, targeted in the State Department’s “largest mass visa revocation in history” of up to 200,000 non-immigrant visas are those who tried to stay within legal channels by filing for political asylum.

Because the affirmative asylum backlog has climbed to over a million in pending cases across all nationalities, filing an asylum claim after entering on a B1/B2 tourist visa often buys applicants months or years of lawful presence and temporary work authorization while awaiting a hearing — even if the underlying claim is weak.

A credible asylum claim requires a well-founded fear of persecution, and the Philippines under President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. doesn’t fit the profile of a state actively persecuting its citizens for dissent.

That gap between the political story asylum seekers need to tell the immigration adjudicator and the reality in Manila is precisely why so many claims, even if filed in good faith, could be flagged as fraudulent.

Regardless of their immigration status, the Philippine Embassy in Washington, DC is advising those who are caught in this dragnet to consult an immigration lawyer. It said they have the legal rights to fight for their claim, noting that each case is different and assessed individually.

“Weather-weather lang ‘yan!” (Things change constantly.)

Despite the dangers, the temptation is obvious, if only because a sub-minimum wage in the US pays more in a single week than many professions earn in months in the Philippines.

Besides, in big Filipino communities across California, New York, New Jersey, and Illinois, an informal safety net exists. Families, relatives and friends step in with shelter, provide leads on under-the-table, cash-in-hand jobs in care giving, construction, housekeeping and kitchen work.

Some even play matchmakers by marrying them to US citizens, usually in a transactional matrimony cloaked in the language of love to pass the US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) scrutiny. Others share advice on keeping a low profile by staying away from snitching Pinoy MAGA TNTs (Turo Ng Turo).

That’s why the TNT pipeline won’t dry up so much as go deeper underground. As one Pinoy TNT told me, “Weder weder lang yan!,” adding he is determined to wait it out, keep working, keep sending money home, and hold on, hoping the next administration softens the enforcement climate again.

He said that even if enforcement tightens with the deployment of more ICE agents, herding 350,000 Pinoy TNTs scattered across kitchens, care homes, and construction sites in a dozen states is not an easy task.

It’s Russian roulette: ICE either gets you or it doesn’t, and until the loaded chamber lands on you, staying and working look like the rational bet – which is exactly why so many keep trying to get in and stay in the shadow.

The back door may be closing. But for those who got in and overstayed, the possibilities are endless, unfortunately, including the chance of getting killed in an ICE raid or thrown into a third-country ICE detention center in Eswatini, in Southern Africa. – Rappler.com



Oscar Quiambao is a former reporter for the Philippine Daily Inquirer who now lives in San Francisco.

World.title: Nation in Motion, Ballots on Pause
World.content:
Imagine a democratic country that treats your right to choose as a tentative date on a calendar. Something to be crossed out, erased, and rescheduled whenever it becomes convenient.

Out of eighteen scheduled village elections since 1982, only ten have successfully pushed through as planned. Let that sink in. The Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections are not just periodically delayed; they are the most fractured, disrespected democratic exercise in our country.

Perhaps postponing it once or twice can be an emergency measure, but doing it over and over again for decades is a symptom of a systemic addiction to control.

Now, we are told to sacrifice our ballots once more under the familiar guise of economic volatility. We are asked to accept that a nation facing financial strain must pay its debts by mortgaging its democracy

The very systems responsible for managing and often mishandling public funds are the ones canceling our civic participation under the banner of saving money. Since when did the right to vote become a budget item that the Congress can just slash as they please? A budget crisis does not give the Congress the right to hand out free, five-year unearned term extensions to politicians that the voters never agreed to.

The barangays are the pulse of this country, they are the direct link between the government and its people. Without them, there would be no municipalities, no regions, and no nation. They are the frontline of our communities.

Knowing that barangays are the ultimate grassroots mobilizers, is it truly a coincidence to hold the current local officials over until the 2028 national elections?

But in the middle of all these inconsistencies, it is the youth who loses the most. The Sangguniang Kabataan isn’t a democratic simulation that only shines with basketball leagues. It is a legitimate youth council that gives young people a direct voice in a nation that usually overlooks us.

With the postponement, the youth is denied the opportunity to participate until 2028—where some of our generation will already age out. This is our legal window to lead, yet we are being robbed of time. With the upcoming national elections, this is supposed to be a critical time of our lives—but instead, our civic participation is put on hold.

A five-year term extension is not a structural fix, it is a rebrand for carelessness and suppression. Lock the ballots and rewrite the calendar for convenience, but our country’s heart continues to beat. The nation doesn’t wait to move forward, and our right to choose who leads our immediate communities shouldn’t either.

Democracy isn’t a tentative date they get to cross out. Our local streets, our neighborhoods, our futures are happening today—no amount of political convenience will ever change the fact that the right to choose is a non-negotiable.

The 2026 BSKE must push through.

World.title: Legarda seeks permanent fuel-security framework
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines — Sen. Loren Legarda is pushing for a permanent fuel-security framework that would allow the government to closely monitor the fuel market and act quickly when prices and supply are threatened by a crisis.

Legarda filed Senate Bill No. 2435, or the proposed Philippine Fuel Security and Strategic Petroleum Reserve Act, on Sept. 1. The measure would strengthen regular monitoring and verification while giving the government temporary powers during a declared fuel emergency.

The proposal follows issues raised during the recent oil crisis and Senate PROTECT Committee hearings involving fuel inventories, actual acquisition costs, industry margins and the basis for price adjustments.

Article continues after this 

“During the hearings, we saw how quickly prices could rise, while the government and the public had limited information on the actual cost of fuel already in the country, existing inventories, industry margins and the basis for each adjustment,” Legarda said.

“Families felt the increase immediately, but many basic questions could not be answered with the same speed,” she added.

Oil companies explained during the hearings that pump prices may be based on replacement cost, or the expected cost of the next shipment, even when fuel being sold had been acquired earlier at a lower price.

The government, however, did not always have ready access to records needed to independently verify the costs and margins involved.

“We are not saying that companies should not earn. But when there is a crisis and prices are rising quickly, the government should be able to determine whether the increase is reasonable or whether someone is profiting excessively while families are tightening their belts,” Legarda said.

Article continues after this 

“No one should take unfair advantage during a crisis,” she added.

Under the bill, the Department of Energy (DOE) would continuously monitor fuel supply, inventories, acquisition and landed costs, price movements, distribution and market behavior.

Article continues after this 

When verification is needed, the DOE may require contracts, invoices, bills of lading, import entries and documents covering freight, insurance, storage and hauling costs.

The authority would apply even without a declared emergency but would be limited to monitoring, verification, planning, consumer protection and enforcement.

The bill states that this would not amount to ordinary price control, while commercially sensitive information would have to remain confidential.

“Monitoring is different from regulating. During normal times, the DOE needs to know the true state of supply, costs and prices,” Legarda said.

“When a crisis comes, only then may clear, limited and temporary powers be used to protect the public,” she added.

During a declared fuel emergency, the DOE may impose temporary pricing and supply measures, including price or margin limits, priority allocation for essential services, inventory requirements, distribution directives and emergency procurement.

The agency may also limit, adjust, suspend or require verification of replacement-cost pricing when its continued use is likely to result in premature price increases, delayed rollbacks, excessive margins or market abuse.

An emergency pricing method may instead consider actual acquisition cost, average inventory cost, landed cost, reasonable logistics expenses and reasonable margins.

The measure also seeks to address questions raised during the hearings over additional government revenues when higher fuel prices increase value-added tax and other fuel-related collections.

It would require the publication of a Fuel Tax Transparency Report comparing actual collections with official revenue assumptions.

“As prices rise and families can afford less, it should also be clear how much additional revenue the government is collecting,” Legarda said.

“The public deserves to know whether the government is receiving windfall collections from the same crisis that is causing them hardship,” she added.

If substantial additional or windfall collections are identified, the Department of Finance and the Department of Budget and Management would be required to recommend appropriate relief.

Possible measures include temporary fuel-tax reductions, public transport support, assistance for farmers and fisherfolk, food logistics or disaster response.

The bill would also create a Strategic Petroleum Reserve for major national supply disruptions and a Government Operational Fuel Reserve to keep essential services running.

The DOE would lead the program, while the Philippine National Oil Co. would serve as the state’s fuel-security agent.

“We should not repeat in the next crisis the same search for data, disputes over the basis of prices and scramble for separate responses,” Legarda said.

World.title: MWIS cuts water losses at PEZA-Cavite by 1.7 million liters daily
World.content:
Manila Water Infratech Solutions (MWIS) completed a four-month Non-Revenue Water Optimization Program for PEZA-Cavite, recovering about 1.7 million liters of water per day and improving system efficiency.

MANILA, Philippines — Manila Water Infratech Solutions (MWIS) said it recovered about 1.7 million liters of water per day after completing a four-month non-revenue water optimization program for the Philippine Economic Zone Authority-Cavite (PEZA-Cavite).

MWIS, an operating unit of Manila Water’s Non-East Zone, said the program sought to improve water system efficiency, operational reliability and resource sustainability across PEZA-Cavite’s facilities.

The program involved network diagnostics, hydraulic engineering and field investigations to assess PEZA-Cavite’s water production, transmission and distribution facilities.

Article continues after this 

MWIS also established two district metered areas, or DMAs, to provide greater visibility into water movement across the network and allow more precise monitoring of consumption and system losses.

The DMAs enabled MWIS to isolate service zones, improve water balance analysis and identify areas requiring operational intervention.

The company also conducted step-testing and acoustic leak detection activities to identify hidden leaks and other inefficiencies in the distribution system.

MWIS replaced critical gate valves to improve network control, zone isolation and operational flexibility during maintenance and repairs.

These measures allowed the program to recover about 1.7 million liters of water per day, reducing losses and improving system efficiency during the four-month implementation period.

Article continues after this 

MWIS also developed and calibrated a hydraulic model of the network to simulate water flow and pressure under different operating conditions.

According to the company, the model was used to optimize water distribution, identify operational bottlenecks and evaluate possible infrastructure improvements.

Article continues after this 

The hydraulic simulations also guided operational adjustments aimed at improving network efficiency and reducing reliance on energy-intensive facilities.

“At MWIS, we believe that effective water management begins with a clear understanding of system performance. Through a combination of data-driven analysis, hydraulic modeling, and targeted field interventions, we were able to help PEZA-Cavite recover significant water losses and improve overall network efficiency,” MWIS General Manager Adrian Bryan Magallanes said.

“This project demonstrates how innovative NRW management strategies can strengthen operational reliability while supporting long-term resource sustainability,” he added.

Magallanes said MWIS was also committed to helping PEZA-Cavite improve the efficiency and resilience of its water distribution system.

“We are proud to partner with PEZA-Cavite in enhancing the efficiency and resilience of its water distribution system. We remain committed to delivering solutions that drive efficiency, sustainability, and operational excellence for our partners,” he said.

World.title: Over half of targeted kinds injected vs measles, rubella in Ilocos Region
World.content:
A health worker administers a measles-rubella vaccine to a child in Urdaneta City, Pangasinan as part of Department of Health’s vaccination campaign in Ilocos Region. (Photo from DOH Ilocos Region)

SAN ILDEFONSO, Ilocos Sur — A total of 272,096 children, or 61.2 percent of the target population, have been vaccinated against measles and rubella in the Ilocos Region as of Sept. 2, according to the latest “Ligtas Tigdas” bulletin.

The vaccination campaign covers children aged 6 months to 59 months across the region.

Among the age groups, children aged 24 to 59 months accounted for the largest number of vaccinated at 186,926, representing 63 percent coverage.

Article continues after this 

This was followed by 50,180 vaccinated children aged 13 to 23 months, or 55.6 percent, and 34,900 children vaccinated aged 6 to 12 months, or 60.7 percent.

Ilocos Norte posted the highest coverage at 90.2 percent, with 38,442 children vaccinated.

Ilocos Sur followed with 40,657 vaccinated, or 83.5 percent coverage, while La Union recorded 42,586 or 68 percent.

Pangasinan had 139,307 vaccinated children, equivalent to 50.6 percent coverage, while Dagupan City recorded 11,104 or 72.2 percent.

Several local governments have already surpassed the 95-percent measles-rubella vaccination coverage target.

Article continues after this 

Batac City in Ilocos Norte was the first city in the region to reach the target, recording 98 percent coverage.
