World.title: Cats v Blues player ratings: From Geelong’s ‘Superman’, to those who had ‘horror’ nights for Carlton
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Opinion Cats v Blues player ratings: From Geelong’s ‘Superman’, to those who had ‘horror’ nights for Carlton

Loading

The fairytale had to end at some stage for the Blues, and it happened at the MCG in front of more than 96,000 fans as the finals-hardened Cats flexed their muscles right when they needed to most. Danny Russell (Geelong) and Sam McClure (Carlton) rate every Carlton player’s performance from the blockbuster elimination final. Bailey Smith celebrates on the siren after the Cats knocked the Blues out of the finals race. Getty Images Geelong



(2) Jay Polkinghorne: The latest to suffer the curse of the big forward during this finals series, he found it hard to break free and was monstered by Jacob Weitering in several marking contests but did manage a goal. 4/10 (3) Bailey Smith: Struggled to shake off a Cooper Lord tag early and would have been annoyed that his opponent kicked two goals. But he is impossible to keep down and got busy in the third. 7/10 (4) Tanner Bruhn: One of Geelong’s best early, and looks to have found his niche across half-back. He was able to become a spectator as the game wore on and the Cats shifted the match into their forward 50. 6/10 Jeremy Cameron (left) was nowhere near his best, but still walked off the ground a winner of yet another final alongside Shannon Neale and Oisin Mullin. AFL Photos (5) Jeremy Cameron: Harder to spot than Where’s Wally in the first half. He didn’t get near the footy. He started at half-back before moving to the wing, but struggled to have any meaningful impact. He’s clearly not right. 3/10



(7) Shaun Mannagh: He has yanked himself out of the “opportunist/goal sneak” pigeonhole to become a damaging midfielder. Close to the Cats’ best as he rotated through the square and found stacks of the ball. 8/10 (9) Max Holmes: Is it poor taste to say the operation was a success but the patient died? He ran the game out and, after a long lay-off, will be better for the run, but he could not find the footy and had little impact. 3/10 (11) Michael Edwards: His biggest moment was being crunched by Blake Acres in a third-quarter marking contest. It was a relief to see him get up. Other than that, he was probably shaded by Marc Pittonet in the ruck. 5/10 (14) Connor O’Sullivan: He probably wished they had another week off when the Blues came out firing in the first quarter, but was able to put the bus in cruise control thereafter. None of the big Blues got off the chain. 6/10 View post on X



(17) Lawson Humphries: Created one of the pivotal moments of the match when he spoiled a Carlton kick-in at full speed at the start of the third term. It set up a Mannagh goal, and sparked the Geelong avalanche. 5/10 Related Article AFL 2026 Dockers v Hawks player ratings: From a skipper’s career night, to the gun forwards who disappeared (21) Oliver Wiltshire: He kicked three behinds. Had they been goals, he was right up there with the game’s best players. While others shaded him on the stats sheet – he had 22 disposals – he was vital to the Cats’ turnaround. 6/10 (28) Oliver Dempsey: Even though he was short of his brilliant best, was still the game’s best winger. He took two marks deep in the forward pocket in the first and third terms, but could not convert either. 6/10 (30) Tom Atkins: He looked bamboozled, or even slow, when Sam Walsh and Jagga Smith were creating havoc in the opening term. But the never-say-die fan favourite combined with Mannagh to help swing the game back on Geelong’s terms. 6/10



(32) Gryan Miers: More reliable than a box of matches, he was one of the chief fire starters for Geelong in the second term, streaming through half-forward. Not bad for a guy on a wonky knee. He kicked two. 7/10 (33) Shannon Neale: It’s funny how the game works. He was odds-on favourite to be worst on ground in the first half, a poor showing that included a butchered shot on goal. But he lifted to kick two after the long break. 5/10 (34) Oisin Mullin: He will be popping up in Jagga Smith’s nightmares for the next six months. He was shaded by Sam Walsh in the first term before switching to the dangerous Smith and rendering him helpless. 7/10 View post on X (35) Patrick Dangerfield: Clearly the game’s best forward and best player overall. He had a touch of the Clark Kents early, fumbling some marking contests, but found the Superman cape and became unstoppable. And if that wasn’t enough, he booted five. 9/10



(36) Ollie Henry: Started on the pine and had his typical flashy moments. He needs to sit down and watch Dangerfield’s game to understand the difference between promising and delivering. 5/10 (38) Jack Henry: Another of the Cats’ unsung heroes, he provides reliable cover deep in defence that allows Tom Stewart to strut his stuff. He often picked up Harry McKay as he pushed up the ground. 6/10 (39) Zach Guthrie: With another solid night in defence, he had 16 disposals and took four marks. Not a bad output. He was instrumental in keeping the small Carlton forwards quiet. 6/10 Finals experience matters: Tom Stewart and Patrick Dangerfield were superb on the big stage yet again. AFL Photos (42) Mark O’Connor: Started on the bench before being swung into the midfield to shadow Carlton skipper Patrick Cripps. If you measure his performance on Cripps’ output (24 disposals) he’s had a good night. 6/10



(44) Tom Stewart: You can see why the Cats were lost without him in last year’s grand final. He was huge in the first half as he almost single-handedly stemmed the Carlton surge. He was big all night. 8/10 (45) Brad Close: He continues to be a poster boy for the long-sleeve brigade. He started to get busy in the second term when the Cats needed a spark, and booted a goal with his third kick of the evening. He finished with 17 disposals. 7/10 (46) Mark Blicavs: He started forward and provided cover in the ruck. He was serviceable without being responsible for any big moments. Had 19 hitouts and six tackles. 5/10 Carlton



(2) Lachlan Cowan: Held his own when the defence was under considerable pressure in the second half. 6/10 (4) Oliver Hollands: He kicked an important goal but was a bit fumbly under finals pressure. 5/10 (5) Adam Cerra: Wasn’t able to display the kind of kicking proficiency that he’s shown previously under Josh Fraser. 5/10 (7) Jagga Smith: He was unbelievable early but well-tagged in the end and his impact was reduced. 5/10 Jagga Smith was brilliant early until copping the dreaded Oisin Mullin tag. Getty Images



(9) Patrick Cripps: The skipper tried hard all night and kicked an incredible goal. 6/10 (10) Harry McKay: He presented really strongly and was probably unlucky not to get rewarded with one or two more frees. 6/10 (11) Mitch McGovern: He was terrible – he had the sort of night he’d rather forget. 2/10 (12) Ben Ainsworth: He looked likely all night but couldn’t finish like he’s been able to do all year previously. 5/10 (13) Blake Acres: He missed a sitter early but competed really hard all night. 6/10



(14) Oliver Florent: He has been a real leader in the back 50 in the second half of the year and worked hard all night again against the Blues. 7/10 (15) Billy Wilson: He has quickly become one of their most important players, finishing with 26 disposals. 7/10 (17) Brodie Kemp: He’s had a great year and still hit the scoreboard, but he does go missing from time to time. 5/10 Sam Walsh was once again the Blues’ best player in a final. AFL Photos (18) Sam Walsh: The Blues’ best player, he just continued to break lines and run both ways. 8/10



(23) Jacob Weitering: He stood up under immense pressure, especially when Harry Dean went off for his concussion test. 8/10 (27) Marc Pittonet: He dominated the ruck for large portions of the game but couldn’t use his aerial presence to great effect. 7/10 (29) George Hewett: He dug in for the majority of the night and was typically tough. 7/10 (33) Lewis Young: He had a horror night, including making inadvertent contact with Dean’s head, which forced him off for a HIA. 1/10 Harry Dean was left bloodied after copping some friendly fire. AFL Photos



(35) Harry Dean: He copped a loose boot from Young that effectively ruined his night. He still tried hard every minute he was out there. 6/10 (36) Cooper Lord: Two goals on the wing in a blockbuster MCG final is a great night. 7/10 (39) Talor Byrne: He just couldn’t find a way to have a genuine impact. 3/10 (44) Francis Evans: He was the best player on the ground early and finished with two goals. 7/10 (46) Matthew Cottrell: He plays an important role as a conduit and did some important things again in this one. 6/10

World.title: Latrell produces hit of the year as Rabbitohs crush Roosters in Arrow’s finale
World.content:
For one brutal, bone-crunching moment, all of rugby league held their breath. Except for poor old Toby Rodwell. He was trying to find it.

Latrell Mitchell, undisputed king of the NRL jungle, hit the rookie Roosters halfback with the most exquisite, most monstrous assault you could ever dish out without having to front court afterwards.

Loading

And as poor old Rodwell, 84 kilos, two games into his career, lay prone wondering what had hit him, all of rugby league wondered if Mitchell had hit him high.

Had the game’s most magnetic, single most-watchable player, just hit the kid in the head and rubbed himself out of the finals?

Nope, the replays showed. Mitchell had hit him square in the chest. Thank the big man above. Especially because Rodwell was showing signs of life. He was soon on his feet too, slowly making his way to the sideline, where Spencer Leniu had the crowd in raptures as well.

Leniu had, an hour earlier, goaded and growled at Souths fans sitting behind the Roosters bench on his way from the field. He had clashed with opposite number Keaon Koloamatangi from a kick-off, and twice again shortly afterwards, with the Rabbitohs prop winning the exchange, baiting Leniu into blowing up and a penalty being blown.

Spencer Leniu clashes with South Sydney’s Keaon Koloamatangi. NRL Photos

As the big screen cut between shots of Mitchell and Leniu, cheers rang out for the Rabbitoh, jeers for the Rooster. Leniu lapped it up, grinning with a touch of the madness that all the good front-rowers possess.

Despite the 50-20 scoreline, the Roosters had held their gloves up. In Leniu’s case, with eyes spinning like poker machines, he did so literally. Rodwell had his moments too.

And the Rabbitohs, with Jai Arrow leaving the Prime Minister emotional, along with 39,999 others at Allianz Stadium, they put their old enemy to the sword.

Before a ball was even kicked, the Dolphins’ narrow win over the Gold Coast meant the Roosters had to win or they would be locked into fourth place. Whether they head across the ditch to face New Zealand or west to take on Penrith won’t be confirmed until the final whistle of the regular season.

Loading

Barring a 41-point loss from fifth-placed Cronulla to Melbourne, the Rabbitohs will now finish sixth and host Newcastle in week one of the finals. Moments from Mitchell – even before Latrell’s scene-stealing 77th-minute shot – and David Fifita again spelled out the impact both men can have in the post-season.

When Fifita took on four defenders from dummy-half in the fifth minute, there was only going to be one winner, and the bullocking back-rower had Souths’ first try.

Tries to Bud Sullivan, Alex Johnston and Campbell Graham ensured the Rabbitohs had plenty of breathing room and a 20-4 half-time lead, before the Roosters found fortune giving the ball air.

Rex Bassingthwaighthe finished off an excellent long-range right-side shift in the 50th minute, before Butcher did the same when the Bunnies were busted up the middle a few tackles later.

But with Cody Walker pulling the strings, the veteran No.6 ensured Souths weren’t ever truly threatened. He helped himself to a try with some light stepping before Adam Elliott, Graham again, Mitchell and Brandon Smith all joined him on the scoreboard.

And Mitchell, he proved once more why he’s the biggest show in town. Just ask poor old Toby Rodwell.

World.title: The night two tribes put 120 years of feuding aside to honour Jai Arrow
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 The night two tribes put 120 years of feuding aside to honour Jai Arrow Adrian Proszenko September 4, 2026 — 9:10pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Jai Arrow stepped onto South Sydney’s (sometimes) home ground. A packed house, much like the man of the moment, struggled to contain its emotions. They came for what preceded the match as much as for what occurred during it. Loading The clangs of the Legacy Bell, rung by Ron Coote, reverberated around the stadium before the opening notes of Stand By Me rang out over the PA system. And then the moment we had all come for. With both sets of players on the field, it was time for one of the most enduring sporting anthems of them all. You’ll Never Walk Alone.



Those words were also plastered on the banner Arrow walked through after emerging from the tunnel to raucous applause. Arrow, wearing jersey No.23, acknowledged the crowd. Even the Roosters players put their hands together. And thus Arrow brought up an Australian sporting century as unforgettable as any ever struck by Don Bradman. This was Arrow’s 100th and final game in the cardinal and myrtle. It was a moment imagined by Wayne Bennett, who, only a week earlier, had helped the larrikin forward put his socks on for game 99. Tonight, Bennett held the interchange card that allowed Arrow to be replaced by his great mate, Cody Walker. Everyone came together to make the milestone happen. The NRL and the players’ association granted Arrow special dispensation to “play” following his retirement after being diagnosed with Motor Neurone Disease.



There was, however, one last obstacle. The Roosters, a feuding foe for well 118 years, needed to agree. Not only did they provide their blessing, their chairman Nick Politis was one of Arrow’s most generous benefactors. “We don’t always see eye-to-eye with the Roosters, but we also know that celebrating Jai tonight will bring us all together,” said Souths chief executive Blake Solly. Jai Arrow’s wife, Berina, and daughter Ayla watch on. Wolter Peeters “On behalf of the Rabbitohs we would like to thank the Roosters for their support of Jai since his diagnosis, and we thank them for supporting this concept of Jai reaching 100 NRL games for our club.” During a half-time interview with Nine’s Danika Mason, Arrow expressed his appreciation for the support he had received.



“It means the world … for me, it’s a great moment,” Arrow said. “I’m so thankful for everyone. I love you all.” Related Article NRL 2026 Latrell produces hit of the year as Rabbitohs crush Roosters in Arrow’s finale The guard of honour comprised Rabbitohs old boys, who led fans on a march along Driver Avenue from the Sydney Cricket Ground. Among them was another past player doing it tough, Jason Death. One of the inaugural captains after the Pride of the League was reinstated into the competition, Death has been recovering from a brain bleed suffered after a fall in his Warriewood home. Yet he also wanted to pay homage to the former Maroon. Arrow’s life expectancy is unclear. Yet earlier in the day, he promised to fight on.



“No, no, don’t worry about me,” Arrow told Triple M. “I understand the disease can be very confronting. I give myself every hope to be around for 10 years, at least.” The memories he created tonight will last forever. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Brisbane’s best burger? There’s a new contender in Newstead
World.content:
Eating outFood Brisbane’s best burger? There’s a new contender in Newstead This expansive venue from one of Australia’s best craft brewers is serving classic pub fare with a fun and imaginative twist. Matt Shea September 4, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There are Neighbour regulars who will never visit Range Brewing, Matt McIver reckons. “And there are people who love Range for what we do – the beers, the weekly releases – who will never come to Neighbour,” says McIver, who co-owns both venues. Neighbour opened in mid-August at Gasworks Plaza. Markus Ravik If that sounds like a counterintuitive basis on which to open a new bar and eatery, McIver says to think of it as a Venn diagram: some of the punters will overlap, many won’t. Range has become good at this. When McIver and business partner Gerard Martin opened the venue in Newstead in 2018, it quickly developed a reputation for being a craft brewer’s craft brewery. Every week new beers would be released, creating a constantly rotating line-up – one that was actually worth knowing about.



Related Article Fish Lane unveils a glamorous, old-world cocktail boozer Their first expansion was a taproom in Melbourne in 2020 (it subsequently closed in 2024). But ever since, the enterprise has been more well-rounded, with strategically located venues that focus as much on food as they do beer. First there was Patio By Range in Paddington in 2023. That was followed by Rays in Camp Hill the following year. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up “Eight years ago, we probably didn’t foresee where this was going … But that modern culture of independent pubs having elevated food menus and nice wine lists and good beer is what we’re trying to create,” McIver says. Neighbour’s fitout feels like a reference to old-school public bars, without being too kitschy. Markus Ravik “We’re not reinventing the wheel, we’re just trying to do the classics well and with love.”



Neighbour opened late August in the Gasworks premises previously occupied by Botany, and it’s the clearest expression yet of that approach. And you can see what McIver means about the Venn diagram: the food menu could be shorthanded as the ultimate pub offering, with a bunch of classics given fun and imaginative twists. There’s a crispy-fried mozzarella in carrozza (think, a fancy cheese toastie) served with a vodka sauce; raw tuna tostadas with salsa macha, cucumber and radish; a parmigiana topped with stracciatella and fresh basil; and an Insta-worthy (and very good) wagyu cheeseburger that’s served on a bed of pepper sauce. The menu pushes pub cuisine in fun and creative directions. Markus Ravik There are also a bunch of smaller snack plates, and a woodfired pizza menu. “It’s meant to be modern Australian pub cuisine,” McIver says. “We’ve taken elements from our other venues that work well and gone from there. It’s food that’s meant to make you go, ‘I can’t stop thinking about that parmy or that steak frites’.”



For drinks, there are six taps pouring Range’s core frothies, backed by a wine list that lines up relatively esoteric Australian producers alongside drops from France and Italy. There’s also a cocktail menu that dishes up classics done “your way” alongside a bunch of approachable signatures. Neighbour’s cheeseburger is up there with the best in town. Markus Ravik All this is served in a fabulously realised fitout by Kate McLean from Soma & Sol that’s slick but welcoming, with glass-brick walls, timber panelling, tile-topped tables and high bars, and burgundy-and-cream houndstooth fabrics. It feels like a reference to old-school public bars without being too kitschy. On a Tuesday night, the place is buzzy and a manager tells me it’s been heaving on the weekends, confirming McIver and Martin’s instinct for what’s been a slightly under-loved space barely a stone’s throw from the original brewery. Neighbour’s bar is serving six tap beers alongside cocktails and small-producer wines. Markus Ravik



But it’s also another expression of a business strategy that’s become sacrosanct in craft beer circles: sell as much product as you can over your own bar. “From the get-go, it was our plan to move as much beer ourselves through our own channels as we could,” McIver says. “We’re still selling 20 kegs of beer through the new venue – that money goes straight into our bank account.” Open Mon-Thu 11am-9pm, Fri-Sat 11am-10pm, Sun 12-9pm 76 Skyring Terrace, Newstead, (07) 3110 1397 neighbourbyrange.com
