For subscribers Matt Shea is Food and Culture Editor at Brisbane Times. He is a former editor and editor-at-large at Broadsheet Brisbane, and has written for Escape, Qantas Magazine, the Guardian, Jetstar Magazine and SilverKris, among many others.

World.title: Four injured after car crashes into Dunsandel pub in Canterbury
World.content:
Four people have been injured after a car crashed into a pub in Dunsandel in Canterbury this evening.

RNZ understands the pub in question is the Dunsandel Bar and Cafe.

Police said they were called about 6.15pm after a car collided with a building on Main South Road near Boundary Creek Road.

Two people suffered serious injuries, one moderate injuries and one minor injuries.

Police said it appeared the injured people were inside the pub, although a person in the car may also be among those hurt.

World.title: UN human rights commissioner visit to West Papua on track, says Indonesia
World.content:
Indonesia's government has indicated that a visit by the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights to West Papua is on track.

This comes as Melanesian Sperarhead Group (MSG) countries agreed to push Jakarta to facilitate the visit, after years of apparent inaction.

A request for the visit was made by Pacific Islands Forum countries back in 2019, but it has still not gone ahead, despite ongoing human rights violations in Papua.

A statement issued by MSG states from this week's Pacific Forum leaders meeting in Palau appeared to reflect frustrations that the visit has still not been facilitated.

The statement said that if a visit by the UN Commissioner's office was not facilitated by Indonesia in order for a report on human rights issues in West Papua to be produced by their next summit in 2027, then Indonesia's associate member status in the MSG will be reviewed.

The full members of the MSG are: Papua New Guinea, Fiji, Solomon Islands, Vanuatu and New Caledonia's FLNKS Kanak Movement. The United Liberation Movement for West Papua has observer status at the MSG, and Indonesia has associate member status.

In a response to RNZ Pacific following the statement, a spokesperson from Indonesia's embassy in New Zealand said there was "no discussion to review our membership within the MSG".

"We are always in constructive discussion on the issues deemed important by other members of the MSG, and we can also confirm that the said proposed visit is on the right path.

Ongoing conflict in Papua

The long-running conflict between the West Papua Liberation Army and Indonesian military forces in Papua has escalated in recent months, causing mass displacement of some Papua village communities in the region around Highland Papua province.

In the latest reported violence, human rights workers told RNZ Pacific that four members of the Liberation Army had been arrested and killed by Indonesian forces in Yahukimo Regency in recent days, and another member seriously injured, while six civilians were also arrested during the incident.

The spokesperson for the embassy said that during the 62nd Session of the Human Rights Council, the High Commissioner assessed "that force must not be used to pursue territorial claims or political demands".

"The sovereign equality of States, territorial integrity, and non-interference remain the foundation of the international order; respect for international law and the principles of UN Charter is non-negotiable."

World.title: New Zealand Transport Agency cuts road funding for some councils
World.content:
The NZ Transport Agency is cutting the amount of funding it gives some councils to help with essential infrastructure, prompting calls for a review of how the calculations were done.

Among them is Tararua District Council, which said the agency's decision to cut it's contribution to the roading network will cost the district more than $1.2 million over three years.

Tararua District Council is one of more than a dozen councils that have seen their Financial Assistance Rate, or FAR, from NZTA reduced over the next three years.

The move has left councils struggling see how they can fund road maintenance, public transport and other costs at a time they're also being forced to keep rates down.

NZTA currently contributes 73 cents towards every eligible dollar spent on Tararua roads. Next year that will reduce to 72 cents, before dropping again to 71 cents for the following two years.

Tararua District Mayor Scot Gilmore told Checkpoint while a couple of cents doesn't sound like a lot, it will all add up.

"It's going to be close to $1.3 million for our ratepayers... we've got to make a decision of whether our ratepayers can afford that and whether we're not going to be able to invest as much in our roads as what we need to. So it leaves us some really tough choices."

Gilmore said the funding amount was calculated using metrics of population size and how much roading a district has.

"The Tararua district, if you laid our roads end on end, they would go right from the top of the North Island right down to the bottom of the South Island. So we've got almost 2,000 kilometres of roading that we're looking after."

He said it was a huge amount of roading to look after with a fairly low rural population base.

Gilmore said the reasons NZTA had given for the cut were an increase in the number of ratable units, a number which he said was "very small", as well as a reduction of reported deprivation.

"We're sort of looking into those statistics... we certainly don't feel that on the ground."

While the council was being told by residents that they need to be doing more on the roads, Gilmore said they were in a difficult position.

"The two choices that we really have in front of us is to reduce investment in our critical infrastructure or to ask our ratepayers to cover the funding cut."

He said the council intended on having discussions with the community about the options moving forward.

With rates caps potentially looming, Gilmore said it would be tough having such a huge shortfall.

"Because we've got such a huge, huge length of roads, over 2,000 kilometres, we have to make sure that we're investing in those continually. If we take our eye off the ball with that, it's just going to end up being more expensive for everyone down the track."

He said they would be writing to the board of NZTA and the minister to ask for a review on the decision.

The Far North District council was also facing cuts, despite previously asking for an increase to it's FAR.

Far North District Councillor Anne Court told Checkpoint that the amount lost in FAR co-payments was subject to final checks by the finance team but it was roughly $1.4 million.

"This kicks in next year from our long term plan which is when rates capping kicks in, so what do we do? Find another $1.4 million from rate payers, or do we cut programmes or reduce levels of service.

"It's a scary conversation we have to have."

The Far North has the largest roading network in the North Island, with 723 bridges and 28,000 culverts but just 11 ratepayers per kilometre of road, she said.

The Council had made a case for an increase to its FAR - "an enormous piece of work for our staff" - but had not put a specific number on the increase sought.

Instead, NZTA has decreased the co-payment from 71 cents towards every dollar spent over the past three years, to 70 cents for the next three years (2027-2030).

The Council was planning to go back to NZTA to "test their assumptions and modelling".

The Buller District Council said its Funding Assistance Rate would progressively reduce from 75 percent in the current year to 74 percent in 2027/28, 73 percent in 2028/29, and 72 percent in 2029/30.

It was too early to put a single dollar value on the change.

However, NZTA has separately confirmed that the Karamea Special Purpose Road will retain a 100 percent FAR for maintenance, operations, renewals, emergency works and low-cost/low-risk activities throughout the period.

Buller District Mayor Chris Russell said that provided certainty for the community.

"These roads are essential lifelines for northern Buller, connecting residents, businesses, emergency services and visitors. Had the funding rate been reduced, the cost would ultimately have fallen on local ratepayers or required Council to reconsider the timing and scope of planned maintenance and renewal work."

NZTA said councils could raise concerns about their new Funding Assistance Rates calculations, but those rates were set using a national methodology and may not result in any change.

"The FAR's have been recalculated using updated affordability data to provide a nationally consistent, transparent basis for comparing councils' ability to meet their share of land transport costs."

It acknowledged those receiving reduced funding would feel an effect but noted the reductions would be a maximum of 1 percent a year, to help councils plan and manage the changes.

World.title: Man and woman dead after shooting in Nelson
World.content:
Two people have died after a shooting in Nelson.

Nelson Mayor Nick Smith said the incident had left many people traumatised.

"The alarm was raised when a shotgun was stolen from Hunting & Fishing in Quarantine Rd and then the offender has gone on to Parkers Rd where the tragedy occured".

Police said just before noon on Friday they received information about the theft of a shotgun from a store in the suburb of Annesbrook. The offender then left the area in a vehicle before officers arrived at the scene.

A short time later, police were alerted to a firearms incident on Parkers Road.

When officers arrived, they found a man and a woman, both dead.

Initial enquiries suggested the two people who died knew each other, police said.

RNZ/ Samantha Gee

Acting Tasman District Commander Superintendent Blair Macdonald said this was an isolated incident and there was no ongoing threat to public safety.

However, people were asked avoid the area, and cordons were in place.

Smith said police told him no-one further was being sought in connection to the events.

"Nelson prides itself of being a safe city and this tragedy impacts on us all. Our hearts go out to all those affected and particularly the families of the deceased," Smith said.

"My thanks to Police and St John for their professional response, keeping others safe and care for those directly impacted."

Nelson MP Rachel Boyack said "this is an extremely sad day for our community".

Police said a shotgun was stolen from a store in Annesbrook, just before noon on Friday. RNZ/ Samantha Gee

One ambulance and one operations manager had responded to the incident, a Hato Hone St John spokesperson said.

World.title: 'We can do a whole lot more': NZ-Canada trade announcement coming soon, minister says
World.content:
Trade Minister Todd McClay says New Zealand is working on deepening its trade relationship with Canada - and an announcement on two-way trade is coming soon.

He made the comments during a press conference with visiting Australian Trade Minister Don Farrell, who raised concerns about how global trade had broken into two camps - one that is pro-tariff, the other pro-free and -fair trade.

"I think Canada is in the space of free and fair trade, at least as it relates to Australia and New Zealand, and I think we can do a whole lot more," Farrell said.

"We've had a great friendship with Canada."

Farrell said Australia would be sending a trade delegation to the upcoming G20 meeting in Wisconsin at the end of October, adding that Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney had addressed the Australian Parliament during a recent visit.

McClay said he had been talking trade with his Canadian counterpart, Dominic LeBlanc, with a focus on how the two countries could make more of the opportunities offered by the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP).

For example, Farrell said Canada had been active in South East Asia.

"When we were in Singapore a few weeks ago to discuss with the Singaporeans how we might get continued guarantee of supply of oil and fertilizer, they made the point to me that for the first time they were using Canadian oil to substitute for the oil that had previously come from the Middle East."

He said there were other opportunities for trade with Canada.

"I also think that from Australia's point of view, we can do a lot more in the wine space.

"I think there are opportunities for both Australian and New Zealand companies to access the the Canadian liquor market."

McClay said the tit-for-tat escalation of the tariff war between the US and Canada had not been helpful for global trade.

"It creates uncertainty. It drives up prices for consumers. It makes it very, very hard for businesses to plan and to invest.

World.title: Rotorua Curtainbank's supply runs dry
World.content:
Curtainbank calling out for donations as supply runs dry Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

A dedicated crew of volunteers who have spent thousands of hours helping families in need by mending curtains are now turning to the public in an appeal for help.

With their shelves looking bare, the Rotorua Curtainbank is calling for donations to replace its dwindling supply of curtains.

The group, formed by 17 women aged from their 60s to 80s, collectively dedicates thousands of hours each year to hemming, measuring, mending and stitching window coverings for those in need.

Co-ordinator Judy Gregor told Checkpoint curtains were vital in terms of keeping warmth inside a house.

She said they had seen many people coming to them who were living in cold, damp and mouldy houses.

"[It is] affecting the health of the inhabitants."

The group donates curtains to people who have referred themselves with a Community Services Card, or people who have been referred by a social organisation.

Rotorua Curtainbank. Supplied

Gregor said that quite often they were having to deck out entire houses with repurposed curtains.

"Just over the last 18, 20 months, we've been moving out to more rural areas... where it does get very cold... [the houses] they were not insulated, they were cold and increasingly damp."

She said a good curtain could make a great deal of difference in keeping the cold and damp out.

"When they're good, used curtains, they will keep out a lot of the cold, and they will also, as long as the houses are aired every day, they will keep mould-free."

Rotorua Curtainbank. Supplied

Gregor said they had heard that their curtains had helped people avoid respiratory problems that they had been experiencing before.

She said that in the past the Curtainbank had been donated a large amount of curtains from motels and hotels from around the Rotorua district, but now they desperately needed more.

The group is looking for any used curtains in good condition to be donated.

World.title: The hidden costs of loyalty programmes
World.content:
Shoppers using loyalty programmes are benefiting retailers more than themselves, new research says.

It comes as Bunnings launches its first rewards programme, offering a $5 reward for every $500 spent.

Edith Cowan University professor of marketing and service science Sanjit Roy said the loyalty market globally was expected to grow in value from US$17.38 billion (NZD$29.49 billion) in 2026 to US$51.65 billion (NZD$87.63) by 2034.

He recently produced research based on 800 supermarket customers, to better understand their interactions with loyalty programmes.

Is there any point in KiwiSaver if I'm on a total remuneration package? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 10m

"Many customers don't have the time to do mental cost-benefit analysis. What am I getting and what am I giving up? Retailers know this, so they'll prompt you at the till before you pay, either at self-serve checkout or by a customer serviceperson asking: do you want to scan your rewards card? Retailers know how to reinforce our habit," Roy said.

"But as customers we are losing more than we are gaining. If we earn one point for every dollar spent, and every 2000 points we receive a $10 voucher - is it worth handing over our personal data when discounts and promotions aren't being personalised or tailored to our buying habits as a reward for our loyalty? Therefore, is it worth signing up for the loyalty programmes?"

In New Zealand, the Woolworths Everyday Rewards programme offers a $15 voucher for every 2000 points.

Roy said loyalty programmes were likely to become more sophisticated over time as retailers made more use of the data they collected about shoppers.

"We live in a data-driven economy and every time we use these loyalty rewards cards, or we are a member of any loyalty programme, what we give up is our personal information.

"Every time we go to a shopping trip and we scan our card, whatever we buy, including the types of items, everything gets recorded.

"I think in this data-driven world, the AI-enabled economy, the retailers have all the tools to examine and analyse consumers' buying pattern and accordingly target.

"I think they can do a lot more than they are doing at the moment... they could design loyalty programmes which are actually beneficial for customers, at the moment that's not the case at least in the supermarket sector."

He said rather than making people wait for rewards, as at present, shops could target specials to customers according to their needs.

"If I'm a young parent and I need nappies and somebody has tracked my purchase behaviour I don't have to wait for 2000 points... somebody has analysed my previous purchase pattern and says 'okay, probably you are running out of nappies, and here is a discount if you come and buy your nappies at this point in time. It's creating instant gratification that may lead customers to engage more and more with the loyalty programme."

Consumer NZ has previously warned that supermarkets could use data from loyalty programmes to bump up prices in places where they felt customers would pay.

Roy said the schemes would benefit supermarkets more than customers.

"It's an open truth.

"Companies always have the upperhand."

He said his research showed customers needed to trust retailers to properly engage with loyalty schemes.

"Customers know they're just a datapoint. Supermarket retailers should focus on advancing their offering by establishing a personalised dialogue with customers and making their loyalty benefits more human-centric. Creating a personalised dialogue is a precursor to building trust."

World.title: MAPAS review hasn't proven scheme is 'clear case of racial discrimination' - Seymour
World.content:
David Seymour discusses Maori and Pacific access to med school Midday Report Download MP3 10m

ACT leader and Deputy Prime Minister David Seymour says a university medical programme that targets Māori and Pacific students is built on "racial discrimination", and a new review hasn't proven otherwise.

But the University of Auckland is backing the programme, which it says plays a "vital role in closing the gaps" and building up the Māori and Pacific doctor workforce.

ACT has been staunchly opposed to the Māori and Pacific Admissions Scheme (MAPAS) at the Auckland and Otago universities, which the universities say is intended to grow diversity of health professionals by removing some of the barriers to study.

The review of MAPAS was part of the National-ACT coalition agreement and the Ministry of Health has now completed the review, but it is yet to be released publicly.

The universities also have a regional rural admission scheme that selects students based on their rural primary and secondary school attendance.

Seymour told Midday Report he has no issue with that element.

"I oppose racial discrimination. I don't oppose living in the country. I don't oppose, for example, trying to train rural GPs. I don't oppose bonding people to work in the countryside where it's hard to get people… those are separate issues."

Seymour says the MAPAS review is being held by Associate Health Minister Matt Doocey, who will release it "in good time".

In the meantime he has had a briefing on it and says it "appears it does not do what I sincerely hoped it would do".

Professor Warwick Bagg, dean of the University of Auckland's Faculty of Medical and Health Sciences, is calling on the review to be released urgently "so the public can judge its findings for themselves".

"All medical students, regardless of admission pathway, must meet the same academic, clinical and professional standards before they graduate," Professor Bagg said.

"Every student selected to study medicine at the University of Auckland has earned their place and is expected to demonstrate the competence, professionalism, and commitment required of a future doctor."

But Seymour doesn't believe the review has done what it set out to do.

Warwick Bagg. Supplied

He says it was intended to demonstrate "what is a clear case of racial discrimination" has a purpose and effect that is consistent with the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination.

New Zealand is a signatory to that convention, and if it is "to be violated then it should only be for specific, effective and temporary purposes to overcome inequalities of the past", he said.

In the case of this review Seymour doesn't believe universities or government departments "have been able to provide that justification".

Seymour says the onus on the report writers has been "misunderstood".

"They seem to believe that the onus is on anybody who opposes racial discrimination to justify stopping it.

"I take the opposite view that anyone who believes people should be discriminated against based on their race has to justify why that's necessary, and that is certainly the position taken in the international convention that New Zealand's been a signatory to for some decades," he told Midday Report.

Seymour hasn't seen the full review, but in the briefing he has had, he says it appears "the review's authors were under the misapprehension that their job was simply to show that some good might be done by this discrimination - not that it's consistent with New Zealand's international obligations".

"Frankly, what any right-thinking person should believe that we don't do racism, and if we do, there'd better be a bloody good reason for it, and it should be a temporary measure for a specific purpose."

He says the review says the programme should continue, but Seymour says that conclusion is based on the wrong assumptions.

"I don't like hearing from constituents and members of the public saying that myself or my child missed out on entry to medical school, even though they had much higher grades than people who did get in on the grounds of race. That is absolutely abominable."

If the report had concluded the discrimination was justified as a "temporary and effective measure" Seymour said he would be happy to see the programme continue.

"The report does not do that. It leaves us in a no man's land where the report writers seem to think that you can casually justify racism and it should just continue. Well, I don't accept that. The people that I talk to, people who miss out on going to medical school based on their race, they don't accept that, so that leaves us campaigning to end it."

'Long way to go'

Speaking to RNZ's Checkpoint on Friday afternoon, Bagg said he had not seen the final version of the report, but had seen a near-final draft, which he said backed keeping the scheme.

"From what we've seen of the draft report, the scheme is achieving what it was set out to do, and so very much we would be delighted to see the final report and have it released."

He said there was a "long way to go" to get both "demographic equity" as well as equitable health outcomes.

"We have seen a steady increase in the number of Māori and Pacific doctors over time. But for Māori, they are still only just over 5 percent of doctors, for Pacific, around 3 percent."

He said it was taking time to improve university entrance rates and success for Māori and Pacific people in the field, but "we are making steady progress every year".

The still-low percentage of doctors of Māori and Pacific heritage was partly down to a growing number of overseas-born doctors, he said.

"I'm not problematising that because I'm one of them. But the pool of doctors is getting bigger every year, so our job of growing the Māori and Pacific doctors is also challenging, because the denominator is bigger."

Bagg said it was "absolutely not the case" that doctors enrolled via the scheme were inferior to others.

"Every student has to pass exactly the same assessments. Patient safety is our utmost goal, and delivering safe and equitable health care remains paramount for us. All of our students need to meet those goals in order to go into a health workforce."

He said there was no truth to claims others would miss out because of a quota, because there was no quota. The target was for 40 percent of the intake to be Māori and Pasifika, because that matched the demographics of the youth population in the North Island - and they were not even meeting that target at present.

World.title: Fancy cars and hanging with mum, the paradox of Aussie's EPL teen dream
World.content:
Lucas Herrington has gone to number one with a bullet in 2026, at a speed so dizzying it would leave many teenagers' heads spinning.

Turning 19 this weekend, he is fresh off a breakthrough World Cup, has a multi-million-dollar contract in the best football league in the world, and has fans fawning over him.

But true to his persona on the pitch, the central defender is calm, level-headed and capable of tackling any challenge.

"My parents have always instilled that factor of humility in my life and having that humbleness to stay grounded and just to keep working hard," he told Australian media on a call from Hull.

"I'm always trying to get better. So I think it's always having that positive mindset that I've still got a lot of things to work on. And I'm not the finished product."

Herrington was one of Australia's best players throughout the recent World Cup. (Stefan Koops/EYE4IMAGES/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Herrington made his bolt-from-the-blue Socceroos debut in March, which turned into a maiden World Cup appearance a few months later.

His impressive efforts in North America captured interest from some of the biggest clubs in the world including Barcelona and Liverpool.

But he settled on Hull City, newly promoted in the English Premier League, and a five-year deal for a transfer fee reportedly worth $33 million with add-ons, to become the most expensive Australian player ever.

Alessandro Circati recently joined that rich list with his transfer from Parma to Benfica.

Herrington with his manager, Buddy Farah, after signing his record deal with Hull City last month. (Supplied: Hull City)

The money is astronomical for an Australian footballer, and despite his down-to-earth nature, even Herrington was lured in by the EPL stereotype of fancy, fast cars.

"It's a nice car park. I do have a car right now; it's nice. I'm enjoying it," he laughed, almost sheepishly.

But when he speaks about his off-field highlights in his few weeks in England, the teenager goes back to keeping it real.

"Mum's here at the moment. She leaves soon, so I've just been exploring around with her," he said.

"So that's been really nice, some great quality time with her."

Advice from a legend

Herrington made his debut for the Tigers off the bench in their upset win over Manchester United.

"It was only a week and a couple of days from when I landed to that game against Man United," he said.

"Great moment for the city and for me personally, with my mum and my agent in the stands, it was a super proud moment for me.

"And it was a great match, very grateful for the opportunity to be there."

Herrington celebrated the Tigers' upset win over Manchester United to open their season. (Getty Images: Molly Darlington)

He was again used as a substitute in a win over Coventry, while he started the EFL Cup penalty shootout win against Stoke.

A strong show of confidence for the youngster, who is the only Australian in England's top flight.

"It's probably the best league in the world. So to be here at 18 is super special," he said.

"I've always wanted to play in the Premier League, so I'm very grateful for the opportunity from the coaching staff and the club to do so. And I've loved my first three or so weeks here.

"It's a league with the best players in the world, so to be up against them every week is really special and a great challenge for me as a young defender.

"It's just about trying to learn as much as possible from the older boys in the team and just try and take every game as a lesson."

And don't mistake his modesty for meekness; he knows he belongs.

A message reinforced by former Sweden international Zlatan Ibrahimović, who publicly supported Herrington after missing a penalty in the Socceroos' World Cup round of 32 shootout loss to Egypt.

Herrington received plenty of public support after Australia exited the World Cup. (Getty Images: Alex Slitz)

“This is just the beginning of your career," Ibrahimović said on Fox Sports USA's post-game analysis.

"You stepping up there, you show a lot of courage. Not everybody would do that. My friend, you're the best. Don't listen to the rest. Listen, Herrington, if you want to reach out, I'm here."

Ibrahimović made good on his promise and ended up calling the Queensland product himself.

"He just said, really don't fear anyone. I'm here for a reason, so just go enjoy," Herrington said.

Dreams do come true

Herrington's meteoric rise means he has not yet played for Australia in his home state.

Herrington is hoping to play in the Socceroos' upcoming friendlies against Brazil in Queensland. (Getty Images: Dean Mouhtaropoulos)

Something the former Roar product hopes to do in the Socceroos' friendlies against Brazil later this month, in Townsville and Brisbane.

"It'd be a dream come true to play for the Socceroos in Brisbane," he said.

"Something that I've always wanted to do, and to play in front of hopefully a packed-out Suncorp would be a dream, and in front of my family and friends would be awesome."

And he is happy to be a role model for others.

"Just trying to be an inspiration for all the young Australians that there is really a pathway to the Premier League," he said.

"I think a lot of young footballers in Australia like me wake up at all hours in the morning to watch the Premier League.

"So hopefully I can make them proud, make Australia proud.

"Just to keep working hard, enjoy the process, and to have big dreams because dreams do come true."

World.title: Tigers coach defends Luai amid 'irrelevant' criticism over PNG trip
World.content:
Benji Marshall insists Jarome Luai is entitled to spend his downtime as he pleases, dismissing "irrelevant" criticism of the Wests Tigers star's recent trip to PNG.

When Luai asked to change his flight out of Townsville following last week's loss to North Queensland, Marshall was unaware his star player would be travelling to his future home country to attend a golf tournament.

The trip came only days after Pepsi unveiled Luai as a brand ambassador ahead of his arrival at the Chiefs for their first NRL season in 2028.

Luai's trip to Port Moresby, and the first of what is likely to be many promotional opportunities with PNG brands, come while he remains on a seven-figure salary with the Tigers.

Loading Instagram content

The five-eighth will also join Parramatta on a one-year deal before his first pre-season with the Chiefs, which begins in more than a year.

Marshall described media concerns over the optics of Luai's enthusiastic PNG links as "irrelevant to me".

"He paid to change his flights [from Townsville] and not come back with us, which happens quite often with players," Marshall said.

"From my opinion, it's his time off.

"What he chooses to do in his time off, that's up to him. In one week's time, he's not going to be here anymore and we're not going to have to worry about any of those things."

In signing Jarome Luai, Papua New Guinea's power has become real Jarome Luai's decision to sign with Papua New Guinea is a showcase of the economic power behind the Chiefs and marks the start of the greatest rugby league gold rush since Super League.

Marshall said, in time, Luai's move to the Chiefs could help transform him from villain to hero in the public's eye.

"He always gets painted as the villain for some reason," Marshall said.

"But he's about to walk into a country in about 12 months' time where he's about to be the hero, so it's going to change for him."

Four-time premiership winner Luai arrived at the Tigers last year with hopes of finally reinvigorating the long-struggling joint venture.

Instead, Luai's decision to sign with the Chiefs coincided with a sharp downturn in form that consigned the Tigers to a 15th consecutive year out of finals.

Marshall previously admitted he had let the saga become a distraction for the 15th-placed Tigers, who had been in the top four when Luai signed with the Chiefs.

Benji Marshall (pictured) has no problems with Luai spending time in Papua New Guinea in his downtime. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne)

"There's obviously a lot of things probably both sides wish went a little bit better, but we are where we are and we've got to move forward," Marshall said.

Marshall still believed Luai's signing was a success for the Tigers, who face top-two side Penrith in their last game of the season.

"There's no regrets from our side about bringing him here whatsoever because he did the job we needed him to," he said.

"I'm sure a lot of people probably have their opinions about what he hasn't done here, but all I've seen are the things he has done here and the impact he has had on the club.

"I'm sure he would admit himself that he would have liked to have contributed more on field performance-wise but all in all, he'll leave here having had an impact on our club."

AAP

World.title: How Swans midfielder is supporting banned housemate amid trade rumours
World.content:
Sydney's James Rowbottom says he must "separate the person from the problem" in trying to support suspended teammate Nick Blakey amid a club crisis and finals campaign.

Blakey is one of five Swans players stood down for the remainder of the season for breaching the club's behavioural standards in a post-AFL match hotel party in August.

Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, James Jordon and Riley Bice have also been suspended from Sydney's finals campaign.

As the club mulls a call on the group's playing future, Blakey is reportedly searching for a trade following a deterioration in his relationship with the Swans.

Nick Blakey is reportedly keen on a trade out of Sydney as he sits out of this year's finals. (Photo by Morgan Hancock/AFL Photos/via Getty Images)

Swans midfielder Rowbottom says he has only spoken to close mate Blakey about his welfare.

"I haven't spoken to Nick about any sort of details [about a trade]," Rowbottom said today.

"It's been a challenging period for him, and I'm just sort of reaching out as a friend.

"Living with him is another layer to the situation, and so I've reached out as a friend but, no, we haven't spoken about any of those sort of specifics.

"You've got to sort of separate the person from the problem when you live with someone, to try and offer support.

"I've been trying to do that."

The player suspensions are separate to a police investigation into sexual assault allegations and the events at East Melbourne's Pullman Hotel after Sydney's round 23 game against Essendon on August 16.

No charges have been laid and there is no suggestion of any wrongdoing on the part of the five suspended players.

Rowbottom would not be drawn when asked if he was open to the five players returning to the club before the end of the season.

The group won't be at the SCG for the club's qualifying final against Brisbane on Saturday, but have individually spoken to teammates in the lead-up to the clash.

Rowbottom (right) and teammate Errol Gulden (left) will be relied upon heavily in the absence of Sydney's suspended quintet. (Getty Images: Russell Freeman)

"It's a lot more complex than what I think or believe," Rowbottom said.

"The club is working through that with them and the relevant party. Honestly, it's above my pay grade."

Heeney and Warner's absence has meant Rowbottom has taken on the bulk of the midfield work with Errol Gulden and Jai Serong.

Rowbottom had returned to the side for the round 24 clash against North Melbourne after missing two weeks with a broken hand.

"For me, personally, I just do what the team needs and I have done that for the last eight years or so," the 25-year-old said.

"My role has been ever-changing this year. I've played a lot of half-forward, a lot of midfield, a bit of wing.

"Football's ever-changing, and I'm happy to take it as it comes."

AAP

World.title: Fan-built roller-coaster sets new standard in match-day choreography
World.content:
Tifo displays have long been a ubiquitous sight in football stadiums around the world.

Typically displayed before kick-off at major matches, fan-led displays have become increasingly elaborate as rival supporters look to outdo one another with the scale of their devotion.

But German second-tier side VfL Osnabrück have taken things to an entirely new level.

Ahead of their German Cup tie against defending champions Bayern Munich, the supporters created a fully functioning roller-coaster in the stands of their 16,100-capacity stadion an der Bremer Brücke.

VfL Osnabrück fans truly surpassed themselves on this occasion. (Getty Images: Lars Baron)

A track was built in sections and had a cart, complete with dummy passengers, which was towed around the track on repeat.

To one side of the stand, a separate "photo" banner was displayed after the cart passed a flashing camera, delivering the authentic experience of what the supporters called the "Funpark Bremer Brücke".

Loading Instagram content

Accompanied by a sign saying "VfL Osnabrück — a roller-coaster ride!" the not-so-subtle message was that supporting the club, based in Germany's north-western Saxony region, was full of ups and downs.

The club has only just been promoted back to the 2. Bundesliga after a five-year stint in the 3. Liga and has a reputation as a club that yo-yos around the leagues.

VfL Osnabrück brought the pyro to their party against Bayern Munich. (Getty Images: picture alliance/David Ebener)

Welcoming Bavarian giants Bayern in the first round of the DFB Pokal was always going to be a tough ask, but the roller-coaster theme continued when the hosts took a shock 1-0 lead thanks to a 30-yard shot by Robin Meißner after just five minutes.

The defending champions soon hit back though, Harry Kane scoring twice either side of goals to Tom Bischof and Michael Olise to give the record 21-time winners a path through to the second round.

But Bayern, who are not strangers to spectacular tifos of their own at their cavernous Allianz Arena home, will have to up their game if they are to manage something as impressive as this for their next home game, against Bodø/Glimt in the Champions League.

Bayern are partial to the odd display of mass choreography. (Getty Images: sampics/Stefan Matzke)

Germany has been something of a trendsetter when it comes to tifos in recent years, although the practice originated in southern Europe and Italy.

Starting out as supporters holding up cards to create a display across a grandstand, Australian fans can think of a tifo as something similar to the fan-made banners AFL teams run through pre-game, only on a much larger scale.

Tifo is short for tifosi, the Italian for supporter, and has become known as a way for fans to display their passion or to mock their rivals.

Tifos originated in Italy, with San Siro home to some of the best. (Getty Images: AC Milan/Diego Puletto)

In 2017, Western Sydney Wanderers provoked the ire of Football Australia, then known as Football Federation Australia, for displaying a homophobic banner during the Sydney derby.

The banner, depicting a blue-faced man giving oral sex, was put up in the Wanderers' support area during the second half of the game.

"FFA is aware of the unauthorised and totally unacceptable banner that was displayed in the Western Sydney Wanderers area during Saturday night's Sydney derby at ANZ Stadium," then-A-League chief Greg O'Rourke said.

"The discriminatory nature of the tifo has no place in society and will not be tolerated in the A-League."

Not all of Western Sydney Wanderers' tifos were vile, most were excellent. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Clubs can play a role in the content of tifos, but often they are ways for fans to make their point about an issue they feel strongly about.

Given the increasingly elaborate designs, Arsenal were heavily criticised by their own fans for a bland rectangular tifo ahead of a Champions League match at the Emirates against Paris Saint-Germain in April 2025.

PSG are known for their extravagant displays — particularly in the Champions League — so perhaps it was fair for Arsenal to be mocked.

Paris Saint-Germain fans are increasingly keen on displaying tifos. (Getty Images: UEFA/Stuart Franklin)

However, since then they have upped their game significantly.

Still, we're yet to see a roller-coaster of any sort at the Emirates, so there's clearly still room for improvement.

As fans of Lechia Gdansk know, the devil is often in the detail. (Getty Images: Mateusz Slodkowski)

World.title: Shifting Ayrton Senna plaque a sign of things to come for Adelaide's MotoGP
World.content:
A plaque installed after F1 driver Ayrton Senna died in 1994 is among a swag of changes to Adelaide's famed street circuit for the MotoGP next year, but an industry stalwart says it represents "transition" rather than the end of an era.

The government wants to return parts of the circuit to its original F1 layout, including the 900-metre Brabham Straight along Dequetteville Terrace, but is also proposing to shift Senna Chicane further into Victoria Park and dump popular Supercar components.

This includes the "staircase" and its challenging succession of 90-degree turns along the CBD's east edge.

"It's a new life, a different life for one of the best locations for a motor racing circuit in Australia," said Motorsport Hall of Fame chairman and longtime industry journalist John Smailes.

The Senna Chicane is a historic turn in the Adelaide Street Circuit that harkens back to the F1 days. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

"It still sits in Victoria Park where [track designer] Bob Barnard placed it in 1985, so you're talking about a rich 41-year history of Victoria Park hosting probably the best Grand Prix that's ever been held in the Southern Hemisphere for cars.

"It's so close to town; it really does involve the whole city and, to that end, whatever the layout may happen to be, the geography remains pretty much the same."

A popular circuit

After the Grand Prix moved to Melbourne in 1996, the circuit was reduced to 3.2 kilometres for the 1999 Adelaide 500, which became the most well-attended leg of the Supercars Championship and grew a reputation for challenging corners, bumps and upsets.

Loading...

One of the Adelaide street circuit's major drawcards, however, is that spectators can be seated close to the action for much of the course.

The MotoGP, on the other hand, requires very large gravel traps along the far edge of corners to slow a dismounted rider safely, meaning spectators will be set a significant way back for bigger stretches of the circuit.

Mr Smailes pointed out there were parts of the current Phillip Island MotoGP course where "you can get up close and personal with the bikes", and expected the same in Adelaide.

The proposed MotoGP street has wide gravel pits along much of the course. (Supplied: SA government)

Viewing areas for the current Adelaide street circuit are largely close to the action. (Supplied: Daniel Kalisz)

"There'll probably be places where the aficionados will scope out the best parts to stand where they can still get the buzz of being close," Mr Smailes said.

" And when you cop the full force of a 320 kilometre-per-hour MotoGP bike pushing the air in front of you, it's like being hit by a glove from a heavyweight boxer. It's amazing. "

The state government said the MotoGP track will be reconfigured for the Supercars Grand Final, which will take place about 10 days later.

Five-time Supercars champion Mark Skaife said the kerbs would remain "punishing and the walls will be inches away".

"The new Senna Chicane will be unforgiving," he said, and the track will be "super quick, with lots of overtaking opportunities".

MotoGP bikes are expected to hit speeds of 340 kilometres per hour on the Adelaide Street Circuit. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

A larger sticking point

The MotoGP's larger footprint, however, is behind its most controversial sticking point for a lot of Adelaideans, which is its requirement to remove trees from the city's national heritage-listed Parklands.

Angered by tree removals for a revamped golf course, a large protest movement has emerged that marched in the thousands on August 23, while a petition of 43,784 signatures tabled in state parliament has triggered an inquiry.

The state government has responded by promising to replace every tree 10 to one, and arguing that of 377 trees that needed removal, 42 were significant, 88 would be transplanted, and the rest were either "unregulated, invasive species, dead or in poor health".

A protest against tree felling for the MotoGP in late August drew thousands of people. (ABC News: Daniel Taylor)

Mr Smailes believed the issue was of bigger consideration than Senna's memorial plaque.

"I don't think Ayrton Senna would be at all concerned if you moved his plaque to another place. I think that's a very small consideration," he said.

A spokesperson for the South Australian Motor Sport Board said the plaque "commemorating the life of three-time World Champion Ayrton Senna was a part of the folklore of the Adelaide Circuit".

The plaque is currently located adjacent Senna Chicane in Victoria Park. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

"The intention is to keep it adjacent to the Senna Chicane, but the exact location won't be determined until the consultation process has concluded and the final circuit design is confirmed," he said.

A 'spectacle for sure'

Adelaide motorsport fan, Simon, told the ABC he was a "car guy, but the MotoGP is probably the most exciting motorsport to watch at the moment, given F1 has become so sanitised and tech-driven", and he would most certainly be attending.

"I'd prefer the F1 to come back, but MotoGP is a spectacle for sure and has a huge global following," he said.

"I also like the fact the infrastructure could be used for the Adelaide Motorsport Festival [AMF] as well, and could see that event become Australia's answer to the Goodwood Festival of Speed [England].

"[AMF owner/CEO] Tim Possingham is a very switched-on guy and I'm sure he has a vision for the AMF to grow and succeed."

A map showing the design for the MotoGP street circuit in Adelaide. (Supplied: SA government)

Mr Possingham said he had been in constant communication with the state government about the incoming MotoGP and was working with it closely with respect to its build times and how the AMF would fit in.

Adelaide MotoGP circuit gets lukewarm motorsport review Adelaide's new $96 million MotoGP track has received mixed reviews from motorsport fans and riders.

"We're also mindful that the Formula One calendar hasn't been released yet, so there's a couple of moving parts we need to fit in with," he said.

"Anything that remotely comes to look like the great track we had in the 80s and the 90s and, in some way, shape or form, brings back that grandeur of a truly international event here in the city of Adelaide is very, very powerful.

"I think that that will be realised maybe after a year or two of the event being delivered here, and I think there's some foresight there of what might come in the future, and the government's looking further afield than national events with MotoGP."

Works have begun for the Adelaide Street Circuit in its current configuration for the final time. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

A public consultation period for the proposed MotoGP track is open until September 20.

World.title: De Minaur crashes out of US Open in shock straight sets loss
World.content:
Alex de Minaur has been dumped out of the US Open in the second round, falling in straight sets to Dutchman Botic van de Zandschulp 6-4, 7-5, 6-2 in two hours and 43 minutes.

De Minaur had never lost to the 30-year-old world number 70 in their previous four meetings, including earlier this year at the Rotterdam ATP event, which the 27-year-old Aussie won.

But on a night where he committed 29 unforced errors to van de Zandschulp's 21, as well as seven double faults in a sub-par serving display, the Australian world number seven faltered badly.

"I always had really difficult matches against Alex," van de Zandschulp said on court.

"Some tough ones as well, some close matches, but today I served very well, I think that was the difference today."

Alex de Minaur was far from his best. (Getty Images: Julian Finney)

De Minaur saved three match points in the final game, but it was not enough, the Aussie leaving himself far too much to do.

After a brief pause where he stood on court in contemplation at his exit, de Minaur exited without looking back.

The defeat is de Minaur's earliest exit at the US Open in five years, at a slam where he has three times reached the quarterfinals.

With Novak Djokovic and Félix Auger-Aliassime both crashing out, de Minaur had been the fourth-highest seed left in the tournament.

But he was unable to make that opportunity count.

Sweeny soars into US Open last 32 Australian wildcard Dane Sweeny has posted the biggest win of his career, upsetting dual grand slam semifinalist Lorenzo Musetti to make the US Open's last 32.

De Minaur was forced to wait until day four to get his tournament underway after rain caused the postponement of his round one clash with Italian qualifier Andrea Guerrieri.

The victory is van de Zandschulp's second over a top-10 player during this US hardcourt swing after he beat world number eight Daniil Medvedev at the Montreal Masters in August.

The one-time US Open quarterfinalist has made a habit of pulling off shock victories at Flushing Meadows.

He beat Casper Ruud on his way to the quarterfinal in 2021 and, in 2024, knocked out third-seed Carlos Alcaraz in the second round with a straight-sets win.

De Minaur's exit means wildcard Dane Sweeny is the only Australian left in the men's singles draw at Flushing Meadows after his 3-6, 6-1, 6-2, 6-2 victory against world number 14 Lorenzo Musetti.

World.title: Kyrgios free to compete after accepting one-month cocaine ban
World.content:
Nick Kyrgios has entered a treatment program after accepting a one-month ban for testing positive to cocaine.

After admitting his "huge mistake" when initially suspended for failing a drugs test on June 22 at an ATP 250 tournament in Spain, Kyrgios is allowed to compete again from Friday.

Kyrgios, who had been provisionally suspended since August 4, had faced a ban ranging from a baseline three-month period to up to four years.

During an interview with International Tennis Integrity Agency (ITIA) investigators, Kyrgios explained his use of cocaine had occurred socially during a night out, days before he was due to play in Mallorca.

The ITIA consulted an independent scientific expert at a World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA)-accredited laboratory, who stated the explanation was consistent with the level of cocaine found in his sample.

As a result, the ITIA accepted Kyrgios's use of cocaine was outside of competition.

Nick Kyrgios has entered a treatment program. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Under WADA rules, the default suspension for a breach of this type is three months, which can be further reduced to one month if the individual commits to a treatment program approved by the ITIA.

The 2022 Wimbledon finalist also forfeited the 6,570 Euros he won in Mallorca for losing in the first round to countryman Adam Walton.

But his suspension was reduced for agreeing to enter a treatment program.

The ITIA said Kyrgios, whose career world ranking peaked at number 13, could appeal against the provisional suspension, but he opted against doing so.

"I recently failed a drug test in Mallorca after testing positive for cocaine," Kyrgios posted on Instagram last month.

"I made a huge mistake and I take full responsibility for it.

"I'm sorry to my fans, my family, my sponsors and everyone close to me. Above all, I'm sorry to the kids who follow me. I know the example this sets and I'm deeply disappointed in myself."

Kyrgios, who played only four official singles matches on the elite ATP Tour this year, has battled knee and wrist injuries in recent years and has all but conceded he is finished as a singles force.

"I'm not going to make excuses, but I do want to give some context about where I've been," he wrote.

"The last couple of years of injuries have taken a huge toll on me, both physically and mentally.

"My body hasn't been able to do what my mind expects it to do, and coming to terms with being near the end of my career has been harder than I ever imagined."

Nick Kyrgios has been beset by injuries. (AP: Charles Krupa)

But the polarising Canberra-born drawcard said that did not excuse his actions.

"I've always said I didn't choose tennis — tennis chose me," he wrote.

"But letting go of something that has been my whole life is one of the hardest things I've ever had to face. At times I've felt helpless and alone.

"None of that excuses what I did."

Kyrgios said "the good news is that this has given me a wake up call".

"For the next 28 days, I'll be stepping away from social media and public life while I focus on getting myself right.

"I'd ask that people respect my privacy during that time, and most importantly the privacy of my family.

"I'm sorry. I'll do the work and come back better."

The ITIA said Kyrgios was suspended for a ‌positive test for benzoylecgonine, a cocaine metabolite, with a World Anti-Doping Agency laboratory confirming the positive result on July 17.

The 31-year-old was banned from playing, coaching or attending any tournaments sanctioned by the men's and women's tennis tours worldwide and national-level events in Australia.

Kyrgios last played in the men's doubles at Wimbledon in London on July 2, when he and partner Alexander Bublik lost in the first round.

AAP

World.title: Australian battler crushes Italian star in US Open boilover
World.content:
Dane Sweeny has won a real-life David-versus-Goliath battle to rock the US Open with a stunning second-round upset over dual grand slam semi-finalist Lorenzo Musetti.

The unheralded Australian wildcard took down the 14th seed 3-6, 6-1, 6-2, 6-2 on Friday morning (AEST) for the biggest win of his career.

Standing only 170cm high, Sweeny rose to the occasion to reach the third round of a grand slam for the first time and earn a minimum pay day of $US290,000 ($A402,750).

For a couple of heady hours it looked like his underdog countrymen Tristan Schoolkate and Alexei Popyrin would join Sweeny in round three.

Osaka, Keys mount thrilling fightbacks Naomi Osaka wobbled through the second set to fight back and beat Kateřina Siniaková in three, while Madison Keys staved off five match points to keep her US Open dreams alive on day of high drama at Flushing Meadows.

But Schoolkate's inspired run from qualifying finally came to a halt at the hands of fifth-seeded French Open runner-up Flavio Cobilli.

Schoolkate snatched the first set before the Italian showed his class to prevail 3-6, 6-3, 6-4, 7-5 after two hours and 41 minutes in New York's scorching summer heat.

And two years after upstaging Novak Djokovic in the US Open's third round, Popyrin fell short of a place in the last 32 once again, losing a tense four-set battle with Chilean Alejandro Tabilo.

Like Schoolkate, Popyrin took the opening set before the 25th-seeded South American claimed two pivotal tiebreakers, then the match 2-6, 7-6 (7-4), 7-6 (7-3), 6-2 to seal a likely third-round date with German top seed Alexander Zverev.

But ranked more than 100 places below his world number 14 opponent, Sweeny is savouring a mighty breakthrough after bossing Musetti into submission.

He ran the 14th seed ragged and had the Italian looking in particular distress when he required a medical time-out after falling behind a double break at 0-3 in the all-important third set.

Even after clawing one break back, Musetti — who has made the Wimbledon and French Open semi-finals over the past two years — continued remonstrating animatedly to his courtside box.

Despite sporting a massive ice pack on his right elbow after his first-round win, Sweeny continued diving like Boris Becker for acrobatic winning volleys at the net.

And the 25-year-old was duly rewarded with a last-32 shot at another Italian, world number 22 Luciano Darderi on Saturday (AEST) — and a rankings rise to a career-best 115 in the world, or better.

"I'm just grateful to be even able to compete in grand slams. The tennis journey is such a rollercoaster," Sweeny said.

"And to soak up the atmosphere and get a win, a couple of wins, in front of this crowd, is awesome."

AAP

Tech.title: Alienware’s refurbished 16 Aurora is almost $200 off at Woot
Tech.content:
is an editor covering deals and gaming hardware. He joined in 2018, and after a two-year stint at Polygon, he rejoined The Verge in May 2025.

Gaming laptop deals aren’t what they used to be (stares daggers at RAMageddon), which is why I consider Woot’s deal on a refurbished Alienware 16 Aurora gaming laptop with Nvidia’s RTX 5050 a pretty good deal at $927 for new Woot customers (with code WOOTALIEN used at checkout). It costs $1,029 for returning Woot shoppers, which is a decent discount off the new $1,099.99 price at Alienware’s site. Notably, this refurb unit includes a one-year Alienware warranty.

These days, most configurations with Nvidia’s RTX 5060 GPU sail well over the $1,200 mark, which is just too much if you ask me. If you’re in the market for a relatively speedy and well-designed machine, perhaps this one will be a good fit for your needs and budget. The Aurora has a 1600p 120Hz 16-inch screen, Intel’s capable Core 7 240H processor, 16GB of DDR5 RAM, and a 512GB SSD. Its RTX 5050 GPU likely won’t be able to play most games at max settings, especially at its native 1600p resolution, but you should be able to get respectable frame rates and visual fidelity with some tweaking.

As for its condition, the company says “it’s as close to new as you can get without technically being “new.” The 16 Aurora features two M.2 slots, letting you greatly boost its included 512GB SSD with other drives. It also has two SO-DIMM slots, so you can upgrade the 8GB x 2 (DDR5 5,600MHz) down the line to 16GB x 2 (it tops out at 32GB RAM). If you have other specs you want to dig into, check out Dell’s comprehensive spec sheet within its support site.

Other great Verge-approved deals

Loch Capsule dishwasher that Live in a really small space? Perhaps, an RV or a van equipped with power to run appliances? Thethat my colleague Thomas Ricker tested is 20 percent off for a limited time through Labor Day. Normally $459.99 for the skinny dishwasher, it’s down to $367.99 with free shipping at Loch’s site . Now, folks with setups large enough to accommodate a bigger dishwasher shouldn’t consider the Loch Capsule. But it might be just what some are looking for. It can clean and dry (even sanitize) dishes and pans in a 20-minute cycle. It doesn’t require plumbing, and its design isn’t an eye sore. If you can look past its flaws (mainly that it’s sort of loud), it’s worth considering during the sale.

Zeppelin Pro is 29 percent off at There are no other speakers that look like the Bowers & Wilkin’s Zeppelin. Not only is its design striking, appearing to levitate, but it boasts a powerful sound (ask me how I know — it was the sole speaker used during my wedding’s afterparty). Itsis 29 percent off at Amazon in the black color option, costing $639 (originally $899). We haven’t tested this particular model, but it seems impressive, featuring five drivers (one being a six-inch subwoofer), plus Bluetooth, AirPlay 2 and Spotify Connect. It also has an optional downward-firing light that gives it a unique presence in the room.

ultrawide Odyssey OLED G93SD costs now at You can tell that Samsung is trying to get rid of monitors when it’s selling a whopping 49-inch OLED gaming monitor for $999.99 (originally $1,699.99). That’s how much itscosts now at Best Buy . Its width is roughly equivalent to sticking two 25-inch 1440p monitors next to other, then curving them inward slightly for a more immersive viewing experience. The full resolution is 5,210 x 1,440 and it features a 240Hz refresh rate. The screen has a 110 pixels per inch density, which isn’t great, though it’s the standard for most QHD OLED gaming monitors. The monitor includes a three-year warranty protecting against defects, however, Samsung’s warranty page doesn’t explicitly mention burn-in.

Tech.title: What to expect at Apple’s September 9th launch event
Tech.content:
is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Apple’s September 9th launch event could be one of its biggest in years. It will be Apple’s first event since John Ternus took over as CEO on September 1st, stepping in for Tim Cook, and will likely feature the first models in Apple’s iPhone 18 lineup. That could include the long-rumored foldable “iPhone Ultra,” coming just a couple months after Samsung debuted its own passport-style foldable, the Galaxy Z Fold 8.

Here’s how you can watch the event live, and a few possible highlights to keep an eye out for.

How to watch Apple’s September launch event

Apple’s “Surprise and shine” event kicks off on Wednesday, September 9th, at 1PM ET / 10AM PT at Apple Park in Cupertino, California. It will be livestreamed on Apple’s website, Apple TV, and YouTube.

The iPhone 18 might be a no-show

Last year’s iPhone 17 might not get a successor just yet. Photo by Amelia Holowaty Krales / The Verge

Apple usually announces new iPhones at its September event, but the base iPhone 18 might not make the cut this year. It’s reportedly being held until early next year, and it might end up launching alongside the iPhone 18E and an updated iPhone Air. So, if you’re looking to upgrade to one of Apple’s less expensive phones, you’ll likely need to wait a while longer.

The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max could launch with a price hike

The iPhone 18 Pro could be more expensive than last year’s iPhone 17 Pro. Photo: Allison Johnson / The Verge

While we might not get a new base iPhone, Apple is still expected to launch its new lineup of phones on September 9th with the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max. Both models are rumored to have larger batteries than their predecessors, and possibly a smaller Dynamic Island. They might even get a variable aperture camera upgrade that’s been rumored for years now. Leaked photos supposedly showing dummy models of the phone also hint at this year’s slate of colors, which could include black, silver, light blue, and a dark cherry purple.

Unfortunately, there’s also a good chance the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max will get a price bump over last year’s models. Apple raised prices on nearly all of its products earlier this year, and those price hikes might finally reach the iPhone during the September 9th event.

Apple might announce its first foldable phone

One of the premium phones Apple launches on September 9th could be the rumored foldable “iPhone Ultra.” Images of an apparent dummy model of the folding phone leaked earlier this year, showing a passport-style design similar to Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 and the Xiaomi 18 Fold. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 has been well received so far, with The Verge’s Dominic Preston saying it “feels like the future.” Will Apple’s first foldable be able to compete, despite being fashionably late?

The ceramic Apple Watch may finally return

The Apple Watch Series 11’s successor could have an option for a ceramic case. Photo by Amelia Holowaty Krales / The Verge

Last year’s September Apple event included the Apple Watch Series 11 and Ultra 3, and there’s a good chance both watches will get an update again this year. According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, the Series 12 could bring back the premium ceramic case option. Gurman also says the Series 12 will have new band colors and configurations, but most likely won’t have any big redesign. Aside from new cases and colors, Apple might also announce new health features for its wearables, like always-on heart rate sensing.

Apple could launch new AirPods, but probably not with cameras

It’s been a couple of years since Apple released the AirPods 4, so they’re due for an upgrade and could make an appearance at Apple’s September 9th event. However, Gurman says the camera-equipped AirPods that leaked last month won’t be released until 2027. So, if Apple announces the AirPods 5 at its upcoming event, they’ll likely be an iterative upgrade, potentially including a new chip and some new health sensors.
